**9.7/10 — 105 hours in, and I'm still having a blast.**  Yeah, I'm still kind of a noob, but after around **105 hours** of playing CS2, I can confidently say this game is insanely fun.  The **competitive gameplay** is easily my favorite part. The gunplay feels great, realistic, and satisfying without being overly complicated. Every kill feels rewarding, and every death makes you think, *"Okay... what did I do wrong?"* 😂  The maps are also really well designed. **Dust II** is probably my favorite — it's just one of those maps that never gets old.  The graphics and sound are **excellent**, and honestly, I was surprised by how well the game runs on my relatively old PC:  **i5-3470 | 24GB DDR3 | GTX 1050 Ti** **1024p 4:3 High — ~120 FPS**  So yeah, optimization has been pretty good for me.  The matchmaking is decent, and I haven't really had problems with ping or lag. The updates are also generally good and keep the game feeling alive.  But there's one BIG problem:  ### The anti-cheat.  Cheaters seem to be getting more common, and that's probably the biggest thing hurting CS2 right now. The game itself is amazing, but running into obvious cheaters can completely ruin a match.  If Valve improves the anti-cheat, I honestly think CS2 could be even better.  Overall, there's a lot to love: **the gunplay, maps, graphics, sound, competitive gameplay, and just the feeling of playing CS.**  Would I recommend it?  **Absolutely.**  Even if you're a complete beginner, give it a shot. Just don't expect to be good immediately. 😭  **Final rating: 9.7/10**  Would've been a straight 10/10 if the anti-cheat situation was better.

Everygame is a complete stomp. Either you stomp them entirely or they stomp you entirely. There is no inbetween. People will bully you out of roles you want to play and force you into roles you don't want to or know how to play, then they flame you for 'greifing' and report you for not playing a role you've never played at an expert level. This is hands down the worst matchmaking and worst new player experience I've ever seen. New players get grouped against players with 10000 games and 15 years experience.  When you ask about the terrible matchmaking, experienced players tell you that ranked queue is the only good queue, because it actually matches against your MMR, but you can't access this for 100 hours. No, that's not 100 hours of the game running, that's 100 hours of being in a match playing the game. So if you install this, prepare to sit in many many games where you get completely stomped by extremely experienced players.  The game balance is also terrible. Towers do barely any damage at all, so if your opponent gets any lead on you, they can easily just walk under tower and kill you without any repercussion. This means if you get behind at all, the only thing you can do is just leave lane entirely so you stop feeding. Forget defending the tower, they will just kill you for being in their vision. If you get behind too early, you're double ♥♥♥♥♥♥, because you can't even farm the camps because they take all of your health to kill just one, so you ahve to run back to base after each camp just to get more health. So what do you do then? Maybe split push and try to be where the enemy is not. But remember, these people have 15 years experience on you, so they expect this and appear out of no where to kill you because your team has no wards up because all of them were purchased by one player that is just saving them for the next game and your team has none left. So what do you do then? You wait at base because by now, all your towers are pushed in and your team is going out one at a time and dying to their 5 man roaming gang. You think you're safe at base though? Wrong again. They will just walk past the towers and kill you instantly using the lead they've been multiplying all game.  You know what would fix this? Maybe matchmaking should put new players against new players so those new players can learn the game and actually be matched against their actual skill level. You cannot learn anything if every game you play, you get absolutely stomped with no clear path to catch up in gold and xp.  Save your sanity and don't even give this game a shot. There are far more balanced mobas out there with superior matchmaking mechanics.

Worst Moba on the market, here is why:  -Last Hit Mechanic : an outdated mechanic that forces you to wait until the enemy minions are extremely low before attacking them so you can get the most important thing in the game, gold. This was extremely frustrating for me since I don't like someone else doing my job for me.  -Shop Confusion: Searching for items in the in game shop requires you to play around 20 hours to learn WHERE and item is then another 5 hours to learn each item individually as to what Attribute they give then another 2 hours per item to learn if you should build them on your hero.  -Broken Champ  Logic : Dota goes on the logic that if all champions are broken then no one really is.. not how it works, this results in a character like Invoker having 5 stuns and slows that he uses on you which renders you unable to play the game   -Carrier: Cool idea bad implementation. I struggled to use it because the logic behind it is.. crazy. So I have to be close to a "secret shop" for me to buy an item and when I do.. the carrier has to come with the item from the base to me to bring it??? What? I bought it FROM THE SECRET SHOP so give me the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ item instantly, why is the carrier bringing the item FROM BASE if I wasn't allowed to buy it FROM BASE????  -Bugs: I have less than 10 hours and I already had a pretty annoying bug where the finished item wouldn't be built for some reason.. the result was me selling one of the item components and then buying it again, resulting in a 300 gold loss for me (gold that is hard as ♥♥♥♥ to earn because of that dumbass last hit mechanic)  -Queue times: For a game of 500 THOUSAND players having a 7 minute queue time is insane, absolutely crazy. Other games have less than 10k people and it takes you 1-2 minutes to find a match to play. Something is wrong with your server connections.  It's such a shame, the game did really good on some other things, such as: -allowing you to see if the people in your queue have good karma or good skills (why you would reject the match after a 7 minute queue is beyond me tho) That's.. it.. there is literally nothing else.  Dota is not "helpful" towards new people in any way, they like their old systems and won't change them for nothing, even if they are extremely badly implemented and flawed beyond touch.   Dota: 2/10

## An Anatomy of Disproportion: Why KRAFTON’s Indefinite Bans Harm Rather Than Protect the PUBG Esports Ecosystem  The competitive integrity of professional esports rests upon clear boundaries, unbiased adjudication, and proportionate enforcement. However, KRAFTON’s decision to issue indefinite, global competitive bans against prominent Vietnamese players—notably Himass and TanVuu—following infractions during an exhibition/showmatch event highlights an overreaching, heavy-handed regulatory approach. Rather than reinforcing governance, the publisher's handling of the situation exposes fundamental flaws in tournament operations, a lack of graduated sanctions, and a disregard for regional ecosystem stability.  ---  ### 1. Disproportionate Penalization and the Absence of Graduated Justice  In established sports jurisprudence and mature esports titles (such as Valve’s CS:GO/CS2 or Riot Games’ League of Legends), lifetime or indefinite bans are traditionally reserved for structural corruption: **match-fixing, illegal betting, or deliberate software-level cheating/hacking**.  * **Conflating Infraction Severity:** Receiving unauthorized outside information or stream sniping during a third-party, online showmatch is unquestionably an infraction that compromises fair play. However, treating such misconduct with the exact same finality as an organized match-fixing ring or an aimbot/wallhack script completely eliminates any sense of proportionality. * **The Principle of Remediation:** A professional sports regulatory framework should deter misconduct while providing avenues for rehabilitation. A standard penalty structure for first-time information-related offenses ranges from temporary suspensions (e.g., 6 to 12 months) and forfeiture of prize earnings to probation. Jumps straight to indefinite bans eliminate due process, leaving no incentive for reform.  ### 2. Deflecting Operational Failures onto Individual Players  A major weakness in the publisher’s ruling is its failure to account for the loose operational standards of the event itself:  * **Inadequate Supervision:** Unlike official Premier circuits (PGS, PGC) that operate with strict refereeing, point-of-view (POV) recording mandates, localized camera feeds, and robust stream delay buffers, third-party exhibition matches frequently run on bare-bones operational protocols. * **Scapegoating Talent:** When an organizer fails to enforce mandatory delays, secure communication channels, or proper monitoring, they create an environment prone to integrity lapses. By imposing the absolute maximum penalty on individual competitors while avoiding any formal acknowledgment of structural administrative shortcomings, the publisher shifts the burden of organizational negligence entirely onto the players.  ### 3. Destruction of Regional Infrastructure and Long-Term Ecosystem Damage  Southeast Asia—and Vietnam in particular—has long served as one of the most passionate and commercially vital hubs for competitive PUBG PC. KRAFTON’s abrupt and unyielding verdict inflicts immediate, collateral damage on this regional foundation:  * **Erosion of Team and Sponsor Confidence:** Esports organizations invest substantial capital into salaries, housing, mental coaching, and branding. When the publisher unilaterally ends the careers of flagship assets over an ambiguous exhibition incident, teams face immediate existential risk. The subsequent withdrawal or scaling back of major organizations illustrates how uncalculated regulatory shocks destroy investor confidence. * **Stifling Competitive Competence:** Himass and TanVuu represented the highest tier of Vietnamese mechanical skill and international LAN experience. Removing them abruptly from international contention directly degrades the regional competitiveness of the APAC circuit, lowering the quality of regional representation at events like PNC and PGS.  ### 4. Lack of Transparency and Independent Arbitration  The ruling highlights an ongoing issue inherent to publisher-dominated esports: the absence of an independent arbitration body.  * **Prosecutor, Judge, and Jury:** KRAFTON acts simultaneously as commercial rights holder, league organizer, and sole judiciary. Without an independent appeals commission or an objective ombudsman, players have no formal recourse to contest findings, present mitigating circumstances, or challenge the proportionality of the punishment. * **Precedent of Volatility:** A governance model that relies on punitive displays of force rather than transparent, predictable guidelines alienates the professional player base. Competing under a rulebook where penalties can swing arbitrarily to the maximum threshold creates systemic anxiety and drives talent to transition to more professionally governed esports ecosystems.  ---  Preserving competitive integrity does not require the immediate destruction of player careers and regional ecosystems. By applying an absolute, irreversible punishment without a graduated framework, transparent mitigating review, or acknowledgment of administrative vulnerabilities, KRAFTON opted for a blunt-force public relations statement rather than sound regulatory leadership. The resulting fallout damages the game's competitive credibility far more than the infraction it attempted to punish.

Overall, this is a really fun game with multiple ways to earn money and progress, which keeps things interesting.  The biggest downside for me is the amount of cheating and connection abuse I’ve encountered from some players. There are situations where the game runs perfectly smooth until you get near certain players, and then the lag suddenly becomes severe. Once you move out of their area, everything returns to normal. Whether that is lag switching or another connection-related issue, it can make PvP extremely frustrating. Better regional matchmaking or stronger enforcement against players abusing the game would help considerably.  Gunplay could also use some improvement. Aiming and shooting sometimes feel delayed or unresponsive, almost like the game does not react as quickly as it should.  The experience for lower-level players can also be rough. Going up against level 100 players when your weapons barely do meaningful damage can take some of the enjoyment out of progressing. Some additional balancing or protection for newer players could make the early game much more enjoyable.  Despite those issues, I’m still having a lot of fun with the game. There is plenty to do, several ways to make money, and a lot of potential. With better server performance, stronger anti-cheat measures, and some balancing improvements, it could be even better.

If you want to fly logi or transport and they build AA, and your team doesn't have its own rocket heli, mortar, or artillery then you can't fly logi or transport. ANECDOTAL: This game is not for everyone, and that's okay. This game is in Early Access and has balancing issues that are being addressed. It took a bit for me to understand the basics of the game and to slow down my desire to sprint in, guns akimbo and I paid for each moment I decided to get impatient (literally and figuratively).  You'll have good matches where you fight like the dickens over a hill that isn't important, with weapons you didn't spawn with and people you just met making callouts or asking for help. You'll have bad matches where an idiot will crash his helicopter in spawn and one team will run the the entire match and you'll lose out on so much money. This game will piss you off and force you to take a break. Then it'll give you some of the most hair-raising firefights and engagments in modern gaming.  EXPERIENCE: I run settings on high and don't get frame drops, I have VSYNC on to keep 120FPS.  the base FPS mechanics are good. You will need to use the Firing Range so that you can learn some basics of how different classes of armor affect your damage potential. You will need to learn what different color smokes have different meanings, that helicopters are not easy to fly without practice, that the physics can be wonky on trucks going over hills. The UI is a bit weird so it will take some time for your clicking flow to get up to speed to navigate the shop interfaces. There are many settings and small technical bits of information that you will not learn until either you see someone do it or you get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up by it.  GAMEPLAY: If you sprint in the middle of a road without taking into account vantage points, cover in a 360 degree radius, sit in the middle of windows staring at the horizon, try to slide cancel, loot a body in the middle of a firefight, you will die. If you do everything perfectly and have 350 degrees of cover with just enough view to see, you'll get headtapped by a Mosin still. You will die a lot. However, if you play the game, scout adversaries, build in the base, or even just sit in the zone, you will make money back and typically profit. It is a pain in the ass getting the first few assault levels to get optics that will allow you to reach out and touch someone at range. But the experience and the way you're forced to slow down instead of grinding kills and matches forces you to learn how to approach different types of engagements.  WHY ARE YOU NOT GETTING TO THE DIRECT POINT: Because this game is not for everyone, and instead of complaining about getting my face blown off constantly I'd rather talk about what my first 10 hours in this game has been. I don't play shooters much, instead I play a ♥♥♥♥ ton of Old School Runescape. My FPS experience begins with CoD 3 for the PS2 and ends with... well, MW3 for the PS3. I played a little Battlefield, but couldn't get into it. If you enjoy the modern shooters, you're going to need to learn self control, patience, and to slow the hell down. If you come from Tarkov or Arma, you'll probably find it a bit arcadey but a lot of the methodical movement will come in handy. No matter who you are, watch gameplay videos beforehand and then try to play two or three matches. If you don't like it, refund it. Nothing wrong with a video game not being designed for you or for me - there are plenty of fish in the sea.

Let me preface by saying yes. I think the gunplay and the concept of earning cash to be very fun and appealing. That said I'm still going to give the game a no because I can't give a mixed review and I think there are plenty of people who have said a lot about what Wardogs does right.  So lets talk about what's wrong with Wardogs.  1. The Progression System - I can't think of many other games with a progression system that is this unfriendly to new players. It is demoralizing to finally unlock the sks for example and learn that it takes like 4 or 5 bullets to put down a guy in level 4 armor while you died to a stiff breeze from his vector. I'm not saying I'm better than the man in level 4 armor nor do I think a loadout that's cheaper should be able to consistently beat out a more expensive one without outplaying it. I will say that AP ammo being locked to like level 80ish is beyond baffling. As a new player you are not even given the opportunity to buy the proper tools to even compete. If you run into a guy with level 4 armor as a new guy who hasn't even hit level 30 yet you will get absolutely eviscerated in most of your engagements unless you get lucky. This kind of polarizing interaction means that eventually you will not be receiving any new players and be driving off any that even try.   2. The Level Reset - I'm a little hesitant to say I will fully understand the ramifications of the level reset, but I will say that it took me 48 hours to hit level 60 and the game is supposedly resetting its levels in roughly 2-3 weeks. By the time I supposedly hit the levels to even use AP ammo, the deagle, or level 4 armor I probably will have less than a week to use it. Cool. The reset is more of a problem to me that compounds with how awful the progression system is. I saw people already using the artillery tank (which is level 90) in the first week. Running into these people made the early level experience absolutely horrendous and potentially going through it all over again starting October 15 just because I didn't spend 48 hours playing in the first two days of a reset? Yeah pass.  3. Winning Matches and Cash - I find it very interesting how little these two correlate with each other. This game kinda inspires a Tarkov or Hunt Showdown effect in players because they paid money for their loadouts and would prefer generally not losing them. This dramatically slows the gameplay and adds a lot of tension to your engages and decision making. That is not inherently bad and I think is a good point of the game. However, the incentives to try to win the game are not generally tied with how to make the biggest bucks. The most money I've ever made in this game is either doing logistics, buying nothing but a spotter scope to just spam spot, or mass building on a FOB. Notice how none of that encourages a player to be fighting or going to the hotzone(hz) which results in either 1 team sitting in the hz the whole game wondering where everyone else. That doesn't mean this is always true as the matches where all 3 teams are aggressively fighting for the hz is the most fun I've had in Wardogs. What I'm saying is that it's hard to get those experiences when it feels like the games systems are punishing you for actively going out and fighting as the most profitable way to play is to not play.  4. Team Balance - I don't have the stats to exactly explain this so this is more of my gut feeling/general experience so take this last point with a grain of salt. My general experience in this game is one of extremes. Either 1 team dominates so damn hard you could probably go afk in the HZ and never die. Or 2 you are on the team getting stomped into oblivion and you don't even want to buy a 5k loadout because there is no point. It's hard to articulate the frustration when you are on the teams that are getting absolutely stomped. Dying immediately on drop to a -10k on your bank and wondering how you'll get to the control zone again only to repeat the exact process. Or seeing 25 out of your team of 33 players sitting in FOB the whole game while you watch the entirety of one other team sitting in the HZ just winning. I think getting rolled in games like this are inevitable but something about Wardogs make it feel like it happens far more than other games to me. I could try to explain why I exactly thinks that happens but I think I'll leave it off there for now and hopefully Bulkhead reaches a more clear answer than anything I could produce.   So should you buy Wardogs? Eh... maybe? If you have lots of free time and a casual tactical shooter with larger scale warfare is up your alley. Yeah go for it. For a more general audience? I think you'll find yourself more frustrated by the grind than anything else. And maybe that's fine. Not every game needs to be for everyone, but if the goal is to make a more smoother experience for the average player I think these 4 points need to be looked at a little more closely. Overall though make an informed decision for yourself and don't listen to just me. Watch videos, read multiple reviews, and use steam's 2 hour refund policy to really decide if you want to commit to Wardogs.

If I could give it a middle rating I would.  There's lots of things to appreciate about the game, the sandbox, the creativity, the moment to moment gameplay. The game is great in many ways.  However, it's something that almost every time I boot up now, I am no longer having any fun.   There's a few reasons for that, if you haven't poured a ton of hours into the game, you will have a lot of moments where things will feel very unfair, or unfun. If you are below rank 50, and don't have any points in assault, you might get lucky, get the drop on someone, land all your shots, and the enemy might be slow to react, but in probably 9/10 encounters, the guy with T4 armor and an M4 will delete you the second they see you.   If you have the default gun, you need to land 2 full bursts from it on a T4 armor guy's head to kill him. Or 3 full bursts and 1 extra bullet if it's body shots. If you have T2 and below armor, it's 6 shots in the body from the M4, with a faster fire rate, and more controllable recoil. T4 armor also covers your arms, which all other armor does not.  This is one of multiple pieces as to why this game has grown quite frustrating. Even me with over 100 hours, I have not yet unlocked the M4, because I made the *idiotic* decision to level up and try multiple types of gameplay. I'm about even in everything but piloting.   To list a few other things that make things even more frustrating, people are unlocking .50 cal sniper rifles, alongside infrared spotter scopes to be able to see you through foliage, smokes, etc. Spotting you from anywhere, ranging the shot, and one tapping you through all but T3/T4 body armor, not to mention absolutely ripping apart your armor even if it doesn't kill you. I was killed yesterday through a smoke, through a sandbag wall while prone on the ground from 400m away. The only counter play to the infra scope is the guillie suit which I also have not unlocked yet.  Then the worst of the worst. The havoc. The only counter play is to have a FOB setup and build anti air, specifically the CIWS because it's the only thing that cannot be flared. However, you can easily be killed off of it by the Havoc's missiles or explosive rounds. It can tank at least 2 RPG rounds even if you free-fire at it.   To exacerbate the issue above, the enemy can spawn artillery tanks at the very start of the match, and immediately start blowing your FOB to pieces before you can even build anything. There are only a few means of counterplay to this, build inside a warehouse/building (most are not tall enough to fit the FOB, and this means you cannot really build proper anti-air), find and destroy the arty tank (requires extremely specific setup like C4s, likely being stranded in the space between the enemy spawn and the zone due to vehicle cleanup, and they might just hop in the turret and gun you down), or use a missile littlebird and hunt them down (requires relatively high pilot XP).  The real trouble is how all of this culminates into games that, when two teams randomly decide to focus on you, it means you essentially cannot play the game. Add to it times where people will lurk outside the zone to get easy kill because they have enough money for it to not matter, camera being attached the any arty/mortar rounds so people can see exactly what they are shooting at, and things like gun humvees/proper tanks, and you have a desperately unbalanced experience.   Similar to using the starter gun, you might get lucky and have a fun game after a few weeks post-release, but 9/10 times, you probably won't. -$6k to -$20k in the hole depending on what you decide to go with, because you flew in and your pilot crashed, or you get SAM'ed or someone planted a mine near your spawn. Or you get out of the vehicle and get gunned down with no teammates around. Some guy in a guillie suit picks all of you off with a suppressed gun from a nearby bush.   I'd consider myself pretty good at shooters, but if I'm just being completely honest, the first 5 days of the game release were some of the most fun I've had in any game, maybe ever. Now I don't really even feel like booting at all. I went from "you gotta get this game right now" to "Eh, maybe after the wipe" but damn, it's hard to recommend a game that might be fun for 5 days every season.

TLDR; Unless you plan on playing this as your main game every day, it's unfortunately just not worth it.  - You can't buy a full suit of armor, until you grind long enough to not be able to do a (steam) refund. - You only get a secondary after unlocking it and buying it (and the first one is completely useless). - One of the better ways to make money is by transporting players, but all the best transport vehicles are the high-season-level unlockables, thus making it essentially impossible for anyone to make money using anything else. - Forward bases also essentially obsolete the existence of most vehicles entirely (inevitable, unfortunately). - I kept getting shot through walls and rocks, but it's probably just early-access jank that will get smoothed out. - VC broke entirely for our entire team at one point, and we lost 100-78-15 because we couldn't communicate (again, early-access jank; will be fixed). - Trying to heal people is really inconvenient and inconsistent. - Reviving takes 20 seconds when people die in 2, which leaves you as a sitting duck for being a good teammate. - 90% of the map is just dead space nobody will ever go to, nor is there any reason to. I appreciate the open-world map truly being open-world, but there's just no point in going anywhere. - Stream sniping is concerningly easy, given helicopters and field artillery can beam people across the map at will. - The long respawn process is just bad. Spending 30-120 seconds buying a new setup to get sniped the moment you land gets old very fast, and you can run out of money very quickly on a bad streak. - Lower level players are essentially delegated to playing minecraft at the forward base, since they have nearly no combat capabilities, useful vehicles, or special weapons to use on anything. It wasn't bad, but it just didn't feel like I was actually playing the game, doing that. - RPGs aren't killing people on direct impacts (EA jank). - Seasonal resets of all your unlocks will kill this game of any remotely casual audience, and people aren't going to bother spending hours re-grinding any of the useful stuff.  Overall, I like the concept, and I don't really mind the gameplay part of it. However, trying to play it solo just sucks most of the time. Trying to play as a medic is very frustrating, with how hard (and how long) it is to actually heal your teammates. The respawn vs TTK ratio is not good, and there's ultimately no actual reason to put the main bases 2 miles from the base camp. I love the team behind this, and their transparency, sense of humor with it, etc. But it's just not a game a casual audience will enjoy playing. If you brain-off it for hundreds of hours I'm sure it's fun, but people don't have time for that.  I feel like (and I hope this is proven very wrong) the general and any casual audience will leave the game the moment the big streamers do (such is the life of video games), and it's not going to recover from that. I can see it being one of those games where one bad session is easily enough to make someone think "why am I even playing this game?" and never come back. I do want the game to succeed (as with most passion projects), but I just don't see it happening long-term with this one.

Apex is an amazing game buried under some incredibly frustrating decisions.  The movement and gunplay are still elite. Sliding, wall-bouncing, climbing, strafing, and combining abilities with gunplay makes Apex feel more mechanically satisfying than most shooters. When you have a good match, there are few FPS games that feel this good.  But then you play for a few hours and remember why the game can be so damn annoying.  The matchmaking can feel miserable. You can have one decent game and suddenly you're fighting players who look like they haven't missed a shot since 2019. Meanwhile, your teammates can range from genuinely good to people who seem to have forgotten they're playing a team game.  Solo queue is especially painful. You can spend 15 minutes looting just for your teammate to launch themselves into a 1v3, die instantly, and leave.  The ranked system can also make the grind feel exhausting. You can play well for multiple games, lose one bad fight, and suddenly feel like all that progress meant nothing.  And honestly, Apex has one of the highest "I should stop playing" to "one more game" ratios I've ever seen.  The game is frustrating, sweaty, sometimes unfair, and occasionally feels like it actively hates you.  But you still queue again.  Final verdict:  Gameplay: 9/10 Movement: 10/10 Gunplay: 9/10 Teamplay: 7/10 Matchmaking: 5/10 Solo queue experience: 4/10 Addiction: 11/10 Overall: 8/10  Apex isn't a bad game. It's a great game that sometimes makes you wonder why you still play it.

Procedural Generation! No small thing. I love this.  You spend a ridiculous amount of time just hauling your stuff, in small batches, to bases etc. Tedious conservative item storage. You have 24 squares or 300lbs. whatever comes first. The first log takes a square and weighs 2units:  the first dandelion takes a square and weighs .1 unit. Each take a whole square from your 24.  You have standard equipment choice: Weapon(s), Shield, Helm, Tunic, Pants, 3+ types of arrows. Each equip takes one of your 24 squares.  Food is well done and interesting. It is expressed as Health (keeps you from dying), Stamina (gives you energy to fight or defend etc...). Without food you die super easy so you are best to have a choice for stamina and health.  And you guessed it, having a choice comes out of your 24squares.  Helm, tunic, pants = 3 squares Bow, Arrows = 2 squares (1 arrow type) Weapon, Shield (Shield has a big bonus to Parry) = 2 squares Food 3-5 squares  You can easily have half your stuff space taken up by equipment and food leaving you to shorten trips and backtrack to your chest.  Your starting chest has only 10 squares.   After a while it feels like all you do is prepare, not game. Most game discussions talks of defending your base. I don't think people feel free to enjoy the considerable random world. Other game discussions talk about needing more space and not having to count what you wear (or equip) as what you are carrying.   For me, its a huge issue with a simple solution. Devs need to not count defenses in the 24 squares and raise the storage space. I bought the game, I feel like I'm in a trial version. There will always be people wanting to carry more stuff, but this level really is harming the enjoyment of a remarkable game world.

This game is a mixed bag for me. I wish there was an option for this, but I'll lean towards recommending it. I do truly think that this game is worth trying out, it is an impressive game in its own right.  Some great things about Valheim: - Music I think the soundtrack fits the game perfectly and sounds great  - Art style Graphics are killer, I love the aesthetic  - Building system Actually cool building system with a surprising amount of cool things you can make  - World design Some of the coolest biome designs I've seen for a game  There's nothing that really feels out of place thematically, I feel as if everything has its place in the game.  The negatives:  While I do genuinely enjoy the building system, there's a handful of things I dislike. My biggest complaint is needing to use various different crafting benches to simply build certain things. You want a fermenter? Sorry, you have you have a forge here. You want a cauldron? Bring over the forge. I understand, there is metal, but this doesn't make the game more fun, it simply adds tedium. Stone needing stonecutter makes sense, no complaints there. The terrain tool, the hoe, could be much better. I'd like more control over how ground is raised.  The combat has not changed at all since this game has come to EA in 2021. 5 years and we have not seen a single improvement to how combat plays. It is awkward, cumbersome, and annoying. There is little nuance besides damage types, and even then it is as deep as a puddle. There are more interesting weapons later in the game, but the system as a whole just feels bland and boring. Attacking locks you into the animation, if enemies are not on the same level as you (especially a bit lower) you will either have difficulty hitting them or simply cannot.  Enemies spawn during boss fights and quite honestly this irritates me to no end. It takes away from the encounters and makes me spend more time fighting fodder than enjoying what I thought would be a cool fight. And... well they generally just aren't. Boss fights are extremely underwhelming, probably due to the extremely barebones combat.  It just feels like a lot of things in this game are weirdly tedious for the sake of being tedious. I do appreciate that we now have the ability to change world settings like difficulty, death rules, and resource drop multipliers, but I just wish the systems themselves were less frustrating. I work full time, I don't have a whole lot of time to spend chasing my corpse to grab my loot. After hours of frustration I changed my death rule to casual, I just wanted to relax, aaaaand I still drop all my items except my armor and equipped weapon. Come on, man.   Despite my extremely arguable and subjective criticisms of the game, I do think there's a great formula here that's bogged down by pointlessly frustrating systems and a boring combat system.

If you consider sailing for many hours at a time, with no sign where to even go in the first place, hard * Some trader items could be crucial to progression and yet if you happen upon Haldor day 1 (for example), half of his inventory is useless to you. You are then left with 2 Increadibly expensive items that you can actually use (if you have finished the 2nd biome and gathered the money from there) - Death penalty is unlike any other game ever made, not in a good way either.  *After you die you spawn either at your bed or at the centre of the world * You spawn with no food in your gut, thus making you get oneshot by any creature past the 1st biome alongside a stamina bar so tiny, you can't even sprint for more than 4 seconds. Nails don't float either so all you get back from your old boat is wood, not the iron or bronze you spent so much time getting - Bossed are underwhelming.  * Their hp bars are insanely big. Bonemass has resistance to 2 out of 3 damage types available to you at the time of the swamp. Slash and pierce * Bosses regenerate health as you fight them * Their movesets consist of 3 moves those being: some type of rock throw, an anti mellee AOE (the most reskinned move and a theme of all the bosses excluding Eikthyr), basic swing left, basic swing right * The average time to kill without exploits on playing on normal is 8 minutes, close to 20 minutes or even an hour if you play on hard (Do not play on combat settings higher than hard) - Biome progression is gatekept in the most zealous ways possible * Blocking with a shield is only ever useful in the biome prior to your current one * Enemies like Drakes, Deathsquitos (Deathsquito? Really? That's the name for a flying bug in a viking game? Come on, øyestikker was right there. As scandinavian devs they have no excuse.) etc. serve as a make sure way to NOT let you play too far ahead of what you currently should be doing * You are only ever supposed to build in: Meadows when you start, Plains after you reach them in progression. Anywhere else the game will tell you that farming here is forbidden and in this game, that's not something you can just skip - Enemy AI behaviour is at atrocious * Terrain, path finding is so bad, you can probably beat the game without ever dodge rolling if you just have a hoe and some stones on you at all times, I will not go into detail * Enemy tactics consist of: run at the player, shoot at the player I need to add here a comment I saw at some point which describes it perfectly - "They run at you, swing, throw, do a little dance, repeat" I cannot credit who said this, I cannot recall, but it's the funniest and most tragic thing i have ever heard about this game. - Gear needs to be crafted, then thrown right away * No class or role identity when playing with a group * Forge of potential has been added you further hinder your progress if you ever felt cocky enough to use it, by having a 35% chance of destroying your items and giving little resource back  This game is not about reaching a reward but avoiding punishment. Played this several times during Early Access and tried our hardest to play through the 1.0 launch.  Best way to describe this game: Tedious Base Builder with a side of Survival Craft.  I know I’ve put hundreds of hours into games that are far more tedious — looking at you, Warframe — but this one... man, does it take the cake.  Trees / Physics: It’s only funny getting killed by a tree doing a 180-spin the first few times. After a while, you start wondering how you can use the trees to kill trash mobs, who somehow can tank a full-grown oak landing on them, while you get one-tapped by a slightly rolling log.  Travel: You mean sailing 1/4 of the way to your destination, only for the wind to change and blow directly against your sails, leaving you trapped in the ocean for hours?  You can’t tack effectively when the wind seems to know exactly where you’re going and says, “Nope.”  Traveling with a friend? You mean keeping them prisoner on the same hellish voyage you’re on? They can’t do ANYTHING.  At one point my friend asked, “Why can’t I row the boat when there’s no wind?”  I could not stop thinking about that.  Eventually, I started putting the boat in reverse everywhere we went.  Fishing: I won’t spoil it, but good luck finding a fishing rod.  Combat: Combat is either really engaging and fun — I parried a bear and punched it to death until I got its trophy — OR you’re completely overrun by trash mobs / one-shot by the big boys.  There is some genuinely satisfying combat in there, but the difficulty curve can feel wildly inconsistent.  Base Building: Actually really good.  Almost like this game is secretly a base builder disguised as a survival craft game.  The problem is that the game seems to push you toward either enabling portal travel with materials or living a nomadic lifestyle and constantly building bases as you progress.  If you enjoy building, this is probably one of the strongest parts of the game. If you want to establish one awesome home base and actually use it as your central hub, the progression systems can make that surprisingly tedious.  Crafting: Yeah, it’s there.  I would love for crafting stations to automatically pull materials from nearby chests. That said, I understand why they didn’t implement it, especially considering how heavily the game pushes the nomadic lifestyle.  Story / Lore: Lots of cool lore moments, but ultimately pretty typical survival-craft storytelling.  Length: This is a LONG game.  Be prepared to sink a lot of time into it.  Hand-Holding / Guidance: “Caw! You need something to survive this area... Caw!”  What? What do I need?  “Oh, you’ll figure it out.”  The game gives you just enough information to know that you’re missing something, but sometimes not enough information to actually figure out what that something is.  The stark lack of GOOD Viking games makes it really sad to give Valheim a negative review.  There is a genuinely great game buried in here. The combat can be fun, the building is excellent, the world is beautiful, and there are plenty of moments where Valheim absolutely nails the Viking survival fantasy.  But there are just too many tedious systems and questionable design choices that turn what should be an exciting adventure into a slog.  If some of the more tedious features and/or poor design choices were improved or made optional, I would absolutely recommend this game.  For now, though, I just keep asking myself:  “How am I still sailing directly into the wind?!"

Not Recommended — 1,263 hours played  Valheim is a great game buried under systems that increasingly waste your time.  The first part of the game is fantastic. Later progression becomes disproportionately punishing, especially solo. Vanilla grind makes this even worse. If you value your time, I strongly recommend at least 2x resource drops and allowing all items through portals. Even then, the later game still feels designed to punish your time rather than test your skill.  After 1,263 hours, I finally reached the point where I don't want to do it anymore. I had a lot of great time with Valheim, but I cannot recommend the full solo experience in its current state.

Don't pretend to be a "hardcore" game because of this. The Souls series can be considered as such because you have to learn "complex" mechanics or boss patterns to progress. 239.4 hours on record Last played: December 2, 2024  I don't hate Grand Theft Auto V. I had fun with it, but after 239.4 hours, I eventually realized how repetitive the experience had become. GTA V was once something I could easily spend hours playing, but over time, the appeal faded & the game started feeling less like entertainment and more like an endless checklist.  GTA Online has an enormous amount of content, but that doesn't necessarily make all of it meaningful. You earn money, buy something, use it to earn more money, unlock another item, complete another activity, then repeat the same process. There is always another vehicle, property, business, outfit, weapon, cosmetic, event, achievement, or collectible waiting for you.  Eventually, I started asking myself: what am I actually working toward?  The biggest problem is the pursuit of exclusive & rare content. GTA Online has accumulated years of limited-time items, event rewards, promotional content, rare vehicles, clothing, liveries, tattoos, collectibles & other items. Some can still be obtained through specific requirements or returning events, while others have been removed or are no longer normally obtainable.  That creates a strange situation where someone can spend hundreds of hours trying to build the "perfect" collection, only to discover that something they wanted was tied to an event from years ago.  If the item is no longer obtainable, there is no amount of grinding that can get it back.  That's what makes the completionist mentality particularly frustrating. You're not simply trying to finish a game. You're trying to keep up with an ecosystem that has been evolving for years, while some of its history is permanently locked behind time-limited availability.  And even the items that remain obtainable can require an enormous investment of time.  For example, GTA Online's money-making activities often involve cooldowns, preparation missions, travel, matchmaking, setup, completion, & repetition. Even one of the game's major solo money-making activities has a cooldown between finales. Multiply that type of waiting & repetition across the countless things a player might want to purchase, unlock, or collect, and the hours add up very quickly.  My 239.4 hours alone equal roughly 9.98 full days of continuous time.  That's almost ten entire 24-hour days of my life spent inside Los Santos.  And that's only the recorded gameplay time.  It doesn't include time spent researching how to obtain items, watching guides, waiting for events, comparing prices, sitting through loading screens, or deciding what to do next.  That's where the opportunity cost becomes impossible for me to ignore.  I'm not saying video games need to be productive. They're entertainment, and entertainment has value. But once a game stops being entertaining & you're continuing only because you've already invested so much time, it becomes worth asking whether that time is better spent elsewhere.  GTA Online can make that especially difficult because there is always something else to obtain.  You can never quite be finished.  Another update arrives.  Another vehicle is released.  Another business becomes available.  Another event begins.  Another exclusive item appears.  Another achievement becomes something to chase.  Then the cycle starts again.  One sequence of the game eventually replaces another.  And eventually, Grand Theft Auto VI will replace this generation's attention with a new world, new characters, new gameplay systems, new content & potentially another online ecosystem to explore. Rockstar currently lists GTA VI for November 19, 2026.  That's not a criticism of GTA VI. It's simply the natural progression of the franchise.  My concern is how much time people can spend trying to completely exhaust an older game before moving on.  You could spend hundreds of hours collecting vehicles, grinding money, unlocking cosmetics & pursuing exclusives, only for the next Grand Theft Auto to arrive & give everyone another massive world full of things to collect.  The sequence never really ends.  That's why I'm no longer interested in chasing every GTA V exclusive simply because I don't have it.  If an item is available, great.  If I miss it, I'm not going to let a virtual item dictate how I spend my time.  Some people genuinely enjoy collecting everything, and that's perfectly fine. But for me, the collection itself eventually became more burdensome than rewarding.  I also don't think GTA V deserves to be treated as a bad game because of this criticism. It has had an enormous impact on gaming, GTA V's single-player campaign remains memorable, & GTA Online has maintained an extraordinary amount of content for years.  My criticism is much simpler:  There is such a thing as having too much of a good thing.  After 239.4 hours, the repetition became difficult to overlook.  The game went from:  "What should I do today?"  to:  "What else do I still need to unlock?"  That distinction matters.  At some point, you're no longer playing because you genuinely want to. You're playing because there's another box left unchecked.  And I don't want a game to become a second job.  My last session was December 2, 2024, and I'm comfortable leaving it there.  I don't regret every hour I spent in GTA V. I had fun, experienced the world, played with other people & made memories. But I also recognize that my time has value, and I don't want to spend hundreds more hours chasing increasingly obscure items simply because the game provides an endless list of things to obtain.  Grand Theft Auto V was fun, but it became repetitive.  GTA Online has more content than most players could reasonably exhaust, yet that abundance can also become the problem.  With GTA VI arriving, I'm choosing not to spend more of my time trying to complete an ecosystem that was never designed to truly end.  I do not recommend it anymore.

TL;DR: Card bloat, excessive debuffs, simplistic build breaking mob/bosses, simplistic smash head into player filler mob/bosses, action point limitations, shift into a "hardcore" mentality at the expense of fun factor, and nerfing certain mechanisms/builds.   Note: I have only played StS2 single player.  I am a StS1 fanboy with an ungodly number of hours logged and all characters at max Ascension level.   This is a negative review largely due to StS2 not meeting my expectations of what I envisioned it could have been, so you decide if that is a fair criteria.  This is a 50/50 review that I decided to fall onto the negative side.  Most of my negative points do exist in StS1, but the over-reliance of them in StS2 gives this a significantly different feel, a feel that adds frustration at the cost of fun factor. To paraphrase a famous quote, “quantity is it’s own quality”, in the case of StS2, a decidedly negative quality.   Regarding the inevitable knee-jerk responses that read, “How can you give a game you put so many hours into a negative review?”, in two words, completionist compulsion.   Being a StS1 fanboy, I am determined to get all of my characters to A10, and I won’t let the lackluster game design stand in my way. I am on my last character, who is currently at A9, and I am determined to check that A10 box, at which point I will walk away.   In StS1, I felt a joyous feeling of accomplishment at completing a new Ascension level. In StS2, my feeling was much more of a “f*** you”, and then readying myself for an even more frustrating ascension experience. I expect when I do get this last character to A10 I will feel a joyless sense of achievement, perhaps like finally completing an overly complex set of tax forms?  I like it when DLC and new editions add positive features that retain the gameplay feel of the original, repair what might be considered negative, and tweak the fun factor.  This is a fundamentally different game from StS1 that feels like a StS1-clone made by devs who didn't understand what made the original so fun and decided to give it a more hardcore edge. I don't see the point as that is what Ascension levels are for, and while all my hours in StS1 at max ascension level might qualify me as "hardcore", I still think there should be a larger space for more casual players to enjoy StS2.  There are arguments whether StS2 is more difficult than StS1. I'll cut to the chase, yes, it is more difficult.  A practical example illustrating this is where the red pillow was a nice relic to have in StS1, in StS2 it is one of my most desired, pointing to how health attrition is greater.   In StS1, I virtually never used the rest areas to heal; my attitude was if I couldn't survive the level without resting then I played poorly (+/- unfortunate luck) and so resting relics were irrelevant.   In StS2, there is a greater unavoidable nickel-diming effect on health, translating into a greater need to rest, which is at the expense of card upgrading.  So, while StS2 is more challenging, much of the increased difficulty is due to greater unavoidable health attrition.  Other negative issues:  Card bloat - More isn't always better, which is a trap less astute devs fall into. Adding more cards sounds cool, but dilution makes putting together your favorite builds more difficult.  Excessive build-breaking mechanisms - Deck builders are all about the thrill of crafting a deck that maximizes synergies and feels OP when all the gears mesh. The over-reliance upon debuffs, and mob that cap, handicap builds, and lead to an experience of learned helplessness, watching your health drain as all of your clever combos, and upgraded cards are functionally nerfed into meaninglessness. These mob design “strategies” are lazy, simplistic, and boring.  Simplistic mob/boss design – Speaking of lazy, simplistic, and boring mob design, there is an over-reliance in mob/boss design amounting to virtually nothing more than them streaking across the screen with single/simple-minded high damage attacks. There is nothing exciting or even interesting in these combats. They are lazy filler thrown in simply for player health attrition. Making one look like statue versus a bird, and so forth, doesn’t detract from the boring central mechanism.  Action Point (AP) limitation - A player’s ability to increase action points is severely limited compared to StS1, which again undermines the feeling of increasing greatness that was present in the former.   Design choice to foster hardcore experience, prioritizing frustration over fun factor – The forums are full of prideful gamers telling frustrated gamers to get good. As I am about to complete all characters at A10, I feel I have gotten good, and yet I understand the non-hardcore gamers’ frustration. Making a game more difficult does not directly translate into making it more fun. Simplistic and lazy design choices for the sake of increasing difficulty may feed gamers whose identities thrive in telling others to not suck as much, but there is an internal standard of a difficult game that IMO is far more enjoyable, StS1, the latter which also succeeded in spanning interests of casual through hardcore gamers.   Nerfing certain builds – This a far less concerning negative point, but I’ll mention it anyways. The curse-based relics in StS2 feel like the devs forgot to remove them given the lack of other mechanisms synergizing with curses. I will scum restart every time I receive one those dead-in-the-water curse proc'ing relics.   To reiterate, most of these negative points were present in StS1, but to such a lesser degree that one could see them as a momentary bump in the road, whereas in StS2 the form an integral part of the gameplay loop, which is focused on making the deck design experience feel disempowered instead of that wonderful feeling of breaking the game in a godlike fashion, i.e., StS1’s crazy fun factor.   StS2 is a StS1 clone, but IMO not an improvement, but a lesser, albeit bloated version.

Not sure if I've ever posted a review before, but I felt compelled to write one about this game.  Simply put, if you're a masochist then this is a great game for you. The game is just too damn difficult unless you're a sweaty min/max nerd that finds all the exploits.  It's a fun game for a time, especially with friends, but it gets to a point where the effort returns so little fun that I don't want to play anymore. The constant hopeless beatdown from the enemies is infuriating sometimes. I have 42 hours into this game and 3/4 of that is playing by myself; I'm not sure I've ever made if to the end alone, probably not. I mostly die at or before the beginning of the 2nd level, and horrendously. It wasn't even fun getting there, as I know I'm already going to fail halfway through the first level.  Another thing is the card draws barely feel random, as you constantly get screwed with cards you do not need at the worst times. If you think you're going to get the card you need on the next draw, you can forget about it. For example, I cannot tell you how many times I have been given zero or only one attack cards when the enemy is on a non-attacking round (so you don't have to block), but then on attacking rounds you receive more attack cards, or useless other cards.  I've had cards that are meant to synergize (and be powerful) but rarely draw them together in a manner that would make them work together, negating my build.  I've started a build and needed certain cards that help with that build and you'll never be afforded any opportunity to assist that build.  There will be enemies that steal certain cards in your deck that make or break your deck, and there are enemies that completely negate your deck altogether, and it's supposed to be "random".  I played a four player coop, we were all rouge, and we went an entire run without any of us having an opportunity to add the one specific card to our decks that we purposefully all played rouge to build around, and it's not a rare card.  Is there some skill issue in here? Yea for sure, I'm a very average player. But I'm not a scrub either, I know how decks and abilities work, and the game just becomes too difficult to enjoy after a certain point. I may only play it COOP from now on.   The game does run great, and the presentation is all awesome; it looks great, I love the artwork. It's a quality game with very few explicit bugs. I just can't support the difficulty of the game. At $25 it's probably worth the entertainment value you're going to receive in return before you hit the wall that I have, but just know it's coming.  Lastly, I just read another review saying this game used to be easier, but some streamers exploited the game and the devs reacted by making it more difficult, so go figure.

The game could be alot of fun, but as it stands now its neither a good rouge-lite nor a good deckbuilder. It really feels more like a slot machine than a game.  The fun in a deckbuilder is to find combination of cards and synergies between them, that elevate their usefulness far beyond the singluar card themself. By integrating those combinations into a deck I create a strategy that works towards a win condition I want to reach.  Slay the Spire doesn't let me do that. I can choose one of three randomly chosen cards. But I have no influence on what those three cards might be. I also have no idea, what any of the  reward cards of the future might be, so it's impossible for me to setup my deck any coherent strategy. My choice devolves to chose whatever card seems to be most useful right now, even if that clashes with whatever cards I might get in the future. Theoretically, I can buy     cards at the store, but what those offer and at which price is also random and not predictable. Usually its better to just buy artifacts, but for those the same criticism applies.  The game is also inconsistent about removing a card. Sometimes it cost a lot of resources, sometimes  removing a card from deck is a cost itself, rarely am I able to choose at which point I might want to loose a card. It seems  like in  general that the game treats randomness as a cost, at least in events, which reinforces the idea that it doesn't want the  player have much agency.  As I said, it isn't really a good rouge-lite either. Sure, there is some tree to traverse with different nodes. Outside  the node type, there is no information available of what might be encountered there. There are some artifacts in particular that manipulate what can be in a node or how to choose a node, but those are as well random events. So player choice is almost always limited by clicking 1 -  3 things and hope for the best. I would prefer if at least I could skip a battle and forfeit the rewards  for a few times.  In most card games, the only lifepoint that matter is the last. That  is based on the assumptions that lifepoints are restored after a match. Thats not the case in Slay the Spire. There is one type of node that reliable regenerates some lifepoints (as well as the end of each level). Every battle will likely cost at least a few lifepoints. The random events might give or take lifepoints but are completely unpredictable. I like  that lifepoints  become a part  of resource  management on the world map, but why can't I buy life potions at shops?  The card game itself is fun. Each character has several different strategies, the cards synergize nicely and there is a decent amount of complexity without the game becoming cumbersome. I really  wish they could transplant the card game into something that feels less random. I understand that not having real choices  is part of  the underlying themes  of the game, but in order to feel the magnitude have having agency  taken away,  the  game would need to give me some in the first place.

[h1] Aniimo Review — 9/10 [/h1]  If you’re looking for a game that scratches that Pokémon itch on PC, Aniimo is absolutely worth checking out. It captures that sense of adventure, creature collecting, and discovery that makes these games so enjoyable, while still offering an experience that feels like its own thing without trying to do too much.  One of the things I’ve enjoyed most is the story. It’s engaging, gives you a reason to keep exploring, and makes the world feel worth spending time in. The music is also fantastic, adding to the atmosphere and making those moments of exploration that much more enjoyable.  The camp and base-building mechanics are another highlight. Having a place to call your own adds a great personal touch to the experience, and it’s genuinely fun to build, customize, and spend time there. It’s one of those features that makes you want to keep coming back and putting more time into the game.  What really makes Aniimo stand out, though, is just how much fun it is. Whether you’re exploring, collecting creatures, progressing through the story, or working on your base, there’s a lot here to enjoy. It delivers that familiar creature-collecting feeling without being overly ambitious or straying too far from what makes the genre fun.  And considering that it’s a free-to-play game, Aniimo is absolutely fantastic. There’s a lot to love here, and it’s easy to lose hours just enjoying everything the game has to offer.  Overall, I’d give Aniimo a 9/10. If you’ve been looking for something on PC that scratches that Pokémon itch, I’d highly recommend giving it a try. It’s a great time, and I’m excited to see where the game goes from here.

I started reluctantly playing this because my partner is playing, and honestly, not disappointed. I'm not really into FTP "Gacha" games (Like genshin and all that) but I do love me a creature collector. I'm sure the gameplay will slow down as time goes on and get a bit more grindy, but for now I'm so in love.   TLDR; Exceptionally better than I expected. Best creature collector out there right now. Your own home and massive outdoors area to make beautiful (and have your aniimo run around in). Great gameplay, beautiful world, but be careful of the transmogrify gambling trap. UI needs option to hide elements, too much visual pollution.  Pro's: 1.Pretty in depth character design. Little skins for now, but the game is new.  2.Creature design is off tap. Cute, weird, eccentric, dark, light, beautiful and deadly creatures alike, and all of them interact with the world seamlessly. It's so cute watching them go about their days doing there own thing as if they would've done this whether you were there or not.  Side note, please, PLEASE twine with the same creatures as the ones you're around sometimes. They chat to each other, and can even chat to you sometimes! Seeing what they say to each other is super freaking cute. Please don't make this something you miss out on.  3.Your own little home. (Spoilies, but if it'll make you wanna play the game more, please read)  You get your own little RV, with a simulated world inside that is absolutely huge. You can grow veggies, make teas, watch your aniimo play dance dance revolution... its pretty cute. Totally didn't need to be there, but the fact that it is, makes this game so special.  4. Gameplay. All you're aniimo have their own style of fighting. Each of them unique, including all the elemental animations. And, if that wasn't enough, you can choose to fight AS them. Your character can also help along side them, but that's just another one of the cool things that totally didn't need to be there but is.  5. Exploration. The world is SO dang beautiful.   Con's: 1. UI. Not as bad as some of the other games like this, but also doesn't give you the option to remove any of the UI on the screen while you're out in the world. Makes gameplay less immersive. The option would be great, so I can see the beautiful world they created without big ass buttons and quests in the way.   2. Voice acting. All of the voices sound AI generated and very samey. It takes away from the story which is actually pretty interesting.   3. Clear "gacha" system within transmog.  To be clear, I am thankful that this game is FTP and in the state it's in because people are willing to pay for this stuff. But the way they've gone about it, is super greedy. I should be able to grind the cr*p out of this to unlock the transmog to it's full extent, if I want. But because I can't, I won't spend ANY money on the transmog. Honestly, If it wasn't this greedy and I had the choice, I would've just bought the skin for $60 as a direct skin, not as the gamble that it is. That's just my opinion though.

The main end-game systems need some changes for solo players and F2P players. In egg heists, if you group up you can rez teammates, solo players just die and lose their stuff. Solo players can run around 80-90% of the map and not find a nest, not a problem when you're grouped as you've got 2 other people and the same 15 minute timer to find egg nests. Then there's the Prismana nurturing. You spend weeks filling up a bar, catching the same mons over and over and over again, just for the Prismana mon that spawns to be a range from common to perfect. That means you either waste a premium cube catching them to guarantee at least an epic or a perfect, or you can potentially have wasted an entire week of time gated resources. Oh, and perfect isn't perfect, each rating is a range of 2, so that perfect you caught isn't a perfect, you have to use even more premium resources to catch a perfect 10/10, which they inevitably will balance this game around.  The game is pretty, it's got creature collection, and it's free. But there are slippery slopes all over the place already, some they've already started sliding down, like the parity and equity between solo and grouped players.  Also, the game does have in game chat and voice coms, so I'd keep kids away from it.  Until they remove the coms and chat, and change it to all emotes. Create some loot parity between the solo and grouped players in end-game modes. And change the nurtured Prismana's to guaranteed perfects. I'd say pass on this.

I genuinely don't know why I subjected myself to this much torture over the years.  As a day-one player, with over 1,300 hours on console, another 700+ hours on Blizzard before migrating my account to Steam, and now another ~350 hours here, I can honestly say that Overwatch has been one hell of a ride.  There have been some genuinely great memories. Playing with friends, laughing at ridiculous plays, pulling off insane clutches, discovering new heroes, and those rare games where everything just clicks and your team actually works together. At its best, Overwatch is an incredible game.  The problem is that the longer this game has existed, the more I find myself looking back at what Overwatch used to be and thinking: maybe it should have just stayed that way.  Because somewhere along the way, the game stopped feeling like the game I originally fell in love with.  This game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ exhausting.  The developers have allowed greed, monetisation and constant power creep to slowly chip away at what made Overwatch special. Every new hero seems to introduce another mechanic, ability or gimmick designed to sell the character and shake up the meta, but the result is an increasingly bloated game where older heroes struggle to compete and the overall gameplay becomes less about understanding fundamentals and more about dealing with whatever ridiculous combination of abilities is currently being thrown at you.  And as a tank main, this is especially apparent.  Tank is simultaneously the most important role on the team and seemingly the role everyone blames when anything goes wrong.  I can be outperforming the enemy tank, have more kills, more damage, more objective time, more mitigation and generally be doing everything I possibly can to keep the team alive — and somehow, I'm still the reason we lost.  I'm consistently the person actually playing the objective. I'm contesting. I'm pushing. I'm creating space. I'm taking the damage I'm supposed to take. I'm trying to make plays and create opportunities for my team.  And somehow I'm still watching the rest of the team stand five miles away from the payload.  How is the person whose entire job is to absorb pressure and create space also ending up with the most kills and damage on the team?  How am I simultaneously expected to initiate fights, protect everyone, contest the objective, create space, survive the enemy team AND somehow compensate for teammates who aren't doing their jobs?  And then, when the inevitable loss happens, it's:  "Tank diff."  No.  Sometimes the tank isn't the problem.  Sometimes people simply don't understand how to play as a team.  Overwatch is fundamentally a team game. You can be mechanically incredible and still lose because you aren't coordinating with your team. You can have the best aim in the lobby and still get nowhere if nobody pushes the objective. You can have a phenomenal tank, DPS or support player and still lose because four people are doing completely different things.  Yet there seems to be this bizarre obsession with finding one person to blame.  It's especially frustrating when you're genuinely trying your hardest to carry a game, sweating your absolute ass off trying to clutch a fight, while teammates are repeatedly dying alone, refusing to group up, ignoring the objective or simply refusing to work together.  And yes, sometimes I am the one playing badly.  I'm not going to pretend I've never thrown a game or made stupid decisions. I've been playing this game for thousands of hours — obviously I've had some absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ games.  But that's the point.  It's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game.  Games are supposed to be fun.  I'm not supposed to finish a gaming session feeling like I've just worked a second shift.  Overwatch has reached a point where I can genuinely feel my stress levels rising the longer I play. I'll tell myself, "one more game," queue up, get put into a lobby where nobody communicates, spend the next fifteen minutes desperately trying to keep everything together, lose, get flamed, and then wonder why the hell I am doing this to myself.  And the worst part is that I KNOW what this game can be.  I've experienced it.  Those games where everyone is actually working together. Where the tank creates space, DPS capitalise on it, supports keep everyone alive, people actually group up, ultimates are coordinated and the whole team feels like a single functioning unit.  Those games are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fantastic.  But they're becoming increasingly outweighed by the miserable ones.  I also can't help but feel that the game has progressively moved further away from what made the original Overwatch so enjoyable. Instead of refining the fundamentals, it feels like every update needs to introduce something bigger, louder or more complicated. More heroes. More abilities. More counters. More monetisation. More things happening on screen.  At some point, you have to ask whether all of this actually makes the game better.  For me, it hasn't.  I don't hate Overwatch because I think it's always been a bad game.  Quite the opposite.  I hate what it has become because I remember how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good it used to be.  I've spent thousands of hours on this game. That's an absurd amount of time. I've met people through it, made memories through it, raged at it, laughed at it and probably sacrificed several years of my lifespan to it.  But I think I'm finally done.  I'm no longer going to torment myself because some part of my brain keeps convincing me that the next game will be the one where everything clicks.  There are too many other games out there that I can play, have fun with, and then actually walk away from feeling better than when I started.  So this is where I finally get off the ride.  Thank you for the memories, Overwatch.  ♥♥♥♥ you for the rest.  I'm going to go play something that doesn't make me question my life choices.

Marvel Rivals is an incredibly fun hero shooter that captures the superhero fantasy better than almost anything else on the market right now. The core gameplay loop is phenomenal. Diving into a fast-paced 6v6 arena with a roster of iconic characters feels dynamic, punchy, and deeply satisfying.  The game shines brightest in its mechanics. The unique hero synergies—like Rocket Raccoon riding on Groot's shoulders or Iron Man supercharging Hulk's gamma attacks—add a brilliant layer of strategy that rewards teamwork. Combined with beautifully designed maps featuring destructible environments, the moment-to-moment combat is genuinely thrilling. When the game clicks, it is an absolute blast.  However, all of that brilliant design is currently being dragged down by a profoundly frustrating matchmaking system.  To put it bluntly, the matchmaking is currently a nightmare. Instead of placing players into balanced lobbies where both teams have a fighting chance, the algorithm frequently serves up painfully one-sided stomps. The experience feels entirely binary: you are either completely steamrolling the enemy team, or you are getting trapped in your own spawn room unable to play the game.  The system seems completely incapable of balancing skill levels or accounting for party sizes. As a solo player, it is incredibly common to be thrown into a team of uncoordinated beginners while facing off against a highly coordinated, fully grouped-up squad. Climbing the ranks—or even just trying to enjoy a casual match—rarely feels like a test of skill; it feels like a coin toss decided before the match even begins.  Marvel Rivals is a fantastic, top-tier game trapped inside a deeply flawed system. If the developers can overhaul the matchmaking algorithm to ensure fair, competitive matches, this has the potential to dominate the hero shooter genre. But until that gets fixed, be prepared to mix your superhero excitement with a heavy dose of sheer frustration.
