3,000+ Hours Later: The Actual State of Marvel Rivals  Peak Rank: Celestial / High Grandmaster  I have over 3,100 hours in Marvel Rivals on Steam, peaked Celestial / GM, and played through every season from launch to Season 10. I am not writing this out of blind hate—I spent thousands of hours here because I genuinely wanted this game to be good. But right now, the game is in the worst state it has ever been, and there are serious structural problems with how it's being run.  Here is an honest breakdown of what is actually happening with the game: 1. No Server Region Locks (Playing on 200+ Ping)  There are zero ping or region locks in matchmaking. Players from NA, EU, Asia, and the Middle East can queue into whichever servers they want. In almost every high-rank game, half the lobby is on 150 to 250+ ping.  In a fast-paced shooter with mobile heroes like Spider-Man, Iron Fist, or Magik, high latency breaks the game. Abilities connect on your screen but don't register server-side, players rubberband, and high-ping players get massive peeker's advantage around corners. Competitors like Overwatch or Valorant lock regions or prioritize ping for a reason. Rivals lets everyone queue everywhere, and match quality suffers because of it. 2. The Ranked System Gives Out Free Points  The ranked ladder does not use a real Elo or zero-sum MMR system. In Gold, Platinum, and Diamond, you get around +25 to +33 points for a win and only lose about -15 to -20 on a loss.  If you play 20 games and go 10–10, you gain over 100 free points just for maintaining a 50% win rate. Because of this inflation, players with 38% to 45% win rates grind into Grandmaster simply by spamming 400+ matches. Displayed rank doesn't reflect skill—it reflects playtime. When these players end up in Celestial lobbies, matches turn into coin flips based on which team got the carried teammate who doesn't understand basic positioning. 3. No Role Queue & The "Performance Points" Penalty  The game still has no role queue. The matchmaker balances teams based on average badge rank, not what roles people actually play. One team gets two Tank, two DPS, and two Support mains, while the other team gets five DPS one-tricks forced onto Tank.  On top of that, the "performance points" system benchmarks your stats per 10 minutes against the rank average for that hero. If you swap off DPS to Tank or Support to help your team comp, your off-role stats lag behind dedicated one-tricks. The game marks your performance as below average and docks you more points on a loss. The system literally punishes you for flexing.  Instead of fixing role queue, NetEase just banned 4-stacks and 6-stacks in high ranks and capped Celestial at duo-queue. They restricted friend groups instead of fixing lobby balance. 4. Dumbing Down Mechanics & Skill Ceilings  Instead of balancing around skill ceilings, the devs keep lowering mechanical execution:      Black Widow (Season 9.5): The devs stated they couldn't balance her sniper against mobility. Their fix was to completely remove the one-shot headshot from her normal Aim-Down-Sights kit and lock it behind her Ultimate. Then they widened bullet hitboxes and buffed body-shot damage so players who miss headshots still get free kills.      Regenerative "Green" Shields: Season 9 gave dive heroes shields that heal them for 30 to 60 HP a second after 5 seconds out of combat. If you dive in, mess up, and have bad positioning, you just run away for 5 seconds and get full HP back without needing a healer or a health pack.      Kits like Scarlet Witch’s lock-on beam or Captain America’s Lucky Loan reflection rely on auto-aim and automatic deflections rather than mechanical aim and timing.  5. The Team-Up System Keeps Breaking  The Team-Up mechanic was sold as the core feature of the game, but the devs cannot balance it. Every season, synergies get deleted or reworked. They completely removed the flagship Fantastic Four team-up in Season 6.5 because they couldn't balance a 4-hero passive.  In Dev Vision 19, devs admitted designing team-ups was burning them out. In Season 9, they scrapped the Anchor system and split heroes into dual loadouts. That created so many balance issues that they had to rebalance 80% of the entire roster in Season 9.0 and another 70% in Season 10.0. Reworking most of the characters every two months destroys any meta stability. 6. Triple Support Stall & The 6-Ban Draft  High-rank matches are dominated by sustain bunker comps (Triple Strategist, Stratpool, immortality fields, revivals). Teamfights take forever and turn into visual clutter because nobody dies. Even after a global 20% nerf to ultimate generation in Season 7, teams with worse mechanics still win simply by picking unkillable sustain and out-stalling cooldowns.  By Season 10, instead of fixing character kits, the devs added an alternating snake ban draft (1-2-2-1) locking out 6 heroes per match down to Gold III. When mid-tier ranks need six mandatory character bans just to stop cheese comps, roster balance has failed. 7. Smurfing, Broken Moderation, and Bot Appeals      Smurfing: You need a verified phone number just to type a message in the official Marvel Rivals Discord server. But to play Competitive Ranked on the actual game, you need zero phone or 2FA verification. Anyone can make infinite free burner accounts and stomp lower lobbies with zero barrier to entry.      Moderation: Voice chat slurs and toxic behavior go completely unpunished. Meanwhile, the text filter aggressively censors normal words, foreign phrases, and political terms like "Gaza" in player handles.      Automated Bans: When NetEase announced stricter penalties, they turned on automated ban waves based purely on report volume with no human review. Several players and creators (including Black players who publicly shared clips) got banned automatically with zero human oversight.      The Bot Appeal System: You cannot appeal bans in-game or via a web portal. You are forced to join their Discord and open a ticket, which is answered by automated bots that instantly close appeals with copy-paste rejections.  8. Performance and Technical Instability  Compared to shooters like Overwatch 2 or Valorant, Marvel Rivals runs poorly:      Severe micro-stutters during 12-player teamfights due to shader compilation issues.      Crashes on Intel 13th/14th Gen CPUs and recurring Nvidia driver problems.      PlayStation players regularly getting hard game crashes (error CE-34878-0) during heavy fights.      The game's install size bloated so heavily that they had to rip the 35GB high-res textures out into a separate DLC.      Every minor seasonal sub-patch completely corrupts and wipes match replays, making it impossible to review VODs or track progress without third-party recording software.  9. Monetization and Devaluing Playtime  NetEase constantly brings back old battle passes and cosmetic vaults. While accessibility for new players is fine, it completely removes any prestige or value for veteran players who grinded early seasons. On top of that, they locked basic chroma color variants and ultimate VFX behind separate currencies like Unstable Molecules to squeeze extra cash out of players. Summary  I put over 3,100 hours into this game because I wanted it to succeed. The character designs and core concept are fun, but the competitive side of the game is completely cracked right now.  Between open servers, free rank points, lack of role queue, dumbed-down mechanics, broken moderation, and constant technical stutters, it's exhausting. Right now, Overwatch 2 handles netcode, role queue, and competitive match quality way better.  Unless NetEase actually overhauls the netcode, fixes the ladder math, and adds real role queue and human moderation, I can't recommend spending your time here.

This game is a mixed bag. It has a lot of hype moments but it can also be very depressing and annoying at times. You can have a lot of fun playing one of many characters (especially if you are a Marvel fan), but there are a lot of issues that have persisted for MONTHS, with devs ignoring the feedback. Below i will list some upsides and downsides, so you can decide if the game is worth your time.  UPSIDES - game has great music and voice acting - devs constantly put out a lot of new content (events, new gamemodes etc.) - it is free, and has no p2w really - you can get a lot of fun cosmetics just by playing and paying for them with in-game currency you earn that way - it is many things, but boring is surely not one of them - the game is very fast-paced and demands your near constant attention with a ton of action.  DOWNSIDES - the game has a lot of visual clutter - because everything is so colourful it is often hard to see what exactly is going on - developers use generative AI. It was visible on multiple occassions in the background art (ex. weird letters that do not make sense on the banner in the background) or even cosmetics (for example on the spray you could get by watching Twitch streams the characters "melt" in certain places or have features that AI added that did not exist previously because it confused them with a similar looking character from another game (I think it was Street Fighter)). The voice lines in-game captions are also AI generated, because they often contain mistakes that are very easy to catch if you speak English at passable level. They probably just used AI instead of real people cause it is faster and cheaper. If that is something you do not want to support, do not play this game. - BOTS. Marvel RIvals has a gamemode where you can play with bots. That is fine. But when you try to play the quickplay gamemode (that is supposed to be just a quicker verison of ranked) oftentimes it will match you with bots, so you can stomp them to "boost your morale". It will not tell you that they are bots, but if you played the game long enough you will learn how to spot them. If I wanted to play against an enemy who can not even kill me because they are so bad, I would have queued for a bot game. I want to play vs REAL PEOPLE so I can improve. - balancing varies very much between seasons - there are times where the game is in a really good place, and sometimes it's unplayable for anyone who doesn't play one of the 5 OP heroes - lack of penalties for cheaters, throwers, and leavers. The anticheat is bad. I am a plat player (which is a rather average rank) and I had cheaters with autoaim and wallhacks in my lobbies. It is even worse in the highest ranks. But the most annoying things got to be leavers. Especially in quickplay there are little to no penalties for just leaving in the middle of the match which means that in roughly 50% of the games you will have (a) player(s) ragequit after 2-3 deaths because he/she is only having fun when he/she is stomping. - developers being very selective about the feedback they listen to. They will hear some guys crying on social media that the champion they play is weak and will act differently depending on the hero. God forbid poor Luna Snow (which is a comic character created by one of the chief creators for this game fyi) is not a great pick for LITERALLY ONE DAY. Devs will do an emergency patch buffing her 24h after new season (and I say this as someone who has Luna as the most played hero). But if Blade is a useless troll pick with more bugs than I care to count the devs will take months to adress the issue (if they even do at all). There have been some allegations of racism (especially racism towards dark skinned characters) connected to that (and skin distribution and quality), but I am not that deep into this topic, so I advise doing some own research if that is something important to you. Devs clearly have favourites and unfortunately it does affect gameplay quality.  Overall, I would not recommend this game to most people. If you do not care about the stuff I mentioned in the downsides, you should give this a try, especially since you can just uninstall the game if you do not like it. Otherwise this is a hard pass. I spent a lot of time with this game and ultimately decided that it is not good enough in its current state to spend more. If devs make some changes and fixes maybe I will reinstall, but for now Marvel Rivals causes me more frustration than joy and there are other games more deserving of my time.

These missiles have flawless fire-and-forget capabilities and TV-guidance data-links, plunging straight down into your roof armor for an instant overpressure kill. Western helicopters have nothing that even compares.  A Developer Trapped in Statistics: Gaijin balances this game strictly based on global win-rate statistics. Instead of fixing broken damage models or giving Western vehicles their historically accurate performance, they just pump out overpriced premium vehicles to print money. They demand classified military documents to fix blatant bugs on Western vehicles, yet uncritically accept glossy sales brochures from Russian manufacturers as gospel truth. [h1] I didn't want to, but the game is wasted potential [/h1]  War Thunder provides very good design and sound for vehicles, including tanks, planes, and ships; battles feel realistic and on a large scale when they go well. The aspect of the game surrounding these features, however, is set up to frustrate players until they decide to open their wallet.  The grind  The progress is extremely slow. To get a vehicle you first need to earn research points, then spend lions to buy it, and afterwards carry out more silver and crew training in order to operate it. In each vehicle tree the initial models do a poor job until the various modules have been unlocked. It is frustrating to play a tank with no upgrades against players who have completely researched and trained their crews. The problem gets worse at higher ranks and to reach the top-tier vehicles it takes hundreds of hours. Even when you lose a match time is still taken up and a weak team can leave you with nothing.  Premium vehicles and pay to progress  War Thunder uses two types of currency. One is gained gradually as a result of playing the game, and the other can be bought with actual money. Premium vehicles are promoted as ways of saving time; in practice they often perform just as well as or better than standard vehicles that have the same battle rating. The purpose of premium time and boosters is mainly to make the process of earning silver through normal gameplay seem extremely unpleasant. The prices are very high since a single vehicle costs as much as the full price of the game and bundles cost even more. Players also feel that their progress is connected to how much they spend, because the free method is so slow that many of them feel they have to buy premium vehicles in order to earn silver at a faster rate.  Economy and repair costs  The costs involved in repairing your vehicle and the costs of spawning vehicles penalise you for the way that War Thunder encourages you to play. If you lose a high-tier vehicle the amount of silver you lose in a match will be greater than the amount you earned. Even if you have a premium account or premium vehicles you can still win a match but will end up losing money. It is hard to enjoy trying out different vehicles when each death has a cost.  Balance and matchmaking  Battle ratings are intended to ensure that matches remain fair. The system is generally compressed and inconsistent. You will frequently come across vehicles that are much better than yours, for example ones with armour that you can't penetrate, weapons that have a greater range than yours or aircraft that have obvious advantages. In top-tier matches the contest is often often one of who has the most expensive vehicle. Balance changes can be slow and difficult to predict and problems which spoil matches for months are not corrected.  Gameplay and other issues  The ground combat aspect is hampered by a dependence on air support and a great deal of downtime after a player dies. Although the Realistic and Simulator modes provide a certain level of depth, the number of players is small and games tend to either turn into camping situations or become chaotic. Bugs and problems with hit registration continue to occur from time to time and some of the game's mechanics seem inconsistent. The interface is messy and confusing for players because of the excessive number of currencies, modes, menus, and store prompts. The developers have often given poor communication regarding changes and have not adequately responded to community feedback. Players frequently feel that they are being ignored.  Verdict  Even though War Thunder might be one of the military games ever created, the design decisions always get in the way. The game places a greater emphasis on monetization and slow progression than on respecting the players' time. People who enjoy spending hundreds of hours grinding or who are willing to spend money might well have a good time. However, if you are looking for a rewarding experience, then you should look elsewhere from the beginning.  [quote=schmuck]There is neither gold nor silver nor treasure. Rather, the true treasure is what is dear to the heart.[/quote]

As it stands, the game gets progressively worse in terms of performance, bugs and overall quality of life. Balancing is a matter of rolling the dice to see if your favorite new gear gets nerfed into uselessness with the next update. Other than yourself, the devs are also rolling the dice, just in terms of significant changes to the game. There have already been multiple occasions, where something in the game got changed in such an obviously unnecessary, bad and sometimes even game-breaking way (for example a very common, medium-armor-enemy now getting heavy armor), just so that the whole community revolted against it and the change got reverted after a few days.   Some mechanics in the game seem to simply be there to sell a solution in the form of an armor passive, coming with warbonds, rather than reviewing them in terms of it's contribution to the overall fun of the game. Ragdolling always has been and is still one of the most frustrating aspects, that serves no purpose, other than randomly forcing you in a situation where you cannot do anything and just die, no matter how good you play. Warbonds are hit or miss most of the times and generally not really worth 10-15€. I really wished the developers would take a step back from churning out warbonds and fix the game's major problems first. I am certain, that this alone would boost both player numbers and retention.  It is unimagineably saddening to me, that such an amazing game gets handled in such a disrespectful way. I really think the game and it's surrounding community deserves better. At it's core, Helldivers 2 is phenomenal, but this core is currently a dim light getting overshadowed by questionable decisions and abysmal community handling. If you don't own the game, I sadly cannot reccomend a buy. If you do, please don't pay for the warbonds, grab a few friends and farm the credits instead.  To be clear, I do not harbor any ill-will against the developers in any way. Developing and maintaining a game of such scale is a monumental task. And what has been accomplished so far, for better or worse, deserves acknowledgement and respect. But I do question if the devs have the right priorities right now.

Helldivers 2 is, on paper, exactly the kind of game I love. It’s incredibly fun, creative, chaotic, and has a fantastic amount of replayability. Every mission can play out differently, and there’s something genuinely satisfying about dropping in with a group of friends and watching everything descend into glorious chaos.  The graphics are also fantastic. The environments can be absolutely stunning, and there are plenty of moments where you can stop and appreciate just how good the game looks. The developers also deserve credit for consistently updating the game, adding new content, weapons, enemies, missions, and other things to keep the experience evolving. There’s clearly a lot of effort going into keeping the game alive.  Unfortunately, for me, the community has taken almost all of the fun out of it.  What should be a goofy, chaotic co-op shooter has developed a surprisingly sweaty player base that seems to take the game way too seriously. Make a small mistake, bring the "wrong" weapon, accidentally kill someone, don't follow the exact strategy someone wants, or simply play differently than they do, and suddenly you're getting kicked or lectured like you've just ruined a professional tournament.  The whole appeal of Helldivers 2, at least to me, is the ridiculous chaos. You're supposed to make mistakes. You're supposed to accidentally blow up your teammates. You're supposed to have things go horribly wrong and then somehow pull off a victory. That's where a lot of the fun comes from.  Instead, too many players seem obsessed with playing perfectly and enforcing their idea of the "correct" way to play.  I've reached the point where joining random games often feels more stressful than fun because I'm constantly worried that one minor mistake is going to get me kicked or criticized. And when a game that is supposed to be about blowing things up with friends starts feeling like a job where you're afraid of making a mistake, something has gone wrong.  I still think Helldivers 2 is an excellent game. The gameplay, creativity, visuals, replayability, and continued stream of content are all genuinely impressive.  But unfortunately, the player base has completely killed the fun for me.  If you have a group of friends to play with, I can absolutely see this being an amazing experience. Playing with randoms, however, has become an increasingly frustrating experience for me.

This is a really fun game with a ton of stuff to do. Playing hard levels and increasing your skill level over time is one of the most satisfying things I've found in any game. The level editor, while very complex and hard to learn, lets you make some really cool stuff for other people to play as well and is another very satisfying thing to figure out.  The problems with this game start to emerge once you're done creating your level. As many others have said, the rating system of user levels in this game is AWFUL. If you aren't a major figure in the community, the system is purely luck-based and incredibly unfair to small creators like myself. To make that even worse, RobTop (the game's developer) recently cut half of the team of mods/rate advisors (people who suggest levels to be rated) in what is potentially the worst decision ever made in the history of the game's development.  But the main issue with the mods getting cut isn't how it makes the rating system worse. The mod purge is symbolic of everything wrong with this game's development. It was done with almost no communication and entirely no explanation as to why certain mods were picked to be demoted. Most of the ones who were actually very active in the community were on the list of the ones who got kicked, and many of the remaining ones haven't touched the game in months.  To make this even worse, the game has a serious issue with child predators, likely second only to Roblox. Mods and players have asked RobTop to do something about it several times for years and he has ignored them every time. The upcoming update for this game is set to make it even worse, with the addition of private group chats between players. And on top of that, some of the mods who were demoted in the purge have speculated that RobTop specifically picked people who were telling him to fix the child predator situation to be demoted, so that's nice.  In summary, this is a great game with a horrible developer who has created major issues with the game and doesn't seem to want to fix them. Despite everything the game does right, I don't think I can give it a positive review until the child predator problem is fixed, and I really hope that happens soon.

The gameplay would also be incredible, but the game is plagued with one of the worse balance possible, and is essentially holding together by the first three things I mentioned. It's a blend of band aid fixes turned into load bearing systems for endgame builds. The endgame itself is so poorly handled, builds for it are more about ignoring it than finally engaging with it. The game runs on outdated design decisions from more than a decade ago when it was trying to be another genre, and no move is made to correct it. And there is so, SO much more, but you get the idea. it's a game that's going to be fun in the first half (or until you run into those endgame builds who the devs allow to just suck the fun from everyone else in a multiplayer game), and will then become boring the moment you are presented with steel path, as it's where all the option, build diversity you had goes to die.  If you want to play it for the story, it's absolutely valid, but the gameplay isn't worth it and I would, above all else, still advise to not spend money on this game, for the devs are currently making no effort to respect your support by making quality gameplay. Warframe is a fascinating setting. The art direction is incredibly cohesive and distinct, the music, sound and voicework is great, and the writing establishes a lot of long term intrigue. And having watched some of the most recent content without really knowing anything about the game, it makes me want to find out why the hell a big title card update quest ends in making your space ninja kids dinner. And why their adult selves are sitting at a table with you in the past, feeding the past version of their sibling. That is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy hook and it made me want to try and unravel what on earth gets you to that point.  But Warframe just cannot escape the fact that it is an MMO, and I just don't find Unlocking New Gear being the main pillar of gameplay to be compelling. The combat has great feedback, but its just. Not that interesting to actually play the combat. The quest stories are good, but the missions themselves are indistinguishable from the missions you grind for resources outside of some unique dialogue. And don't get me started on the new player experience. Even after the tutorial revamp, its just terrible. If you don't have a friend who's already heavily invested in Warframe to guide you through how certain systems work or when you should be expecting to get to new content, its a complete mess. Finishing the tutorial would have me think that the next thing to do is start the next quest, which will then progressively lead me through the solar system. But no, as a more experienced friend told me, the idea is actually to go and unlock most of the map, which then grants you access to the next quests. A lot of Warframe is very unintuitive to people who haven't played an MMO before, and its incredibly confusing and offputting.  I know that's just MMO gameplay, but despite how interested I am in getting through to the story and learning more about the setting and its characters, the game itself just isn't fun to me as someone who's primarily motivated by the narrative. This hasn't been my first attempt either, I've had three separate goes of trying to get into Warframe. Its unfortunate that a game that keeps capturing my attention just isn't capable of keeping me engaged. If Digital Extremes ever decide to make a Warframe game in a different format, I'd definitely be interested in trying it out.

Let's start with the "negatives".   Most people are put off Limbus due to it being a gacha. Does this game have P2W? No. The only thing you are buying if you want to spend some money is the battlepass. And due to this game having seasons last almost a year, you'll be getting insane mileage out of this battlepass, because it has repeating levels after the last one. This has to do the Shard system. There are Identities for Sinners (aka Characters on banners), and you can Shard them. Every level past the last one gives you boxes with Identity Shards. With the pass you get more. Farm those, boom, you have almost all of the IDs in the game without gacha.  The next point is a little bit more niche. There are people who are fans of Lobotomy who dislike both Limbus and Ruina, unwilling to engage with the plot and new gameplay mechanics. To them, I say that it's very sad. Kim Ji Hoon is clearly doing the same thing as he always does with different coats of gameplay. I can't say I am also a big fan of what he's doing gamewise, but lore and characterwise he is almost never missing. Of course, he IS missing sometimes, but that's exactly WHY I love Project Moon's projects. They are alive. They are breathing, and also dying sometimes. So if only LobCorp stuck with you, maybe you're not a PM fan. Maybe you just like monster management. And that's okay.  But WE, and I mean WE are here for the ride for all of the shenanigans the company pulls.  The next one is somewhat between a negative and an Eh. It's the amount of content. To be real, there is almost nothing to do in the game. Story is absolutely incredible and the game is still going on, but that's a live service and you have only TWO real gamemodes. Excluding the main story, that's ONE. There is also endgame "content", but it's for insane people and even I don't like where it's going because I am a filthy, filthy casual.   For example, I've played HS:R Virtual Reality gamemode for quite a while and enjoyed building different stuff and trying out stuff. I don't like Mirror Dungeon as much, even though i've put 400x the time in Limbus. Mirror Dungeon is just kinda Meh. A mean to an end, rather than something you actually want to be actively playing for 8 months between Cantos.  This is a serious negative side if you care about this sort of thing, but I'm there for the STORY so I don't really care, although a more pleasant way to farm BattlePass levels would be nice. But KJH does whatever he wants, so I can't dictate my wants to him.  Okay, let's talk about the good stuff now.  Obviously. Story. It is absolutely incredible. Yes, it's an acquired taste here and there, and it's a little bit special, but it's a billion times better than whatever any other gacha game has. The characters are vibrant and great to follow, even with some of them getting less limelight than others, this game doesn't abandon it's characters because there is a STRICT 13 main characters lineup that is holding incredibly well. You are not getting random new characters like in Hoyoverse slop titles, this is a real story that is progressing for three whole games at this point! And this one tells it's own story in the subsection of this massive world PM has built. It's a pleasure.  Music is top notch. EiM and Mili are cooking some real bangers time after time after time AND even though some LobCorp fans complained about new music I say they are dumb and wrong and all of the games have peak sound design and music, no matter who does them. It is just so rich.  Art is also very good and gets better. Yes, we lost Nai_Ga and that is very sad, insert your political opinion on the topic, but Vellmori is also great and whoever does the character sprites is great. Also, now we have RPGmaker in the game for some reason, and it's also PEAK. Animations for fights and in-game sprites are also very good.  The gameplay. It's solid, it's good. It's nothing special and I can't say it's my favorite, but I like it. It's about 30-40% of why I play a PM game. The Challenge when it comes is absolutely incredible to overcome, tipping it more to 50%, but I am more of a storyhead.  Overall Limbus Company is a 9/10 game and Project Moon is easily my favorite gaming company in the industry. Vroom-vroom to victory!

These are my main complaints after playing Canto X.  First of all, I found the new gameplay system to be uninteresting. The game has shifted away from its traditional combat system and adopted a top-down RPG style, but the result feels shallow. Most encounters boil down to walking into enemies and repeatedly pressing buttons, and the controls themselves do not feel particularly smooth or responsive.  I also do not understand the decision to make such a drastic change to the core gameplay after players have spent years with the previous system. It feels as though the developers are filtering out players who enjoyed the game for what it originally was.  Another issue is the level sync system, which makes previous character progression feel largely meaningless. I understand that the story’s setting provides an in-universe explanation for the reduced levels, but even with that context, the enemies feel significantly less threatening and less impressive than those encountered in Canto IX. As a result, the overall sense of tension and escalation is diminished.  There are also other problems, such as excessive fetch quests that seem designed to pad out playtime and the game’s tendency to explain specialized terminology with even more specialized terminology, making parts of the story unnecessarily difficult to follow.  Overall, Canto X currently feels like a step backward. The new gameplay system lacks depth, the pacing suffers from unnecessary padding, and many aspects of the experience feel less engaging than previous chapters.

The Season 8/Canto X update is shockingly bad. I'm fine with alternate game modes making an appearance to shake things up, like Spring Cultivation, but the Grand Sisyphe (the "RPG" gameplay) that makes up essentially the entirety of Canto X's story so far is just so, so bad.  To start off, you walk with the arrow keys. There's no options for WASD movement. This might seem like an incredibly small thing that you can deal with, but it shows a lack of care that's present throughout the entire update. It gives the impression that PM did absolutely zero player testing, because using an alternative control scheme as the only option will inevitably lead to complaints. Then there's the actual combat in the RPG section. Spam X. That's it. You can get an item that stuns enemies pretty early on, and it completely breaks the combat, because nothing can attack you, not even the final boss of that gameplay style. There's another item you can get that reverses the breaking, because it knocks back enemies when you hit them, which pushes them out of your range so you can't stunlock them. I would be willing to give this the benefit of the doubt, because knockback effects make sense when enemies have attack ranges, except that the knockback doesn't move the hitbox of the enemy's attack. If they're about to hit you with a 1 tile melee attack and you knock them so they're two tiles away, their attack stays on top of you, disconnected from the enemy. That item is optional to get, but cannot be turned off once acquired. Again, it feels like this just wasn't tested at all, because this is the natural result of buying all the items and pressing the singular combat button.  Then we get to the normal gameplay that was present. There were only like four required fights, and they were all pretty easy. I only had to read enemy skills once, the rest were easily reduced to just winning the clashes. But that level of difficulty is pretty par for the course with the main story by now. No, what really bothered me was the level progression in the Grand Sisyphe. As you buy items in the Grand Sisyphe, your levels go up. It doesn't matter how much time you've invested into playing the game before. All of that time was wasted. I don't know why they even bothered increasing the actual level cap if they're not going to give the players any content at the new level cap. I'm aware that this was done in order to allow for new players to do the story skip to Canto X (another bad idea that I'm surprised got approved), but it completely devalues the effort that enfranchised players have put into the game over multiple years.  And then there's some other random stuff worth mentioning. The Grand Sisyphe has a lot of minor graphical bugs: Stuff doesn't layer properly. Characters on the edge of the screen can be seen popping out of existence. Certain cutscenes will pause character movements but those characters retain their walking animations. Those same cutscenes will cause all corpses on screen to despawn and then respawn when the cutscene ends, and when they respawn they all replay their spawn animation, so you get a bunch of bodies popping onto the screen with an audible splat. There's no choices in what items to buy because you're always flush with enough cash to buy everything. There are items that are extremely useless, my favorite being the item that gives you "Invuln Frame +0.05 seconds when hit" which equates to exactly 3 frames of invulnerability after getting hit, which is basically nothing.  The story wasn't even that good, it felt like they rushed through all of the parts that I had been anticipating, and then had the Grand Sisyphe, which was 90% filler that didn't matter. The ending cutscene for the Grand Sisyphe was around 5 minutes of repeating the same couple of sentences phrased in different ways, equating to "Look at how things turned out due to your actions, are you really happy with your choices here?" Imagine an ending to Undertale, except it lacks any semblance of subtlety and keeps hitting you over the head with it. On top of that, it's unclear at this point if there are actually different endings to the Grand Sisyphe section that you can get with different choices, or if we'll be seeing different endings to it in the later parts of Canto X. I think it's the latter, which would defeat the entire point of the ending cutscene, (because it *wasn't* my choices that led there,) but I could be wrong about that. Either way, it wasn't a fun experience, and it's weird that it's what PM *wants* new players to experience by implementing the level skip, considering it isn't representative of the rest of the game at all.  Project Moon, and KJH in particular, need to learn that not everything should be in one game. If they had made the RPG section as a standalone project, they could've expanded it into a holistic experience, rather than tying down its mechanics to Limbus Company specifically. As it is right now, it just dilutes the Limbus Company experience into something worse than it used to be.  **Update**  Part 2 of Canto X has dropped, and man, I have more to add. First, they added some keybinds! You can now rebind keys to WASD. You can also rebind some other keys! But only keys in the Sisyphe, no rebinding the awkward shortcut keys for the normal gameplay. And you can't bind some keys you might want to bind, like the mouse buttons, or Tab, or Spacebar. So it's a very half-baked solution, in my opinion, but it was added, so I felt it necessary to correct that part of my review.  Now let's talk about more problems, though. Part 2 continues the RPG gameplay, and it somehow gets worse. It's just completely pointless in this part. There are a couple of wave defense sections where you spam the attack button more than before. There's a couple of bosses, except the RPG combat doesn't matter for those bosses because you're forced into a normal battle with them anyway, once they reach certain HP thresholds (and lowering their HP in the RPG combat doesn't affect the normal combat, so it's pointless). Throughout the Sisyphe there are non-hostile NPCs you can choose to fight if you want to, but part 2 introduces a required upgrade that automatically attacks nearby NPCs, including non-hostile ones, so you now have to fight *everything*, whether you like it or not. There's a large diagonal hallway that's fairly empty, but the movement is four-directional instead of eight, so it feels really awkward to navigate. When you're fighting a lot of enemies, the light increases for some reason, to the point where it can be exceptionally difficult to see what's going on. Speaking of the lighting, it sometimes suddenly changes after cutscenes now. There's one section of part 2 where you get a fetch quest that requires visiting seven of the eight floors in the Sisyphe (which you've already explored twice at this point, once in part 1 and once getting to this section of part 2), and for some godforsaken reason, they decided to remove the fast travel option for this section only. If at any point you enter a safe room on any floor during this section, or if you somehow die, you get sent back to the bottom floor, as far away as possible from progressing. Just... awful design. Due to story shenanigans that are similar to a time loop, (but not exactly,) a decent amount of scenes are repetitive, adding very little over part 1. I would go on about additional problems, but I'm nearing the maximum length of a Steam review. PM just needs to do better.

(Written at end of S7 / Canto 9)  Tl;DR: Too much bloat to make this "game" worthwhile. If you want to watch characters talk about something for 45 minutes before moving the plot a fraction of the way to completion, then this is the game for you.  The game's selling point is the story, but it's just kind of... rough? It is quite decent in its themes and overall plot, but there is a lot of narrative bloat to sit through to actually move said plot due to poor narrative momentum and pacing. The music is great; the characters are enjoyable.   Despite being a gacha, very friendly to f2p. Even if you only buy the season pass (like 15 bucks for 6 months), it is extremely worthwhile value and will net dozens of characters if you play weekly. I've only bought one pass, and I've gotten nearly 20 characters out of it in this past season playing only 5 minutes a day, plus one two-hour session a week for the boring mirror dungeon/endgame 'content' grind.  Gameplay is just kind of present. It takes little thinking at times if you build a good team or just whichever team is being pushed at present. Often, just hit the "Win Rate" button until victory is the equivalent of the 'gameplay'. Yes, there are some enemies that if you don't build exactly into, there will be a need to think. However, these enemies that requiring actually reading and planning are only a couple times per few month stretch, and once they are beaten, there's no real reason to come back once rewards are claimed. Certainly, there is the 'extreme' version of the endgame activity that does require thought later on, but it's a 2–3-hour slog of fighting trash enemies you're stronger than until one shows up and kicks your teeth in in the last 2-3 floors of the 15 floor dungeon. Even with this in mind, half of the hard battles are less 'use strategy' and more dealing with clash power inflation in later cantos, which very much can be a loss on the team screen rather than in the battle itself. Very much a second monitor game.  If you're okay with a slow and bloated story, average gameplay befitting a mobile game, and willing to sink time into it, then this game is decent. Otherwise, would highly recommend finding another game. The heights of the story do not outweight the lows or sitting through the many tactics used to extend the plot beyond reason. It's more like a time-gated novel that circles the same plot point several times before acting on it. This is mostly a fault of the visual novel-isms employed, but it could still be reduced to provide an overall more streamlined and effective narrative. Not to mention, a greater majority of 'missions' have random, almost forced combat encounters in them that just inflate the story for no reason that aren't even fun to play.  Overall, I just can not recommend this game. It's too much work to be considered a 'game', and its story is too conflicted with trying to be a game to be truly enjoyable.

I have played this game for awhile, and I have a lot of feelings about Terraria as a game, I'm not an expert at this game, I'm not super well-versed in everything this game has to offer but I've spent a lot of time dealing with its mechanics, the gameplay, and lots of things in-between, and after all that I have come to say that I don't recommend this game at all.  The game is a series of small frustrations that keep piling on top of each other, things you may or may not want to do that you have to keep doing in order to progress or do better damage, things that may or may not be fun depending upon who you are, and the game is for all intents and purposes one gigantic slot machine, a slot machine you can slightly rig in your favor but a slot machine.  Do you want a better weapon or tool? Well fight this boss an unknowable number of times for its ONE drop you want! Want an item to traverse the world easier? Kill 800 of this enemy! Want the item that displays everything? FISH! Want buffs? Place a bunch of planters, and get flowers that all have different growth conditions! Want a permanent buff to your magic? Click this Crystal Ball! (Why isn't the buff permanent???????)  It's this, constantly, over and over and over again. Things you might want to do, but things you also might never want to touch, and you have to do them if you want certain things. You need to look up how to even get these items most of the time, what even drops them, or how to even obtain the materials. Then there's the things that are never explained to you, like luck.  There is a lot in this game, a lot of things that don't mesh together, a lot of inconveniences that stack up, and it just all comes together to make a game I don't like playing at all. The Ship of Theseus is a thought experiment about whether an object is the same object after having all of its original components replaced with others over time. It is also an incredibly fitting paradox for my feelings towards Stardew Valley.  I always thought I dislike farming games. As it turns out, farming games were never the issue, Stardew Valley was. I am usually the type of gamer that wants a game to keep as much of its original aesthetic as possible and usually refrain from using any gameplay overhauls so I can honour the original creator(s).  This was entirely impossible for me when it comes to Stardew. Frankly, I think the artstyle is atrocious and the gameplay is much more stressful than relaxing, especially when you play the multiplayer version of it. Cutscenes neither stop time nor do you have the possibility to slow down the passage of time in a day, meaning that you have to plan ahead whether you want to socialise or grind to make grandpa happy. This often meant that my co-op player had to do all the farming and grinding while I played my own little social sim.  My pixelated neighbours also didn't really draw me in - at best, I can say I liked Sebastian (how original) and disliked Lewis. At worst, I have to question how much of this stems from fan-interpretations of the characters and the mods I had installed. The fact that I mostly have no strong feelings about any of the other characters isn't a good thing. Cue me installing Stardew Valley Expanded and at least getting a little bit more out of the game, with some additional characters that ended up being more interesting than the ones I was initially given.  The worst part is that some emotional scenes didn't hit the way they were intended to - a certain character on the beach, talking about his backstory with some... less than stellar pixels to set the scene - as the cutscene actually looked so ridiculous that I couldn't take it seriously, and naturally my character was forced to drink in other scenes, even though I dislike alcohol. Same old. At some point in the game, you also just simply lose the drive to keep going, which is not a great sign either. And I tried to give this game multiple chances, as I know some of my loved ones enjoy it.  Frankly, after having experienced RRRR once (which plans to break away from Stardew modding and instead intends to become its own game), I don't think I can ever go back to a version of Stardew without it. A meaningful romance option, with changes to the characters and his character arc beyond the initial wedding, with children that matter? Stardew Valley could only DREAM of this. I am also simply tired of people calling everything a Stardew Valley clone when Harvest Moon came first (and I never even played it, so it's not the nostalgia speaking here) and other games, like Fields of Mistria and Coral Island, simply do the formula better AND are prettier, no mods required. It also seems hilarious to me that the creator now scrambles to finally update children after years of not giving a care and other farming sims deciding that they wanted to do better. Will we get non-binary options as well and meaningful updates to the characters, or will this just be a half-hearted attempt to keep being "the best"?  I ended up having a lot of fun with my co-player in the end - but the question is at what point am I truly still enjoying Stardew Valley instead of all the modders' additions? Roman aqueducts were one of the most impressive engineering achievements of the ancient Roman world, allowing cities across the Roman Empire to receive large and reliable supplies of fresh water from distant springs, rivers, and underground sources. Despite often being called “water bridges,” an aqueduct was actually an entire water-supply system, much of which ran underground or through tunnels, with the famous stone arches only being the most visible sections. Roman engineers carefully surveyed the landscape to create a very gentle and continuous downhill gradient, allowing gravity to carry water from its source toward a city without the need for pumps. The water travelled through channels known as specus, which were commonly lined with waterproof cement called opus signinum to reduce leakage. When valleys or low areas interrupted the route, engineers sometimes constructed enormous rows of arches to maintain the necessary gradient, while hills could be passed through tunnels. Some aqueducts travelled for many kilometres, and the longest systems could extend for well over 50 kilometres when all their branches were included. Once the water reached a city, it was often collected in a settling and distribution tank called a castellum aquae, from which it could be directed through smaller pipes to public fountains, baths, houses, gardens, and sometimes industrial facilities. The Romans built aqueducts throughout their empire, with particularly famous examples in Rome itself, where numerous aqueducts supplied the rapidly growing population. The Aqua Appia, completed in 312 BC, was Rome's first aqueduct, while later structures such as the Aqua Claudia became famous for their enormous masonry arches and sophisticated construction. Aqueduct water was not simply a luxury for wealthy Romans; it played an important role in public life, especially through the enormous public bath complexes that became central social and cultural spaces. The supply of running water also helped support fountains, public toilets, street cleaning, and firefighting. Roman engineers used surveying instruments such as the groma and chorobates to establish accurate routes and gradients, demonstrating an impressive understanding of practical engineering. They also had to account for problems such as sediment buildup, leaks, erosion, and changes in terrain, so aqueducts included maintenance shafts, inspection points, settling basins, and access routes. Contrary to the popular image of Roman aqueducts being completely straight, their routes often followed the natural contours of the landscape, sometimes winding considerably to avoid difficult terrain. The construction of these systems required huge amounts of labour and materials, including stone, brick, concrete, timber, and lead or terracotta pipes. Roman aqueducts therefore represented much more than impressive architecture: they were complex pieces of infrastructure that combined surveying, hydraulic engineering, construction, administration, and regular maintenance. Their success helped Roman cities grow to remarkable sizes and provided a level of urban water management that was unusual for the ancient world. Many Roman aqueducts remained in use for centuries, and some sections of ancient systems were incorporated into later water networks, demonstrating just how durable and effective Roman hydraulic engineering could be.

At this point we all know that the story mode of GTA V is fantastic, and it's one of the best selling games of all time. That being said, I would like to use the opportunity of this review to try and have a critical view of this game, as I think that the success of GTA V is the worst thing that happened to Rockstar/Take Two Interactive.  But before getting into that, even though recognizing the undeniable qualities of the game itself, and the fact that this enhanced version looks absolutely gorgeous for a 2013 game at maximum setting with full RTX, I would like to point out the things that went, in my eyes, backwards compared to the previous games. I recently replayed all of them from GTA III to GTA V, in order. And I can say the biggest downgrade in my eyes compared to any other GTA game is the characters and the story, outside from GTA III of course that was just a precursor. I remember, if not in all details, most of the stories of Vice City, San Andreas and IV, but even though this is technically my third playthrough of V, I could not remember at all what the story was besides a few missions like the boat chase on the highway or the jewelry store heist. And that's because the missions are not memorable in this game. Don't get me wrong, they are action packed, fun and much more varied than in the previous title, but they don't have any impact on a storytelling point of view. They are more like GTA San Andreas than GTA IV. But the problem to me is not just the story itself but the characters that we are given. Just compare them to CJ and Niko, the best character Rockstar has ever written for GTA with so much depth, ambiguity and history, and then look at what we're dealing with here: Franklin, Michael and Trevor. Franklin is an absolute empty shell, he has barely any personality and is by far the most superficially written main character that Rockstar has ever cooked. I hate playing as Franklin, and I didn't even remember his name before replaying the game for the third time. Then we have Michael. The fact that he has a family and is going to therapy could have been interesting, but all of it is treated again very lightly and as a joke, that nothing lands for me. He's clearly supposed to be the main protagonist out of the 3, and I can not care for him honestly. And then we have Trevor. Everybody's favorite, and mine too. But he's a meme character. He's literally insane, and has zero layers, it's just the crazy character that is funny, but he's so insane that nothing can carry any weight with such a character, because nothing really has any consequence when you're dealing with insanity in that matter.  Beyond that, there are things that are also clearly missing from the previous two titles, such as the surprising lack of interiors! Buying businesses also has nothing interesting besides being a way to sunk the money you make somewhere. You can literally never get inside any of the businesses you buy, have procedurally generated random missions from time to time that bring nothing to the game. Vice City had better business missions than this game! The Euphoria physics engine has been tuned since GTA IV, and the physics of vehicles is much less frustrating, but the combat feels also much less impactful and visceral, enemies just feel like pawns that you kill in crazy numbers. There's more action, but less consequences I'd say. Also, I forgot how terrible the controls can be in this game sometimes. There's inconsistencies with them depending on vehicles or point of view. For instance, on a PS5 controler, R2 accelerates most vehicles, but not bikes, it's X! In 1st person, up goes up underwater, but in 3rd person, it makes you go down, etc. One last thing on the topic of comparison with other GTA games. Every one of them was a revolution that moved the industry forward. GTA III was the first 3D open world that felt like a real one for the time. Vice City brought actual story telling to an open workd and was among the first games to have actual movie stars voice over such as Ray Liotta for Tommy Vercetti. San Andreas brought an entire region, varied, with 3 cities, 100 main missions, many side missions, dating, gang wars, etc. It gave a life sim aspect to the game as never seen before at the time. GTA IV brought a revolutionary physics engine, a city that felt like real life like never before and more mature storytelling.  As big and cool as GTA V is, what did it bring? We've already established that it was not the story our protagonists. The physics is a refined version of the previous game. The world is huge, but is that an industry breakthrough? Liberty City felt like such a packed and atmospheric place, that was alive and with very clear distinctions between each districts. Los Santos is huge yes, but also feels very empty to me. Yes the large streets are probably like the real Los Angeles, but they're so big that there's never enough cars and pedestrians to make it feel like the big city it's supposed to be. And besides the obviously rich parts of Vinewood hills, I can never tell any district of the city apart. They are incredibly detailed, but also not distinct enough and too empty. There's no more dating or friends (I discovered this time around that you can actually hang out with the other main characters, but it brings nothing compared to GTA IV). They brought back some stats from GTA San Andreas, but they are completely meaningless and I cannot tell the difference between a level 10 in shooting and a level 100. The characters are thematically different and have different animations, but besides that they play all exactly the same, where CJ back in the days had clear progress with his stats and could learn 4 different fighting styles! So what did GTA V bring that was new? 3 characters instead of 1? Sure, but like I said they are more like meme characters devoid of substance than real fleshed out protagonists, and it's not like it was a brand new idea. We could already play as Batman or Catwoman in Batman Arkham City for instance. First person for the first time? Again, it's not like no game before allowed you to switch between perspective, I'm pretty sure Morrowind already had that! And I personally don't care about this perspective in that type of games anyway (they're not bringing it back for GTA VI, so this is also proving my point).  GTA V brought something that was a, thankfully, short-lived trend with AAA games back then: a freaking companion app for Franklin's dog that you had to download on your real life phone! That was mandatory to make it progress and very obnoxious. Of course now that the app has been discontinued, the dog is completely unusable in the "enhanced" game.  No, what GTA V brought that really made a difference was the freaking GTA Online mode! And that's what's in my opinion the worst thing that ever happened to the company. Because despite being an awfully glitchy, bug-ridden, unstable and cheaters-filled mess, this mode is bringing BILLIONS to Rockstar, with a freaking B! Because of that, Rockstar stopped making anything else and started comparing everything to what amounts of money GTA Online was bringing. And since nothing compared, everything else got canned. Rockstar used to make very varied and interesting games such as Bully, L.A. Noire, Max Payne 3, Manhunt or The Warriors. Now Rockstar only does GTA. Even Red Dead Redemption 2, one of the best games ever made, fell short of their expectations if you can believe that because the online mode didn't bring the same load of cash as GTA Online. That's also why there's been 13 years between GTA V and GTA VI, Rockstar just kept making content for their cash machine instead of new games. What's also funny, on a side note, is that we know that capitalism has the capacity of swallowing its criticism and monetize them, and that's what Rockstar, the giant corporation, is doing by making fun of practices in their fake movies or games in GTA V that they indulge themselves in!

Steam Review — Why I Don't Recommend Rust  The game itself is good. The problem is what Rust can do to your time.  Rust is undeniably a well-designed survival game. The building, PvP, raiding, progression, exploration, teamwork, and unpredictable player interactions can create some incredible gaming moments. However, after looking at the experiences repeatedly described by both positive and negative Steam reviewers, I think there is a much bigger issue worth warning new players about: Rust can consume an enormous amount of your time while constantly making you feel like you need to keep playing.  The biggest problem is the repetitive gameplay loop.  You gather resources, build a base, farm more resources, research, craft weapons, collect better loot, defend your base, raid someone else, get raided, lose your progress, rebuild, and repeat the entire process after the next wipe. At first this feels exciting because everything is new. Eventually, however, you can realize that you're repeatedly performing the same tasks just to get back to where you already were.  Rust has no real finish line.  There is always another wipe, another base to build, another resource run, another raid, another weapon to obtain, another enemy to fight, or another reason to log back in. That can make the game extremely difficult to put down. Instead of playing because you genuinely want to, you can eventually find yourself playing because you feel like you need to keep up.  The wipe system makes this even more frustrating.  You can spend countless hours building a base and accumulating resources, only for a raid or server wipe to erase much of that progress. Then you're expected to start over. For some players, that constant reset is the appeal. For others, it eventually becomes exhausting because hundreds of hours can amount to repeatedly rebuilding something that is never permanent.  The time commitment is the biggest hidden cost.  The $40 purchase price isn't necessarily the expensive part. Your time is. If Rust becomes a game you play 20–30 hours a week, that's roughly 1,000–1,500 hours per year. Those are hours that could have gone toward school, work, career development, exercise, family, friends, traveling, learning something new, or simply getting proper sleep.  Gaming is supposed to be entertainment. It becomes a problem when the entertainment starts competing with the rest of your life.  Rust can also create FOMO and an obligation to log in.  You may think, "I'll just take a few days off," but then you start worrying about falling behind, missing progression, getting raided, losing your base, or letting your teammates down. Eventually the thought becomes, "I have to check the base," or "I need to farm tonight." That's when a game can start feeling less like recreation and more like another responsibility.  The community can make the experience considerably worse.  Not every Rust player is toxic, and there are plenty of good people you'll meet. However, the game naturally encourages distrust, competition, raiding, betrayal, trash talking, door camping, griefing and revenge. Someone can spend hours specifically making your experience miserable simply because the game allows it. Losing a legitimate fight is one thing; having somebody repeatedly grief you after you've already lost everything is another.  Cheating is another major concern.  Rust has a long-standing problem with cheaters, and Facepunch has publicly reported hundreds of thousands of bans and millions of cheat reports. Even with anti-cheat measures and bans, encountering a suspected cheater can be especially frustrating in Rust because you're not simply losing one match—you can potentially lose hours or days of accumulated progress.  The high-stakes PvP system can also make ordinary gaming sessions unnecessarily stressful.  When you hear footsteps, see another player, hear gunshots, or notice someone building nearby, you're constantly evaluating whether you're about to lose everything. That tension is part of what makes Rust exciting, but after enough time it can become exhausting. You can spend a large portion of your gaming session worrying about protecting progress rather than actually enjoying yourself.  Then there is the financial side.  The game isn't necessarily limited to the initial purchase. Rust has DLC, cosmetics, skins, marketplace items and other ways to spend additional money. One skin might not seem like much, but $5 here, $10 there, another weapon skin, another building skin, another cosmetic, and eventually the total can become surprisingly large.  Be especially careful if you're someone who enjoys collecting things or feels compelled to have the newest or rarest items. Virtual items can become a very real expense.  The sunk-cost mentality is another trap.  You might eventually think, "I've already played 500 hours, so I can't quit now." Then 1,000 hours becomes 2,000. But the hours you've already spent don't require you to spend even more. If Rust is no longer improving your life or providing enough enjoyment to justify the time you're putting into it, you're allowed to walk away.  Ironically, some of the game's strongest positive qualities are also its biggest problems.  The persistent world, wipes, raiding, progression, competition, social interaction, resource gathering and unpredictability are what make Rust unique. They're also what can make it incredibly time-consuming and difficult to stop playing.  My biggest warning to new players is simple: don't judge Rust only by whether it's fun. Ask whether the amount of time it demands from you is worth it.  A game can be fun and still consume too much of your life.  A game can be well-made and still become unhealthy for you.  A game can have an amazing community experience while also exposing you to cheating, griefing and toxicity.  And a $40 game can eventually cost far more than $40 when you include DLC, skins, marketplace spending and, most importantly, hundreds or thousands of hours of your life.  If you can play Rust casually, set boundaries, avoid unnecessary spending and walk away whenever you want, that's one thing. But if you notice yourself sacrificing sleep, work, school, relationships, finances or real-world goals just to keep up with a virtual wipe cycle, it's probably time to reconsider.  Rust isn't necessarily a bad game. That's exactly why the warning matters. It's good enough to keep you coming back.  Don't let a game designed around endless progression convince you that you have an obligation to keep progressing. Your real life doesn't have a wipe button.

I feel like my playtime speaks for itself, broadly speaking. If you enjoyed the first two games, this one is better (some Warhammer 2 folks may disagree - their arguments shouldn't be discounted, WH2 was a more solid experience with less imbalance imo from what I remember), though the most content is in WH3.  Having over 1k hours in the first two games, I'm sticking with the third since it's got the most overall content and the more active portions of the modding community. Despite my gripes, I strongly recommend WH3 to anyone who enjoys strategy games, and if you enjoy Warhammer Fantasy... I assume you already own it, because you ought to.  On the DLC Pre-End Times: There's a lot. Yep. Looks horrible doesn't it? While I don't know everything about CA's business practices, they're owned by Sega, and Games Workshop requires a sacrifice in their name if you breathe near the IP too loudly, so I don't find it surprising. Look at gameplay footage of individual lords to figure out if their unique spin on things is worth your money. I think most (if not all) of them add some new units too, so that helps add some value to it. If you see 75% off, just get it unless you really don't think you'll ever play them.  On the End Times DLC: It's lots of fun, though Nagash and Thanquol got the lions share of cool stuff by a mile. Unfortunately its initial release is so buggy you'd think a different studio made it. I've gotten glitches like the Black Pyramid investment getting refunded and set to random numbers (it went to -20 for some reason and I never figured out how or why), quest battles starting on black screens and forcing me to restart the game, armies unable to move for a turn, lots of effects not actually applying in particular with the Black Pyramid, but with all the DLC lords. I am so f***ing tired of Total War's campaign design.  The Supply Lines mechanic has been around in some form since Rome II, and it still f***ing sucks. Playing an entire early and mid game where your economy basically forces you to survive with one or two armies is not interesting strategy. It is not meaningful decision-making. It is just restrictive and frustrating.  And province management is barely management at all.  For most factions, you have maybe two or three useful province templates. Once you understand what works, there is almost no reason to think about it anymore. You just repeat the same buildings everywhere, over and over again.  Provinces are basically giant tax bills that demand money from you every few turns.  Build this. Upgrade that. Repair this. Pay for another settlement upgrade. Pay to remove a Skaven infestation. Pay to remove Chaos corruption or whatever other campaign mechanic has appeared in your territory.  Meanwhile, because your economy is garbage, half your empire is still sitting there with Tier 1 income buildings because upgrading everything costs a fortune.  And why would you even invest heavily into those provinces?  You cannot reliably protect them anyway.  Your TWO F***ING ARMIES are fighting a war somewhere on the other side of your empire, while some random AI army walks through your territory playing f***ing whack-a-mole with your settlements.  This has been the Total War campaign loop since Rome II:  Spend the entire early and mid game with one or two mediocre armies.  Build the same province templates again and again.  Pay for the same boring upgrades again and again.  Then chase AI armies around your territory because they deliberately avoid your main forces and attack whatever settlement happens to be undefended.  I AM SO F***ING TIRED OF PLAYING WHACK-A-MOLE WITH THE AI.  And then we have GARRISONS.  LET US CUSTOMIZE OUR GARRISONS.  This problem has become even worse in Warhammer because magic and high-tier units can be insanely destructive, while our settlement garrisons are still filled with absolute garbage.  Tier 1 units.  No experience.  No upgrades.  No meaningful customization.  No real strategic choices.  Why can't I decide how I want to defend my own empire?  Let me spend more money on a settlement if I want to station stronger units there.  Let me decide whether a province is supposed to be an economic center, a recruitment hub, or an actual F***ING FORTRESS.  If I want to spend a ridiculous amount of money putting elite troops into an important border settlement, LET ME DO IT.  Instead, I can upgrade every settlement in a province to Tier 3, build defensive structures everywhere, and the garrison still f***ing sucks.  You build walls.  You build the garrison building.  You invest thousands into the settlement.  Then an enemy army arrives and wipes the entire place out in one turn anyway.  Great defensive strategy.  And WHY THE F*** DO WE HAVE TO PAY TO DESTROY SKAVEN NESTS OR CHAOS INFILTRATIONS?  This is Total War.  YOU HAVE A BATTLE SYSTEM.  Why couldn't these become small special battles, similar to quest battles or missions?  Give me an actual gameplay event.  Let me send troops into the tunnels.  Let me fight the Skaven hiding underneath the city.  Let me fight the Chaos cultists.  That could actually be fun.  But no.  Apparently the solution is:  "Pay 5,000 gold."  Amazing gameplay.  The fundamental problem is that Total War's campaign mechanics have barely evolved since Rome II.  The economy still restricts the player to too few armies for too much of the campaign.  Province management is repetitive.  Garrisons are terrible.  Defensive strategy is almost nonexistent.  And enemy armies constantly turn the campaign map into an exhausting game of whack-a-mole.  I DON'T WANT TO PLAY WHACK-A-MOLE ANYMORE.  I WANT TO SEE ENEMY ARMIES COMING.  I WANT BORDER DEFENSE TO MATTER.  I WANT TO DECIDE WHICH PARTS OF MY EMPIRE ARE HEAVILY FORTIFIED.  I WANT TO CHOOSE WHAT UNITS DEFEND MY SETTLEMENTS.  I WANT TO MAKE ACTUAL STRATEGIC DECISIONS ABOUT HOW I DEFEND MY F***ING EMPIRE.  Give us customizable garrisons.  Give us meaningful defensive infrastructure.  Give us more ways to maintain several armies without completely destroying the economy.  Turn infestations and cults into actual gameplay instead of another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ invoice.  LET US MAKE SOME ACTUAL DECISIONS.

The gameplay underneath is solid, but Creative Assembly has officially settled back into its favorite habit: testing how far they can squeeze a loyal player base before the dam breaks again. Following the massive backlash over Shadows of Change, management released solemn statements promising to rebuild trust, re-evaluate their monetization strategy, and listen to the community. That remorse lasted just long enough for the PR fire to die down. With Lords of the End Times, the total bundle price quietly creeps past $30—half the cost of a full standalone game for four lords and an asset pack.  Their concession is offering the factions à la carte for $9 apiece. It’s a neat bit of pricing theater designed to deflect review-bombing, but the broader math hasn't changed. They took Boris Todbringer—a character fans have asked to see fully realized since the first game launched nearly a decade ago—and parked him behind this paywall knowing full well that nostalgia and completionism would do the heavy lifting.  I don’t mind paying for good work, and the developers and artists clearly put effort into these models and rosters. But executive leadership views this community as an extractive asset rather than a customer base. They push prices until people revolt, take one step backward with a polished apology blog, wait twelve months, and then take two steps forward again.If you want to spend $30+ on a single DLC pack every release cycle, that’s your business. But don't mistake corporate amnesia for good faith. They learned nothing; they just learned how to slice the invoice differently.
