Honestly, Warhammer 2 is the better game. This beats it on scale and map size and number of factions, but Total War: Warhammer 2 is the tigher, objectively better balanced and optimised grand strategy game.  My play time has been limited but I feel like combat has regressed massively between the two games. Not just in terms of the noticeable lag between issuing orders and the unit actually doing anything, but in particular ranged units no longer work because of the awful new line of sight system. What has been a satisfying game mechanic for decades they've now changed, and not for the better.  Siege battles have gone from epic wall battles to tedius settlement building that is fine the first few times but quickly becomes incredibly repetitive. Compared to the old system, this is really horrible.  I can appreciate that they want to keep evolving the formula and trying new things but I don't really see the sense in changing core mechanics of the series when there was nothing wrong with the original systems - I'd rather they improved on the series' weak points: for example the (much improved) diplomacy system, or the shoddy AI. On the former they've actually managed some improvements, on the latter they've overcorrected to what I think may be one of the most ludicrously overaggressive AIs I've seen in any Total War game to date.  I held off on this review because I figured in the time since release they would have optimised and balanced the game to the point where it was as fun as its predecessor. More than 4 years later and while I'm wowed at the dizzying array of paid DLC - there are so many paid DLC factions, to the point where when I start a campaign I feel a bit like I'm playing the demo version of the game - I'm really disappointed by the lack of attention and focus paid to the core of the experience.  I would still recommend this game as they do get a lot right - the sheer scale of it, lore, the flavour and character of the factions, the visuals, the diplomacy system... this is a really professionally made game that stands on the shoulders of many grand campaign games before it. But for me, even now over 4 years after release... I still can't get into this one. For me, the fundamental sticking points have not been addressed at all, which is a huge shame.  This is is a "don't recommend" for me - not because it's a terrible game, because it isn't. Simply based on the fact that TW: Warhammer 2 is by some distance still the better game, and your hard-earned money would be far better spent on that.

The game definitely shines when it comes to assets. Unit designs and their animations range from imaginative to absolutely hilarious; voice and sound design are solid, and music is there too. A lot of thought and effort was invested in this, and clearly a lot of fun was had in the process. When it comes to the "game" part of the game... well... the gameplay consists of two parts. The "world map/strategic" part is a lobotomised version of "Heroes of Might and Magic" that pretends to be a lobotomised version of "Civilization". The smaller "real-time combat/tactical" part of the game with its physical projectiles reminds me of a lobotomised version of "Myth: Fallen Lords/Soulblighter". So it scratches, if poorly, both HMM and Myth itches that cannot be scratched by many modern games. And that is the best compliment I can give. The downsides of the game are multiple. • There is a huge number of factions to play, but don't be mistaken: the gameplay is very "wide", but not even remotely deep. All factions follow the same basic principle, with small faction-unique gimmicks thrown on top. Half of the gimmicks are useless, underdeveloped, obsolete or boring. Be it Repanse's "wasteland water supply" that is either unnecessary or does not work in most deserts; Mother Ostankia's hex crafting that is so poorly implemented interface-wise, it becomes a chore after tenth repetition; or whatever undercooked monstrosity the whole Changelling gameplay is. Etcetera, etcetera, etcetera. • The AI is bad. Bad politically, strategically and tactically. Like "gives you an obscene amount of gold and enters war against its ally in exchange for a useless settlement" bad. Like "will pay you forever to cyclically trade the same settlements for no reason" bad. Like "will send five armies across the continent and forget why, so they'll just graze around some field, while the capital burns" bad. Like "does not comprehend that to take a city one needs not only defeat the defenders, but also take the city" bad. Like "what is this 'unit cohesion' and 'tactics' things you are even talking about?" bad. Like "sieges are not just broken, but actually depressing to watch" bad. Like "squad got stuck in terrain and will not move again" bad. It is impossible to say that AI is "buggy", "cheesable" or "easily exploitable": bugs in this game are the only way of its operation and are indistinguishable from features. • The narrative is, well, basically non-existent. Which is bizarre, because Warhammer Fantasy/Old World has rich and deep lore with many interesting stories to tell. The game fails to tell any of them. The missions, campaign goals and victory conditions are grotesquely empty and unsatisfying. Considering that AI is too dumb to even role-play and properly pursue its lore-accurate goals, the narrative each campaign manages to present is as rich as the story mode of original Tetris. And there is no story mode in original Tetris. • The interface of the game is an abomination. Pages over pages of bloated lists and menus that somehow hide important data in even more submenus. Pop-up windows in the corners of the screen that do not attract players' attention but partially block controls until closed (I repeat: partially, not fully, and with no explanation, so when something stops working, most newbies don't understand why). Pathfinding previews that often fail to properly indicate the path your lords will actually follow, or if they will be able to reach the destination this turn at all. The assets that obscure critical objects and UI elements. The camera that falls in every decorative hole on the map or makes it impossible to click the terrain when placed on a hill. The unit figures that are often too small to distinguish or interact with without severely zooming in. Unit banners that do not have enough variations to distinguish units and are often obscured by everything from UI elements to tree shadows. I competitively played RTS games for decades, but I fundamentally cannot properly micro in this game. • Performance is meh, but "meh" in this case is unexpectedly high achievement.  So. Should you play this game? Yes, as long as you like Warhammer Fantasy, don't take the game too seriously and don't expect much from either gameplay or story. The game basically provides you with a set of great animated figurines and a jumble of mechanics, and leaves the rest of the game to your imagination and the modding community.  Should you buy this game, especially for the full price? Absolutely not. The game is basically a Chaos Dwarf project: owned by unrepentantly evil and greedy slave-drivers, and developed by their starved, questionably sapient greenskin slaves.

I actually forgot I ever bought this. The launch was a mess, I reckon I snagged it on sale. And. I hate to admit it, but I'm still pretty disappointed with the game overall. It's not buggy (at least, not as far as I can tell); and it runs pretty decent on my 3080 (even if it does sound like a jet engine taking off), it's just...  I'd consider myself a Total War veteran - I've been playing since the original Mediaeval days. Yep, the clunky one. And it's been interesting to see the direction that Total War has taken these past two decades, it really has - Warhammer seemed like a no brainer. Each time, I've bought into the idea behind the mythos, and I've given them a good go. Each time, however, I've found that some areas of the game have been oversimplified (since Rome II, everything's been a bit downhill in this respect), others have become overcomplicated. Like, there are SO many different units for Chaos that it can become a bit too much.  Still, however, I see many of the old problems haven't been resolved. AI being able to field multiple armies without their economies crashing being the primary problem. The overall unevenness to battling on the field (like, some armies just feel downright indestructible to play against). And maybe I'm just not that good at the game, even on Normal.  That raises the final problem I have. This is really 'half' a game. The prologue is a bare-bones, on-rails teaser for a faction you still need to purchase as optional DLC. The Immortal Empires campaign has the same problem - half the factions are locked behind paywalls. And that's just about all the game really has to offer.  I think what's happened is, Total War have made things a mile wide, but inches deeper in terms of gameplay. I wonder if they'll be able to strike that balance again with the upcoming 40k universe (it'd be nice to see a mash-up of space and land battles, perhaps smaller sized squad fights). That's another kettle of fish altogether. But if you're thinking of dropping full price on THIS particular bad boy, I feel like you're not going to get much out of the experience if you've already played Warhammer 1 and 2.

I have very mixed feelings about Battlefield 6. I'm still trying to understand how a game with gunplay this fun could end up like this. Underneath the constant reshuffling and identity crisis, there is a genuinely good FPS. Early on, it even looked like Battlefield might pull off something difficult: bring fast-paced FPS players and the traditional large-scale Battlefield crowd into the same game. Almost a year later, they seem to have managed to piss off both. That's quite an achievement. For context, I'm not a traditional Battlefield player. I'm an objective-focused, infantry-oriented FPS player, and I fundamentally dislike the asymmetry vehicles introduce. There is something uniquely Battlefield about winning several gunfights, carefully pushing an objective, and then being reminded by a tank 200 metres away that your tactical mistake was apparently being born with skin and having only stones to return. But that's fine. For years, my conclusion was simply: “Battlefield isn't for me.” Then I played the beta and had an absolute blast. In retrospect, someone like me having this much fun in a Battlefield game should probably have been the first warning sign. Instead, I did something regrettable: I gave EA 70€.  And in return, Battlefield 6 greets me with all the elegance of the modern live-service storefront: battle passes, bundles, weapon packs, notifications and flashing rectangles begging to be clicked. Sometimes it feels like there are more ways to buy things than ways to play the game. Which makes what followed even stranger. Almost a year later, Rush isn't something I can simply expect to find as a permanent official playlist. Modes rotate, experiences come and go, and Breakthrough increasingly puts vehicles front and centre on several layouts. Why? You already made modes for players like me. They existed, they worked, and they helped convince me to buy the game. So why make them increasingly inconsistent to access? Maybe players like me simply weren't the priority. Maybe Battlefield needed to return to its roots and focus on the people who actually love Battlefield. Fair enough. I'm the tourist here. If sacrificing some of what attracted me meant making Battlefield better for Battlefield players, fine. So at least the traditional Battlefield players must be happy now... right? Oh. Apparently not. While infantry players complain about vehicles becoming oppressive in certain objective modes, traditional players complain about Conquest maps too constrained for 64 players, restrictive combat areas, limited flanking and vehicles squeezed into spaces that barely let them behave like vehicles. Infantry players ask “Why am I constantly fighting vehicles?” while vehicle players ask “Why are these maps so hostile to vehicles?” Rush players wonder where their permanent playlist went. Conquest players wonder where the scale went. Who exactly was all of this for? Battlefield doesn't need one magical compromise where infantry players learn to love tanks and vehicle players learn to love corridors. That's what modes are for. Give infantry players room for infantry combat and combined-arms players room for combined arms. Give Conquest players Conquest. Give Rush players Rush. Not every part of Battlefield needs to appeal to everyone; it just needs to stop taking away the parts that already appeal to them. And that's where the grotesque live-service interface becomes harder to laugh at. Battlefield 6 seems remarkably uncertain about what it wants players to play: which modes stay, which rotate, how large Battlefield should be, how dominant vehicles should be. Yet one part of the game never seems to suffer from this identity crisis: the store knows exactly what it is. Modes rotate, playlists disappear, the game's identity oscillates, but don't worry, there will always be something to buy. That's what makes Battlefield 6 such a waste. Not that it's a terrible game, but that the pieces of a great one were always there. Battlefield didn't need to choose between Call of Duty and Battlefield. I genuinely thought it could found a way to be both. Somehow, it ended up being neither. Almost a year later, it still doesn't seem entirely sure what it wants its players to play. It just seems remarkably confident that it wants players to keep paying while it figures it out.

This game should have been amazing, this game should have been the greatest FPS of the decade. I should have been playing this game every week since launch, instead I got bored after a month of desperately trying to like the game and hoping the devs would fix the issues within its first month of release.  I came back to this game recently, thinking surely they would have fixed the bugs that plagued it early on, surely they would have added far larger maps with better flow and balancing, surely they would have fixed TOWs, reblanced classes with weapon locks and reworked the Squad system to make working with your squad as important as it has always been in Battlefield.  Instead, I felt like I was playing the game at launch again, only this time there were neon soldiers running around and I was getting crack-shotted by people with ADHD. I jumped in a tank which still had my old TOW setup and got about 20 player kills and multiple aircraft kills on my second game in.  They never fixed anything, the maps are still tiny, the flow still feels like COD, squads are still pointless and classes can chose any weapon they want, making them completely pointless. Oh and TOWs are still OP.  If you liked modern COD, you will enjoy Battlefield 6, and I wont take that away from you. But if you enjoyed the old Battlefield games of 4, 1 & 5, you will not enjoy BF6. EA has milked this franchise dry, the menu is a horrific mess trying to get you to buy Season Passes, skins and bundles. Classes are pointless, maps are either too small or too big with no flow, New York is pretty much every second game. Games are just constent firefights with enemies seemingly appearing everywhere and no chance to rest, regroup and push with your team, and speaking of team, you don't feel as though you are part of a team in the traditional Battlefield sense, you feel as though you are playing a COD game and all you care about is kills & K/D, not actually capturing objectives to win the match. In Battlefield 6, the match isn't about the teams performance, it is about YOUR performance. It honestly feels like the only reason they still have a Squad System in place is because the fans would get upset if it were removed entirely, despite the fact it wouldn't change the game at all.  Maybe the next game will be better, I doubt it. All I know is that I have completely lost faith in DICE. This isn't a battlefield game, it's a COD game with vehicles and slightly bigger maps. You may enjoy it but I certainly don't.

TL;DR - the game is very repetitive; it doesn't have interesting gameplay variety and it's designed around killing your character soon, so there's not much content after the first few in-game days. I am not a fan of "there's a mod to fix X". If the game were good, I wouldn't need to keep tinkering what mods I need to fix my problems with it.   Project zomboid's design is based on quick permadeath loops, with complicated systems that will increase the likelihood you'll die for something silly, like getting a scratch for not checking if your shoes are still wearable or getting too slim and dying from not eating enough calories to keep your weight (which is different from dying from hunger, yes.)   This design hides a major problem that the game has - if you learn how to survive past the first few hours/days, you'll realize there's not much to do. No NPCs, no quests, no factions, no progression that unlocks gameplay variety. There's nothing. It's just an endless grind loop to increase some stats so you can live forever, like farming, carpentry or fishing. And they don't really offer new gameplay.   Combat, for example, is really repetitive: lure a few zombies out from the pack, push the zombies to make them fall, stomp their heads, repeat. If you can, camp behind a fence so they fall down when climbing it and you stomp them faster. Guns are useless cause the ammo is very scarce and you'll attract way too many brain eaters to your position. It's a death sentence most of the time. And by the time you have good guns and skills, you'll already be bored to death anyway. Cars get destroyed instantly if zombies hit them (in case you find one that is semi working and has some fuel), so no use. Molotovs are far in between. Melee weapons have no variety and break very easily, so it's best to just push and stomp. In the end, you're always doing the same stuff. Stomp stomp stomp. Even Mario would get tired of so much stomping.   I think this design problem comes from the fact most of the dev time was spent on making complicated independent systems to kill your character in the first hours. I think if those were simplified and we got more dynamic gameplay loops, this game could be really good. But as of it right now, the "fun" in this game, in theory, is seeing how your character died in a stupid way and restarting. It's a sandbox game that really doesn't make me want to go back to it.   If you do survive, best case scenario, you'll get an autonomous farm going. Sure, you can spend time on the farming mechanics in this game, but you might as well play a farming simulator. You won't have to restart your farm every time you forgot to check for something. Here, it's a very tedious grind based on RNGs - did I find the book fishing 1 and fishing 2? no? oh so now you'll have to spend hours and hours grinding because you can't get xp fast enough.   A lot of people recommend innumerous mods to fix X, Y or Z problem with the game. Instead of spending my time to try to fix the game with X, Y or Z mods, I would prefer just finding a game I can plug and enjoy with less frustrations.  I can't comment on multiplayer. I ain't got time for it, but the YouTube videos seem fun.

I tried numerous times to enjoy this game on different occasions. I understand the sentiment of "the game gets better the more you play it!" and "it has a huge learning curve" and that the game itself is meant to be difficult more than anyone, I've tried to enjoy it so many times with so many people. I just  can't.  Despite how it looks, if you play the game long enough, you will eventually begin to fall in love with the Sims 1 graphics. For me, personally, I felt like the developers had crafted a genuinely amazing world with such detailed scenery. The amount of times where I'd just read a skill book whilst being in a vehicle (which, might I add, for some reason takes an absurd amount of time unless you change it within the sandbox settings) and my friend is driving through towns and roads, and I can just admire the attention to detail for an apocalyptic world they've created. However, as great as this is, most locations within this game are redundant. Most locations within the world have loot which isn't of interest, and more or less is just junk you can find or "collect" for the (numerous) crafting systems to interact with later on in your playthrough. I felt like I was hoarding a bunch of useless things, telling myself over and over that eventually they will become useful (they never did).  This resorted to me and my friend/s looking at the interactive map online to see where the "major loot" hotspots were, since the community is very expressive about where these locations are.   Considering how expansive this map is, it makes no sense to me that you unlock the map throughout playing. You either have to be lucky and survive an entire playthrough (until you get bored) by unlocking each location on the map, or you have to die repeatedly in different locations to unlock it. It baffles me that the map isn't fully unlocked. However, like most things within this game, this can easily be fixed with mods or changes to the settings. The vanilla game itself is such a slog IMO, that outside of the unnecessary grind, you are faced with so many difficulties that mods cannot fix. For us, we had to the mod the game to the point where there was so much QoL, that my friend felt like he was a member of the developer team. The fact that some very basic things, such as ladders not being climbable, are not in the base vanilla game is slightly concerning to me.   The game itself revolves around a "sort-of" permadeath loop, which is fine, but it often means you could spend months and months alive, only to then die to a tiny cut on your hand because you didn't bring enough medical supplies with you. This is fine, and I have no issues with permadeath games, in fact I actually love them, but it becomes an issue when your character has to relearn the hours of progress in order to be able to do certain actions. The progression loop in this game is not fun to repeat at all. It also becomes an issue when, despite picking what area of the map you want to spawn in, you still spawn in the middle of nowhere and are completely isolated from everything. You then have to pick a random road (unless you're lucky enough to have the map fully unlocked without a setting change or mod) and follow it, hoping that it leads somewhere useful but more often than not you'll end up wasting real-world time walking through a desolate road with about 4 or 5 zombies on the entire trip which is incredibly boring. But hey, at least you'll find an old 2 CDs, a magazine and some lipstick in one of the run down cars along the way.  The driving in this game is.. interesting. There is a reason why I'm banned from driving, and that is because it is a buggy mess. For some reason, whenever I'm behind the wheel, if the car itself clips any solid object, whether that's a tree or a building or a fence, the car (and trailer) will be launched so far from our original destination that we will have no clue where we are, and we will be at near-death. To make it worse, the car itself will be damaged beyond repair, meaning we then need to ditch it. If I'm the designated passenger princess, then I am sat idly watching the terrain go by whilst my character reads the 90th skill book, only for our car to randomly be damaged to the point that it is inoperable.   The progression in this game is relatively boring. You essentially dismantle everything in sight with a specific tool to increase your level in said skill. Only then can you actually do the enjoyable elements of the game. 5 minutes later you will die in a zombie interaction and lose all of your progress by the way.  The combat in the game is not enjoyable. It's weird and clunky, and you essentially "S hold" (or just walk backwards) from the zombies until you're at a range where you can attack them. If they're at a close range, you may as well just let them kill you, because your character can do numerous 180's or even 360's whilst your mouse is aimed at the zombie. For some reason, the combat in this game is horrendous up close. If you fail to push a zombie over, you'll end up with your back to it and then it's essentially game over, or you have a wound that lasts several sessions of gaming.   I could honestly rant and ramble about this game for ages. On paper, it's great, if you can ignore the graphics, and the ridiculous amount of bugs, but on a deeper level I feel like this is less of a survival game and more of a "apocalypse scenario simulation".. I love difficult games, especially permadeath ones, but the uninteresting gameplay loop is very off putting. It's infuriating losing your character to something so meaningless, or the car decides to evaporate into the sky, or even the combat just messing up on you.   I'll continue to play the game, probably, and if it gets to a point where I do enjoy it, I'll change my review but for now I just could not recommend this.

This game is a 16-year-old piece of software that still somehow runs better than half the modern live-service slop being released today. Congrats, Valve. Your ancient zombie shooting gallery from the Obama administration still hits harder than most $70 “AAA experiences.” The AI Director will either drown you in a tidal wave of Special Infected the second you dare to breathe near a safe room, or it will fall asleep and leave you wandering empty streets like a lonely sad bastard for ten minutes. The Specials still have the pathfinding intelligence of a concussed raccoon. Smokers will drag you through walls. Chargers will yeet you into the void. Jockeys will ride you like you’re their personal mechanical bull while your teammates watch and laugh. And the Tank? The Tank will clip through geometry, no-scope you from three maps away, and then despawn out of pure spite. Versus mode is a gladiatorial arena of pure toxicity where half the lobby is cheating, the other half is throwing, and everyone is screaming racial slurs in voice chat. It’s beautiful. Yet here I am. 121 hours later. Still loading up this dusty old relic every time I want to feel something. Because when the chaos clicks—when your team is coordinated, the Director is on one, and you’re screaming while a Tank is chasing you through a burning building with a chainsaw—nothing else comes close. It’s janky. It’s old. It’s held together with duct tape and Valve’s pure refusal to let it die. And I still love it. 10/10 would get charged into a wall by a 500-pound zombie again.

Hate to say it, but I don't "get" TF2. If people lose their mind about the great feel of CSGO/CS2, TF2 is the polar opposite.  This never really was for me. I tried to get into it and I think I might just be too... young, or too late to the PC gaming scene to really get the appeal of TF2. I always felt like the recipe was better executed by other games, but I'm also not really one for "goofy pvp games."

Pro's:  So to begin I'd like to say that this game is not inherently BAD. I found that TF2 is a brilliant game for those who want a casual and positive gaming experience, you'll never find someone in a TF2 lobby that does not want to be there and you will most certainly never get ripped in on for ANYTHING. It's a refreshing environment for a shooter to have a community that wont be inclined to call you are slur for a minor mistake. TF2 is also a nice place to make friends, a goldmine if your into internet trolling and meme culture. You'll never get stressed out on TF2, frankly I don't think anyone takes the game seriously enough to.  Con's:  This game is FAR FAR FAR from a "competitive" game in my opinion. Strictly focusing on the gameplay, majority of characters felt totally pointless to pick up, like it became very clear very quickly to me who was a useless pick and who was going to bring some kind of support to my team. Frankly, I don't enjoy the fact that if I shoot someone point blank in the face with a rocket launcher or a shotgun, they can survive or even kill me one nano-second later. The selling point of this game very much seems to be on the side of funny = good, which makes it enjoyable for those who are not particularly the most adept at games that are competitive by nature.  This is strictly my opinion on the game, hope it was insightful.

This is a social game, which means your enjoyment very much depends on the people in the worlds you go to (outside of portal worlds like Portal fishing or Portal library), most worlds are based on you finding people to talk to and to have fun with, which for the socially anxious or socially less skilled, this is daunting, but remember; if someone is playing this game, they opened it, they're probably in a similar boat to you, and if they do mind you talking to them, they shouldn't have went into an instance with other people in the first place, you have the right to talk to others, and they probably want to talk to you. Conversely, socializing is hard, because it requires you to be in the right world, in the right instance, find the right person amongst(?) as compared to the wrong people who you wouldn't vibe with, at the right time for the right person, and at the same time as them. This is to say: Socializing isn't a science, and hoping for anything about a 4/10 socializing success rate, is beyond ambitious, understand it is a bit of a numbers game, hell, if you have a 1/10 success rate, that means that every 10 times you try you succeed, which is already good.  VRChat socializing does have some stuff I had to learn the harder way, which is: Go to an avatar world, and choose a normal avatar, I made the mistake of choosing a *meme* avatar, which no one wanted to talk to me, and only later did I realize, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ avatar like that is associated with people that yell slurs like it's a concert, so make sure to choose an avatar that isn't a meme avatar, avatar doesn't matter that much, but the wrong avatar does, so just have a more sensible/normal set of avatars (and try to get ones that have good performance ratings if you can; other people's systems are going to have to render your avatar, so don't bog their FPS if you can), I'm not saying you can never have meme avatars, but you just need to establish yourself as not a troll.  World choice is the second biggest thing, worlds I would say are the best for this is: Fish! Combat likely won't challenge most people due to the extreme amounts of XP the game grants unless you elect to fight the bosses again on Hard/Ultra Mode. Aside from that, the game is a power fantasy sandbox where you build bases and catch pals to run them while exploring the world to make numbers go up.

Pallworld is... not a great game, it's a sandbox you can make some of your own fun in, but it's systems are a bit limited and lacking. If you just want to randomly catch some pals for a hundred plus hours, ok... if you want a game with real depth, quality combat, interesting mechanics that require thought in the moment, and good challenges though, you'll be disapointed.  At it's core, the pacing and polish is just really lacking. You start off for the first hour or two ok, level 1, slowly growing your pals and base, but after that first bit, you quickly find yourself in the situation of either over leveling, or under leveling everything. From then till the very end of the game, you will find 90% of your encounters end in one or two attacks, not even really fights, or will end you in one or two attacks and probably require a hundred plus to bring down. The number of times there is a fight that feels like it's not auto win, or auto lose... is very rare, and the ones then that have any mechanical depth to learn the enemy moves and counter are fairly few.  Also for having all those pals, there's not much difference, the vast majority are fights that end up as I fly over towards them, launch one attack, and if I have mercy ring on then I toss a ball and start trying to catch them, possibly over many attempts, and if I don't, they just died in that one hit. Honestly, the combat side never felt that interesting, and pal hunting, while ok, also got very repetitive after doing it 1k plus times, it never really changed much.   Then there's the base building and resource managment. You'll spend a lot of time manually going around and farming/mining/killing for various materials, the bases wont fully cover everything, especially since it constantly has new materials that completely replace all the previous things you are upgrading for. This gets very repetitive... I personally wouldn't care about most of these either, you rapidly far outlevel what you can actually build, easily being ten levels higher than you need to unlock all the key parts for a new material and its infrastructure buildings... yet you haven't even entered that area, I've at multiple points unlocked and had two plus levels of full tech over what I was actually using as I didn't want to just skip exploring parts of the map in their entirety. I tried lowering the XP multiplier, it helped at the early/mid game, but late game gets so grindy on resources for just your needed pal spheres and it wasn't like it was enjoyable that it wasn't worth slowing it down anyway. In the end, base building wasn't the most enjoyable, base management wasn't the best feeling, and while there's enough it's interesting at first, not nearly enough to keep it good for the entire play session.  My overall thoughts are, largley a waste of time that I only pushed through because I don't like leaving games part way through. If you have friends to play in multi, like all things it'll be funner, though for many there'll be other games you'd probably prefer over it so... meh. It's probably most enjoyable in the first ten to twenty hours, beyond that, it just turns into a giant grind, and oh god does it keep going. As a result... while I don't want to say it's bad... given the price, honestly it is for most people probably a waste of their time. This has way more in common with a "base building" level-up mobile or Facebook game than one with meaningful content and challenges supported by "progression" (rather than the other way around).    There's tons of padding, virtually nonexistent narrative/lore drip feed, arbitrary scaling or damage formula, quests that give dubious rewards (like an MMO), or even expire in the case of food (yes you can get a "freezer" later, lots of hoops to possibly address obstacles--not challenges--the devs put in). So many "mechanics" in the game become pointless and trivialized an hour into the game, such as hunger.   Others continue to be nuisances like inventory weight for mining ore, needed to build the buildings to automate mining ore to unlock the next level of ore and ingots which you must make manually until you build the things that let you automate the next level of ore and ingots. Rinse repeat. This is not a content loop for any self-respecting human's time and efforts. All enemies/bosses are just damage sponges that you grind to deal a "reasonable" amount of damage to. Level 40+ and no boss or battle was anything beyond a statcheck and timecheck. Endgame doesn't seem worth it.   The above made it go from a good game to a very mid game but not worth writing a bad review about. The following did that:  Co-op is pointless if one person plays even a few hours more than the other and the level scaling makes them do 10x the damage of the other where one either one-shots the enemies or the other does "why am I wasting my time on this alt+f4" damage.   Devs made the co-op in this game fit the category of "hey everyone let's all play our own single player game but occasionally bump into each other to feel that spotlight on our egos, share our tales and conquests (which obviously cannot be unique or even RNG'd)."  Conclusion: It's probably an entertaining game for anyone under age 20--because the average quality of games being released these days is abominable--or for who really miss the nostalgia and enjoy "building stuff" for the sake of building stuff. Not recommended for anyone who has "expectations" for a game, budget notwithstanding.

If you are reading this, then you probably already know the positives of Baldur’s Gate 3: freedom of choice, great voice acting, strong quest design, memorable companions, and the ridiculous amount of ways you can solve problems. I'm not going to sit here and pretend those things are not impressive, because they are.  But because those parts have already been praised to death, I want to focus on what, in my opinion, makes the game overrated.  Baldur’s Gate 3 is clearly a good game, but I don’t think it is the flawless masterpiece people make it out to be. To me, it is also bloated, clunky, awkward, weirdly horny, and surprisingly weak when it comes to the feeling of progression. I will address each of those in the following sections.  [h2]Weak Progression[/h2]  One of my biggest problems with BG3 is progression. For such a huge RPG, I rarely felt genuinely excited about my character becoming stronger.  The story moves forward, the stakes get bigger, and the locations become more dramatic, but my actual character build often felt weirdly static. Gear progression especially felt underwhelming. It is very possible to find strong equipment in Act 1 and keep using it through Act 2 and even into Act 3.  I understand that this is probably good for balance, as it avoids the usual RPG problem where every item becomes useless after two hours. But from a player perspective, it can feel boring. You defeat major enemies, explore dangerous areas, open some impressive-looking chest, and then the reward is something you instantly send to camp because your old gear is still better.  I mean there is clearly something wrong when I'm deep into Act 3 and still wearing gear from Act 1 without feeling much reason to replace it. Loot should be exciting. I should look at a new weapon, armour piece, ring, or cloak and think, "Oh, this changes my build." But too often in BG3, loot just feels like mildly interesting clutter.  [h2]Underwhelming Level-Ups[/h2]  Leveling up has a similar problem. Because BG3 follows Dungeons & Dragons 5e, progression is more restrained. Yeah, I get that it is faithful to the tabletop rules. But as a video game RPG, it can feel really underwhelming. There is no proper skill tree, no big long-term upgrade path, and not many future unlocks that made me excited.  Some classes get fun powers, but plenty of level-ups feel minor. You get one spell, a passive, a feat, or some practical option that feels fine but not exciting. Many of the coolest choices can be taken early, and after that you often just pick whatever is left or whatever seems vaguely fitting.  A skill tree would have helped. Not some bloated mess with 300 meaningless icons, but something that gives a stronger sense of direction. Something that lets you look ahead and think, “Oh wow! I cannot wait to unlock that!” In BG3, I often didn't feel like I was building towards some powerful fantasy version of my character. I felt like I was just selecting from a small menu of practical options.  [h2]Combat: Great Ideas, Clunky Execution[/h2]  Combat is a mixed bag for me. When it works, it can be genuinely great. Positioning matters, height matters, surfaces matter, spells matter, and the environment can completely change a fight. You can push enemies off ledges, block routes, set traps, summon creatures, buff allies, debuff enemies, and turn the battlefield into complete chaos.  But when combat does not work, it becomes slow and clunky. The camera is often terrible, especially in multi-level areas. Trying to click the right enemy, floor tile, ledge, ladder, or doorway can feel harder than the actual fight.  Pathfinding can also be stupid. Characters walk through fire, acid, traps, or other hazards like they are trying to speedrun natural selection. You finish a fight, relax for half a second, and then someone casually strolls through burning ground because why the hell not.  The hit chance system can also feel awful. I know missing high-chance attacks is part of D&D. But that does not mean it always feels good in a video game. Nothing kills the heroic fantasy faster than watching your trained warrior miss a point-blank attack while some goblin with the posture of a wet sock crits you from across the room.  [h2]Inventory Management: Fantasy Warehouse Simulator[/h2]  Then there is the inventory system, and oh boy, it honestly deserves its own prison sentence.  By mid-game, your bags are full of scrolls, potions, arrows, keys, books, notes, quest items, food, rings, amulets, dyes, tools, random bones, and 46 pieces of equipment you are keeping "just in case." Managing all of it becomes a chore.  The game gives you so many items, but sorting through them is tedious. You constantly move things between characters, send things to camp, compare gear, check whether some random note still matters, and try to remember which companion has the potion you need.  Somewhere in your backpack there is probably a useful item. Good luck finding it.  [h2]Act 3: Too Much of Everything[/h2]  The pacing also becomes a problem, especially in Act 3. Act 1 is strong because it has mystery, danger, discovery, and a good balance between freedom and direction. Act 2 has a strong atmosphere and feels more focused. But Act 3 is where the game starts drowning in its own ambition.  The city is impressive, don't get me wrong. There is a lot to do. But sometimes there is just too much. Every building has secrets. Every NPC has a problem. Every street corner threatens to become a side quest. You can’t walk 20 metres without someone asking you to solve a murder, uncover a conspiracy, rescue someone, investigate a basement, enter a portal, or confront a god.   The amount of content is impressive, sure, but this density hurts the pacing.  [h2]Romance Writing: Too Fast, Too Easy, Too Awkward[/h2]  The romance writing is another big issue for me.  The issue is not just that the companions are bisexual. That alone I can survive. The problem is that nearly every companion feels player-sexual in the same way. Instead of feeling like complex adults with different preferences, boundaries, and emotional pacing, the party often feels like they all joined the same fantasy dating app and instantly matched with the player.  You meet these people, survive a few fights, avoid being completely evil, and suddenly half the camp starts acting like you are the most desirable person in Faerûn. Ridiculous.  The romance feels too easy and too fast. It does not feel like trust is properly earned. It feels like romance unlocks because you picked enough polite dialogue options. I even had scenes that felt weirdly romantic when I was not trying to romance that character at all. I was just choosing normal polite or supportive options, but the game seemed to assume I was interested.  The silent protagonist makes it even more awkward. A companion pours their heart out, becomes vulnerable, or expresses attraction, and your character mostly communicates through silent staring and vague hand gestures. Instead of two people building chemistry, it can feel like one fully acted character falling in love with a mute wax figure.  [h2]Conclusion[/h2]  That is why I cannot see Baldur’s Gate 3 as the flawless masterpiece people make it out to be. It is ambitious, reactive, and impressive, but also bloated, clunky, awkwardly paced, and surprisingly weak as a progression-based RPG.  I respect the game a lot, and I understand why people love it. But for me, the weak progression, messy Act 3 pacing, clunky combat moments, silent protagonist, and weirdly rushed romance writing hold it back too much.

The best save-scumming simulator since Pathfinder: Kingmaker.  Baldur's Gate 3 looks fantastic and has all the ingredients of a great RPG: an excellent story, incredible voice acting, cinematic scenes, interesting classes, and plenty of quests. Unfortunately, the dice-based gameplay completely kills the experience for me.  So much of what you do comes down to dice rolls that even characters who are supposed to be good at something can constantly fail at it. What's the point of making a decision or building a character around certain strengths when the game can just decide that your character is suddenly incompetent?  Pros:  - Great story, graphics, and cinematic scenes that make you want to keep playing. Probably the best voice acting I've ever heard in a game. - Extensive and interesting class and character building. - Lots of well-designed and memorable quests. - The game encourages multiple playthroughs if you want to see everything. - The amount of choices and possible outcomes is genuinely impressive.  Cons:  -The heavy reliance on dice rolls can make your character choices feel meaningless. Even with a high chance of success, you can still fail at something that should be routine. -The constant failed rolls can turn serious situations into a comedy show. At some point you could put circus music under almost every encounter and it would fit. -Some characters and dialogue feel more like edgy teenagers than actual adults, which can really hurt the immersion for me. -The constant save-scumming becomes almost mandatory if you don't want important situations decided by an unlucky roll. This reminds me a lot of Pathfinder: Kingmaker. -Loading saves repeatedly gets especially annoying when you already know that a failed roll was the only reason something went wrong.  Overall:  I understand why so many people consider Baldur's Gate 3 one of the best RPGs ever made. The production quality, voice acting, visuals, story, and character building are absolutely top-tier.  But personally, the dice system ruins too much of it for me. I prefer RPGs where character progression actually makes you reliably good at something. If my character has the skills for a task, I want that to matter instead of constantly watching him trip over his own feet because the game rolled a 1.  For me, Dragon Age: Origins and Dragon Age II are still much closer to what I want from an RPG. Baldur's Gate 3 is incredibly well-made, but the core gameplay philosophy simply isn't for me.

Baldur’s Gate 3 - Overwhelmingly Tedious and Boring  I genuinely tried. Seven hours in, multiple sessions. Somewhere around the middle I had a tiny moment of “okay, maybe I’m starting to see it”- that lasted about five minutes. This is one of the most boring games I have ever played.  BG3 feels like taking every slow, fiddly, overcomplicated part of tabletop RPGs and turning it into a video game - then making every single action take three business days. An Indian drama...  The introduction is atrocious. You are dumped into a wall of classes, races, abilities, resources, dice rolls, actions, bonus actions, movement, spell slots, concentration, inventory, companions and unexplained mechanics with barely any useful explanation. Character creation somehow manages to be both absurdly detailed in places and bizarrely restrictive in others. I spent more time fighting the character creator than creating a character. I eventually made a Wood Half-Elf Ranger because “stealth sniper -> get spotted -> RAAAAAGH” is basically my natural playstyle, but the game certainly didn't make understanding my choices easy.  Then there is the actual gameplay.  Combat is an RNG simulator where my greatest enemy is apparently the number 1. Miss. Miss. Miss. Critical Miss. Miss. Miss.  Congratulations, you have successfully spent several minutes positioning your character so that a dice roll can tell you to go f*** yourself.  And the damage progression? Incredible. Hour 1: 1–9 damage Hour 7: 4-11 damage Absolutely revolutionary.  The combat is painfully slow. Every movement point matters, every action takes ages, enemies take their turns one by one, animations drag on... Pathfinding is janky and a single misclick can send your character climbing some invisible wall or walking somewhere you absolutely did not intend. I have played games with clunky controls before, but BG3 somehow makes most games' control schemes look like divine intervention.  Exploration isn't any better. You click on a ladder: “You can't go there.” Click again: suddenly you can. Click beside a doorway: your character attempts to scale the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Himalayas. Try to scout around a corner: congratulations, you've been teleported into combat. I repeatedly felt like I was fighting the interface rather than the enemies.   The world itself has not grabbed me either. I explored the Grove, picked up a pile of vaguely described errands that they call quests, fought some goblins, got annihilated by an owlbear, got blown up by a statue, stumbled into fights I wasn't prepared for. Spent half my time rummaging through containers for mediocre garbage. The game constantly tries to give the impression that there is supposed to be something fascinating around the next corner, only for the reward to be another conversation, box of junk or fight.  The loot is particularly underwhelming. Forget about finding cool gear and becoming noticeably stronger.  You get another item with slightly different numbers, same ugly piece of armor, pile of useless arrows and another 20 minute inventory-management session.  And yes, I understand that the game is about player choice and role-playing rather than conventional power progression. That doesn't make the gameplay engaging.  The story, after seven hours, is essentially: YOU HAVE A PARASITE. FIX THE PARASITE.  FIX THE PARASITE. FIX THE PARASITE.  I KNOW. I HAVE BEEN TOLD. PLEASE STOP BEING A BROKEN RECORD.  The characters haven't done anything for me either. The voice acting is generally good but great performances cannot make characters interesting if I don't care about what they're saying. Shadowheart is probably the closest I've gotten to actually liking a companion. Still not enough. Astarion is entertaining to listen to but insufferable. Lae'zel is an aggressive noseless ♥♥♥♥♥, any line coming out of her makes me physically cringe and want to put my hands on somebody (the writer or smth...). Gale is a parasitic f*** who has 3 moves, then becomes utterly useless until you go rest. And the whole party has so far felt more like a collection of personalities I am managing than people I actually want to travel with.  The romance system also feels hilariously prominent for a game that otherwise tries to take itself so seriously. Apparently everyone is horny enough to jump you after approximately three conversations. Fantastic. I'm sure this has nothing to do with the soulless gooners that actually LARP sh** like this.  The music is underwhelming at best. It's competent but repetitive and generic compared with games whose soundtracks actually stick in my head. I ended up wanting to turn it off, replace it with actual good OSTs, like The Witcher's or Lies of P's...  And then there's the technical side.  The graphics look MEDIOCRE for a 2023 game, yet the performance is absurd. My PC gets hotter running this heap of trash than Cyberpunk 2077 on max settings with Ray Tracing. It's artificially big and visually inconsistent. Manages to make my hardware work overtime while I stare at two people standing in a room talking about a spermatozoid...  The funniest part is that I can understand why people like the freedom. BG3 clearly allows variying approaches to situations. That's the only place I can really see effort put in. But for me, that is not enough. I need the actual GAMEPLAY to be fun. Not "options to potentially make gameplay exist are vast"... Empty theatre room.   This feels less like an adventure and more like administrative work with dice. Pick up item. Miss item. Open door. Miss door. Walk somewhere. Accidentally climb something. Sort inventory. 9/10 I was not entirely convinced at first but upon learning the game, this has got to be the best battle royale ever made. Picture Sekiro-like combat on a set of different battle royale maps with a lot of characters, each having their own (gimmickey) set of abilities and playstyles that you can choose.  It's melee favored, because ranged weapons are mainly used to poke the enemy before engaging or to catch them from escaping. Tare limited to durability and that takes time to replenish amidst the fight and to collect beforehand, upon other things that you will loot during the match. But that's of course not everything in the game.  The combat is really high quality and despite what noobs might want you to believe; button mashing will quite literally get you owned. There is an increidbly in depth attack system full of combos, for every single weapon that can dictate your entire playstyle or approach to combat and a set of souljades that go from neat stacking buffs to literal alterations that enhance your current weapon attacks.  There are some annoying and spammy ultimate abilities, however they can only  be used once per fight and most of them leave you unable to chase, which makes securing kills pretty hard, as the movement in this game is probably the most important part.  Whatever can't catch you, can't fight you. And whatever can't fight you, can't kill you. With that being said, when starting out freshly, there certainly should be a lot of players that will be able to defeat you, since that is how niche competetive games work. With not enough casuals the sweats start cannibalizing eachother and thats not even neccessarily a bad thing, but as a new player with an unrecognized MMR you will mostly fight against bots in the beginning until the game starts dropping in real opponents, Even if I know that the guy that chased me down through the whole match will probably end me, I can at least start learning his attack pattern, like with some Sekiro boss. Or maybe I could just sneak away and let him take out his wrath on some other unfortunate souls. That kind of experience is entirely unique to Naraka.  The game is completely Free to Play and everything I describe in the following segment are purely optional cosmetics that do not alter the mechanical gameplay. The in-game store is detailed and if you don't find luck with mostly free lootcrates that have an unmissable chance system, should you get unlucky enough, You could also purchase some cosmetics directly from the store for mostly real money. However, the game to me seems quite generous and whilst I spent some real currency, I also got multiple legendary outfits, weapon skins and cosmetic accessories and extremes (even rarer) just by playing. Since the community on asian servers (f.e. china) is so large, there are tons of events where they hand out free stuff and I managed to get quite lucky with some legacy lootboxes.  Sadly the only negatives I have to give is the games incredible size on my harddrive. Whilst that can be explained by tons of modes. Next to the usual battle royale casual, and ranked with solos, duos and trios, with some vanilla - like event modes or a team deathmatch. We also have f.e. the whole single player/ coop stuff the extraction mode, some event mode,.. Whilst everything is semi-regularly maintained, you can occasionally hit the 10-20+ GB seasonal patch, but that's probably just an internet (skill) issue on my end. It runs surprisingly stable and you will quickly have patched access to the newest settings (upscaling algorythms, etc) The only real bad thing that to me isn't objective is, that the game keeps getting shoved into a direction that to me looks more like a mobile game. Flashy new characters that basically force a disengage when ultiling since they will statcheck you. That#s not really bothering me though. What's awkward to me is the powercreep that leaves older and more beloved (and balanced and more fun to fight) characters in the dust.  Then again, with enough gamesense on these aforementioned characters you can definitely still perform. Just maybe not as easily. Naraka: Bladepoint is one of those games that feels strange at first, but once the combat finally clicks, it becomes incredibly hard to put down.  The biggest strength is definitely the combat. Fights are not just about having better gear — timing, positioning, counters and knowing when to attack actually matter. Every weapon feels different, and there is always something new to learn. The movement system makes it even better, especially the grappling hook and climbing. Chasing someone across the map or escaping a fight by flying over rooftops never gets old.  I also really like how much room there is for improvement. At the beginning, you will probably get destroyed by more experienced players, but after some practice you start understanding combos, spacing, counters and different hero abilities. Winning a difficult duel after that feels much more satisfying than winning a typical BR gunfight.  The game also has a great visual style. The characters, weapons, animations and environments give Naraka its own identity, and the combat often feels more like a martial arts movie than a traditional battle royale.  There are definitely some frustrating parts. The learning curve can be rough, matchmaking is not always fair, and ping/netcode issues can make certain fights feel completely out of your control. These problems can be especially annoying when you are trying to improve.  Still, the core gameplay is so unique that I think Naraka is worth trying even if you normally don't like battle royale games. If you enjoy competitive combat and games where getting better actually changes how you play, this one can be seriously addictive.

Monster Hunter: Wild- Oh boy, this is going to be a long one. I love this franchise and want to bring the right people in and share my thoughts on how it could improve. I will make this review as thorough as possible, so let us get into it.  CHAPTER 1: The Story ______________________________ Unlike all other Monster Hunter games I have played, this game takes a much more traditional approach to its storytelling. Instead of having brief story moments tied to key quests unlocked after a long phase of grinding, or having the narrative run through the entirety of LR and HR, this game instead puts the story front and center. It is a story-driven ride in which you never HAVE to grind to progress, but can if you really feel like you need to. This does come with its benefits because, for once, Monster Hunter can actually take itself seriously and show and imply the devastation that monsters can cause. On the other hand, story has never been a focus of MonHun games for a good reason. While the premise is incredible, as it is with every MonHun story, the execution is pretty damn bad, and while it has its moments, even those are ruined by characters constantly needing to explain what is going on like you are watching some modern Hollywood slop. There is one exception to this, however: the main villain of the game, Arkveld, is genuinely one of the best-written video game villains I have ever fought against, and it is the only villain in all of my time spent playing games that has actually made me dread it.  Aside from that, the story also lacks any stakes whatsoever; the game is simply way too easy at this stage, and it leads to not one battle (aside from that against Arkveld) feeling intense or emotional.  CHAPTER 2: High Rank _______________________________ The post-game grind is what makes or breaks a MonHun game, and while this may be an unpopular opinion, the grind in this game is my favorite out of any of the Monster Hunters I have played. Something about actually needing to look for when and where a monster appears to create the quest, and the ability to choose how difficult you want it to be by deciding between tempered and normal, just does it for me. Maybe it is because you are...brace yourself...actually HUNTING a MONSTER, which is something that the game otherwise completely fails to get across. A lot of quality-of-life changes also make this grind just all the more bearable, while still keeping it lengthy and grueling; I mean, just look at my playtime. While the actual monster roster for the post-game is majorly underwhelming when compared to the story, it still brings in some neat new additions that help spice up the gameplay on your journey to reach Hunter Rank 50.  CHAPTER 3: TITLE UPDATES _____________________  This is where things get intense, literally. The game up to this point has been on the easier side, but these title updates punch out some of the hardest battles I have fought so far. Aside from the fact that the difficulty curve is nonexistent, this secondary post-game is quite good, with some really cool and some, sadly, very bad additions being brought to the monster roster of this game, alongside even harder versions of beasties you have already bested. Tho I must say that I love how some of these actually force you to create custom builds for them, wish it would have been like that from the start.  CHAPTER 4: Comparison _____________________________ While I still believe that Monster Hunter: Rise and 3 Ultimate are the best choices when it comes to picking up a base game to play, this game is certainly a close second/third. Its combat is basically that of World, just majorly improved, and the roster of new monsters introduced in this game might just be the best in the entire series. The music and the visuals are spectacular as always, and performance appears to have been mostly fixed, with the only problems I ever encountered being a single crash, some stuttering in the Gogmazios fight, and a single area in the ruins of Wyveria. Sadly, there are also some aspects where this game is a whole lot worse than the others. For one, the maps are...eh... The first two are great. The Oilwell Basin is visually stunning but not that fun to fight in, and the last two just feel kinda rushed. Other things that suck are the support hunters. While I love that they have become a recurring thing in these games, in this one their AI appears a whole lot worse than that of Sunbreak, and all except for one are just random people who have no contribution to the story or personality. Also, the UI is horrible beyond belief, and the fact that you can no longer abandon quests is stupid as heck.   CHAPTER 5: End ______________________  In conclusion, Monster Hunter Wilds is a game I highly recommend to fans of Monster Hunter and other similar games. It brings a whole lot of good to the franchise, while also dumbing down stuff that should not have been dumbed down. People looking for a good story, likable characters, and a good difficulty curve should, however, instead turn their attention to Monster Hunter: Rise. Meanwhile, people who actually want to HUNT THE DAMN MONSTERS should just go play World and Iceborne.  In the end, I want to actually hunt stuff again, bring back Zamtrios, and obliterate Alma with a dragonator...thanks for listening.

Monster Hunter has always been a series I loved in concept but usually struggled in some form with gameplay. I remember playing World and Rise and just sitting in the back of my head was a sensation of "man, I really want to like this, but something bugs me about it". There's really nothing off the top of my head or even if I delve deep into the depths of my head void to explain what 'bugged' me about other titles, but I can say that World and Rise always left me with a sense that something's missing.  In my opinion, Wilds adds those missing pieces, particularly ones that I didn't even know were there. It's a lot more casual player accessible and just feels nicer to play and control compared to before, and I had a lot of fun with it. I think people who haven't played much or want to try it will have an easier time getting into this title (or World) than older games in the series, while more experienced players will catch on to things quickly and potentially breeze more smoothly through its challenges (common for long running series with dedicated fanbases, though, to be honest).  The general highlights I enjoy about it is being able to more freely travel between the regions, rather than lock into a specific quest before going. Traveling on the Seikret is also nice, but I found myself often just walking on foot and looking at everything that I thought was interesting. I still do that sometimes when playing, just walk around and watch the endemic life or track a monster for a while and observe it before hunting it.  It's also fun to just sit and people watch in the grand hub, but that might just be a me thing. I usually play by myself or with a dedicated team group of people I know, so when I wait for them in the hub I'll sit at a table and look at names and how others customize their hunter.  The story is something I think is enjoyable. It's not overly complicated, and it's rather easy to follow in its scheming, and I think it's perfectly OK that way. It doesn't have to be a big, complex thing. There's layers there for savvy players to look at but it's not super required to know of things.  Overall really fun game! Very pretty. I like how accessible and easy all the weapons feel to use. Getting a mount on monsters is something difficult for me so it feels rewarding.  Be sure to check if your specs are good with the game though. I'm just barely dipped out of it and below min reqs, and that really tanks the experience. This was the game that had me go the route of a temporary GeForce Now subscription to play it before switching to console to play more regularly.

Sadly, this is probably the weakest entry in the Monster Hunter series.  The developers focused too much on making sure everyone could get through the story easily, and in doing so removed many of the moments that make Monster Hunter memorable.  During the story, there's no real sense of fear or progression. You never hit a wall where you have to improve your gear or skills to overcome a difficult hunt. Instead, the game spends around 50 hours feeling like an extended tutorial before you finally reach the content that makes Monster Hunter fun.  The endgame is where the game finally starts to shine, but by then you've already spent dozens of hours waiting for the challenge to arrive.  What worries me most is that Capcom seems happy with this direction, and it looks like the DLC may follow the same philosophy.  I just hope they stop treating difficulty as a problem to solve. Monster Hunter's identity has always been overcoming incredible monsters through preparation, practice, and better gear. That's what many longtime fans come for, not a story that prioritizes getting everyone to the credits as smoothly as possible.

The biggest problem with Wilds is that it removes almost all friction and with it, a lot of what made Monster Hunter feel like Monster Hunter.  Almost every mechanic that used to require preparation, decision-making or knowledge has been streamlined away.  You barely walk anymore. Seikret handles most of the traveling, lets you heal and sharpen on the move, and even gets you back on your feet after taking a hit. Items don't need to be picked up anymore, just shoot them with the Slinger. Monster drops teleport straight into your inventory.  Resources are basically infinite. Money, points, consumables and materials never feel scarce. There is almost no grinding. Most monsters only need to be hunted a few times to get everything you want, and even decorations and Artian gear are extremely easy to obtain.  The Palico handles healing and status recovery for you, capture thresholds are practically impossible to miss, and mechanics like tremors, wind pressure, blights and especially stun barely matter anymore. You can cook and restock whenever you want, even during a hunt. Fainting barely has any consequences because you keep your food buffs.  And then there is the actual combat.  There is almost no challenge. Monsters spend huge amounts of time knocked down or locked into wound-break animations. You don't really have to learn their moves or earn openings anymore, just attack wounds and the monster falls over. Triple-carting feels almost impossible because the monster will often die before it can seriously threaten you.  The result is that you don't really need to learn the maps, prepare for hunts, manage resources, understand monster behavior or grind for gear. You just fight the monster, collect everything automatically and move on.  And that's the biggest disappointment for me.  Wilds is polished, beautiful and fun, but it has streamlined so much of Monster Hunter that it removed a lot of the reason I loved the series in the first place.

So, at this point in 2026 it's a good game. Not absolutely mind-blowing, but GOOD in the sense of coming from Fallout and Elder Scrolls games. This would be the next logical step from Fallout 4 even thought it's entirely different company and universe.   The game still has some flaws, bugs and glitches, etc. just like the Bethesda games but they do not detract from the immersion too much.   The graphics: For a game with 2015 graphics it runs like crap, at times dropping below 40 fps even on a 4070Ti Super with the ray tracing turned off and DLSS on performance mode. It just reminds me of Fallout 4 and Skyrim all over again. The ray tracing is all a gimmick, it doesn't run well at all. The game engine could have been coded a lot better to handle distant objects, LODs, crowds of people, multiple vehicles and what not. The engine SUCKS. HARD.  If you looked at GTA V and expected this to be better than that, forget it.   The driving is wonky and feels like a slip'n'slide with the delayed steering and constant drifting around. I hate it, and only use vehicles to get to the next fast travel marker.  Combat is good, very satisfying to watch body parts explode during the more intense scenes, but only with the right weapons/implants. Most Pistols/SMGs/Assault rifles feel like pea shooters and enemies become bullet sponges. Avoid those.  The weapons system is more akin to Borderlands, with different stats, strengths and classes like many other RPGs (Diablo, Divinity, Borderlands, etc.), but also modifiable with some weapons having extra mod slots for scopes, larger capacity clips/mags, less recoil, etc. It gets confusing, so for most of the game I stuck with throwing knives and high damage sniper rifles because they're pretty OP.  Implants, same again - confusing and a burden to keep travelling to-and-from ripperdocs all the time so I just stuck with what worked.  There's a lot to do in the game aside from the main story line. A lot of these are just the usual "steal this vehicle" and "kill this bullet sponge" side quests, which earn you discounts on the vehicles and such. There's no real point in doing them if you hate the driving like I do.  A lot of the side quests are tied to the main story and are actually fun and involving to play. The dialogue and story on these are far superior to the previously mentioned fetch and kill quests and left me feeling satisfied once I completed them.  The endings are all quite depressing. No spoilers, but you will see if you spend as much time in the game as I have.  Buy this game with the Phantom Liberty DLC when its on sale. But only if you like the Fallout and Elder Scrolls games.

At first, I only played Cyberpunk 2077 for about an hour because I thought the game was a little too dark for my taste. A couple of months later, I decided to give it another chance—and I'm glad I did.  The more I played, the more I realized how much the story, gameplay, and open world kept improving. What surprised me the most was how much some of your decisions and dialogue choices can affect the story and its endings.  My first playthrough was... painful. 😂  I was playing on Hard difficulty with a weak setup and poor equipment, and unfortunately, I wasn't able to save Takemura. I was under a lot of pressure during that mission, ended up fighting the TAC Team, and eventually followed Johnny's suggestion to get out.  I also misunderstood Hanako's relationship with Takemura, so I thought she would somehow make sure he stayed alive. That definitely influenced my decision.  Then came the ending.  I'm naturally a pacifist and someone who tends to deal with problems alone, so when I reached the ending choices, I picked **The Devil**. I thought it was the safest option because I didn't want other people to die because of my own problems.  And then Johnny reacted with:  *"What the ♥♥♥♥ was that?"*  That's when I started thinking:  "Oh... I might have made a mistake."  And I was right.  The more I progressed through The Devil ending, the more uncomfortable I became. It felt like I had sacrificed my own principles and conscience just to find a solution. I was basically handing myself over to the corpos—the same people connected to Jackie's death.  The aftermath honestly felt like psychological horror to me.  I eventually chose to return to Earth, and I remember thinking:  "Well... anyways I did'nt sold my soul to the corpos."  I didn't even know the other characters would leave messages during the credits, which made the whole experience hit even harder.  That night, I genuinely couldn't sleep properly because I kept thinking about whether I had made the wrong choice. I started wondering if my real-life personality—being a pacifist and preferring to solve problems alone—had actually influenced my decision.  So I went back and tried the other endings.  The Aldecaldos ending was fantastic. One of the funniest moments was when I gave my speech to the clan and suddenly realized I wasn't wearing pants or shoes.  Don't ask me how that happened. 😂  But the ending I liked the most was **I Don't Fear the Reaper**.  The idea of fighting alone so that nobody else has to die because of my problem fits my personality perfectly. I didn't even know this option existed at first, and if I had known about it, I probably would have chosen it immediately.  The mission itself was incredible. Johnny's dialogue throughout the entire sequence really felt like he was pushing me forward. Playing it on Hard made it even more intense because dying meant the whole attempt was over.  During the final fight, I noticed my HP getting lower and lower and initially didn't understand why. Later I realized it was because of the worsening effects of the Biochip/Relic.  Despite that, this ending felt the most "me."  Ironically, I think Cyberpunk 2077 taught me something outside of the game:  **Sometimes you shouldn't try to solve everything alone.**  Sometimes you need to accept help from other people. You're not alone in the world, and other people can help you carry your problems.  Overall: **4/5**  The game definitely has bugs. I experienced a blocker bug once or twice where a character or vehicle was positioned incorrectly, causing a scene to get stuck and preventing the story from continuing. But those issues didn't ruin the overall experience for me.  My personal ending ranking:  1. I Don't Fear the Reaper 2. Aldecaldos 3. Johnny & Rogue 4. The Devil 5. Jump, Jump  Really memorable game. I'm glad I gave it a second chance.

Cyberpunk 2077 is my personal favorite RPG I have ever played. Despite it's messy launch back in 2020, CD Projekt Red got to work and fixed (most of) it soon after, making this world I was very excited to immerse myself in that even better. I played (and finished) this game for the first time back on PS4 launch day, and have returned to it countless times for a plethora of playthroughs on PC.  Cyberpunk 2077 story, world, and characters are all eerily derived from our real world, albeit more theatrical. While the corporations of Cyberpunk rule with an iron fist, the corporations of our world rule with whispers behind closed doors. I truly enjoy how important many of the characters are in V's story. Specifically, depending on your playthrough, how the characters you meet over the course of V's desperate fight for survival slowly become a greater reason to stay alive as opposed to V's dream of becoming a legend.   Now into spoiler territory (for Phantom Liberty),  [spoiler]Not only is the base game amazing, the DLC Phantom Liberty is just as good or even better. The characters, setting, and story of Phantom Liberty is amazing. Specifically, In the beginning of Phantom Liberty, you are tasked with the rescue of the President of The New United States of America (NUSA) from a shot down Space Force One by Songbird (So Mi). As the events of Phantom Liberty play out you soon learn that Songbird played a role in the grounding of Space Force One, despite a less violent plan in mind. Doing this in order to hopefully find a cure for her ailments caused by accessing the Blackwall often.[/spoiler]  [spoiler]Although some may blame or hate Songbird for this, I see her story as a reflection of V's own path in certain ways. So Mi's efforts to save her life mirror V's own efforts in a way. Both So Mi and V both do anything to survive in their respective stories.
