**Not Recommended: I waited six years for this game to work.**  I was a day-one buyer of Cyberpunk 2077. I was there for the launch, and I swear I encountered just about every bug that ended up documented online.  So I waited.  I saw what CD Projekt Red had done with The Witcher 3 over time, and I genuinely believed Cyberpunk would get the same treatment. I wanted to experience this game when it was finally ready, rather than ruin my first playthrough fighting through technical problems.  Six years later, I still can't play it.  For me, it's the infamous audio crackling/popping glitch. If you've searched for this problem, you already know the worst part: everyone seems to have a different "fix," which means there really isn't one.  I've changed audio refresh/sample rates. Updated and reinstalled drivers. Turned SFX down and completely off. Disabled spatial audio. Used Windows spatial audio. Tried Bluetooth headphones, wired headphones, laptop speakers, desktop speakers, and monitor speakers. I've verified the game files, uninstalled and reinstalled the entire game, restarted the computer, turned it off and back on, and done all the other obligatory troubleshooting steps. I've gone through forums, Reddit threads, videos, and troubleshooting guides.  Believe me, if you're about to suggest a fix, I've probably tried it.  And before someone points at my Steam playtime as proof that the game must have been playable, those hours are extremely misleading. A huge amount of that time was spent with the game running while I was trying to troubleshoot the problem, testing settings, restarting, loading back in, driving around to see if the crackling returned, and repeating the process. Yes, there were stretches where I actually got to play the game, but I'd estimate maybe 25% of my recorded hours were spent genuinely playing rather than trying to make the game work.  And that's what makes this so disappointing. I *want* to play Cyberpunk 2077. I bought it at launch, watched CDPR spend years rebuilding its reputation, watched the game receive major updates and an expansion, and deliberately waited to give it the experience I thought it deserved.  But I've never once been able to actually play through the game.  Six years of patches, updates, fixes, and second chances, and a game-breaking audio issue that has been reported by players for years still makes the game effectively unplayable for me.  So, for the final time, I'm uninstalling Cyberpunk 2077. At this point, I have to accept that I'm probably never going to finish what I genuinely wanted to be a superb game.  I'm sure Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game when it works. I genuinely wish I could have found out.

Look. I know a lot has been said about this game, both good and bad. I'm not breaking new ground here. The pros of this game are the immaculate vibes and graphics. Being locked in on a mission makes the game flow and can be, at times, fun. And if this game was just an on-the-rail story-driven FPS, then yeah, I wouldn't have much to complain about (besides the hard crashes and game-breaking bugs that are still rampant, even now).   The thing is, I can't let what happened be excused. I know CDPR pulled a "NMS" here and spent the last few years fixing it up, and that's good. But to glaze this game now only excuses the absolute fact that not only did they sell me an unplayable mess at start, they also sold me a DIFFERENT GAME. I pre-ordered this game because the makers of TW3 promised me an OPEN WORLD RPG, just like TW3, but cyberpunk. That is not what this game is. Night City is empty, a vacuous window-dressing void of any and all content save for the rare "work for the police by killing some dudes" (in a "punk" game, you sure do spend a lot of time doing the police's dirty work). No factions, no meaningful choices, all the shops and doors are closed, I could go on and on. Walking around NC is fun for the vibes, but it gets incredibly boring, and then depressing.   I wanted to love this game so much. I was ready to lose myself in it. But even after waiting years to get this game in a playable state, it's clear this game is not 'open world' in any meaningful sense. It's not a 'role playing game' beyond choosing your combat style. Nothing you do really matters. Hop in a car (which are still absurdly hard to control on mouse/keyboard) and all the lights turn green, all the traffic disappears. Nothing you do matters, in the open world or in the story missions, as everything leads to a single "pick your ending" moment. In some ways, I'm more disappointed now than I was on launch.  If you want to just hang out in a cool futuristic cyberpunk city, this is the game for that. If you love story-driven on-the-rails FPS games, this is a great game for that. But if you want an open world role playing game, I can assure you that this is not that game. Don't reward bad corpo behavior, choom. Stop glazing this still-buggy mess of a failed promise.

Eight hours of planning, resource management, and flawless execution were gone down the drain due to one simple bug. Playing Repo is a game of high stakes, where a single wrong move can undo hours of hard work. But there is nothing worse for a player than to finally reach level 22 only to realize that their efforts have been in vain due to a game glitch. This is an utterly heartbreaking scenario for any player, who has put a significant amount of effort into the game.    Repo is one of those games where the tension is built-up throughout the play until the very end. At the beginning of the game, it is relatively easy to earn points and upgrade one’s character. However, as the level progresses, the tasks become more challenging and require more effort and time to be completed. For this reason, players tend to become more serious and focused when approaching level 22. After spending eight hours in the game, one does not want to quit right away, so they decide to invest more effort in order to beat the game. The higher the levels, the more exciting it becomes to watch your character take on the seemingly impossible odds and overcome them due to one’s effort and skill.    However, once a player reaches level 22, all progress can be overturned due to one simple game bug. One is bound to feel particularly disappointed if they have managed to survive due to their own skill only for the game to end due to a technical error. There are several reasons why such a scenario would be more disappointing for the player than a traditional game end. When facing an enemy attack, there is nothing wrong with dying due to enemy engagement. After all, the player knows that they have a reasonable chance at surviving the encounter. But bugs eliminate the possibility of fair play, as the player is no longer in control of the game outcome. If the player has mistakenly triggered an invisible trap, fallen victim to a programming error, or simply ‘flew off the map’, they cannot influence the outcome of the game. A game bug is much more disappointing than a traditional game end because it takes away a player’s sense of accomplishment and investment. Looking at the game over screen after spending eight hours in the game is heartbreaking. One’s first reaction to such an outcome would be shock and even anger, but the feeling will quickly turn into disappointment as the realization sets in that the eight-hour effort has gone down the drain with no reward or satisfaction.

Rocket League is easily my favourite game of all time.  I play it every day, and somehow it still never gets old. You can always improve your mechanics, positioning, rotations, consistency and decision-making, which means there is always another reason to queue up for one more match.  What keeps me coming back is the challenge. Some days you’re playing perfectly, other days absolutely nothing goes your way, but I never give up. Every loss teaches you something, every mistake gives you something to work on, and every great match reminds you why you keep playing.  There is no better feeling than hitting a shot you’ve been practising for weeks, making a ridiculous save, pulling off the perfect pass, or winning an intense overtime match where both teams are giving everything they have.  Rocket League can definitely test your patience, especially in ranked, but that is part of what makes improving feel so rewarding. Your progress actually feels earned.  Thousands of matches later, I can still jump on and have just as much fun as I did when I started.  It’s competitive, frustrating, exciting, addictive and unbelievably satisfying.  I play every day. I have a great love for Elden Ring with some caveats.  Having already played through the original Demon's Souls, Dark Souls 1 and 3 multiple times, I believe I have a good enough amount of experience to speak on Elden Ring with some good context.  Elden Ring is simultaneously amazing and yet a little tedious.   The parts I love are why I have loved all the Souls games before it: great exploration and world building, atmosphere, and a wonderful sense of progression as you slowly build your character. Gameplay is top notch and is as varied as it has ever been in terms of weapons and potential builds.  On the other hand, the shift to an open world has introduced some unfortunate open world tropes, such as a lot of emptiness and open space between all the cool and interesting things to do. The dungeons are all hand crafted with the typical souls level of quality, yet the vast amounts of space between them leaves me wishing it was just more of the densely packed and intertwining level design the souls games are known for.  I haven't quite finished my first playthrough, and even though I'm having a great time, I already don't believe I'll want to play through it again immediately like I did my other Souls games, for the open world reasons I listed above.   It's a weird feeling because, for me, Dark Souls 3 was the peak of the Souls formula. The level design was top notch, the world was slightly more linear, but the intertwining design of the levels made it so when you unlocked a shortcut to a previous area it immediately felt so gratifying. Some of that magic is lost in a massive open map. There's lots to do, yes, but it's so much more spread out that you get those magic moments much less often.  While I love this game, and I do highly recommend it, enter into it knowing the drawbacks of any open world game.   Thankfully, this is not the open world formula you may be familiar with in Ubisoft games, where the map is just littered with side quests that pad the run time but leave you feeling empty inside for pursuing. In Elden Ring, there are virtually no markers. You need to go find them for yourself. Exploration is almost always rewarded with some cool item or spell or weapon. But the amount of time spent wandering between these cool moments can sometimes feel quite long, especially if you like to explore every nook and cranny like I tend do to.   If you go straight for the main quest markers, your time with Elden Ring will likely feel quite different. But for me, I like to take my time and uncover everything. I think my natural tendencies may be why I haven't enjoyed it as much as DS1, or 3. As there is simply so much to explore and so much nothingness between the true points of interest.  If you're a fan of the genre, though, this is a must play. Enjoy it in the way you enjoy playing these games, and be ready for an incredible journey.  PS I have also experienced much of the game on a Steam Deck. While not the ideal way to play, it's well enough if you can tolerate 40fps. Only very occasionally did it dip from this, so it's a decent way to experience the game if you're not able to use your computer or tv for any particular reason.

This isn't a good Souls game.  Firstly, let's get this out of the way: Souls fans, this review is not for you. You already bought the game, completed it six times and are busily posting a long rant nobody will read about why whatever weapon is underrated/overpowered.   For the rest of us, who might dip in and out of Souls games from time to time: this is just a Souls game but worse. The only thing that makes it any different from Dark Souls 1, 2, 3 or any other Fromsoft game is the open world - and the open world makes literally everything worse.   Don't get me wrong - it was the correct decision to put an open world in. The game isn't for me, it's for the Souls fans who've played every game FromSoft release a dozen times over and just need something new. For those people, the open world is the least harmful breath of fresh air possible.   If you're not sick of the sight of Souls games, though, the open world is a terrible addition. Pacing is dead and buried, the usually stellar map design is relegated to only existing in dungeons, and you have no idea where you're supposed to go next. If you don't look it up you can guarantee you'll miss a region entirely, then have to choose between never experiencing it or doing it while horribly overlevelled. Speaking of which, if you like to explore and find everything, you'll be overlevelled anyway; I didn't grind once and yet was 30+ levels ahead of where I should be for virtually the entire game simply because I refused to skip content.  The worst thing, though, is the bosses. Bosses are FromSoft's selling point, and they're usually both well-designed encounters and also very visually impressive. In this game, however, thanks to the open world they have to put 300 more of them into the game than there should be - gotta put SOMETHING in the open world after all. They can't design 300+ unique bosses, so that means reprints. A LOT of reprints. By the time I gave up on the game I'd fought an estimated six Crucible Knight versions, dozens of lesser versions thereof, half a dozen gargoyles, seven (I think) Ulcerated Tree Spirits, over a dozen Watchdog Statues... the list goes on. The anticipation and impact Dark Souls usually has with its bosses is entirely eliminated because nine times out of ten you'll see the boss health bar pop up and realise it's the same thing you've already fought before. Repeatedly.  To conclude, if you're NOT someone who plays every Souls game relentlessly, do yourself a favour - buy Dark Souls 3 instead. Hell, buy ANY Dark Souls game. If you already own one, play that instead. They'll have proper gameplay pacing, proper map design, and most of the bosses you fight will be unique and interesting.   They'll be better than this, in other words. This was legitimately a boring game.

The open world just destroys the flow of the game. It doesn't feel like exploring, but more like working a 9-to-5 just to reach the next legacy dungeon and finally get another taste of actual level design.  More than half of the game is made up of useless horizontal planes with different textures or, when the game feels generous, those same planes decorated with good-looking solid objects planted into the ground.  The game can often be visually impressive, but that alone contributes very little to the actual enjoyment of the exploration itself.  And the legacy dungeons aren't that much better, to be honest. Excluding Farum Azula, I don't feel like any of them really tries to propose a distinctive or interesting way of exploring in the way almost every area of Dark Souls did. Stormveil is basically a castle, Raya Lucaria is a castle with mages, Volcano Manor is a castle with lava, Leyndell spends most of its time feeling like a traditional dungeon crawler, and the Haligtree is okay but ultimately forgettable.  This doesn't mean the game looks bad. Quite the opposite: very often it looks fantastic. But visuals are only part of the job in a medium built around interaction. It's crazy to me that, despite being the first entry with a dedicated jump button, this somehow feels like the Souls game where exploration is least enjoyable.  The reward structure makes things even worse. The game fills the world with useless items in an attempt to create the illusion that wandering around is worthwhile. Half the time you go out of your way to reach some distant corner of the map only to find a crafting material or recipe whose function you'll forget five seconds after picking it up.  And then there are the catacombs and mines.  I hope you really like those assets, because you're going to see them a lot. They feel almost procedurally assembled: repetitive, unimaginative, full of dead space and absurdly unrewarding considering how much of a slog many of them are.  The entire map could have been one quarter of its current size. If that smaller space had been properly filled and given more attention, I'd probably be the happiest Souls player alive.  But thank God there are the incredibly rewarding boss fights.  Yes, I absolutely love being input-read into an AoE, roll-catching, delayed one-shot attack during a seven-hit tracking true combo. At some point you genuinely start wondering whether having somebody punch you while you're playing would improve the experience, if only because the physical pain might distract you from the spiritual hassle of fighting yet another random boss.  And that's assuming the boss isn't recycled. Be prepared to fight the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing over and over again, or, even better, a normal enemy arbitrarily promoted to boss status for the occasion. It's lazy design taken to an absurd level. There isn't a single boss in the entire game that I genuinely look forward to fighting again. Maybe Malenia and Morgott.  Regular enemies aren't much better, although their biggest problem is less the movesets themselves and more the absurd damage numbers. After a certain point, even with a full tank build, almost everything can practically two-shot you.  That doesn't mean their movesets aren't filled with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, because they absolutely are, but the damage is so aggressively overtuned in an attempt to inflate difficulty that every other problem almost becomes secondary.  That constant feeling of unfairness, combined with some of the least rewarding exploration I've experienced in this kind of game, pushes the frustration to another level.  What keeps Elden Ring afloat is its build diversity and lore. In combat, you can use almost anything and create an enormous variety of viable builds, while the world and its mythology are genuinely compelling. The problem is that the experience surrounding those strengths is often so exhausting that eventually you stop caring about what is in front of you, because everything starts feeling like another chore.  Worst entry in the series, and overall an average to below-average game.  If I also judge it against the minimum level of progress one should reasonably expect from a later installment in an established series, I have to mention how unacceptable the state of the AI is. Enemies are frequently just braindead.  The environmental storytelling has also become strangely self-celebratory. It was one of the defining strengths of the earlier games, but an open world should have been the opportunity to expand that formula and communicate the setting in more organic ways: through cities, settlements, populated spaces, or basically anything that made the world feel more alive.  Instead, despite having exponentially more space to work with, the game often falls back on the exact same formula: empty ruins, cryptic environmental details and item descriptions carrying most of the narrative burden.  At that point it stops feeling elegant and starts feeling lazy.  Bad.

Before I start, I would like to say that this it not a negative review. I have very complicated feelings towards this game. Feelings that could not be measured by a simple like or dislike.   Let's start with the positives. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LOVE the art direction of this game. Each region feels distinct and full of detail, conveying a beautifully tragic war-torn world so well, albeit one that feels as though it can be saved and its not all hopeless, and yet despair lurks around every corner.  I loved a lot of the NPCs, they feel considerably more fleshed out than some of the previous Souls games, not to say they didn't have any, but a lot of them made me really question the choices I was making along the way, in particular Varre, who I found intriguingly creepy as hell. It has some of my favorite character designs as well! Blaaid, Alexander, Godrick, Mohg, Malenia, I could go on! The voice acting is top notch as well, some of the best I've heard in a game.   The music was pretty nice too, unfortunately I'm usually too distracted by my mission or fighting a tough boss to really appreciate it for what it is.    What made me leave a "negative" review, however, was the difficulty. Not that it was HARD, this genre is known for its relatively high difficulty. It was brutally hard, moreso than every other Souls game I have played, (1 and 3, 3 I have the most experience with) but it's not even that!  The difficulty of this game is....is just....all OVER the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ place!!!  Like...ok. You start out in Limgrave. You have barely any health to speak of, so you need to start leveling Vigor. My advice to you all, get that ♥♥♥♥ to 40 IMMEDIATELY. And then towards the mid-late game, get it to 60. I have gripes with this, more on that later. Liurnia, a bit more difficult, but not a huge step up. Every region after that has a rather large jump in difficulty. ESPECIALLY Caelid. ♥♥♥♥ Caelid! But wait!! It gets even WORSE!!  When you get to the late game areas, (Leyndell, Mountaintops of the Giants, Crumbling Farum Azula) the game just throws as much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at you as it possibly can, and doesn't ever hold back. JESUS. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. CHRIST. I have NEVER seen such a horrific difficulty spike in any game up until this point!   The Fire Giant was the first boss to really question my sanity. It is INSANELY tanky, and while largely telegraphable, it will destroy you in 3-4 hits. With 60 VIGOR.   60 Vigor is practically MANADATORY at this stage of the game. Everyone and everyONE will ♥♥♥♥ you up in 3-4 hits. I say 60 because it's the second softcap. After that you get barely anything from Vigor. Which ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SUCKS BECAUSE YOU DON'T EVER GET ENOUGH HP TO WORK WITH!!!  As are summons. The PC version is the definitive version because the online is free. You NEED co-op to beat most of these bosses. Especially towards the end. Spirit Ashes can work too, but here's the thing I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate about this. NOT. EVERY. BOSS. WILL LET YOU. SUMMON. SPIRITS!!!! WHY?!!! This is a HORRIBLE design choice!! They're not even as good as a player can be! Just let me USE them for Christ's sake!!   But THEN....Maliketh.  Maliketh, and the boss you fight at phase 1, the Beast Clergyman, might just be the worst boss I've ever dealt with. And right before, in my mind it was the Fire Giant.   Imagine a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as tanky as the Fire Giant. Now make him INSANELY mobile, have multiple AOE projectiles, and make much of his attacks go through the pillars that LOOK like they're safe, but oftentimes won't protect you from ♥♥♥♥. I mean this to BOTH bosses by the way.  Maliketh, is even worse. Now give him a sword that can DRAIN YOUR HEALTH OVER TIME, AND! Reduce your Max HP, Make him even MORE mobile, and make him tanky too.   I am stuck on this boss right now. You need two summons. Not one, TWO. One is not enough. And many times for some godforsaken reason I hardly get anyone online to help!    There's another aspect of Elden Ring I really don't like, unrelated to difficulty.  It is, by far, the most walkthroughiest game, I have ever played. You NEED a walkthrough for most of this game. After a while I just gave up playing it blind. There's no shame in using one either, especially for games like this. Dark Souls 3 could be like this too, but I used it more for building my character rather than much of the game itself!  NPCs have the most obtuse questlines in the world. They practically DEMAND a guide. How are you supposed to know what to do next, what items to get to progress a questline, without using a guide?! It's ridiculous!!  Pages upon pages, videos upon videos, all just to be able to play this game without losing my mind. And I'm still losing my mind.    Dark Souls 3 could be like this at times, I remember Irithyll being absolute HELL in regards to difficulty. But in regards to difficulty CURVE, that is the big ass difficulty spike of the game, but a lot of lategame areas tend to generally be more fair relative to the area. But I CAN tell you that both of them have twice as much health as the final boss of Dark Souls 3. BOTH. OF. THEM.   It all combines into the most unaccessible, harder than hardcore, not for the faint of heart or the short of temper Souls game, I have ever played. For their first attempt at an open world Souls game, I'd say FromSoft did a pretty good job, but its also meandered with questionable design choices that ultimately lessen what I would've otherwise called the best Souls game! It shows a lot of promise!!....but holy ♥♥♥♥, are the lows some of the lowest I've seen in a game.   I wouldn't give it a flat out thumbs down because I DO like a lot of this game. I ultimately did have fun most of the way through, and if a video game is fun, that's great! I would give it a more, thumbs sideways, I guess???  I say "not recommended" not in the sense that the game sucks, it doesn't, I know I sound like I think it sucks, but its moreso certain aspects that really get under my skin, enough to make me not recommend it for most people. I would just start out playing either Dark Souls Remastered, or Dark Souls 3, if you want to get into these games. Elden Ring is for the most hardcore ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the planet, clearly.   And from what I heard the DLC gets even worse due to certain mechanics, and DLC of Souls games generally being even more brutal than the main game, but that is standard at this point. The late game is brutal enough for me, and honestly I'd say it's too much. I'm not ever getting the DLC.  Also also, WHO CHARGES MONEY FOR CHARACTER CLASSES, ARE WE REAL, PEOPLE?!! CHRIIIIIST!!!   If FromSoft makes another open world in this style, I would like to see FromSoft do a much better job with the difficulty curve, making it a lot smoother and fairer in regards to where you are, and make the NPC questlines easier to follow without a guide. I'm going to write a review on things that are important to me.  I started playing yugioh like many did as a child during the peak of the first anime.  It was a much simpler game but it was still fun.  I lost interest in it though because I was a broke boi and couldn't really figure out how to get better decks so I'd just lose to my friends, I was also a kid playing against highscoolers/adults at locals.  I also played a game for the Gameboy Advance called YuGiOh World Wide Edition and YuGiOh Ultimate Masters 2006.  What was cool about these games is for the most part they were correct rulings and interactions and the games played themselves scripting wise.  I played this far more then the physical TCG so this was my favorite part of "YuGiOh".  I had looked into getting into the TCG again over the years but it seemed way too complicated and there wasn't games like those GBA games that would script all the interactions for you so I never really took the time to learn.  I just stuck with Hearthstone  Fast forward to now that I found MasterDuel (I know the games not new anymore but I just heard about it).  It's for the most part very similar to the TCG and almost every yugioh card interaction is scripted.    THIS IS THE BEST SELLING POINT FOR THIS GAME!!    It wasn't easy and it was very overwhelming but after 50 hours I'm starting to get a bit of a handle on the game and I'm barely scratching the surface.  This game is HARD.  One other thing I was a bit nervous about was how F2P the game is.  I found a lot of conflicting answers but I will say this game is very F2P, especially compared to what I was familiar to with Heartstone.  You need to be smart about your gems though but for the most part any new player can make any meta deck in about a day or 2 of doing the challenges.  Your 2nd and 3rd deck might take a big longer but that's still better then F2P HS.  Finally the gameplay.  This TCG and therefore this simulator isn't for everyone.  It's got the largest learning curve of any TCG I've played.  That means is it takes a long time and experience before your skill expression actually matters.  You can't just drop into this game and and be big brain duelist, it's just not possible.  That's very frustrating for a lot of beginners and that's going to be the biggest complaint you see about the game or the TCG in general.  I think the TCG is generally better in this way though because it does a best of 3 which means you can change your deck depending on your matchup.  In this game you can't do that.  I got some other nitpicks like how ranked ladder works and some of the controls but I think this is a nice f2p TCG.

I say I'd recommend this, but with a MASSIVE asterisk. This is good, but has a couple problems that you should know before you first play.   1. This game isn't good at explaining how the actual program works. I HIGHLY recommend looking up a video on the best way to start playing, as this game is actually very f2p friendly, it just doesn't tell you. My recommended video is the one by TSG Anime, but really most of them will do the job.   2. There is a ton of hyper competitive decks, but 90% of the time they aren't actually that hard to beat, EXCEPT how this game program works you literally don't have time during the actual game to work it out as you play. Which is what I think causes most retuning and new players to get frustrated and think its all BS. Problem one is the turn time limit means the longer it takes you to read what each card in a combo does so you know which ones to prioritize stopping, the less time you have to actually spend stopping them. Problem two is that because everything is automated, even if you had the time to read it can be hard to tell which effect is contributing to what other cards. Infinitely better than Magic Arena or MtG in general. Always will be. But gosh has Yugioh ever dug itself into a rough format. Some of these matches feel as bad as MtG games do with how long it can take people to do their turn and how many cards people play from hand or activate effects on the field.  The monetization is actually really good. You can earn over 8k gems a month playing less than 10 hours a week without too too much trouble. 1k gems opens you 10 card packs which guarantees an SR or if you don't happen to get a UR the next 10 pull a UR is guaranteed. But in practice I find myself drawing 3 or 4 UR on average and regularly see 6 UR in a 10 pack pull. Each pack is 8 cards so that's 80 cards for 1k gems and with 8k gems that's 640 cards. It's a lot more than I'd get in real life without having to spend money that's for sure! Between dailies and login bonuses you get 140 per day just for logging in each day and playing 2 or 3 games every 3 days (You get 3 dailies per day and they stack up to 9 so if you complete them on the third day you're pretty good). In practice I don't get all the dailies done so I just play 2 games every other day and say that's good.  The timer is definitely my main issue though. The fact of the matter is.... this game doesn't have a real timer so people take 15+ minutes on their turn somewhat regularly and it's REALLY bad. They have a counter on the side of the table to count down the seconds for your turn, it starts at 5 minutes. Now this may sound like a timer but I'd STRONGLY hesitate to call it that as it stops for nearly every action and interaction as well as any fancy visuals that cut in occasionally. If we had a hard 5 minute timer this game actually might be REALLY enjoyable even though it would cut out people wanting to play certain decks that just summon 20+ cards. I don't really have a problem with that personally; I think combo slop decks like that are very uninteresting and if you don't have time to set up a full board state like you want to then either that should just be okay or you should consider trying to minimize the amount of actions you're performing on your turn to account for the timer. Since the counter they have already pauses for every action you take and interaction that could be resolved it means there's no threat to anyone having to even think about the timer. Basically the way it is right now you're rewarded for playing the game more and preventing your opponent from playing the game more. They lose more time if you floodgate them and prevent them from taking actions while you gain more turn time if you can make as many actions as possible. I don't like this one bit and it's the main reason for me giving this game a negative review here.  The other thing that's really a problem for me is the heavy restrictions they put on all the events. Most of which seem incredibly arbitrary or just oriented to try to make certain new archetypes look better in hopes people pull for them. I'd much rather be able to play Yugioh when I go to play Yugioh. Finding a deck I enjoy and get into playing ranked more with just for the next event to pop up and prevent me from playing that deck.... It really makes me feel bad.  Unfortunately there aren't really any better online options. Like, there are some online services that let you play duels but nothing as high quality as this. So my recommendation might just be to go play in locals tbh. Being around people and interacting with others might benefit you a lot more than a game like this ever could.

I just killed an innocent man.  I thought it would be fun to be a rat for once. I befriended him at the start of the raid. I gave him some good loot. We traveled together for a while, and all the while I was plotting my move. When the moment came, my finger was swift. I thought his would be too. It wasn't. He took every bullet. He didn't fight back. He didn't even let me knock him down. He just left the game. All that remains with me is his scream. After the first shot, I knew he felt betrayed. I could've stopped. I should've stopped.  I'm sorry, random guy. You were just trying to find a friend, and all you found was my misplaced boredom and mischievousness. I originally wanted to leave a negative review saying I'd probably never return to ARC Raiders. But for a game to make me feel genuinely sick about something I did to a stranger in the form of ones and zeros, to make me sit there afterward actually regretting pulling a virtual trigger, for my eyes to well up with tears. I can't pretend the game hasn't given me something special.  And yet, strangely enough, I think that moment also explains why I'm losing interest in it. After 107 hours, I've looted everything. I've killed ARC. I've killed Raiders. I've searched the same radiator boxes, drawers, cabinets, containers, and corpses more times than I can count. I've gone topside with nothing and returned with a fortune. I've lost kits that took hours to assemble and replaced them the next evening.  Eventually, you realize you're doing the same thing over and over again: Loot. Extract. Regear. Kill. Die. Repeat. At first, that loop is intoxicating. Every item matters. Every gunshot in the distance makes you nervous. Every stranger might become your friend or put a bullet in your back. Extracting with a backpack full of valuable gear feels like you've actually accomplished something.  But eventually the question changes. Instead of asking, "What can I find in this raid?" You start asking, "Why am I still trying to find it?" And I think that's the problem that ARC Raiders will have to solve if it wants to survive long term. The loot can't be the destination forever. Once you've accumulated enough weapons, materials, money, and equipment, another successful extraction becomes just another successful extraction. The tension that made the game extraordinary begins disappearing precisely because there's nothing else to do in the game.  So you start creating your own excitement. Maybe you run worse equipment. Maybe you hunt players. Maybe you camp an extraction. Maybe you betray someone who trusted you five minutes earlier just because you've never done it before. Maybe you kill an innocent man. That poor bastard became more memorable to me than almost anything I looted during the previous hundred hours. And that's both the greatest compliment and the biggest criticism I can give ARC Raiders.  The game's systems created a human interaction powerful enough that I genuinely felt bad about what I'd done. But I only went looking for that interaction because the underlying progression loop had stopped giving me a reason to care.  That's where I worry about the game's future. An extraction shooter can't sustain itself indefinitely on the promise that tomorrow you'll extract with slightly more stuff than you had yesterday. There needs to be something meaningful on the other side of all that accumulation, something that makes the hundredth hour feel fundamentally different from the tenth.  Otherwise, eventually, the loot stops being the reason you go topside. You start looking for another reason. And sometimes that reason is some poor random guy who thought he'd made a friend.  Or maybe that's just the point of extraction shooters, idk.

It's a masterpiece.....  I've got 1,000 hours in this game now, and somehow I'm still playing it almost every day.  I really didnt expect that when I first started.  The game just has something.  The atmosphere, the sound design, the ARC machines, the maps, the whole feeling when you're carrying a backpack full of good ♥♥♥♥ and suddenly hear footsteps 20 meters away.  You never know whats going to happen.  And thats exactly why I love it.  People complain about PvP all the time, and honestly I find it pretty funny sometimes.  I've got over 1k hours now and in my last 30 games, I havent been shot ONCE by another player.  Why?  Because I didnt shoot back.  That's literally it.  I see a player, I dont want to fight, I move on. Most of the time they do the same.  And then you see someone complaining about "too much PvP" while they are shooting every single person they see.  Like bro... YOU are doing the PvP 😂  Embark has also confirmed that matchmaking actually takes your behaviour into account. If you keep playing peacefully and dont start ♥♥♥♥ with everyone you meet, the game takes that into consideration when matching you.  And in my experience, it actually works.  I'm not saying you'll never see an aggressive player. Obviously you will. It's still an extraction game.  But thats the whole point.  You can play peacefully.  You can loot, do your quests, fight ARC, explore the map, help randoms and extract without shooting another player once.  Nobody is forcing you to turn every encounter into a fight.  And I really hope Embark doesnt change that just because some people want a completely PvE version of the game.  There are already plenty of games for that.  ARC Raiders is different.  The possibility of PvP is what creates a lot of the tension. Even if nothing happens, you hear footsteps and you instantly start thinking about what to do.  Do I hide?  Do I leave?  Do I trust him?  Does he have a weapon?  Is he going to shoot me?  That little bit of uncertainty makes the game what it is.  And when you actually have a good encounter with another player, it feels great.  Sometimes people help each other.  Sometimes you just wave and leave.  Sometimes you kill each other.  Sometimes you trust the wrong person and get absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥.  Thats the fun part.  Same thing with cheaters.  Yes, they exist. I'm not saying the game has zero cheaters.  But reading Steam discussions sometimes makes it sound like every second death is a cheater.  In my 1,000 hours, I have met 2 blatant cheaters.  Two.  And in total I've probably had my items returned maybe 6-7 times after getting killed by a cheater. Mostly on Stella Montis.  Could I have played against cheaters that I didnt realize were cheating? Of course.  I'm just talking about my own experience after 1k hours.  And honestly, my experience has been pretty damn good.  For the maps, I'm a pure Buried City enjoyer.  That map just hits different for me.  I love the layout, the atmosphere, the way the fights happen there, and just walking around the city itself. I can play Buried City over and over and still enjoy it.  But every map has its own perks.  Stella Montis has its own feel.  Spaceport is completely different.  Dam Battlegrounds has its own little spots and routes.  Riven Tides, Blue Gate, all of them play differently and give you different reasons to go there.  That's one of the reasons the game doesnt get boring for me.  You can go into a raid with one plan and 10 minutes later you're doing something completely different.  Maybe you find some insane loot.  Maybe you get into a fight with an ARC that you really didnt want to fight.  Maybe you run into two players and somehow end up helping each other.  Maybe you hear something huge behind you and just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ run.  Or you spend 25 minutes looting peacefully and then lose everything in the last 30 seconds.  It happens.  And then you press "play again".  The gunplay is good, movement is good, weapons feel good, the maps look amazing and the audio is probably one of my favorite things in the game.  You can hear a machine in the distance and already know you dont wanna be there.  The world also doesnt feel like some random multiplayer map made just for shooting people.  It feels like a real place.  And thats a big reason why I still enjoy exploring it even after 1,000 hours.  Is the game perfect? No.  There are things I'd change, bugs happen, I'd obviously like more weapons, maps and content over time.  But the core gameplay is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ excellent.  And after 1,000 hours, that's what matters to me.  I've played a lot of multiplayer games where after 100 hours I was completely done.  ARC Raiders somehow keeps pulling me back.  There is always another raid.  Another loot run.  Another "ok one more".  And sometimes that one more turns into 5 more.  So yeah.  It's a masterpiece.....  1,000 hours later and I'm still here.  Maybe the PvP problem isnt always the PvP.  Maybe sometimes people just need to stop shooting everybody they see. 😂  ****10/10.****  One more raid.

Almost never review games, but this one deserves a review.  I know the developers are kind of hesitant about making the game PvE because they originally sold it as a PvPvE experience. But, to be honest, I played for almost an entire month when the game was released, and the main reason I stopped playing was the campers and the really bad experiences that came with them.  I would spend hours farming, fighting, and preparing just to take down a big ARC, only for some guy with a free loadout to take everything from me—or, more often than not, kill me while I was extracting.  I also remember reading for months about the really bad hacker problem the game was dealing with. I never personally played during that period, so I can't speak from experience about how bad it actually was, but seeing all the reports and discussions about hackers definitely made the situation look even worse.  I get it. PvP is part of the experience, and for some people, that's what makes the game fun. At first, I was like that too. I think that's how most people feel when a cool and innovative game like ARC Raiders first comes out. There's something exciting about the constant risk of losing everything and getting into fights with other players.  But at some point, I realized that wasn't what I wanted anymore.  I just wanted to experience the game for what I personally found most enjoyable: fighting ARCs, exploring the world, completing quests, and enjoying the vibrant world that Embark Studios created—a world that, in some aspects, feels more alive than our own.  I actually downloaded the game again after deleting it many months ago, simply because they announced a PvE experience test that will last for a week. They have said that it isn't a permanent update, but honestly, all I want to say is that, for that week, I'm going back to dust off my Raider gear and spend as much time as I can killing ARCs and enjoying the world without having to worry about another player waiting around the corner.  Whatever happens after that week, I'm just glad I get to experience ARC Raiders this way again, even if it's only temporary.

But I cannot recommend a game managed by a studio that only listens to its community out of financial desperation rather than genuine respect for its players.

As always, it seems the Forza Horizon team never misses with these games. Well... almost.  Apart from the obvious cinematic downgrades, like character models being not that great with how stale they look, the driving is pretty nice. Of course, it isn't a real simulation for car driving and it's more arcade-y, that means it is much more accessible and easier to drive cars around the map (well, sometimes). Then, my favorite part of the game was actually the photo mode, how smooth it was, how refined it was. The photo mode blew my mind with how high quality it was, there were so many photos that I took and all of them looked incredible. Loved the photo mode.  But as all games like this, it will have seasonal updates and such coming to the game. But for me, it isn't enough for me to stay for that long. When a lot of the challenges are done and all there is left to do is to just drive around the map, enjoy the scenery, tune cars the way people want to, and just overall to enjoy the game. It isn't a bad game, it is quite enjoyable, but I feel as if there aren't enough content when you're actually done after a lot of the content has been completed.  So, overall, very fun, very enjoyable, very nice game. Just that the content was lacking. Fun for a week or two, then it slid down.

If you like Graveyard Keeper, you will like Graveyard Keeper 2. For the most part, it's exactly the same game. If you've played GK, you don't need any tutorial for GK2. Some things work slightly differently, and there are a few QOL improvements. You get a new graveyard, a new house, a new church, a new town, a new everything. This is Graveyard Keeper 2.0.  Ordinarily, I'd see that as a bad thing. I'm against developers releasing a "new" game that's little more than a map pack and story DLC for its predecessor (looking at you, Assassin's Creed) but in this case, I don't mind it. The gameplay is different enough that I'm fine paying new game price.  So what's new? No spoilers, I promise. Fishing is entirely worse. It is now virtually impossible to tell when you should reel-in and when you should wait. I don't understand why they changed it, but it is what it is I suppose. There's a new thing called "Inspirations," which are essentially in-game achievements. This dovetails with the new system of "masteries." Now you (and your zombies) have numerical stats for how well you mine, farm, embalm, etc. XP is still the same. You get Red, Green, and Blue XP for doing tasks related to manual labor, nature, and intellectual pursuits, respectively.  Without spoiling the story even a little, I'll just say the story is good, and makes a nice... I don't want to say "addition," but... let's call it a nice "companion" to the original Graveyard Keeper. You'll understand what I mean five minutes in.  To me, it always seemed like combat was an afterthought in Graveyard Keeper (and an entirely unnecessary one, frankly). In GK2, that's... not necessarily the case. The story requires you to do more fighting than the original, and the fighting feels more like an actual part of the game, as opposed to something that was shoe-horned in because the developer thought "this game needs some violence."  One nice little touch that I appreciate tremendously: remember the mumbling from GK? Well, GK2 has fully-scripted dialog with proper voice acting. But what's even better is that you can *disable it in the settings and stick with the mumbling!* That's the kind of thing you only get from a small developer who genuinely loves their own games, and I genuinely love it. I started my playthrough with the mumbling, but I've switched over to the voice acting and I'll probably go back-and-forth as my mood changes.  In my opinion, the new mumbling is not as good as the old mumbling. The old mumbling was very... for lack of a better term, "monosyllabic." Every character had at most two vowel sounds, and a few consonants. In GK2, characters don't "mumble" so much as they "gibber." Their speech is gibberish. It sounds a little bit (but not a lot) like Simish. Overall less charming than the mumbles from GK1, but still cute and funny.  In summary: I'm greatly enjoying Graveyard Keeper 2. I'm hoping the fishing gets easier once I get better fishing rods, but so far that's my only real complaint about the game. Having said that: the surprising inclusion of Steam Workshop makes me hope someone will put the original fishing minigame back in. In fact: I'm off to the Steam Forums right now to see if anyone is working on that, and to request it if nobody has yet.  So if you enjoyed Graveyard Keeper, you'll certainly enjoy GK2 just as much.

If you played the original Graveyard Keeper, then this one is better.  I've currently have 17+ hours and am giving my initial review of the game. Starting off, as with the original Graveyard Keeper, is a bit of a grind. The game does not hold your hand and lets you figure out within the research tree what to craft. You need smooth stone, but you also need bronze nails, you need a kiln, just look on the research tree and go down the list to see what you need and figure out how to get it. It's not that hard.  Graveyard management is similar to the last game, but you get a larger graveyard. Better visual improvements, and in my opinion, less of a tedious grind for resources.  Compared to the last game, I feel like getting resources in this game, using your character is far easier than the original. Which is an improvement to me. There is a transition from you producing most resources to eventually getting zombies to automate production so you can do other things.  Fishing has also changed and is no longer like Stardew Valley fishing, it is simpler and honestly better. It respects your time.  How does this game differ from the last? Others have said it, I will repeat it. Panic Reduction (PR). It doesn't feel good. Also, the factory aspect is more annoying than interesting, but its mostly PR.   I can understand the need to throw a wrench into the core gameplay loop, it gives players a challenge to overcome. Typically this is done by giving the player new tools to overcome those challenges. PR doesn’t do that, it’s an extremely binary faith tax, which only has one solution, pay the faith tax.   I think if they wanted PR to punish you, then they could instead affect the amount of gratitude gained, requiring more trades (or scrolls) to reach the same level of gratitude. This would incentivize the player to get PR, so they could use less resources to get the same amount of faith. While still allowing players who work harder to be rewarded with normal faith gains. Effectively giving the player more tools to play with.  So, yeah. The current PR system just feels like a lazy solution. Which is only made worse because it impacts gameplay too much. PR reduces faith production, which means you can’t unlock inspirations, you can't research certain reagents without faith, and most importantly, you can’t reanimate zombies without faith.  Zombies, by the way, are pretty much the core mechanic of the sequel, you cannot complete the game without it.  Zombies are required for your church. Zombies are required for fighting other zombies. The factory crafting stations require zombies to craft, and select items are only craftable in the factory, by zombies.   Ah yes, the factory. The other problematic aspect of this game.  Designing a factory is an iterative process. You make mistakes, need to add new production lines, you might be able to spaghetti a path to make it work.  But GK2 makes this as miserable as possible. - Belts consume power. This means you have a finite number of belts to work with per zombie. Not a bad design choice, if it was the only issue. - Iterating on the factory isn't free; I believe you don't get all resources from a building until you unlock a certain inspiration perk. Which means tearing down a factory to make changes costs you resources to rebuild. Better not make any mistakes. - PR limits the number of zombies available, on top of needing zombies to fight, you'll be shuffling zombies between the barracks and factory until you unlock higher PR tiers later in the game. - Dismantling structures requires you to pick up the dismantled ingredients on the ground before you can place a new building. Items on the ground prevent new buildings from being placed... I'm sure there's a reason, but also... why did they choose this solution? This is really only a problem for belts, as stations need to be torn down manually.  Some other minor gripes;  Why is there no town architect menu? Right now, you have to check every building to see what they need, write that down, then come back. An architect villager (or a mason or whatever) which you could ask for a synopsis would be extremely nice. Especially since rebuilding the town is yet another required mechanic.  Why isn't there a global build menu for the current area? The graveyard already knows when you are in it because it shows the graveyard score. And items on the ground already prevent buildings from being placed, so the game has logic for preventing placement. Being able to just enter an area to build in it would certainly improve the factory experience, and just be a nice QOL feature for the yard, church, graveyard, etc.

I went into this game optimistic - the updates and dlc for GK1 seemed to indicate that the developers understood where the grind and pain points were, so I was looking forward to a game built from the start with that understanding.  And at first I was impressed. Quest NPCs were available every day, so you weren't constantly stranded at the wrong end of the week to do a simple quest hand in. Early faith costs were low and didn't gate most of the early content from being unlocked. I don't like that you have to manually empty every crafting station when it finishes - it means I'm forever hovering around home just to keep the iron smelting, but on the whole it seemed better  Then the early game ended, and it was like they only smoothed out the design wrinkles from the first act. Faith costs soared - you need 5+ faith points to unlock a skill point, and when you get enough skill points you unlock a perk point, and the only perks really worth aiming for are the perks that give you another attribute point, because those are the ones that actually make you better at doing things and most of the perks amount to being slightly better at specific subtasks.  Then the focus on zombies just really grinds the game down - even in the early game, they suggest using zombies to automate your front yard, but you may as well not bother - the zombie supplier doesn't unload your workstations unless they too have a zombie on them, and you won't want to do that because they are so crushingly slow that you might as well craft it yourself. You are given a factory floor which is both very time consuming to setup (hope you like growing flax, simple conveyors use a whole bolt of cloth per single tile), and requires more zombies at every stage - zombies power the factory, run the assemblers, dig up the raw materials and transport them. again crushingly slow, and only worth it for things you can't produce any other way. Combat? Yep more zombies. Each squad requires 4 and you need more squads as you clear combats.  The problem with all those zombies is: A) getting the zombie book from the astrologer is aggrovating - he demands endless favours, and every time you do the thing to get the book he just asks for another one and your character just says "ok" B) FAITH TAX. the game introduces a mechanic that has you use faith to offset the number of zombies you have. You know, the zombies the game has been requiring you to amass? Better pay up. There is one day in per week where you must pay your faith tax. The penalty? Reduction in faith earning. Yes, a person struggling to pay a faith tax is rewarded by getting even less faith. Once again a GK game is massively throttled by faith input - even moreso since you need to go out and recruit your congregation anew every single week, since there's a new "thumbs up" resource that governs church attendance that resets to zero after every service.  Hold on - didn't I say at the beginning how nice it was not to be stuck to specific days too much like in GK1? But there's only one specific day to pay the tax, when it should be fine as long as you pay it some point before the service? Oh yes, that whole dance comes right back, just lightly later into the game. Want to fight zombies? Sorry, only on Moon Day. Need more zombies? Sorry you can only make them on Green Day. Want to help people move into the town? Nope that's red day business, we don't want help on any other day.  I'm not saying all day mechanics are bad mind you - it makes sense for things like there being one day a week where the merchant ship docks and things like that, but plenty of them are just there as "time management" problems, only the only time management you can do is realise you need thing X, and that it's still 4 in game days until X is available, so hurry up and wait.  All in all, this feels like the devs only worked through the initial experience, and are relying on people's investment to carry them through a roughly thrown together mid- and end-game. Save your money for a game that's been designed all the way through - or maybe when this has 3 dlcs fixing its faults, pick it up in a bundle on sale.

The things I liked: +Artwork is still great just like the last game. It's clear it needs a good 6 more months of time in the oven.   [h1]I Wish I Liked Graveyard Keeper 2 More[/h1]  I really wish I liked this game more. I loved the first [i]Graveyard Keeper[/i], although I certainly had my problems with it too. Unfortunately, many of those problems remain in [i]GK2[/i], while some new ones have been introduced.  There are things it does very well. It looks great, the mechanics generally feel more fluid than the first game, and once you get your first zombies working, the automation can be incredibly satisfying.  [b]Unfortunately, that's also where many of my problems begin.[/b]  [h2]The Automation Needs Work[/h2]  Zombies are a great idea, but they're incredibly stupid. If a zombie finishes chopping wood, for example, he won't go find another available task. He'll just stand there while other work sits unfinished.  The obvious solution is to assign multiple zombies to every workstation, which means you frequently end up with a bunch of zombies doing nothing.  Simply allowing zombies to seek out available work within their assigned area would make this system dramatically better.  The zombie skill trees are also unnecessarily restrictive. A zombie can only learn as many skills as the corpse had red skulls, and useful skills are often scattered across different branches. It makes creating specialized zombies feel less like meaningful customization and more like being arbitrarily prevented from making the zombie you actually want.  [h2]Progression Often Feels Backwards[/h2]  The tech tree has some strange progression decisions. Some things are heavily gated behind quests, while other branches are practically wide open.  Graveyard decorations are a good example. You can unlock high-level decorations so quickly that I found it more practical to skip most of the lower tiers entirely. Why repeatedly tear up and rebuild my graveyard when I can just wait for the best decorations?  Which is especially strange in a game called [i]Graveyard Keeper[/i], because the game barely gives you a reason to actually maintain your graveyard.  After the initial quest to improve it, you're largely free to ignore it. I've repaired huge portions of the town and completed countless quests, yet my graveyard still looks like garbage because the game has never really given me a reason to improve it.  [h2]Faith Becomes an Enormous Bottleneck[/h2]  The Faith system is another major frustration.  You don't generate very much Faith each week, yet it's required for seemingly everything: prayers, zombies, talents, and various other systems. Some talent upgrades can cost 25+ Faith just to redeem a fraction of a talent point.  Then the game introduces another system that [b]reduces the amount of Faith you earn because you have zombies[/b], unless you spend even more Faith to mitigate the problem.  So I'm being penalized for using one of the game's primary mechanics, and then asked to spend the same resource to stop being penalized for using it.  That's just frustrating design.  The factory suffers from a different problem: it's barely explained. You unlock complicated machinery without much indication of what the components actually do or how they're supposed to work together. I don't mind complicated systems, but I shouldn't have to reverse-engineer the entire thing through trial and error.  [h2]The Biggest Problem: I Feel Directionless[/h2]  But all of these issues pale in comparison to my biggest problem with [i]Graveyard Keeper 2[/i]:  [h3][b]I don't feel like I'm building anything for myself.[/b][/h3]  Your character is effectively a permanent errand boy for the townspeople. Repair this. Fetch that. Build this. Unlock this so you can help that person.  And for what?  Repairing the town unlocks more residents, which increases your Like cap, which makes your sermons more successful. Then you're essentially acquiring another resource so you can acquire another resource more efficiently.  It feels like [b]busywork rather than progression.[/b]  This is where I think [i]Graveyard Keeper[/i] misses something important about games like [i]Stardew Valley[/i] and [i]Coral Island[/i]. In those games, you're primarily improving your own life and pursuing your own goals. Helping the townspeople naturally becomes part of that process, and building relationships with them actually feels meaningful.  In [i]Graveyard Keeper[/i], NPCs mostly exist to give you quests or sell you things. If you don't currently have a reason to interact with them, they often have nothing to say.  There's very little sense that you're actually becoming part of a community.  And that's especially strange because your character doesn't even seem to have much of a personal goal. He's been isekai'd into this world, decides he's perfectly happy staying there, and... apparently just wants to spend the rest of his life doing errands for everyone else.  [h2]There Is a Great Game Buried in Here[/h2]  That's what makes this so frustrating.  I think [i]Graveyard Keeper[/i] could be a fantastic dark-humor take on the cozy farming/life-sim genre. The foundation is absolutely there.  But I think the series needs to look more closely at [b]why games like Stardew Valley and Coral Island are compelling[/b], and then build its weird, macabre systems on top of that foundation—not in place of it.  Give me goals of my own.  Give me reasons to care about the people in town.  Give me a reason to actually maintain my graveyard.  Make the zombies smart enough to automate the work they're supposed to automate.  Let the game's systems complement each other instead of constantly putting up arbitrary roadblocks.  [hr][/hr]  [i]Graveyard Keeper 2[/i] does a lot right, and there are definitely things I prefer over the original.  But too often, it feels like the game is making my job harder simply because it can.  [b]I really want to like this game. I just wish it gave me more reasons to.[/b]

I was really sure this review will be positive and for the first 15-20h of the game I had tons of fun. I just thought that I'll wait just a little bit longer to make sure the experience stays the same... and it suddenly changed when the factory mechanic came into play.  Let me start by saying that this game has serious identity crisis and doesn't know what it wants to be at its' core, because it's "jack of all trades and master of none". Graveyard Keeper is just the title of the game, not the core of it. You can pretty much completely ignore the graveyard for the entire game and nothing will become of it. Technically you could also ignore it in GK1, but the first game was convincing you to keep caring for it unlike here.  Corpses are also a lot easier and BORING to deal with. You can pretty much just spam one type of embalment to get either lots of white or red skulls and call it a day and this is what the game actually encourages you to do. Just baffling.  The game has some side activities that let you break from the main gameplay loop and spice things up. Something I very much appreciate in games. Here it's tower defense and rebuilding the town. Very unfortunately both are done so poorly that I don't feel the need to do either of those things. I'm not earning anything new through battles, it's always the same loot, battles always look exactly the same. If you seen one battle, you've seen them all. I'm also not really gaining anything of substance by putting all my time and energy into rebuilding the town, including vendors.  And then we have the factory... [b]I absolutely hate it.[/b] It's good to have an option to automate certain things in games, so you can focus on more engaging stuff, but I don't want to automate almost every single thing. I don't want to play Factorio, I also don't want zombies to do everything for me. [b]I want to PLAY the game, not watch it play itself.[/b] At first I was trying my best to avoid using the factory until I realised I won't be able produce lots of stuff without it. I'll be cut off from big chunk of content, which honestly sucks. Why can't this thing be optional? Just let ME craft stuff, even if it takes longer time.  Writing and art quality also took a massive hit. Writing is several levels below the first game. It's not interesting, not amusing, it just... is. Completely without any soul. And art style in cutscenes... It reeks AI. Developers said they didn't use it, but whether it's true or not, artsyle still remains completely hideous compared to GK1.  Overall, feels like developers wanted to create a completely new title, but decided to play it safe and put it all into known and popular game from their own shelf. They mixed it all together and we got.... something I guess.

However, the core gameplay loop gets incredibly repetitive. Ultimately, all you do is constantly gather resources, scan fauna, and craft items across planets that quickly start to feel very similar despite being procedurally generated. Even the aliens you meet feel lifeless and static. While you can build bases, the mechanics feel a bit clunky, and the overall building system ends up feeling somewhat pointless.  Compounding these loop issues is the horrible performance. I am running an RTX 4090 paired with an AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D, and I would expect a locked, stable 120 FPS in a game like this. While space and certain planets run great, most planet surfaces cause my framerate to tank all the way down to 60 FPS, sometimes even dipping into the low 50s due to severe CPU/engine bottlenecks and uneven frametimes. Turning off Low Latency Mode and dropping DLSS to Performance helps slightly, but it makes the game look completely blurry and terrible, which defeats the purpose of having a top-tier rig.   It's a massive achievement, but between the technical frustration and the underlying gameplay lacking the depth to keep me hooked, I just can't recommend it. The main things I like about NMS are the ability to do low orbit flight & seamless flying from ground to orbit. But it's not enough to carry a game. I encountered so many game breaking bugs in 20 hours. The Caveat:  Once again the binary review system means I have to leave a red tick in the box when I really don't want to.  So let me start by saying this and getting it out of the way - I've got a lot of hours in this game.   It's the sort of game you put a lot of hours into.  I've got more than my money's worth and at times I've enjoyed it a lot.  It's not a bad game, the devs seem to genuinely care and I have high hopes for their future projects.  So why the negative review?  Because there is no option.  I can't in good conscience leave a positive review, because of all the things wrong with it.  Do I recommend it?  I guess.  But there are a LOT of caveats.  Slightly Relevant Story Time:  So let me tell you a story.  When I was in my teens, I spent a lot of hours in Frontier: Elite 2.  A LOT of hours.   In Frontier Elite 2 there were two main factions (all human descended) who had spread over a limited area of space, with clear cultural differences between the two.  Beyond that there was a sort of frontier bit and independent worlds, and then.... nothing.  Just planets.  So eventually I tooled up my trusty Tiger 2 with a gas scoop and mining rig and travelled 6 months into the beyond (since you needed to maintain the ship every year lest the engine lunch itself a 6 months journey was pushing my luck) to a pristine earth-like, fighing off a billion bandits to get there... somehow landed the ship on the planet and dropped the mining thingy.   And I felt like a real explorer!  Even though it was just green and the only thing I mined was water.  You see, it wasn't easy to do.  It needed planning, and serious execution.  No matter it was a waste of time in the end and I more or less immediately stopped playing.  Never mind that.  This game was made in 1993, after all.  What is NMS?  No question No Man's Sky is an extraordinary piece of engineering.   And it is awesome when you first scope out new planets and wotnot.   But (extremely grindy storyline aside) there is NO GAME.  It's a cosy base-builder.  Now a cosy ship-builder.   But where's the jeopardy?  Where's the mystery in the universe?  Procedurally Similar:  There are 3 races, who are EVERYWHERE.  There is nothing to distinguish them but their avatars.  They all have the same missions, the same station designs, the same... everything.    If you happen to stumble into a wormhole and end up 167,000 light years away then you'll find the same aliens and the same station design there too!  Wait - 167,000 light years away you say?  No matter, just step into the teleporter and you can go straight back to your base - even if you don't have a teleporter there!  All the above even applies to other galaxies... other dimensions!!!  Even better once you have teleported across inconceivable reaches of space and time, step outside the door and somehow your ship has instantaneously made its way across half the galaxy with its 100ly hyperdrive and no fuel left.   The same goes for your freighter.  In fact, once you have teleports set up you don't really need your ship to get anywhere, unless you're going to explore a bit.    And as for exploration... there's lots to discover, but at the same time absolutely nothing to discover.   It's too easy.  It's all too easy - making landfall on a new planet should be an exciting adventure but it's so easy to jump / teleport / jump / teleport it becomes routine.  It all means that whilst you can explore in theory endlessly because there is no jeopardy there is no sense of achievement in doing so - which is exactly what exploration should be all about.  The Grind:  Honestly, once the novelty wears off, it's a grindy collecting things game.  Which has no idea what it wants to be.  Stung no doubt by the criticism of the lack of content on launch, they've proceeded to shove in every sci fi trope they can think of.  But it just doesn't hang together.  The main story of the game, with all its dark premonitions, even the character of the races, with the slightly threatening Vykeen or the very logical captain Korvax has the immersion broken completely when the NPCs emote cheerily at you just after threatening to rip your throat out.   I see what it tries to be.  It looks at titles like GTA or The Witcher and thinks hell a Pokemon min-game or a fishing challenge are just the ticket.  But they are jarring in this context.  And besides, what both those games had in the first place was an actual game.  So it's highly forgiving, and I get it, not everyone wants to be punished in a game.  Maybe this disconnect is just a product of how I like to play games.  I love Kenshi, and Rimworld, and Dwarf Fortress, and Star Sector, to name a few.  None of those games hold your hand.  But in a game about exploration should make the exploration bit a rewarding challenge, not routine.  And a lot of this is a product of procedurally generated play.  There's no real room for variation, which is the ultimate irony.  Because it's procedurally generated there is no need to go anywhere either - literally no need to go more than one jump from your home system, in order to see the whole game.  I see why the stations are all identical, so people can find things, but you have teleports, can't you have an explorable randomised station with teleports to get to crucial areas at the entrance? Every freighter, no matter what the freighter, is laid out identically.    What I'd love to see (at least as an option):   - If you teleport somewhere, you don't take your ship with you, and you can't instantly call your ship/freighter/whatever from another dimension whenever you want to.  If you want to go to a different system, you have to actually GO there.  No more calling ships or freighters over improbable distances. - Sparser stations.  There shouldn't be a station in every system, and they shouldn't all have the same services.  Also they shouldn't all be identical.  It just doesn't feel like you're travelling anywhere at the moment. - Sensible population distribution.  The nearer you get to the centre of the galaxy or whatever, the more stations there are.  Vykeen/Gek/Korvax zones of influence.  Potential border disputes.   I get it's all procedurally generated, but it must be tweakable.  This would all help immersion no end.  There should NOT be an identical districution of the same races 200k light years away.  It's just nonsensical. - More races.   Where are all the humans?  where are all the races you see travellers being?  Where are they? - Actually, where do all these Gek/Vykeen/Korvax live?  Do they have home systems, cities, whatever?  I suppose they all live at my settlements.  There you go. - tougher planet distribution.  It should be HARD to find habitable worlds.  But they are everywhere in this game.  Again I get that people love finding the 3 legged tube creature from hell, but imagine how much more it would mean if you needed to travel through 10 systems to find it. - Gas giants... WTF?  I know you wanted to do the pretty cloud bands, but seriously, read a science book, guys.  Or read 'The Algabraist'.  I was expecting a whole new game mechanic involving clouds or whatever, it could have given corvettes something else to do, but instead it's just another planet which is a waste really.  Chin Stroking:  I think part of the reason I'm writing the review is because I did put so many hours into this, to discover there is nothing at the end of it.  You think at some point you'll find something, but you never do.  You hope you'll round a corner where you find something new and amazing but it is never there.  The point is, I've wasted a lot of time on it.  Honestly, when I think about it I've spent more time on games I've given negative reviews to than I have on some of my favourites.  I think I am an optimist.  Don't get me wrong, the game is very good at killing hours and hours.  But then most games are.  Maybe I should just get out more instead.  I haven't even seen all the real world has to offer yet.

No mans sky seems to be asymptomatically approaching becoming a good game. Hello games continues to add interesting concepts and systems on top of very flawed bones.  I’m just going to list some major issues. The game is never challenging in an interesting way. Difficulty is added exclusively with grinds. Everything feels same-y. Every system will have a set of identical features randomly tossed a bunch of barely distinguishable planets. Every planet must have all the resources available to survive there easily (taking the form of bright glowing plants), so preparation is almost never necessary. All space stations have the same internal structure with a few color changes. The universe teems with spaceships and life, but none of them do anything or matter.  The game wants to be “casual” to a fault. While a few features require some work to reach (autophages, purple stars etc.) the real meat and potatoes are thrusted upon you at the first possible moment. Features like freighters and settlements are given comically easily.  The multi tool sucks. every single thing is done thru this one thing. Why? It just feels shallow. Would it not be cool to look across the galaxy for the best bolt caster or gravitino coil? Would it not be cool to have multiple tools and  weapons strapped to your character?  Combat is shallow and so easy it’s boring, especially in space. There is little tact or skill to it.  However the devs have not sufficiently addressed any of the core problems. Instead they pump out more interesting concepts with often shallow executions.   They have the whole salvaging thing, and the xeno arena, and fossil collecting, but never a survival overhaul or a combat redesign. Hell they hid better worldgen in endgame content most never see  But it’s not over, I have hope for this game still. The cosmos update was legitimately promising tho flawed. If they have the guts to really switch things up they could make this game a masterpiece.
