TLDR: I think the reviews are overly negative, the game's fun and charming, if you like long ass grinds you can leave on in the background, you'll enjoy late game as well, if not, you'll probably enjoy up to mid-late game, and then stop. I have issues with the game too, but overall my experience has been enjoyable.   Checking the reviews for this game was an experience to say the last, people complain about the big grind, and how hundreds of hours in the game makes little to no progress, now, I understand, If you don't like that, then yes that will be annoying you, the late-game grind of this game takes ages.  However I do want to bring up, that yes, you spent "hundreds of hours" to make little to no progress, but a good 99% of that time was spent, doing something else, its a weird thing to complain about, my PLAY time is probably less than 50 hours at this point.  The game's charming, it's got a style that it accomplishes fairly well, the early game is quite fun, I'd say I enjoyed the middle to early late game part the most actually, hell difficulty was fun to get through, I had to change up my build a ton to make things work, which IS the majority of the fun of this game for me, the build making, having to scrap together what you can to make a semi-good build based on purely theory knowledge about the meta that you will likely never achieve unless you wait another 10k hours to farm it out, and that part, is still there in the endgame for me, in torment, I've had to look at what weaknesses my team still has, and have been slowly adjusting them to make small bits of progress. I should probably add that I do not spend money on games like this out of principal, though I do agree with a lot of the reviews that it is VERY tempting to do so, sometimes you do just want to skip the waiting, that is a fair critique, that they're using this as a source of monetization. On the topic of plaguelands, I will agree that this update is also frustrating, I don't really find other things frustrating in this game, but plaguelands does bug me a bit, I understand the concept, hell, I like the concept, a waaay high level area, that you can grind for ultra rare gear, but takes longer and you have to have an amazing team to actually make waves. The problem, is that, anytime i've farmed plaguelands, it has felt like a complete and utter waste of my time, I think it's a combination of plaguelands having its own rune upgrades, the way longer time to farm a single map, and the insanely low drop rates, two of these by themselves wouldn't be issues, if I had maxed out the runes of plaguelands already, it'd likely be worth farming, but until then, I feel it is useless to me, because I gotta farm another 9 billion coins before it can match the normal levels output items and gold wise.

After playing for 1k+ hours the following is what you should expect from the game.  Early stages you should just be patient, its possible to build arcana grade equipment overtime. Just farm on stages that you can clear.  The good things end there.  After playing for a long time you might be able to get 1 beyond of your level.  You should not expect to see Celestial or Divine in your lifetime that is level 80 or 90. New content reinforces this where there are no drops at all. You can keep the game open for 500+ hours and notice your equipment have not progressed at all. You can synthesize 90 Arcana equipment and end up with 1 Arcana. Do not be fooled by its availability in the Steam Market, said equipment is the privilege only limited to those who played the game at its early stages.  The game will give you offering coins that will sometimes yield beyond items. In reality, its a system to guarantee you get a beyond gear or higher that is low level. Level 50 or lower. The game has many fail safes this way to ensure that your gear is not updated.   Why am I still playing? Sometimes you just want to validate that turning that 1k hour into 10k hours or 100k hours wont matter. You still wont get a level 80 or 90 celestial or divine equipment.

There is no "incremental increase". Your characters reach level 101 and stop. Then it is just farming gear. Slowly, based on luck. To reach higher map levels you have to buy gear for real money or play hundreds of years to be lucky to get the infinitely rare drops.  Forget about selling items on the market yourself. The market is full of bots. You won't sell anything.  I played it for the game, not the market so I tried to enjoy it but seeing the game basically stops once your characters reach level 101 -which I reached after maybe a week or so (incredibly short for this kind of idle game)- there is little to nothing to enjoy.  I usually like to have some idle games running in the backgrounds while I work but this one has no progression.

The Sims 4 is essentially a game in which you spend four hours setting up a family, two hours building a house, and then only thirty minutes playing the game before you decide that your Sim should go through a tragic storyline for no apparent reason.  The game is in fact a lot of fun. You're able to construct houses, create Sims, assign them jobs, damage their relationships, and generally take a hands-on approach to the lives of people who have no notion of what you're doing to them. The range of possibilities is quite ridiculous.  Even so, mods and CC are essentially a must if you want the game to reach its full potential; the vanilla Sims 4 is similar to ordering a burger and receiving only the bun, while the mods and custom content are equivalent to the meat, cheese, fries, and dubious sauce that you didn't realize you needed.  The main drawback is the situation with the downloadable content. There is so much DLC that it would make your bank account sue you for restraint. When you look at the store, you immediately start to wonder why a virtual washing machine has to cost money. By this stage, I believe my Sims have more expansion packs than I have real furniture.  The game does have some decent moments; for example, the Sims will randomly loiter about doing nothing, cancel the action you have specifically instructed them to carry out, fight someone that they are said to love, and then go outside to complain about being cold even though they are wearing a winter coat.  And somehow I still keep coming back.  8/10. I'd recommend it, provided that you're willing to download 47+ mods, 300+ pieces of CC, and then spend the whole of one evening sorting out all the problems following an update.

Hard to recommend at this point, even after around ~130 hours across EA and Steam. The aggressive, anti-player monetization structure that continues to gatekeep QOL and only focused on profit-driven content and gameplay expansions for the majority of the life of the game left a seriously bad taste in my mouth.  EA/Monetization ethics aside, TS4 gets a few things right: - Sheer scope of "life sim" after so many years of expansion is truly impressive. It is very obviously the most developed of it's type not including games with heavy modding communities, and is objectively top dog for that ask. - Surprisingly accessible given the amount of systems present in the game, and surprisingly cohesive as an experience. - Still manages to be "fun" in both a "live mode" capacity and a "build mode" capacity. It is no small feat how many things TS4 is to so many people.  That said, there are some drawbacks: - TS4 definitely feels like the most corporate, whitewashed, family-friendly, neo-conservative game it has always sought to be. It is totally idyllic in nature, which makes it surprisingly hollow in a media market moving ever more towards gritty, authentic themes. - TS4 is amazingly mid in it's performance and of course, riddled with bugs as it holds on for dear life after too many years and too many add-ons. - TS4 is seriously limited by the instancing and some systems that were clearly stripped back from previous Sims games, which really shows the overall age of the game.  I don't know - I can't realistically recommend TS4 in good conscience anymore. The game itself is okay, if severely out of date, and I do think you should consider major up-and-coming competitors like Paralives and InZoi, but I understand they are unpredictable bets to take - and TS4, despite the flaws, is the safest bet for the most robust and best supported out-of-the-box life sim game.

game_name: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition
review_text: Many games since 2011 and maybe even prior have more profound systems and mechanical depth. Maybe the lore of those games is more coherent and themes treated are more mature, There's something about Skyrim however that sets it apart from everything else. Idk if it's nostalgia but the impeccably consistent art direction, worldbuilding through places, people. dialogue. literature, weapons. spells and more when paired up with THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ INCREDIBLE OST and the sheer grandeur of the in game moments, both in the scripted sections and random encounters just makes something click. Goosebumps. Is it immersion or is it a sense of a better era gone by? I am not sure I just know Skyrim is a monumental presence in the history of gaming and my personal gaming journey. I'll take the essence of what this game has made me feel to the grave with me and for that I am grateful. A totally subjective 10/10   Edit: I have played this game on 360 (pirated bootleg copy when i was 12), PS4, Nintendo Switch, VR, Steam Deck. PS5 and PC again, and again, and again. Thats 3 Desktops, 1 laptop, 2 handhelds, 3 consoles and VR. I have thousands of hours in this world though Steam only tracks my Steam Deck/New PC playtime. Just thought it was relevant information to preserve. I am also incredibly saddened by the state of Bethesda and have made peace with the fact that TES6 will not uphold the magic. I have decided instead to cherish how precious Skyrim was. No one and no thing can take that away from me.

review_text: Yes and no (not as good as its popularity would suggest).  - Buggy as hell. After over a decade Bethesda decided to release an update that kills peoples' free mods and pushes more overpriced paid mods but has done ♥♥♥♥ all to address the numerous bugs (things falling out the sky and dying randomly, some equipment not rendering on characters of certain races correctly, inability to progress many quests... the list goes on and on). I'm writing this review in frustration after finding this out having come back to the game.  - Bad game design. Dragons killing all the NPCs (especially bad on high player level). Unbalanced as ♥♥♥♥: rewards you for putting all your points in alchemy, enchanting and smithing, creating super equipment that one-shots anything, while people who want to actually role play a certain style might lag behind as they level.  - Incredibly shallow and limited dialogue for key characters like followers and faction leaders. Only real exception is Serana, who you cannot marry like other NPCs without mods. The Witcher got this right, Fallout NV/4 was an improvement. You need to rely on mods (when Bethesda isn't breaking them) for actual RPG immersion.  - Inability to turn down quests, some (like thieves guild) are shoved in your face and just stay in your journal with the same dumb greetings from NPCs as if you were even thinking of doing their ♥♥♥♥♥♥ quest that goes against the personality of your character. Vast majority of quests are extremely linear with no way to complete them in a way that suits you.  - Perk system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Some perks are OP (e.g. Necromage) whereas entire skill trees are worthless (lockpicking and speech). So much apparent choice in playstyles, but realistically not really unless you want to completely waste your level ups.  That said, the voice acting is well done, the game is generally quite beautiful with a good musical score. There is a lot to do, even though most of it is mind-numbingly shallow and repetitive.

game_name: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition
review_text: TL;DR: Bethesda shipped a patch almost nobody on PC asked for, and it took a sledgehammer to my six months of modding work. The ecosystem is still picking up the pieces.  What happened  On August 27th, Bethesda released the "Additional Hotfix" on top of this month's Creations update, the first game update in two and a half years. For console players and the Creations storefront, it's polish. For the PC modding ecosystem, it was a runtime bump (1.6.1170 → 1.7.99 → 1.7.104) that broke the dependency chain the whole scene is built on:  - SKSE, the Skyrim Script Extender, is the foundation under thousands of mods. It went incompatible the moment the patch hit, and every mod depending on it stayed dead until it got rebuilt. - Address Library, the translation layer plugins use to find game internals, shipped in a new binary format (v5). Older plugins don't politely refuse to load; they fatal-error on boot with dialogs you can't click away. - PapyrusUtil, Papyrus Extender, editor ID fixes, media key fixes: broken, all of them, waiting on maintainers to rebuild against tools that had to be updated first. - Custom setups like ours (a six-month AI-driven SkyNet build with voice, world simulation, Dynamic Economy and companion services) didn't lose data, but the runtime backbone went dark in one patch cycle. Every launch is a wall of "incompatible / needs recompile" dialogs.  Six months of building, silenced by one patch, with zero communication about the damage done to the people who keep this game alive fifteen years after release.  What we got instead  Here's the list of "essential" fixes that justified breaking the ecosystem:  - A crash when opening the on-screen keyboard on the PS5 main menu - A crash when opening the map multiple times on Xbox - A PS4 storage display fix ("14 of 15 GB used" message) - Console mod storage raised to 15 GB - Box art in "stunning" 3640×900 to bring the store "to parity with Starfield" - A "Most Popular" sort button for the Creations store - Creations bundling, WIP bookmarks, and instructions on how to report mods - Updated credits - A pile of Creations storefront bug fixes: sale pricing, version numbers, title formatting, text clipping  Console crash fixes, storefront cosmetics, a sort button. None of it touches gameplay. All of it breaks the free modding scene.  And the part that really stings  PapyrusUtil alone is required by thousands of mods and has been maintained for free for years. Its update has been sitting under review for over a month. In the same patch, the pipeline for paid Verified Creations got achievement-friendly status, new file formats, and Creation Kit quality-of-life updates.  Free modders wait in line for a month to ship a fix the community needs right now. Paid content gets the red carpet. Am I supposed to believe that's a coincidence? Gates and review queues for the free side, a wider door for the paid store — at some point that stops being luck and starts being the business model.  Where we stand  The base is already rebuilt on our side: SKSE 2.3.1, Address Library for 1.7.104, updated Tweaks and Papyrus Extender are in. The work continues, because we still care about this game.  Fifteen years of free labor built this ecosystem. It deserves better than being treated as collateral damage for a storefront refresh.

I really like Street Fighter 6 and would recommend the game because the gameplay itself is genuinely fun. However, Capcom’s monetization is extremely greedy and takes away from the overall experience.  The base game is already $54.99 , but if you want the full roster, you have to spend a lot more on DLC characters and character passes. That feels excessive for a full-priced fighting game, especially when a large portion of the roster is locked behind additional purchases.  I don’t have a problem with Capcom selling extra costumes. What bothers me is charging for basic outfit colours and other things that feel like they should have been included. Characters such as Akuma and Sagat were part of the base roster in older games, so seeing them become paid DLC feels disappointing.  The game itself is great, but Capcom’s pricing makes it difficult to recommend the complete experience without mentioning how expensive it can become.  Overall, I like SF6 and would still recommend it, but I really wish Capcom would be less aggressive with the DLC and microtransactions.

I am leaving a positive review for this game but with a caveat. The gameplay is amazing. This is hands down the best fighting game and I say that as someone has thousands of hours in almost every fighting game you can possibly think of. Street Fighter 6 is an amazing game for both fans of the franchise and newcomers. Modern controls adds an extremely viable option for people who are new to the series or fighting games in general. Classic controls are the same controls we've all grown up with and feel great. Overall, if you like fighting games or Street Fighter, this is absolutely the best game you can possibly buy. That being said, here comes the bad.  THE BAD  This game is insanely overpriced. The base game is fine for the price but the cost of the game with all of the DLC is absolutely insane. There are way to get the game and the DLC cheaper(if you know, you know) but that being said, Capcom really needs to start coming up with a fairer microtransaction policy. If they could somehow fix this or make a really worthwhile bundle, this game would absolutely be a must buy.  The best thing I can recommend to folks who are interested. Look into the characters included in the base game. Use the fighter rental tokens that Capcom gives to rent and try other fighters you don't have. Once you have a good grasp on who your main is(or if you already know because you're not new to  the series), purchase only what you need. So if your main is in the base game, then there you go. If your main is in a particular character pass, get that particular pass or use fighter coins to buy that specific fighter. This will save you on a lot of money.   One thing I hope that Capcom could do is start free weekly rotation fighters so that people who don't have a lot of money could at least try all the fighters and then purchase the ones they want based on their experience.   OVERALL SCORE  9.5/10 for the actual game 4/10 for the microtransactions 7/10 Overall score for the game and microtransactions combined. If they fix their monetization though, this score will definitely be much higher

If you are looking for a game to completely decompress after a long, exhausting day at work, this is it. At first glance, it might look like a casual simulator, but it is so much more. It has become my ultimate go-to game after a stressful day. There is something incredibly therapeutic about driving tractors, managing your fields, and watching your hard work literally grow and pay off. It completely reboots your brain. Beyond just being relaxing, the game is a fantastic tool for developing real-world skills. It heavily rewards good organization and critical thinking. You constantly have to plan your budget, time your harvests around the weather, and manage logistics. It forces you to make smart, calculated decisions—from picking the right machinery to optimizing production chains. Whether you want to play it casually with a podcast running in the background or go full-simulation mode with realistic mods, this game delivers 10/10 value. Highly, highly recommended for both casual gamers and strategy lovers. A perfect escape!

[h1]Farming Simulator 25[/h1] [b]Excellent visuals, but I recommend waiting for a sale.[/b] [i]Updated September 9, 2026. Written as an FS22 player, FS25 server renter, and someone with small-farm and livestock experience.[/i]  [h1]The Good[/h1]  [b]Pumps N' Hoses is finally here[/b] The free Pumps N' Hoses Pack launched on September 8, developed by Creative Mesh and published by GIANTS. This is exactly the kind of farming-focused addition I welcome. I hope returning content continues to be improved and expanded, not simply brought across from FS22 and left there.  [b]Excellent graphics and ground deformation[/b] The detailed graphics look fantastic. Visually, I have little to complain about.  Ground deformation is a genuine improvement. Tires leaving ruts and reacting to softer ground make fieldwork feel more physical. I like how vehicles affect the ground, even though the separate landscaping tool still needs work.  [h1]The Mixed: Not Entirely Good or Bad[/h1]  [b]Familiar gameplay, but familiar limitations[/b] Coming from FS22, the familiar experience makes it easy to settle in. However, some areas feel more like a continuation than a meaningful upgrade.  To my ears, the standard sound design feels familiar too. I have not noticed the same leap in audio that I see in the graphics.  [b]A good animal selection, but limited involvement[/b] I enjoy the variety of livestock, but animal farming should involve more than supplying resources and waiting for products.  I grew up watching my father shear sheep and have raised chickens myself, so the simplified care routines stand out to me.  [b]Reasons for cautious optimism[/b] Beans & Alpacas, scheduled for October 27, 2026, promises manual shearing or hiring a worker. That is exactly the kind of choice I want.  I want that approach extended to existing livestock, especially sheep. I hope GIANTS is adapting, but I am not putting all my eggs in one basket.  [h1]The Bad: Areas That Need Improvement[/h1]  [b]Animal care needs substantially more depth[/b] Chickens are my clearest example: the standard care system requires feeding but no water-refilling task. Having raised chickens, I find that disappointing. A basic water-care option should be a free improvement, not paid DLC.  I also want bedding replacement, coop cleaning, day-and-night routines, and optional illness and flock-health management. Caring for animals should mean more than filling a resource meter.  Breeding could involve rams for sheep and a meaningful rooster role in producing chicks. Hens do not need a rooster to lay ordinary eggs, but breeding chicks is different. I also want to raise young male chicks, not just buy adult roosters.  Sheep should offer manual shearing or hiring a shearer. That should not be an interaction reserved for a different animal in an expansion.  I want deeper links between soil condition, crop and feed quality, storage, pests, and animal health. Advanced systems could be optional. I would consider an animal-care expansion, but basic care should not require another purchase.  [b]Repairs should involve more than a menu[/b] The repair experience still feels too familiar to me. I would like to open the hood, inspect components, identify a problem, order parts through a farmhouse computer, and use the appropriate tools to fix it.  Filters, batteries, belts, brakes, hydraulics, and damaged header teeth could provide practical tasks. Repair skills could improve with experience. Players wanting convenience could pay a mechanic or request vehicle collection and delivery.  Cleaning and maintenance could affect component wear and metal corrosion more meaningfully, creating practical work and a foundation modders could expand.  [b]Landscaping, roads, and fences need better tools[/b] The landscaping interface still feels too close to the FS22 experience. I want more precise controls and an easier way to browse and apply modded ground, yard, and road textures through clearly organized categories.  A connected road tool would help: place control points, adjust curves and heights, and let the road follow or shape the terrain. Fences also need smoother placement and alignment. Building a farm should feel creative, not awkward.  [b]Forestry needs a more noticeable step forward[/b] Logging and chainsaw audio feel very familiar. I wanted better handling and more interaction, not simply more equipment.  I would welcome optional tree regeneration, including a simplified setting where retaining a stump allows regrowth and removing it prevents that regrowth. This would not need to apply to every species. Server owners should be able to disable it.  [b]Weather should interact more convincingly with vehicles[/b] I have noticed rain audio that makes it sound as though rain is hitting the vehicle even when it is sheltered inside a building. That breaks the immersion.  I want more convincing rain and snow effects on windows, with water running across the glass and wipers making a practical difference to visibility.  [b]The server-management interface feels outdated[/b] As a paying server renter, the web panel I use is a frustration. I have not found convenient mod-name searching, useful active/inactive filters, or straightforward bulk selection and removal.  Managing many mods should not require so much manual searching. Removing selected mods or clearing the collection should be straightforward without risking the savegame.  This describes the panel I use, not every hosting provider.  [b]Mod support and content priorities concern me[/b] Modders add enormous value, but the variety available for my interests has grown more slowly than I hoped. I have heard complaints about restrictive approvals, but cannot verify individual cases or blame every delay on GIANTS.  Quality testing matters, especially in multiplayer. I would like a clearer, efficient approval process that supports creative mods without unnecessary restrictions.  The free Emergency Pack from Creative Mesh, published by GIANTS, is not content I personally want on my server. Rural emergencies have a place, but firefighting is not my priority in a farming game. I would rather see more depth in everyday farm work.  [b]Smaller farms deserve more attention[/b] My experience included a small John Deere used for mowing and pulling a wagon, not a fleet of expensive commercial machinery. I want more emphasis on that starting point: compact equipment, hand tools, small trailers, and practical small-farm jobs.  Small tractors exist, but I want stronger gameplay around them and progression toward larger operations.  [b]More optional multiplayer systems would help[/b] I would like a built-in way to list and sell an entire farm to another player, not just manage individual land purchases. Player-run stalls where people buy and sell goods would also make a server feel more connected.  Optional hunger, thirst, fatigue, and workplace injuries could add depth to realism-focused servers. Owners should control these settings and recovery times, with everything switchable off.  [h1]Final Verdict[/h1]  [b]Worth considering at a discount, but not worth full price to me right now.[/b]  FS25 has strengths, and Pumps N' Hoses is a positive step. However, too much still feels like FS22 with improvements around it, not the deeper farming simulator I hoped for.  I want more attention given to existing systems before the focus moves to the next addition. Farming should feel like more than operating increasingly large equipment.  Before buying, watch an ongoing YouTube series from someone who plays regularly. Look beyond trailers and opening episodes, and check which features come from the base game, DLC, or mods.  [b]Overall, it is a decent game with potential, but it still needs substantial improvement. Do your research and buy it on sale.[/b]

Integrated Tools: FS25 includes a simplified, built-in version of Courseplay, though the standalone Courseplay mod on FS22 is still superior if you know how to use it.  Mod Selection: Since most players buy for the mods, FS25 does not currently offer enough modding depth to justify buying it over FS22.  Final Verdict: Stick with FS22 for now or hold out for the next entry, unless you specifically want the updated vanilla features.   Side note: I will not be addressing any bugs as I was only testing base gameplay. I did not witness any besides some light framerate issues.

I love PoE2, but I can't recommend the game at the state it is in right now. The story is fine. Player to Player trading is well done. Crafting is gambling. And my bone to pick, the endgame being an illusion of choice for player power. No matter what build you play, it all comes down to 3 things;  [u]1. + level of skill on gear[/u] Its a must have on every gear you can slap it on and if it's not on your main weapon you can throw that gear away, even if the other stats are best in slot. This also mean that the Unique weapons (legendries) without any "+ level of x skill" becomes redundant as well.  [u]2. Jewels in the Passive Tree[/u] The iconic complex Passive Tree in PoE2 has some node where you can place a jewel in them. these jewels are so over tuned that the best way to increase your player power is to add as many of the "jewel socket" nodes as you can and filling them up with jewels. Ignoring most of the passives nodes on the PASSIVE tree. Though the high end jewels are expensive, that is 99% of every build's endgame goal.  [u]3. How fast your character clears content[/u] Though this point is more extract, PoE2 is trying to stray away from the insane power creep/ speed of PoE1 by making the skills "not as fast as PoE1" (is the best way to put it for me), what this caused is the redundancy of about more than half of the skills presented to us. Skills that have too much setup or slow animations are just deemed useless, (without a "Cast on X"), an example for this is a skill called Parry, it is a mechanic that was introduced with the Huntress on the buckler to help set up combos, but because it requires an enemy to attack first it was deemed too slow and not a single build uses it, not to mention all the parry nodes on the Passive Tree becomes redundant with it.   These are what comes to mind after playing the game for 1k+ hours, I believe in GGG will do something about this, as build diversity is the core selling point of PoE. But I can't recommend this game at the moment with the early access fee.

Disclaimer: I know it's alpha, however, I don't see how issues I will be talking about might change in the future. It seems to me that they are a part of this games nature and can't be simply patched out of existence.  First, my problems with the game (talking about early game mostly):   1. No real tank support, especially close mellee like mace (you are presented with builds to become tanky, but you will mostly have to dodge anyway up to the very end game).  2. Horrible hitboxes for big bosses, again, for mellee build it will be very bad. Get used to being moved around the arena with their bodies as if you were palying some 2005 game and at the same time not being able to land a hit.  3. Incredibly slow pace. I like spending time listening to lore, appreciating the scenery. Unfortunately, you just don't have enough mobility to explore at any reasonable pace. If you really unimaginably enjoy the very map you are walking through and you don't have much to do besides this, well, this is a game for you.  4. Tradies vs HCSSF - you either go around in easy mode buying literally anything at any time and so it ges boring fast or you spend hours crawling through campaign without mandatory items (you will die because of dot quasi-oneshot anyway). In the end it doesn't really matter: it gets boring pretty fast or you just find out that you can't sustain the lifestyle this game demands.  4. The story is literally stolen from Diablo 3, it is so obnoxious it is even a bit goofy, one good thing is that not-Leoric's wife this time was not executed by him, she is a strong and relatively independent woman (like Maghda, she is literally Maghda, you'll see in Act 2).  5. I am sure that there are more endgame issues, there are many problems people were discussing in chat, but I didn't experience some of them, so I won't even mention them.  Cool stuff: normal-size enemies feel alive, they react to any impact, that's really fresh, you movements are also very natural. Gem management is cool and simple, much less demanding than POE 1. Well, in general, it's just like POE 1, but with a few tweaks and even slower.  Conclusion: If it was possible, I would make a neutral review, however, choosing between positive and negative, I choose negative now and mostly because I don't think that the problems I was talking about will ever change. This is a wonderful free game, well, just because it is free obviously, but I don't think it will help if I put "thumbs up" at this stage of development, especially because of the fact that I actually bought it and didn't just receive it for free.

The Myth of Strategy: How Civilization VI Degenerates into a Bonus-Gathering Race Having spent countless hours navigating the tech tree and dealing with the mid-game tedium of Civilization VI, the initial illusion of a grand historical and geopolitical strategy game eventually gives way to a harsh reality. Beneath its polished hexagonal veneer and sweeping orchestral score, the vanilla game suffers from a profound structural identity crisis. It is marketed as a grand strategy masterpiece, but once the curtain of artificial difficulty and mechanical gimmickry is pulled back, Civilization VI reveals itself to be little more than an inflated mathematical spreadsheet—a hollow bonus-gathering race masquerading as statecraft.  Artificial Difficulty as a Substitute for Intelligence The most glaring indictment of Civilization VI lies in how it handles AI difficulty levels. True strategic depth requires an opponent that adapts, anticipates, and counters the player's long-term maneuvers. Instead, the game relies on crude, lazy scaling multipliers. Higher difficulties do not grant the AI superior tactical reasoning; they simply gift computer-controlled nations extra Settlers, massive baseline yields, and compounding percentage bonuses to science, culture, and production right out of the gate.  Because the AI's tactical and operational decision-making remains fundamentally inept, the game resorts to handing out free real estate and resource advantages just to keep the player from winning too quickly. Consequently, early-game survival is not a masterclass in grand strategy, but rather an exercise in overcoming arbitrary handicap imbalances, rendering true strategic outmaneuvering nearly impossible.  The Death of Diplomacy and Genuine Geopolitics A compelling strategy game thrives on dynamic geopolitics, evolving alliances, calculated betrayals, and fluid diplomatic leverage. In Civilization VI, diplomacy is reduced to a rigid, predictable system of static agendas and transactional trade windows. True betrayal, opportunistic cooperation, and long-term strategic alignments do not exist in any meaningful way. The AI operates on erratic, hardcoded logic loops rather than rational self-preservation. Nations will denounce you for arbitrary reasons while ignoring glaring existential threats, transforming international relations into a superficial checklist of agenda-pleasing rather than a tense, living web of power politics.  The Flawed Lottocracy of Era-Specific Leaders Another fatal blow to strategic consistency is the design philosophy behind leader abilities. Many leaders are hyper-specialized around a specific historical era or a single narrow mechanical gimmick. When a civilization aligns with its designated temporal window, it becomes overwhelmingly, absurdly powerful. Yet, the moment that era shifts, or if the terrain fails to cooperate, that same civilization plummets into irrelevance. This creates a deeply unbalanced experience where historical alignment feels less like a strategic archetype and more like a high-stakes, single-use lottery ticket. If you roll the right combination, the game plays itself; if you do not, you are permanently bogged down by structural disadvantages.  Vanilla Desolation and the Illusion of Modded Salvation Perhaps the ultimate proof of the game's core failure is the state of its vanilla version. Out of the box, unmodded Civilization VI is virtually unplayable for anyone seeking a genuine strategic challenge—it is tedious, predictable, and mechanically shallow. To make the game bearable, players are forced to rely on massive overhaul mods (such as AI improvement suites and balance patches). Yet, these essential mods are rarely about adding fresh, optional content; rather, they serve as frantic emergency patches designed by the community simply to fix what Firaxis left broken. When a strategy game requires hundreds of megabytes of third-party patch-work just to function as a competent tactical simulation, the underlying vanilla design has fundamentally failed.

This might be the worse-designed game I have ever played, and I've been playing video games since they were invented.  I made a good-faith effort to learn how this game works, but I was met with extreme hostility when I sought out assistance from fans. You have to memorize SO MUCH. Luxuries like Tea span multiple cities, but CERTAIN amenities span 6 tiles, but SOME only affect the current city, and trade routes move "production" (????) from one city to another somehow, and campuses have to go near mountains (why????) and you can't upgrade your units unless you select this SPECIFIC TECH way down at the bottom (despite already having rocketry and satellites) and if you don't upgrade your units, the XP goes to waste and it doesn't TELL you to upgrade your units. The World Congress ungrays the "Next" button if you spend all your points, so the bad design makes you THINK you HAVE to spend all your points when you don't have to. It's possible to purchase policy changes, but if you lack the gold, the button is completely hidden, so it's possible for the game to NEVER tell you about this mechanic. The game doesn't tell you the pros/cons of open borders or explain that zealots IGNORE borders, or that sending an Envoy to a "Technological" state will boost YOUR tech (why?????). It has icons that look like cities, but it turns out those are just "suggestions" and you can actually plop a city anywhere. Same thing with farms, mines, etc., the icons are misleading. The advisor LITERALLY LIES to you to make you lose, so the new-user experience is awful to begin with. You found a religion and gets tons of faith points, but you can't spend them on anything unless you "build" an Apostle (for some reason?) and the game doesn't explain that OR tell you how to GET an apostle. The tutorial shows you the very basics, but only like, "Here's the purchase screen." It doesn't explain WHY you build ANYTHING or any of the win conditions or what sorts of obstacles you should prepare for. But if you need a tutorial to explain how to click buttons, they got you. You can't learn as you play because it doesn't explain why Spain suddenly, randomly got a Diplomatic Victory or why your units can't compete with another city's units despite the fact that you've been playing for the same number of turns and they're the SAME UNIT. It doesn't explain why building a Taj Mahal gives you a benefit. (Trump destroyed the reflecting pool and nothing happened, so I know that stuff doesn't matter IRL.) There are tons of bonuses to be had, like if you build multiple units of a type, it boosts some Tech or Civic, but none of it makes sense! You wind up doing random things to get bonuses and it's soooo unfocused. Like, I built 3 archers I didn't need, NOW WHAT? Do I just delete those now? It's so dumb.  And if you get a bad start, you could be doomed to lose no matter what you do, so all of that above might not even matter.  Nothing is explained anywhere, nothing just "makes sense" intuitively, and you will be insulted if you ask for help.

Spending 125.4 hours inside OBS Project’s famous recording and streaming program can be an experience that ranges from productive to painfully frustrating. While many creators praise the software for being free and powerful, there is another side to the story—one filled with crashes, confusing settings, endless troubleshooting, and the slow psychological drain of wrestling with technology when you just want things to work.  To begin with, one of the most common frustrations comes from the overwhelming complexity of the settings menu. OBS offers an enormous level of control: bitrate, encoders, rate control, keyframes, scaling filters, color spaces, audio monitoring, scene buffering, and more. For a beginner—or even an intermediate user—this can feel less like a creative tool and more like a cockpit of switches waiting to break something. Over 125.4 hours, a user may repeatedly tweak settings hoping for the perfect recording quality, only to discover that one small change ruins performance, causes dropped frames, or produces blurry footage. The constant cycle of “adjust, test, fail, repeat” becomes mentally exhausting.  Performance problems are another major pain point. OBS relies heavily on system resources, and even moderately demanding recording settings can push a computer to its limits. During long sessions, users may experience lag spikes, stuttering recordings, audio desynchronization, or the dreaded “Encoding Overloaded” warning. Few things are more discouraging than finishing a long recording session only to discover the footage is choppy or unusable. After 125.4 hours, this repeated disappointment can make the software feel unreliable, even if the real issue lies in hardware limitations or configuration.  Crashes and instability also contribute to the negative experience. Although OBS is generally stable, it is not immune to plugin conflicts, driver issues, or random failures. A crash in the middle of an important recording can instantly erase hours of effort. Over time, this unpredictability builds anxiety: users may constantly worry whether the next session will succeed or fail, turning what should be a creative process into a stressful gamble.  Then there is the plugin ecosystem—both a blessing and a curse. OBS plugins extend functionality, but they can also introduce new bugs, compatibility problems, and performance issues. After enough hours, users often find themselves juggling plugin updates, version mismatches, and mysterious errors. Troubleshooting becomes a routine: searching forums, reading logs, reinstalling components, and hoping the next attempt works. This maintenance burden can make OBS feel less like software and more like a never-ending technical project.  Audio is another notorious source of frustration. Balancing microphone levels, desktop audio, monitoring, filters, noise suppression, and sync delay can be incredibly finicky. One small mistake can produce echo, clipping, silence, or distorted sound. Many users spend countless hours just trying to make their audio sound normal. When problems appear mid-recording, the result can be unusable content and wasted time—an especially painful outcome after long sessions.  User interface friction also adds up over extended use. Scene management, source ordering, and nested setups can become confusing, especially in complex projects. Accidentally muting a source, hiding a layer, or misconfiguring a scene can ruin a recording without immediate notice. Over 125.4 hours, these small frustrations accumulate into a sense that the software is constantly working against the user rather than helping them.  Another hidden difficulty is psychological fatigue. Recording or streaming for long periods is already demanding, and technical problems amplify that strain. The more time invested, the more frustrating each failure feels. Users may begin to associate OBS with stress, disappointment, and lost effort. Even when things work correctly, the memory of past failures lingers, creating tension during every session.  Despite all these criticisms, it is important to recognize that much of the frustration comes from the software’s power and flexibility. OBS tries to accommodate countless hardware setups, workflows, and creative goals, which inevitably introduces complexity. However, from the perspective of someone who has spent 125.4 hours battling settings, crashes, and performance issues, it can certainly feel like a deeply flawed and exhausting tool.  In conclusion, while OBS is widely respected and incredibly capable, extended use—especially over something like 125.4 hours—can reveal its harsher side. Confusing configuration, performance struggles, instability, plugin chaos, audio headaches, and mental fatigue can combine into an experience that feels overwhelmingly negative. For some users, OBS becomes less of a creative companion and more of a stubborn obstacle standing between them and the content they want to create.

This game is less about designing your dream dress, and more about making dresses that satisfy rigid criteria and completing tedious tasks. Designing the sketch is probably the most fun part of the game, but you have to keep clicking back and forth to find the cut you want because you can only view one design at a time. I am often making ugly dresses for my clients in order to satisfy their desired criteria, because the gameplay is geared towards ticking boxes rather than designing beautiful dresses (because so much of the gameplay is tedious I don't want to risk getting a bad score and taking longer to progress). However, it doesn't feel very rewarding when a client tells me how much they love my awful dress.  Most of the tasks are monotonous rather than fun. Measuring is so simple that it seems unnecessary, while adjusting the mannequin to size is quick but tedious. Cutting the fabric requires a bit of thought to try to waste as little material as possible, and you have to rotate every piece to its optimal position. Sewing is time consuming even though all you do is make sure the fabric moves in the right direction. In general, gameplay is very repetitive and uninteresting. One toils, step by agonizing step, over the digital sewing machine. Agonizes over the precise drape of the taffeta, the cinching of the bodice, and the delicate, painstaking embroidery that graces the hemline. And for what reward? What grand crescendo awaits the diligent artisan?  Nothing but a hollow, ghostly void! By all the saints of haberdashery, thou art never permitted to behold the finished masterpiece upon the lady’s ACTUAL BODY!  To deny a seamster the divine revelation of the final fitting. To rob us of the sight of our creation breathing life, contouring to the elegant slope of the shoulder and the graceful sweep of the hip is a mockery most foul. A garment without a wearer is but a tragic, limp shell; a silken ghost of unfulfilled potential!

More of a Dress up/Design game rather than a Dressmaking Simulation  I wish you can leave a neutral rating because this game certainly has an audience for it— however when I saw the measuring and pattern cutting in the advertisements I expected something totally different.  Now upon beginning you measure 3 parts, busts, hips, and waist, which would be fine I guess if you were actually cutting the pattern and making adjustments to those measurements but the measuring itself is just a minigame where you get points and does not interact mechanically with the actual garment construction. When cutting out the patterns you place them on a fabric but it's just a minigame as the patterns are readymade and there is no interaction with the measurements you took or any creation of a pattern.  The sewing part is yet again another mini game where you have to follow a line on the garment piece adjusting your keyboard but it is nothing more other than that, you're not going to have any stitch selection or have interactions with the seams between the different pieces of the garment, it's just a minigame where you have to line up the feed dogs using your keyboard.  The characters are cute and the story seems lovely but it's again it's a dress up/management game rather than truly a "dressmaking" simulator. It's more similar to something like Love Nikki  So if you are looking for a game where you can select many parts of a dress with a lot of combinations while managing a shop with a cute story that then this will be perfect for you, but if you want something with deeper mechanics and dressmaking I'm afraid this just isn't the simulation "dream game".

I wanted to love it, especially as my new sewing machine arrives tomorrow. The gameplay loop, though, right now is bad enough I ended up not even finishing my 2nd dress. Thinking of repeating the clunky interaction with each dress in the future made me quit the game with sadness.  1. This is a sewing simulator. I doubt you will like it if you want to try it out for the designing features similar to how people played Sims for decorating houses and finding creative ways of letting your Sims d** whilst never touching the actual game. In dressmaker! it's like...you have to run an actual Sims game to finally be able to arranging the living space. There is no shortcut, no group selection, no fast forward/skipping. Every single piece of pattern needs to be individually selected and positioned on the fabric. rearranging asks you to again select every single piece individually. Cutting them - the same. Putting the cut pieces into your inventory - the same. What might be meditative and calming for some, can be tedious for others. Be aware of this amount of mouse input to get things done.  2. Interface and interaction with it can be wonky and unusual if you're used to play games on a regular basis. examples: When putting cut pattern onto your dressform, you need to find the right angle from which your camera looks onto the dress to unlock the snapp function. This angle can be disturbingly specific and happens often enough to start becoming annoying.  Or: When looking onto your rolled out fabric and layed down pattern pieces, using your mouse wheel does not scroll the screen to the right/left, but rotate the last active pattern piece you have touched, even though it's not actively selected.  Instead you need to click arrow icons to move your camera. I see t challenge of being thoughtful with your positioning in order to save material as a part of the game, though, so if you're used to more common usuage of the mousewheel you have to fight that behaviour pattern. Together with the "click everything individually to do stuff" the gameplay right now incites you to just rush this thinking part to get it just done.  All in all, it doesn't sound as much of a problem to some. But be aware: patterning and sewing is 2/3 of the whole game time wise.   Dressmaker! in this state feels like a soul's game where animation predictions aren't timed right so it doesn't feel satisfying to fight. Some will still play, others politely turn to other titles. I will patiently wait some more time before returning to it and hope it will be in a more polished state.  If you're desperate for sewing games and aren't preprogrammed by other game titles on how smooth things can be interacted with, go for it. Otherwise you might struggle staying immersed.  Also: tutorial is bugged ( eg look at the negative reviews): when you start with your first customer Rose and beginn the patterning process, the turorial ask you to select your chosen fabric. In case your tutorial already started with your chosen fabric selected, nothing on the screen will work out until you select some other fabric so the action can be counted as "done". Just go back to your actual one after that and follow through with the next steps. You can also lay down all patterns first before going for the scissors and cutting them. I'm a min maxer, even in turorials, maybe you are too. Cuz it seems that you will continue the "real" game with the money and material left after your tutorial. And you can hard lock urself number wise :D fun

300 hours across both XSX, PS5 and now PC. This game is finally in a really good spot, and it makes me happy to recommend it. We also finally have the return of a missing fan favorite character, though it was kind of lame. Old Blizz would've had a sweet pre-rendered cutscene that had the character be heroic and amazing, but modern Blizz just had some in-engine cutscene where they just showed up and talked about emotions and hugged... but whatever, I'll take it I guess as long as the game is fun.  And man is it fun now. Building a character feels good! You no longer need to give up and go to Ivy Veins for some OP endgame metabuild. You can reasonably put something together that remains viable in the endgame and I love it. Endgame feels great now too, War Plans are a fun way to get you to cycle through activities and keep the grind from getting stale, and leveling up the activities and tweaking them with their own skill trees is superb.   It took a while, but Diablo IV is finally in a spot where you can play it for hours and not realize the time's flying by. It's just fun now in the same way Diablo I-III are. Really the only crappy thing (outside of some spotty writing) are the cosmetics. $20-$50 for single skins and mounts? I get that you're doing that because the whales will buy them, but how about a little respect for your fanbase? Some of the stuff is really cool looking and I'd drop $5 or even $10 on em, but these prices are ridiculous. At the end of the day, that stuff is easily ignorable, so whatever. Just keep the game at the good fun place it is now and I'll be happy.  Just, for the love of god, take the lessons learned here and apply them to Diablo V

============================================== 50 hours played, Season 15. Made it through "Acts I  & II" ==============================================  TL;DR - Do not spend more than $10 for this. Do not buy the expansions. Do not use the cash shop.  A friend offered to buy this game for me so we could play together. I initially refused on the grounds of giving Blizzard-Activision money, but at $5-10 sale, I felt that the value was warranted.  The game is gorgeous, runs well enough, and is addictive in it's gameplay loop. A lot of what's there to love about Diablo is here, but it is offensively bad in too many ways to recommend for anything more than $10, which it typically falls down to every 3-4 months (Usually with the start of a new season).  The games script was thrown out 9 months before release, completely re-written from the hands of two CD Projekt RED writers they brought in that wrote for The Witcher 1, 2, and Cyberpunk 2077, due to the script containing characters that were victims of abuse.   As a result, the story is now about generational trauma inflicted by your parents. Nyrelle, in particular, is so insanely insufferable that her Act alone left me comfortable skipping cutscenes from then on.   Diablo is no longer a medium where you can indulge fictionally about human suffering. It is about an asian-american girls frustration with the emotional abuse laid onto her by her immigrant mother. It is about doing better to help one another make a better world. It is about treating others with respect and kindness.  It is about being an epic Diablo Hero.  The story is mostly nonsensical, and full of fetch quests and long cutscenes about people being upset and hurt feelings, in a world where writing in that way comes off completely tone deaf.   I'm wearing a belt made out of dead children skulls for a stat boost according to this flavor text, why exactly am I listening to a 5 minute cutscene about someone's feelings getting hurt?  I killed 800 bandits to retrieve a stolen satchel of gems, why am I being lectured about how someone cant trust the church anymore? Do these people understand the setting they're putting these melodramatic, sentimental hallmark movie moments in? I don't think they do.  I will say, I am happy to see Debra Wilson is still getting work essentially, everywhere, AS Debra Wilson in the game. Loved her in MAD TV.   The sub systems, grind, and functionality of the endgame are very bland by comparison to it's modern contemporaries, and the cash shop is one of the worst I've seen in all of triple AAA gaming. For example, right now a set of cosmetic armor runs roughly $35 USD, more for "premium" sets. Sets that appear on your screen on a 1 inch tall character, surrounding by flashing lights and blood SFX.  The cheapest thing in the shop is a $12 pet goat you can wear on your back.   The shop also runs strange, predatory systems where it will show you certain sets of armor for sale based on the character you play, and how often you check the shop and look at certain things. You cannot buy the same things as your friends, it is custom tailored to your habits.  There's a lot more that I could say. I could rant, but I'll drop a few points that feel pertinent to me before I stop;   - Diablo II remastered costs more than this and has more people playing it. (Very good remaster, worth your money!)  - Diablo does not appear in this game, outside of a $20 pet in the cash shop.  - Hamburger Hepler is the lead narrative designer for Diablo V.   Stop giving Blizzard your money.  EDIT: The pet goat is $18.

When I first started the game, it took about 20 minutes to actually get to real game play due to all the "let's get set up and signed in" crap that comes with so many AAA games, nowadays. However, once I got in, the first cinematic was pretty good. Then the game play started and the quality of everything went down, sharply. This game was made to keep you busy. Busy, busy, busy. I really don't think the devs know what fun is, cus the content here is wide-spread and lacking in flavor. Like old butter, spread too thinly upon moldy toast. Monsters are pretty much all the same... or at least it feels like that. The bosses and rares have unique names, but for some reason play no differently than weaker monsters spread around the game world. I have played 11 hours up until this point. I've played over ten dungeons, mapped a lot of the first area (which is way, way too big), done countless event encounters, and seen lots of kinds of loot. The game is vapid and lacking, which is odd because it felt good when you get started.  Alright, let's focus on something specific. Combat. As an action rpg, this kind of game is ALL about the combat and fighting your way through monsters to get loot and get more powerful etc. I'll just say it plainly: the combat sucks. It's repetitive, boring, and lackluster. EVERYTHING is too easy. I have died once, and it was because of a lot of pop-ups that happened mid-combat. Apparently, I leveled up and unlocked a few things, which caused pop-ups to confuse me. So, I pressed ESC, expecting the game to pause... and it didn't. I am playing in single-player mode, with no interest in multiplayer ever, but the game doesn't pause when you're in game menus. WTF?! The devs are not on your side. The devs are not interested in making good UI content or a well designed experience. They want you to play, and play, and play, and play, and play until you can't anymore.   More specifics... all the myriad of ingame currencies. Plenty of people have said this before me so I'll be brief. There are tons of seemingly rare ingredients and resources you pick up and I just can't understand why there needs to be such variety when each thing is used once or twice for very specific things. It's so dumb and wastes the player's time. Does it make sense for a berry bush to give you relics? No. No it does not. Do we need furs and leather and iron to play the game? Nope. It's there for crafting, which doesn't seem to serve any purpose other then giving you more things to waste your time with. Crafting in this game is an afterthought, added because they saw other better games that have it and they had FOMO. Crafting should be useful. Why craft an item mod or item when something better will drop in ten minutes when you level up again. Which brings me neatly to the reason I actually hate this game...  The levelup system and combat difficulty. Why isn't combat difficulty up with the combat paragraph? Because it's intrinsically tied to your character's level. Like the debacle of Fallout 76, all monsters are scaled to your level. Let me say that again. The difficulty of the entire game is scaled to you and your current level. Why is that important? Because no matter how strong you get, the game is tailored to your level. Meaning, mathematically, nothing will ever get harder, easier, or anything other than the same exact difficulty you are having. It is incredibly monotonous. Got a new sword that does double your damage? Too bad, the monsters now have double their previous health. Got new armor that gives you far more defense and higher health, too bad the monsters do more damage and just enough to do around 2-5% of your HP with each hit. There are no stakes. It's just... boring. Monster encounters are procedural, tasteless, and seem to exist just to give you yet another thing to do.   How would I improve the game? Make the maps far, far smaller. Make enemies scale to their AREA, not the player. If you are too weak and you run into an area way above your level, it's supposed to be difficult. That's called "challenge". Challenging content is fun because it makes you overcome yourself and be better. When everything is the same, you never improve because it's (all) (the) (same). I don't understand what kind of mental state led to this kind of game development.   How else can we improve? I've heard that the campaign is fun, but I can't for the life of me get to any of it. There is so much busy work. Walk here. Get there. Do this boss that isn't fun. Talk to them... Oh right. One more big thing. The dialogue is... I have no polite words for how stupid the dialogue is. This game is rated M for mature. The audience are adults. Yet a lot of the dialogue is repetitive, inane, and uninteresting. THERE ARE EXCEPTIONS. But the overall experience is extremely poor. The characters' interactions are obvious to the point that the devs must think we are all as dumb as rocks. "Pick up that controller and mash those buttons because you are dumb and you can't do puzzles or think about what to do."   Playing this game feels like I'm slowly being skinned by an ant wielding a very small, but very sharp spoon. I am not joking when I say this: the "Librarian: Tidy Up The Arcane Library" game was more exciting than this game. It also was more engaging and clearly was created to be fun. This game? Not so much. There's a game coming out where you have to sort through a massive pile of hay to find a needle, and that looks like it would be more fun than this game. I bought this game at an extreme discount (only 13 bucks) and I still feel like I've been cheated out of my money.   To be honest, there are a few things I do/did like about Diablo 4, but they are massively overshadowed by the colossal landfill that is the collection of reasons why I think this game is bad. Do yourself a favor and play Path of Exile 2 (or 1, if you are really dedicated). Or Blue Prince. Or Talos Principal. Or Tyranny. Actually, yeah, go play Tyranny is you want to experience a game with real heart and passion. K, rant over.

CONTROL Resonant is not Remedy's best work, that still handidly goes to Alan Wake II, but it follows up the original with a lot of funky ideas and cool levels that really play into the eccentric aspects of these games. A lot of what I like about CONTROL is here, but what is *not* here is that game's overall structure and de-emphasis of RPG elements, which this game is now fully embracing. It takes some swings and it's not a complete home run, but it struck more than it missed for me.  The shift from shooter to melee combat is a nice shake-up overall, and I'd say they solidly translated a lot of the same health / damage resource management of the original despite a totally different combat framework, but that melee combat is quite simplistic and extremely mashy. It almost feels Dynasty Warriors esque actually, in terms of regularly shifting between filling up resources from trashing adds or focusing on the actual beefier enemies to kill. I was actually enjoying the combat more at the start when it felt like I had to keep my focus up to prevent getting easily murked, but it's really easy to power level and stomp stuff just by doing the game's side content, and the game's runtime makes the simplistic combat a bit tiresome by the end. I'm mixed overall, since a lot of it is *well designed* but it also definitely drags a lot and starts to feel choreish, but this is how I felt with the first CONTROL, funnily enough.  The open world design is also far more conventional, but does give room to a lot of fun secrets, and the puzzles/riddles + traversal challenges are actually real deal challenges, huzzah! Sad the standard is low for the AAA space in this regard. I felt like I was gonna get exhausted with the open world by the end of it, but the later areas ended up having really fun gimmicks made for some of the game's best moments, so that ended up not being the case. That said, I'm not the most in love with this style of open world design personally, but it does play a lot into the superhero action energy that this game is going for, and you know what? We haven't gotten one of those in awhile. Especially not one that's made for a more adult audience.  Ultimately what really tips this over into a recommend for me has to be a lot of the game's many, many other strong suits. The music is excellent, Dylan is a compelling character (as is a lot of a lot of the returning and new characters), and the tone is set so well by both its decent writing and impeccable art direction. There are a lot of *very* memorable, killer sequences in the game that make keeping up with this Remedyverse worth it. All of these components, put together, remind you that there's no one else out there making AAA games like Remedy, and that's particularly refreshing given recent releases.

For a quick summary, this game's great. Some "fine" aspects: Combat, performance, sound design. Not stellar in these respects, just fine. Where the game is stellar is in its story, environments, and gameplay structure. I think it's very important to note, however, this is the most somber of any Remedy title. The game can feel pretty slow, and it doesn't have that constant levity previous games had. There's funny moments, instead of being a funny game. If a more downer experience sounds like a terrible time, come back when you're more willing to give it a try.  [h1]Combat[/h1] To keep things brief, this is an entry point into melee action combat. It starts out deep as a puddle, and deepens more in power usage than raw melee combat. Resource management and build synergy has more to learn than melee combos.  [h1]Movement[/h1] It's quick, and it's fluid. One of the main things one does in this game is move, and moving is enjoyable. Play with a controller if you're having a hard time controlling the movement, and check the options if you'd like easier to toggle on sprinting at the cost of it becoming basically automatic. The game's built on bigger movements instead of precise ones, so it's far more floaty then the original Control, but a lot more fluid.  [h1]Structure[/h1] The game's a proper open world metroidvania-ish experience. You start out with limited access to the world, and gain abilities to access more of that world, re-exploring previous areas encouraged, and sometimes required. They've committed to this hard, with a lot of side content from more radiant encounter style objectives, to one in each zone activities, to some puzzle spots around the entire map for a lore + stat reward. You're properly encouraged to explore, and rewarded for it. The game also splits world mobility and story progression, letting you get ahead in one aspect, until you have to reach a wall you need to complete some of the other to get past. It's not complete freedom, the late game is reliant on you having those mobility tools, so they're unskippable, but they're delayable.  [h1]Environments[/h1] Even after playing the original Control, there's some awesome moments. The early game starts off as a city environment but weird, and the late game gets WILD. It's a proper escalation, where the environments start off less fantastical than the original, and becomes far more in the late game.  [h1]Story[/h1] The themes reach WIDE and maintain the depth those themes deserve. For an experience that not that much longer than the original, that's impressive as hell. It deals with peoples perspectives on each other, people's fears while living a tragedy, the blame placed on one's environment vs one's person, as well as some less directly approached themes that take more analysis to find, which I won't describe given that analysis is a part of what every player ought do instead of listening to it being described. Trust me, the most perfect "explained" video is still worse than finding what stories mean to [b]you[/b]. You'll be more likely to incorporate those lessons if you learn them through the experience rather than a retelling.  [h1]Performance[/h1] It's passable. I can only speak from my experience, however. I've seen some people have awful experiences despite the on-paper specs seeming like they'd be just fine, no idea what's up with any of that. Personally, the game was running with similar framerates to the original on similar settings, generally above 144 fps on high with the smallest amount of upscaling, no frame gen. I didn't try raytracing much, the top preset was still around 30 fps from some short testing. There's the Alan Wake 2 issue of having super blurry screen-space mirrors, but other than that, raytracing isn't that big of a deal IMO. I encountered 0 crashes throughout the game, one instance of missing collision (random wall, not important), one instance clipping through collision, and one instance of getting stuck in collision.  [h3]Note[/h3] The digital deluxe edition is the most minimal of any Remedy title. Some concept art and a title screen music player. It says it includes the soundtrack, but you sure as hell don't end up owning the soundtrack when you have to launch the game to listen to it. It also doesn't include the licensed tracks, those you have to go in-game for. A far cry from Alan Wake 1's entire book and musical score with soundtrack included in its game files, but these have been getting reduced more and more over time. Digital Deluxe is more a donation button than an actual product.

I loved the first Control, was one of the more recent games I completed to its full extent. The story, the visuals, the atmosphere, the gameplay and combat, all amazing. And the lore, somewhere between SCP and RE. So when they announced this one, I was excited. I picked it up soon after release.  The story picks up after the first one and explores outside the Oldest House, in the city of Manhattan. And so far, after about 5 hours in, the story is still pretty interesting. Maybe not as intriguing since the cat's outta the bag about the general vibe of everything, but some mystery still remains. HOWEVER...  The problem is the combat. It just feels weak, at least, maybe in the early game. In the first game, you feel like a superhero pretty early on. In this one, you ARE a superhero, but you don't feel like one. Dylan's attacks have no punch behind them for what the animations look like. Enemies are damage sponges and in any given encounter, there are a LOT of them. Most respawn unless you kill the larger ones, and they all tend to attack at once. One of the bladed enemies (IYKYK) will autistically flail around, hitting you multiple times despite trying to dodge and weave. And most enemies suffer from the new-modern AI enemy behaviour - spin-in-place attack. Even if you dodge at the right time, the enemy's animation will rotate on the spot, locking in on you and still connecting.  That said, after battling my way through a large section of the game, I got to another one of the bosses, in the theater (IYKYK) and it was... underwhelming. Atmospheric, yes. Visually and auditorily appealing, yes. Engaging, meh. The boss had maybe 3 different attack patterns that were easy to figure out, and the rest of the battle was more button mashing. Oh, and when I defeated it, all the previous enemies respawned outside and now they're tougher - despite me being rewarded with only a minor combat ability. Nice.  I'm sure I'm just too early on in the playthrough to unlock and explore most of the better combat mechanics, so I might keep playing it, and I would cautiously recommend it to anyone who liked the first one as it's in the same ilk as that, but the combat is such a slog. And there's a LOT of it. Every objective, every place of interest, every collectible, every mission has a ton of combat, and it's all relatively the same. Dash in, mash the attack button, dodge a few times, maybe use a special attack, button mash again, repeat. Maybe die a few times because of either a touch of jank, or the sheer overwhelming number of opponents. I really want to like it, and I wish there was a rating in between yes and no, so for now I will not recommend it and pray that it gets a little more enjoyable.

I've heard people compare it to DMC combat, which is insulting, because I'm pretty sure DMC ONE had more enemy variety and more combo variety. You just air juggle enemies and then use whatever your designated "damage" setup is, which sounds like it could be interesting, but 90 percent of my combat loop in this game was -> summon, dash attack to air launch an enemy, then hold down my heavy attack button to use my drill, which is just light attack spam into heavy attack spam. It looks like the game has combos, but it doesn't. Most the bosses are actually pretty solid though, oddly enough. The game runs reasonably well (I did have it running like the original control on a base PS4 a few times though (absolute crap)), and some of the environments are pretty cool. I can't even say if you liked the first game you'll like this one, because they're completely different genres. The vibe that the first game had is definitely not 100 percent here, either. I've been looking forward to this for nine years. The original Control (and the two DLCs) is my all-time favorite gaming experience, possibly even my all-time favorite storytelling experience of any kind.  After playing Resonant, I'm not even sure I can enjoy the original any more. Resonant annihilates the first game. It takes the countless hours of exploration, discovery, hard-fought battles and hard-earned wins, the lows and the highs, and it makes them all meaningless.  It's hardly a spoiler, because it's splashed all over every game trailer, but [spoiler]Resonant simply starts its story by saying that the victories of the past are just scrubbed, destroyed. You beat the Hiss, twice? You beat the Darkness? And what happened afterward? Basically just nothing for seven years of game time. The old god Ahti just went on his fishing vacation and never came back while his people were locked in a haunted house full of demons for seven years. People started bowling leagues inside the Oldest House.  And then one day, boom, everything just suddenly breaks loose. The [strike]Plot Device[/strike]Patterning Resonance bursts in, the Hiss escapes, everything looks weird and crazy and kooky! Ooooo! Jesse Faden (who, let's be honest, is the heart of the story and the reason we kept coming back) is just swapped out like a third-season sitcom actor with a scheduling conflict, and we're left with Dylan -- the former living avatar of the Hiss, who should have been an absolutely ferocious lead, but instead is just mopey and sullen and tedious. This is a character who reads like he was written by a teenager who incorrectly thinks that angst makes you interesting.[/spoiler]  Look, I'm only 11 hours in at this point. But I'm already sick of the aimless drifting, the tedious grinding, the obnoxious vendor mechanics forcing me to keep a spreadsheet of which materials I need to buy, the stupid spiderwebs of tiny incremental melee advantages. (Oh, a mysterious [spoiler]ice cream truck[/spoiler] that sells... [spoiler]combat upgrades[/spoiler]. Seriously, Sam?)  Jesse's powers were some of the most iconic and amazing game mechanics of the last decade. Dylan is just a putz who slowly, [i]slowly[/i] learns to swing his weird little sword very slightly better. They even go out of their way to point out that Dylan is [spoiler]unable to bind objects of power, for no adequately-explored reason at all, even though that is established in the lore as a basic ability of parautilitarians much, much weaker than Dylan[/spoiler].  And I'm honestly starving for lore. The Control lore was so rich, the Oldest House was a joy to explore, always finding something unique and bizarre in the files. But this... the depth of the lore is now just a memo someone sent about something that happened two days ago. The paltriness of it is so consistent that I can only blame myself for being disappointed.  So. The game is fine. It's pretty. What are you going to get?  - A Control fanfic that has to keep telling you it's Control, rather than being Control. - Mid-good melee mechanics (that's basically the entire game)  I'll keep playing for a while, at least. Maybe it'll suddenly wow me. Maybe it'll eventually get me back to the place that I'm excited to start the game up again, instead of just making myself do it.

There's not really a combo system that stands out, just kinda mashing and hoping you can see what's happening, which is impossible with all that goes on. I can't even see what's going on half the time because of the effects distorting the air and visuals when in fights with many people, especially in tighter areas. Didn't you love finding Altered Items and learning their stories and dealing with them in unique and interesting ways? Well, let's just split them up into multiple, repetitive and simple open-world slop trash and not give them a real identity or fun.   If you like this tripe, go chase the stupid stroller around eight times and pick out which taxi is slightly different over and over again and somehow, someway be entertained by it.
