There are three words that describe this game for me: performative, contemporary, and contrived.  Performative: Control Resonant performs Control rather than actually being Control. It has all the recognizable elements: surreal imagery, paranormal phenomena, strange architecture, cryptic lore, and weird enemies. But the way those elements are used diminishes the mystery that made the original interesting. The game constantly shows you that it is weird rather than allowing you to wonder why it is weird. The original made the inexplicable feel genuinely inexplicable. Resonant too often feels like it is performing surrealism. Just look at what they did to the board.  Contemporary: The game feels much more contemporary in its characters, presentation, and art direction. I actually loved a lot of the surrealism visually, but the world itself feels too warm and too lived-in for what is supposed to be. Its the aftermath of a catastrophic paranormal disaster and there are people everywhere who constantly talk. To me it takes something away from the atmosphere. If a disaster on this scale has happened, why doesn't the world feel more like it?  Zoe is probably the clearest example of this problem. Her constant presence over the radio makes the game feel like a modern AAA action game rather than an unsettling paranormal mystery. She pretty much is the contemporary tone that I found so annoying.  Contrived: Beneath all the surrealism, Resonant often feels like it is following the same formula as any other big-budget AAA game: constant dialogue, mission objectives, exposition, quips, progression systems, and characters telling you what is happening as you experience it. It is tedious and predictable while simultaneously trying very hard to present itself as unique and quirky. (But what did I expect really...)  Again I'm gonna mention Zoe because she is the formulaic radio companion who constantly gives directions, explains objectives, makes quips, and banters with them while pretending everything is casual and witty. Resonant to me feels close to that formula rather than like the strange, lonely experience that Control was.   However, I don't think Resonant is devoid of creativity. Some of its imagery is genuinely fantastic, and there are lots moments where it captures the surrealism I wanted from a sequel. But for me, the game misses something important. It has the aesthetic of Control without the atmosphere of Control, and the more it tries to make itself approachable and character-driven, the more it loses the sense of isolation, uncertainty, and mystery that made the original special.

I am a Remedy superfan and that is how I know that this is a bad game.  At my 35th hour now, and the words I said out loud to myself when I just closed the game were: “this ♥♥♥♥ is so laborious.”  Laborious. This is a great way to define ‘Control Resonant’. The cutscene direction, immaculate; the graphics, incredible; the act of playing the game? Laborious.  First it helps to know how much of a Remedy fan I am. I will not bore you with my life story but believe me I have been an ardent supporter of Remedy, and I will continue to be, because I think they really tried for something incredible here and in so many varied ways they succeeded, but the core loop of this gameplay is dull, monotonous and lacking in depth.  What went wrong?  Each moment of combat is as follows: X, X, X, X, maybe throw in an RB, X, X, X. These are the buttons you will press, over and over, whaling on a single enemy as they spasm mindlessly with each hit, beating down on them and watching their health bar slowly whittle away. You will do these for each ‘large’ enemy as their minions spawn in infinitely, only stopping once all large enemies are dead.  I am well into the endgame now. I have paired my Mold turret with my fire sword. I have stacked my ability points into buffing my supports. I have invested in other Weapon Forms to boost my damage rating. And the gameplay, each time you face an enemy, is still mainly: X, X, X. Ad infinitum. The health pools of these large enemies are ridiculous. It can take 10-20 seconds of just hitting them with the same 4X combo, over and over, for them to finally die. Rarely will enemies bother you while you’re doing this, you hardly ever need to even dodge allowing you to, again, just keep tapping X.  They’ve made a game with no possible skill expression.  There is a ‘falter’ (poise break) mechanic in here that hardly feels worth using (Y) because by the time you falter them, you may as well just have been hitting X faster to kill them. It adds a false layer of depth to the combat. If it were removed entirely, the game would still play exactly the same.  This extends even to the boss encounters. They are bad. They are, generally, not very good. Once again things go as far as just pressing X, but you will be expected to dodge too. None of these are very hard or very interesting to fight against, and it’s a shame because the build up to, the presentation, the MUSIC, of these bosses are immaculate, and then they are let down very swiftly by a return to the same derivative formula of actual gameplay.  There is ONE exception to this rule and it is The Collective boss. Finally the game demonstrates its greatest strengths, with the fight opening up to gravity jumps and a greater use of the movement abilities. This is easily one of the high points of this game.  Let’s focus on those for a second, the high points. ‘Control Resonant’ is visually stunning. I am amazed by what this team can do with environment design and cutscene direction. They have made a truly beautiful game, beautiful in a way untouched by any other media. The soundtrack, both OST and licensed tracks hit well and at great moments. You can tell they were trying to one-up the Ashtray Maze segment from ‘Control 1’ and they do so, consistently. There are so many good moments in ‘Resonant’. When the world around you is refracting and oscillating within itself, kaleidoscopic shimmering, it is mystifying.  The acting is also a strong suit; all characters are portrayed incredibly well by both the voice cast and motion capture crew. The writing for these characters is quite good, the main plot less so (it’s generic action movie stuff, there are TWO bad guys now), but the actual character writing creates a really solid foundation and goes to interesting places, sometimes confronting, that I was not expecting.  This good writing extends to all other aspects of ‘Resonant’. With regards to the side missions some were incredibly memorable, some of them dealt with interesting themes using the magic of science-fiction storytelling. The plethora of notes to read, just as in ‘Control’ are engrossing, as are the NPC idle conversations. I stopped and listened to every one and was rewarded for doing so with some very funny, and at other times very human, dialogue. Although the core plot might be generic, everything else written around it is stellar, Remedy at their best.  Speaking of their best, the movement in this game is incredible. Insomniac made Spiderman feel good to swing through the streets of Manhattan – Remedy make Dylan feel nice to soar over these same streets. Occasionally something irritating will sever you from that wonderful movement (elevators take far too long, especially that one in The Park), but generally it is a blast to interact with. But all the movement ends up doing is getting you right back to the terrible combat.  This is a ‘Focus M’ game. This is an open world game. This is a game filled with World Events to grind, to slowly fill up your ‘victory metre’ over each Zone, so that you can churn out more currency and materials. It is boring, it is a boring game. So much of it is boring. The combat is boring, the enemy attack patterns, boring, the gravity distortion, frankly also quite boring as to how it’s utilised.  My patient for this game finally boiled over when I experienced the ‘Underpass’ level. This entire area is just annoying to play, genuinely frustrating, and this combined with the combat had me relieved that the game felt it was almost over.  Then it turns out this is just the end of Act 2. Oh my god, I wanted so badly for the game to be over and then you have to go to a new area that has the SAME problems of the Underpass level design and I genuinely almost put the game down but figured I just wanted to finish it.  There are some lessons that I’m surprised weren’t learned from the original ‘Control’. Looking at collectible files is somehow worse? The hotkey to look at them doesn’t open it directly, instead leaving you staring at the collectibles screen looking for it yourself. ‘Control’ had an issue with being almost overwhelming with its assorted currencies and upgrade materials and ‘Resonant’ just adds to that feeling.  I’ve finally stopped playing the game. I’ve played ten additional hours past the final level and have stopped now because the Shum combat minigame had me move to a shrunken play area only to have enemies not follow, so I stood and waited for them to congregate in this new area but they didn’t follow, they just stood out there outside the play area and I had to wait for this temporary barrier to disappear before I could go back to fight them, which impacted my score time bonus, which then lead to me losing. This was when I pulled my headset off my head and said, out loud to my empty room, “this ♥♥♥♥ is so laborious.”  I love Remedy. I love what they tried to make here. But the gameplay is lacking, and that is, frankly, the most important part of a video game such as this. Maybe I’ll play ‘Devil May Cry’ or ‘Bayonetta’ instead.

So far, the plot has been quite boring. It’s kind of an open-world game with a level-based system, meaning there are zones and quests you can’t complete because your level is too low. However, the journal doesn’t indicate the recommended level for each quest. It would be quite handful rather than wasting time on starting the mission, listening all the dialogues and cutscenes and ended up with the high-level enemies. Wasting of time. I’m currently stuck because all the main quests are too high-level for me, so I have to farm… really? In a single-player game? Meh. And this is still at the very beginning of the game. 10/10?! don't think so.   The difficulty is also weird, in a bad way. I don’t really understand the purpose of it. It’s not a Souls-like game, but you’re expected to die over and over just to learn how to beat most enemies, even when you have the required level and have already learned the necessary skills. At least, that’s how it feels. In Souls games, dying repeatedly is part of the game’s design and the story, where the protagonist repeatedly comes back to life (hello, Dark Souls, Elden Ring, etc.). Resonant doesn’t have that narrative justification. So when I finally farmed enough levels to do the main story quests, it didn’t actually help much. I still had to die quite a few times, seemingly hoping to get lucky and make it through the enemies, or quit the mission and farm even more. Honestly, that sucks for me.  With games like Alan Wake and Control, I see them primarily as story-driven experiences, rather than Ubisoft-style open-world games where you’re expected to spend a lot of time farming. And here, farming doesn’t even seem to help much eventually.  I’ve finished all the Souls games multiple times, and I enjoy challenging games when the difficulty feels fair. Here, it just doesn’t work for me. Thank God I found the Assist Mode. It’s also kind of funny that instead of simply having 3–4 standard difficulty levels, the game uses an Assist Mode with some settings inside, but at least it lets me focus on the story and deal with all the unnecessary overcomplicated fights and hordes of enemies.  Maybe I don't understand something, but so far, I do not recommend it.

The wuthering waves ebb and flow.  Flow + Excellent combat system. Switching between 3 resonators. Intro/Outro attacks, special skills, ultimates. Very flashy and satisfying. + Visuals. Not everyones style but I think it looks really good. There is an abundance of beautiful scenery in this game. + Character models. No elaboration neccessary. + Great introduction of Scar. + Story. Good characters. (Jinhsi, Scar, Changli, Phrolova, Mya, Hyuki etc.) Really good world building. Interesting history. I overall like the story, only some bits were not for me like the Black Shore arc or the story bits around Chisa and Lynae which were a bit too slow paced. At some points the story gets a bit too confusing but overall the cutscenes throughout the story are (especially later in the game) well done. + Pretty good voice acting as far as I can tell. + Some fun side activities. There are a few activities in the open-world that I didn't like but overall exploration in this game is very good. + Beautiful open world. + A gazillion of echoes to collect. + Impressive cutscenes. + This game sometimes turning into a sidescroller is pretty cool. + Some really epic OST (Rinascita!) + Some enemies (echoes) have a story about why they exist which is pretty cool. They are described as lingering frequencies, like the Fisalia girls, for example, that didn't pass the trials. + Hyuki!   Ebb  - Parrying doesnt feel good cause it's the same button as your light attack - Mute Protagonist. She does talk at some points but mostly just nods which is odd. - Not every content is being shown on the map and there is no way (ingame) to find all chests, challenges and so on. There is the lootmapper but why not just show it then. - V-Synch and some other graphic options simply do not work. - Some boring, unfun challenges. Very frustrating, bad designed ones. - You spend a bit too much time doing menial tasks, especially in 1.0. - Dialoges in Quest. They are often artificially long and a bit boring. Also they repeat many things and there are quite a lot of grammar mistakes. Some side quests are especially tedious like almost all of the quests in Jingzhu or some of the companion stories. There could also be a little more actual gameplay during main story quests. - Running up walls and climbing often sucks, cause you often end up being stuck on some protrusion. - A lot of the companion quests are quite slow and boring even later when they are part of the main quest. - Gacha-system. If you spend a lot of real money in this game you get significantly stronger. Upgrading your Resonators or pulling for new ones is very expensive. You can however play through the story without the need of a perfect meta team. If you are smart about your pulls, you can actually clear most of the end game content but it still takes a lot of time. That time invested can be swiped away and the game encourages you to do just that. Also you will never get the max amount of wavebands (to make the character the strongest) or level up your weapons with duplicates without spending real money. You have to be ok with the fact that if you decide to not spend an insane amount of money, your favorite team will never be as strong as it could be. - Depending on your team, exploration can get very annoying. I, for example, had no one in my main team that could use free aim and I had to switch teams on many occasions in the open world. This is just annoying and bad. I see no reason why everyone shouldn't be allowed to use free aim for the completion of open world activities. - Annoying weeklies. - The echo menus are horrible. - Movement could be more fluent. - Bad translation. Lots of grammar mistakes and odd writing in the beginning of the game but it gets significantly better the further you get in the game.  Gacha system aside, this game is good. Combat and exploration are well done, story is good aswell but this being a live service game, the story never ends until the game ends so its kinda hard to rate properly. Now that I have rated this game, I will delete my screenshot folder and move on for now.

This game has a lot of pretty chars (yes, I love looking at pretty chars) but they are only side dishes for me.  I'm a casual player and when it goes to playing games, I mainly focus on what kind of story/narrative such games could offer. So, this review will only cover my experience following the story of wuwa (main story, side story, exploration story) and how it handles the worldbuilding/lore within said game.  Please note that currently I'm still in Huanglong and soon to be in Rinascita. This is my initial experience playing the first chapter of the game. Think of it as an opening to the world of wuwa, like a prologue maybe, and whether this "opening" deliver or not, whether it works well to make me fall in love with the lore tidbits or not (I wont talk about character writing because it's not my main focus).  1. I must say that Huanglong starts ... pretty rough. The conflict starts simple (which is good as starter, just like how it should be in any games), with a basic and straightforward premise, but what makes it rough is the driving plot in which your MC does to finish each checkpoint. I dont wanna put it into detail here bcz Im afraid it would be a spoiler. But what I wanna say is that your MC really walks a lot, getting into one place into another, yet the driving plot around these exact checkpoints feels too basic. It lacks narrative that makes me pop like "wow!" or "ooh so that's it!" because everything appears so basic, with a plot that is easy to guess, no crazy revelations, no deep talking bcz most conversations run casually just like everyday conversation (with most of them being repetitive such as when npcs asking rover's opinion, or asking rover's condition and what he/she is planning to do, basically they put too much "care" on rover's wellbeing, and all of these happen even during near-climax when "war is incoming and jinzhou is in grave danger". It kinda feels repetitive, so much information/topic being discussed again and again, even tho it's already clear from the very beginning.  2. Lore dump everywhere bruh. It really breaks the immersion of the convesation that is running at that time; because as an open-world game, they should know how to distribute lore in the main quest and side quest, or even in npcs talking or some archives you can find scattered in some areas, not everything (literally everything) needs to be loaded in the main quest. The characters casually mentioning strange terms, and rover's always asking to elaborate, which ended up the characters giving explanation that sometimes feel so much to grasp. Not to mention that some terms being explained more than once, feels like lecturing instead of the conversation runs smoothly.  3. The plot itself feels long (starting from solving puzzle, fighting overseer, meeting blackshores, go to war with threnodian, handling crisis with the sentinel, then fight the sentinel, etc etc) but it also feels jumpy to move between overaching conflicts. I can feel that the dev just put those conflicts and groups intro (fractsidus, blackshores, midnight ranger, court of savantae, etc) to extend the story, like cram it into one big narrative, yet what I get is just basic conversations followed by lore dump, with no surprise, no reveal. As a nation raging in endless war with threnodian, and crisis with the sentinel vs fractsidus scheme, there is no dialogue full of strategy on how to handle such conflicts. As I said earlier, the conversation in huanglong's arc feel way too casual, and mostly too linear, while lore/info dump sometimes being put out of place (like intentionally being thrown away just to prolong the dialogue, instead of making the narrative feels like a complete puzzle it ended up look jumpy and messy, especially with the constant repetition).  4. Side quest and exploration quest mostly borrows the same formula of the main quest. Maybe slightly worse because they repeat the same explanation about certain lore, the lore doesnt appear as expanding but instead being repeated again and again (different sentences, but same context). I still remember how in the main quest they explain more than once about certain terms like threnodian, retroact rain, taced discord, tacet field, waveworn phenoomena, sentinel Jue's ability of altering time, etc etc and it feels highly redundant. Meanwhile, certain npcs in the side/exploration quest would sometimes repeat that same info/lore as if they really try hard to make rover understand. I know that rover is amnesiac, but I dont think he/she is dumb enough to be constantly in need of such reminder again and again.  Well, that's only Huanglong (jinzhou). I will update my review soon after I finish rinascita, Im gonna review everytime I complete a nation's main quest (apart from some of their exploration quest and side quest) and see how the story/worlbuilding in this game expand more.   6/10 rating for how they handle the worldbuilding/lore and integrate them into the main quest (as of now) -- lore dump, which also falls repetitive. 6/10 rating for how the conversation among characters run in the main quest (as of now) -- way too casual, too basic and simple. 5/10 rating for how they make the conflict appears engaging in the main quest (as of now) -- not much room for the conflict to expand narratively, how the chars handle/discuss the conflict narratively, and how the conflict ends in a plot twist format (turns out no plot twist, even there is no big reveal in the aftermath).  P.S. I play the game on medium spec PC. It runs well but with minimum settings, but still the visual looks decent and yeah no crash or laggy so far.  For the sake of playing and reviewing the game's story at least until lahai roi arc, and bcz I'm still in Huanglong, I will regard this game as RECOMMENDED bcz I dont have much to complaint apart from the story/lore/worldbuilding (as of now).

300+ hours played. Negative review.  A lot of my playtime was sunk cost. WuWa has just enough good stuff that I kept thinking the rest would catch up. Combat is pretty good, quickswapping is fun, Hiyuki’s iai attacks scratch the monkey-brain SHING itch, exploration can be enjoyable, and the elementary-school-level puzzles can be relaxing.  1.X WAS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AWFUL  The opening throws Frequencies, Resonators, Tacet Discords, the Lament and pseudo-science at you before giving you much reason to care.  WuWa too often mistakes information density for depth.  Then 1.0 tries an “Avengers Assemble” moment around the Ovathrax/Threnodian of War climax. The cast rolls up like I’m supposed to scream “♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, EVERYONE’S HERE!” when many barely had enough development to matter. It wanted an ensemble payoff it hadn’t earned.  WUWA HAS LORE. THAT DOESN’T MEAN IT HAS GOOD WORLDBUILDING.  A major concept should roughly go:  1. Introduce it. 2. Develop it until the audience understands how it affects the world. 3. Use, break, exploit, or subvert it.  WuWa constantly goes:  STEP 1 → ♥♥♥♥ STEP 2 → STEP 3.  Tethys. Mount Firmament. Fabrictorium of the Deep. Fortune-telling. Chaos. Journeying Paradise.  These are huge ideas, yet Kuro often introduces them in the same arc where Rover is already exploiting their rules. The lore exists, but rarely gets enough time to become part of the world.  Compare that to Morrowind’s Morag Tong. They are not just “cool legal assassins.” The Great Houses are powerful and full of grievances, so sanctioned assassination acts as a pressure valve for disputes that might otherwise become open war. One faction touches law, religion, House politics, culture and the balance of power.  That is worldbuilding. WuWa too often gives me the PowerPoint instead.  If a phenomenon is supposedly world-changing, show me what it does to normal life: industries, laws, superstitions, religion, politics. WuWa often rushes past that connective tissue to reach the next revelation.  IUNO IS THE BEST EXAMPLE  Put a gun to my head and ask me to explain exactly how we saved Iuno in plain English.  We went into the sea, collected memories, grew a tree, did metaphysical ♥♥♥♥, cut it down, and now she’s back.  I guess???  Yes, there is lore explaining it. That is not the point.  The story introduces the metaphysical rules, explains the exception, and uses that exception to solve the climax almost simultaneously. I have barely internalized what “Chaos” means or what the causal rules are before Rover is already navigating around them.  Fantasy can be completely insane and still feel coherent. The audience just needs time to understand the rules before those rules become the solution. WuWa often introduces the knife five minutes before Rover needs to stab God with it.  That is why supposedly enormous revelations can land as “apparently that’s a thing now” instead of “♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, that changes everything.”  ROVER IS THE CENTER OF THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ UNIVERSE  Fractsidus? Rover. Sentinels? Rover. Ancient systems? Rover. Historical figures? Probably knew Rover. Regional crisis? Rover is uniquely qualified to fix it.  At this point I don’t wonder about a new region’s history. I wonder what Past Rover did there.  Everyone also glazes Rover. Jiyan is THE GENERAL, yet the story bends over backwards to involve the newly awakened amnesiac in military strategy. Important people trust, admire, or attach themselves to Rover absurdly quickly.  I’d kill for someone to ask: “Who the ♥♥♥♥ are you and why should I care?”  ROVER IS ALSO BORING AS HELL  The most important person in history has the personality of drywall.  Calm. Nice. Helpful. Mildly amused. Mildly concerned.  The voice and attitude are so neutral that gigantic revelations land like being told the grocery store closes early.  WuWa is extremely linear, so this is not a blank-slate RPG excuse. I’m not meaningfully defining Rover’s morality or major decisions. The game already decided who Rover is, so why not give them a stronger personality?  I hope Rover gets their memories back someday because maybe their personality is stored in there too.  THE AMNESIA IS A BOTTOMLESS MYSTERY BOX  Planescape: Torment handles amnesia vastly better. The Nameless One’s past creates enemies, victims, relationships and consequences Current Him must deal with. His missing past is the problem, not just a source of cool reveals.  Rover’s amnesia too often feels like an infinite writing coupon.  New ancient connection? Past Rover knew them. New organization? Past Rover was involved. Another revelation? Past Rover researched it. Why doesn’t Rover remember? Amnesia.  Past Rover also discarded the context behind countless failures and decisions. Memory is not just trivia; it is reasoning. Erase your mistakes and you erase what you learned from making them.  Brilliant. We kept the notebook and deleted the scientist.  CHARACTERS FEEL LIKE BANNER ADVERTISEMENTS  Too many characters feel written around their banner cycle instead of integrated into an ongoing cast.  A new character gets major relevance, cinematics, trauma and lore while being sold, then often fades away once the marketing cycle moves on.  Chisa is the perfect example. She effectively loses around twenty years of everyone else’s lives. Her family thought she was dead. Her friends aged without her. She returns to a world that moved on.  That should produce grief, alienation and the horror of lost time. Instead, the reunion and aftermath get nowhere near the weight the setup deserves.  Temporary story content makes it worse. Xiangli Yao’s original introduction was heavily tied to an old event, while Somnoire has recurring lore and characters but event-limited context. New players can hit material that assumes Rover knows people or concepts they never got to meet.  Canon story should not evaporate.  THE MAIN QUEST SOMETIMES BARELY WANTS YOU TO PLAY IT  Some story fights are so protected that failure barely feels possible, and missed QTEs can continue for you. If the cinematic finishes the action anyway, why ask me to press the button? If a fight refuses to let me lose, the boss threatening me becomes theater.  SIDE QUESTS ARE OFTEN BORING AS ♥♥♥♥  Side quests should be where the worldbuilding breathes: local culture, beliefs, politics, jobs, families and how ordinary people live around all this insane technology and metaphysics.  Instead, too many amount to: talk to NPC, walk 200m, press F, kill three enemies, return.  Some companion quests are alright. Most side content is forgettable.  THE GACHA STILL SUCKS  “But it’s better than Genshin!”  I know. I don’t care.  If one guy shoots me in the head and another shoots me in the foot, the second guy treated me better.  I HAVE STILL BEEN ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SHOT.  Older limited characters can disappear for stupid lengths of time while the roster keeps expanding. In a character collection game, that is ridiculous.  Pulling a character and finding their materials, bosses, Echoes or region story-gated is also annoying. Congratulations on your new character; please finish your homework before using them properly.  THE GOOD STUFF IS WHY THIS IS SO FRUSTRATING  Combat is good. Quickswapping is fun. Hiyuki goes SHING and brain goes :D. Exploration can be pretty good. The puzzles are easy as hell, but sometimes square peg → square hole → chest is enough.  That is why I kept playing.  Kuro needs patience. Let concepts breathe. Let characters remain part of the world after their banners. Let people distrust Rover. Let someone else be the expert. Give Rover an actual personality. Stop using amnesia as an infinite generator of retroactive importance.  You have a world.  USE THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ WORLD.  After 300+ hours, I’m negative not because WuWa has nothing good in it, but because it constantly reminds me how much better it could be.  If Steam ever starts refunding human lifespan, Kuro owes me about twelve and a half days.

[h1]GREAT GAME. AWFUL MONETIZATION. F2P PLAYERS DESERVE BETTER.[/h1]  Wuthering Waves is a genuinely good game buried under a monetization system I simply cannot support.  And instead of just saying [i]“gacha bad”[/i], let's look at the actual numbers.  [h1]THE F2P REALITY[/h1]  A normal F2P player receives only [b]60 Astrite per day[/b] from Daily Activity.  One pull costs [b]160 Astrite[/b].  That means an entire day of dailies gives you only:  [b]0.375 pulls.[/b]  [list] [*][b]1 pull[/b] = about [b]2.7 DAYS[/b] of dailies [*][b]10 pulls[/b] = about [b]27 DAYS[/b] of dailies [*][b]80 pulls[/b] = about [b]213 DAYS[/b] of dailies [/list]  And here's the important part:  [b]80 pulls does NOT even guarantee the limited character you actually want.[/b]  The Featured Resonator banner has an [b]80-pull hard pity[/b], but your first 5-star has only a [b]50% chance[/b] of being the featured character.  Lose the 50/50?  You may need another 80 pulls.  [h1]160 PULLS = 25,600 ASTRITE[/h1]  At 60 Astrite per day, that represents roughly:  [h1]426 DAYS OF DAILY ASTRITE[/h1]  [i]For ONE guaranteed limited character.[/i]   [h1]WANT THEIR SIGNATURE WEAPON TOO?[/h1]  The limited weapon banner can require another:  [b]80 pulls = 12,800 Astrite[/b]  So in the worst case:  [b]Character:[/b] 160 pulls   [b]Weapon:[/b] 80 pulls    [h1]240 PULLS = 38,400 ASTRITE[/h1]  That's the equivalent of:  [b]640 DAYS OF DAILY ASTRITE.[/b]  Yes.  [b]640 days.[/b]   [h1]"BUT THE GAME GIVES YOU MORE ASTRITE!"[/h1]  Yes, it does.  You also receive Astrite from:  [list] [*]Events [*]Story [*]Exploration [*]Chests [*]Achievements [*]Endgame activities [*]Patch rewards [/list]  But there is one massive difference:  [b]Most exploration, story, chest and achievement rewards are ONE-TIME rewards.[/b]  Once you have completed them, they are gone.  You cannot endlessly farm Astrite just because you are willing to play more.  Your normal repeatable daily income still remains extremely limited.  For Version 3.6, F2P calculations put the total rewards at roughly:  [b]11,800 Astrite + 12 limited character pulls[/b]  if you complete essentially everything available during the patch.  That's roughly:  [h1]85 LIMITED CHARACTER PULLS[/h1]  during an entire six-week patch.  Now remember:  [b]Worst-case guarantee for ONE featured character = 160 pulls.[/b]  So even completing practically an entire patch worth of F2P content does not necessarily guarantee the limited character being advertised to you.   [h1]AND IT GETS WORSE FOR NEW PLAYERS[/h1]  Some of those Astrite rewards come from difficult endgame activities.  Version 3.6 has roughly [b]2,800 Astrite tied to endgame content.[/b]  Meaning a newer F2P player may not even be capable of earning the full theoretical F2P amount.  So when people say:  [i]"You get around X amount of pulls every patch!"[/i]  remember that those calculations often assume you:  [list] [*]Log in consistently [*]Complete the events [*]Complete the new content [*]Explore [*]Do the endgame [*]Claim all temporary rewards [/list]  Miss content?  [b]Those pulls are gone.[/b]   [h1]NOW LET'S TALK ABOUT DUPLICATES[/h1]  Characters don't simply end after obtaining them once.  Each character has [b]six additional Sequence Nodes[/b].  To fully max out a limited character, you generally need to obtain that character:  [h1]SEVEN TIMES.[/h1]  One original copy + six additional copies.  And then, of course, there is still their separate signature weapon.  So the monetization doesn't stop at:  [i]"Congratulations! You got the character."[/i]  There are additional character copies and weapons waiting behind even more banners.   [h1]THIS IS THE PART I REFUSE TO SUPPORT[/h1]  I have absolutely nothing against developers making money.  Wuthering Waves is free.  Servers cost money.  Developers deserve salaries.  Artists, programmers, animators, composers and voice actors deserve to be paid.  [b]That is not the problem.[/b]  Sell me:  [list] [*]Skins [*]Cosmetics [*]Mounts [*]Battle passes [*]Expansions [*]A subscription [*]A complete character for a reasonable fixed price [/list]  I will happily pay for a game I enjoy.  What I do NOT want to support is a system built around:  [list] [*]Premium currency [*]Limited-time banners [*]50/50 mechanics [*]Pity systems [*]Character duplicates [*]Signature weapons [*]Fear of missing out [*]Constantly rotating characters [/list]  All conveniently designed around making spending money extremely easy.   [quote] [b]A game being free does not automatically make every monetization system reasonable.[/b] [/quote]   [h1]60 ASTRITE VS. 160 ASTRITE[/h1]  This single comparison tells you a lot.  [b]Daily reward: 60 Astrite[/b]  [b]One pull: 160 Astrite[/b]  You don't even receive enough premium currency from an entire day's standard daily activity to make:  [b]ONE pull.[/b]  Not ten pulls.  Not a guaranteed character.  [b]One pull.[/b]  And one pull doesn't guarantee anything meaningful.   [h1]"BUT WUWA IS MORE GENEROUS THAN OTHER GACHAS!"[/h1]  Maybe.  But this argument completely misses the point.  [quote] [b]“Better than another gacha” does NOT automatically mean consumer-friendly.[/b] [/quote]  If one game charges you $1,000 for something and another charges you $700, the second system does not magically become good simply because something worse exists.  The comparison should not be:  [i]"Is this gacha nicer than another gacha?"[/i]  The comparison should be:  [b]"Does this game respect my time and my money?"[/b]   [h1]THE SAD PART? THE GAME ITSELF IS REALLY GOOD.[/h1]  The combat is excellent.  The animations are beautiful.  The world looks fantastic.  The characters clearly have a lot of work put into them.  There are obviously incredibly talented developers behind this game.  [b]And that's exactly why the monetization disappoints me so much.[/b]  A genuinely great game should not need psychological monetization systems designed around limited availability, random outcomes and repeated copies of characters.   [h1]I DON'T HATE WUTHERING WAVES.[/h1]  I actually WANT games like this to succeed.  But I don't want this monetization model to become something we simply accept as normal.  There is a massive difference between:  [b]"I want to support a game I love."[/b]  and  [b]"I feel pressured to spend because the character I want disappears soon and I might lose a 50/50."[/b]   [h1]PLEASE THINK BEFORE YOU SPEND.[/h1]  If you enjoy Wuthering Waves completely F2P:  [b]Good. Enjoy it.[/b]  If you buy a small monthly pass because you enjoy the game:  [b]That's your choice.[/b]  If you spend money on characters because you understand the system and can comfortably afford it:  [b]That's also your choice.[/b]  But please understand what these systems are built around before spending hundreds or even thousands.  Don't let FOMO decide how much your entertainment is worth.   [quote] [h1]GOOD GAMES DESERVE SUPPORT.  PREDATORY MONETIZATION DOES NOT.[/h1] [/quote]  [b]Your money is your vote.[/b]  [b]And this is one monetization model I personally refuse to vote for.[/b]

Absolutely brilliant game, but you will need mods to realize its full potential. Specifically, Content manager, Pure, a post-processing filter of your choice, and then car/track mods on top.  Once you get that, you will have the virtual embodiment of a mechanic's wet dream. You get an incredible handling and physics model, a very expandable visual engine, and an OK soundtrack in the way of engine sounds (currently the most lacking aspect, even after modding). But to me, all of those still pale in comparison to the mechanical sandbox you get to have in front of you with this game. Instead of naming every option you have at your disposal, let me just describe some cars that I built in-game, all just by editing existing mods, or rather their files.  1. The world's strangest presidential vehicle - While perusing the internet one day, I came across the Audi A8 L Security - a 4 ton armored beast meant for VIPs. Now, I personally don't like that gen of the A8, so instead I decided to edit a different car in this fashion. Naturally, it was a Mini Cooper Countryman, because why not. I edited it to weigh 3,9 tons and push 250 horsepower, and adjusted the suspension until it actually carried that weight quite graciously.  2. A safe Dodge Viper - this being a Viper that was converted to be FWD, have ABS and TC, and one which got its V10 replaced with the Fiat 600D's 32 horsepower inline 4. Perfect grocery getter.  3. The most annoying luxury vehicle - specifically, a 2020 Maybach S650 with the engine out of a third-gen Honda Civic. The 7-speed automatic stayed, with its gear ratios adjusted to achieve a fairly impressive 210 km/h top speed.  4. A WRC-inspired Citroen C4 VTS build - which was a more serious, detailed build than the others. Power went from 150 to 215 hp, the suspension went up by 7 cm and was made softer, and the whole thing was tuned for rugged mountain roads and light offroading. Was one of the more fun builds.  I made these and so many more, and still plan on some more goofy builds like a diesel-powered RX7 because again, why not. Point being, you can adjust just about everything on cars. If you are in any way mechanically inclined, this is THE game to play. Plus, it regularly hits 5 euros which is a steal for what it offers. Get the DLC as well.

Assetto Corsa barely feels like a complete game—it’s more like an unfinished sandbox hiding behind the label of a “simulator.”  The base content is laughably thin. Without mods, you run out of things to do in a few hours, making it feel more like a demo than a full release. The graphics haven’t aged well either—flat lighting, lifeless environments, and visuals that already felt outdated years ago.  Single-player is dull and uninspired. The AI is either clueless or frustratingly inconsistent, and the career mode feels like a soulless checklist rather than a meaningful progression system. On top of that, the UI is clunky, outdated, and unnecessarily frustrating to navigate.  Even the much-praised physics aren’t flawless—too unforgiving for casual players, yet not always as precise as hardcore fans claim.

I honestly would have recommended this to anyone who was interested prior to today (1st of September, 2026). The game has undergone an update to dramatically change the UI and they have added a new system that I am not a fan of.  As of today, the devs have added a battle pass system (called the Paw Pass) with both a free lane and a paid lane. They state that both tiers earn Bongo Coins, which are used for purchasing rewards and can be used to purchase the paid tier of the pass. They are also stating that the rewards "do not expire" on either tier. These both sound good, but when you look a little deeper, they are not all of what they seem.  Both tiers of the pass earn 100 coins a month, and it either costs $4.99 or 500 coins to redeem the paid tier of the pass for a month. If you wanted to stay a f2p user, then every 5 months you would earn enough coins to purchase the paid tier for ONE MONTH. That is also assuming you do not use the coins to purchase any cosmetics or anything in the meantime. This is not sustainable to the free users as within a few months, you are so far behind on cosmetics that it does not matter if the things never expire, they are not even remotely all attainable for you anymore as a f2p user.  This Paw Pass is an additional thing added to the game, which already had built in FOMO in the form of the events, and already had a paid market for rare items. Injecting paid FOMO into a free game that already has free FOMO is simply not acceptable to me. Even accepting items on the free tier of the pass requires you to see the items you will not be getting because you are not paying for them.  You may say that you do not have to interact with this new system, and you are correct, you do not *have* to. But this game is about collecting things just as much as it is about hanging with friends or randoms, so you have to be willing to accept that there will be no hope of collecting everything without paying, where as previously there was a chance to. Sure, there were seasonal and event items you would not be able to get retroactively, but that was acceptable as it was. Adding more missable (and paid) items to that is sadly not the right way to move forward IMO.  I understand that this is a good revenue stream for the devs, and on spreadsheets this probably looks like a solid plan. Unfortunately, this system is not friendly to the users, nor does it respect their wallets. In a game that already does not respect the user's time, this is unnacceptable to me.  If the devs reverse this decision, I may come back, but maybe not. This is disrespectful to user's time and money, and is not a good sign for the future of Bongo Cat. In a world where everything is demanding you to open your wallet wider and pay more attention to it, it is sad to see a silly little typing companion game following suit.  Do not recommend to anyone currently.

game_name: Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition
review_text: Most remasters are cash grabs with sharper textures. Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition is something else: a loving restoration of one of the greatest real-time strategy games ever made, rebuilt so thoroughly that it now outclasses nearly everything released in the genre since.  The core design is timeless. Villagers gathering wood, food, gold, and stone; advancing through the Dark, Feudal, Castle, and Imperial Ages; building an economy while scouting, raiding, and defending. More than 25 years after the original, this loop remains brilliantly balanced between economic management and battlefield tactics. Every match is a race, a puzzle, and a fight at once.  The presentation is a genuine upgrade. 4K graphics, remastered audio, smoother animations, and quality-of-life features like build queues and improved pathfinding bring the game into the modern era without betraying its identity. It still looks and feels like AoE2, only the way you remember it rather than how it actually was.  It finally treats the whole world seriously. Where many historical strategy games center Europe and treat everyone else as flavor, AoE2 DE has steadily built out civilizations and campaigns across Africa, South and Southeast Asia, the Caucasus, the Americas, and East Asia. The Ethiopians, Malians, Vietnamese, Bengalis, Georgians, and others aren't reskins; they have distinct units, technologies, and playstyles. The campaigns cover figures like Sundiata, Bayinnaung, and Tamar alongside the familiar European heroes.  The balance is astonishing. With dozens of civilizations, you'd expect chaos. Instead, the developers have maintained a remarkably fair competitive environment through years of careful patches. Nearly every civ has a viable niche, and top-level tournaments show real variety in picks.  The community is its lifeblood. Ranked matchmaking, a thriving esports scene, active content creators, and a huge library of mods and custom scenarios keep the game alive. Few games from 1999 have more active players today than they did at launch. This one does.  The flaws are minor. Newer DLC has occasionally sparked debate over whether additions fit the game's timeframe or design philosophy, and the AI, though much improved, still can't match skilled human opponents. New players may also find the competitive ladder intimidating, since the veterans have had decades to practise.  Verdict: AoE2 DE is the gold standard for how to remaster a classic: respect what made it great, fix what didn't age well, and keep supporting it with meaningful content. Whether you want a relaxed campaign, a chaotic eight-player match, or a sweaty 1v1 on the ladder, this is essential strategy gaming.

Crosshair X is a simple program that does one thing:  It puts a crosshair on your screen.  That's it.  And somehow, I have spent more time messing around with crosshair settings than I would like to admit.  You can choose from a ridiculous number of different styles, colors, sizes, outlines, and shapes. You can make a tiny little dot, a massive neon monstrosity, or something so complicated that it looks like you're trying to pilot a spaceship.  The best part is when you find the perfect crosshair.  You spend twenty minutes adjusting it.  Too big.  Too small.  Too bright.  Not bright enough.  The gap is wrong.  The thickness is wrong.  The outline is wrong.  You finally get it perfect.  Then you play one game and decide you hate it.  So you change it again.  Crosshair X is especially useful for games that don't have a crosshair, have terrible customization options, or simply give you a crosshair that looks like it was designed by someone who has never played an FPS.  It's also hilarious how quickly you can convince yourself that changing your crosshair will fix your aim.  Miss a shot?  Obviously the crosshair is wrong.  Change it.  Miss again?  Change it.  Still missing?  Clearly you need a different color.  Eventually you've gone through 47 crosshairs and somehow gotten worse.  At that point, you realize the problem was never the crosshair.  It was you.  The customization is the real appeal, though. You can experiment with different designs until you find something that feels comfortable across your games, and having a consistent visual reference can be genuinely useful.  It's one of those programs you don't really think about until you need it.  Then suddenly you're wondering how you ever played without it.  Is it revolutionary?  No.  Is it going to make you a professional gamer?  Absolutely not.  Will you still blame your crosshair when you miss an easy shot?  Without question.  10/10. i'd specifically recommend purchasing this game at a heavy discount. i purchased this for $10 in 2016 and forgot about it; played again after 1.0 in 2024, and i am stunned to see a $45 price tag. i've enjoyed my time with it, but it is not a $45 game.  the good: the point of interest system in this game is amazing. every building is a handcrafted experience that isn't present in many other survival games. it is rewarding to follow the easily-marked path through every POI and experience the twists & turns of combat, parkour, and looting. this experience only gets better as the player gets stronger, as each higher tier POI increases in both complexity and difficulty. i'd really recommend upping the zombie spawns/game difficulty as you progress to keep the challenge there, especially if you're playing multiplayer.  the bad: (there's honestly a lot, but here are a few key points) - the crafting system is too entrenched in the attribute skill trees. skill points come at a premium and key to your combat prowess, but tying crafting recipes, reduced item costs, and crafting magazine (perk books) to specific skill trees makes it hard to progress as a solo player. this can be revised by either playing with a group or by editing the amount of skill points received per level, but the intended design is messy.  - the game is ugly. no two ways about it unfortunately; this game looks largely the same as it did in 2016. meshes and textures blend in an unpleasant manner, some zombies are cartoonish, items look janky. i don't need realistic graphics, but these aren't even stylized, they're just bad.  - on the topic of janky, there is an overlying sense of jank to the entire game. enemy pathing, menu navigation, lag spikes. it does not feel like a polished product.  - the devs lack direction. probably the most popular criticism of the game. 8+ years in EA and the game feels unfinished. certain aspects of the game are heavily developed, others feel shallow. game mechanics are added and removed seemingly randomly.  there is fun to be had in this game, but overall like a 5/10.

After 13 years of on-and-off bursts with 7 Days to Die, here's the honest take: it's still one of the best post-apocalypse sandboxes out there, and I genuinely cannot find a better co-op alternative. The game has gone through six or seven major evolutions in that time, and the devs are still cooking.  7D2D is the closest thing you'll get to "Minecraft, but for grownups." It lacks polish in places, but it makes up for it with atmosphere and a brutally addictive core loop. You've got a deep building and crafting system, a world generator with absurd customization, multiplayer with proper PvE and PvP options, a quest and vendor system that stays out of your way, and a premise that hooks you hard: every seventh day, the game tests whether you've prepared well enough to survive. Survive or die trying, those are your options.  Now, the flaws, because pretending they don't exist would be dishonest:  · The melee feels like swinging a pool noodle through wet cement. It's been like this for years. · Linux performance is rough. Don't expect parity with Windows. · Shooting is functional, not satisfying. You'll hit your shots, you just won't feel cool doing it. · There's no physics to speak of. Zombies clip through debris, ragdolls are a suggestion, and it constantly reminds you this is still an alpha at heart, with a production wrapping. · Zombie hitboxes are a running joke in the community, and not the funny kind.  What the game actually nails:  · Building and crafting. This is the whole reason to play. Full stop. · Traps. Traps everywhere. Traps on traps. The game wants you to be paranoid and creative, and the toolkit delivers. · Electricity is genuinely useful, not a gimmick you ignore after the tutorial. · A real variety of melee weapons, each with actual tradeoffs. · Light RPG progression you can tune to taste — not bloated, not an afterthought. · Crafting goes stupidly deep. You'll still be discovering recipes 200 hours in.  I dare you to find another game with building and crafting this satisfying and this customizable. If you've ever fantasized about constructing your dream post-apocalyptic fort, this is the closest you'll get, but go in knowing it's a time sinkhole. There's always another upgrade you can do, and a recipe to find.

I have almost 800 hours in 7 Days to Die, spread across nearly a decade of playing. I’ve had some genuinely great times with this game. I’ve built ridiculous bases, survived hordes that should have wiped us, played with friends for hundreds of hours, experimented with different builds, and come back after major updates more times than I can count.  That’s what makes leaving a negative review after all this time so disappointing.  My biggest problem isn’t that the game has changed. After this many years, change is expected. My problem is that the developers have increasingly felt adversarial toward the way players actually enjoy playing their game.  7 Days to Die has always been at its best when it gives players a problem and lets them come up with their own solution. Here’s a horde. Here are some blocks, traps, weapons, and tools. Figure it out.  Some players build fortresses. Some build elaborate trap bases. Some exploit pathing. Some dig. Some build towers. Some come up with completely ridiculous contraptions that somehow work. Finding those solutions was part of the fun.  But over the years, it has increasingly felt like whenever the community finds a creative way to deal with the horde that doesn’t match the developers’ intended way of playing, the response is to change the mechanics to stop it. Instead of asking, “Is the player having fun?” it often feels like the question is, “Are they playing the way we want them to?”  For a sandbox survival game, that attitude is incredibly frustrating.  For a long time, mods kept me coming back. The 7 Days to Die modding community is fantastic. Modders have added features, quality-of-life improvements, mechanics, content, and fixes that breathed new life into the game for me repeatedly. In some cases, the community implemented features years before anything comparable appeared in the base game.  At a certain point, though, you start wondering why the community has to keep carrying so much of the experience.  Then the Jawoodle situation happened.  Jawoodle is probably the single content creator most responsible for bringing me back to 7 Days to Die over the years. I would stop playing, eventually stumble across one of his new series or ridiculous experiments, and before long my friends and I would be reinstalling the game and starting another world.  His content represented exactly what I always enjoyed about 7 Days to Die: experimenting with the mechanics, finding weird interactions, testing the limits of the AI, building unconventional bases, and seeing just how far you could push the sandbox.  So seeing the situation between him and the developers unfold felt like the culmination of the problem I’ve had with the direction of the game for years.  It reinforced the feeling that creativity is welcome only as long as it stays inside the lines the developers have drawn for you.  After nearly ten years and almost 800 hours, I finally uninstalled 7 Days to Die. Several of the friends I’ve played with over the years have done the same. At this point, I don’t intend to come back.  That’s unfortunate because there is a genuinely great game here. There always has been. I got hundreds of hours of entertainment out of it, and I have a lot of good memories because of it.  But after watching a game that I loved remain in development for what feels like forever while repeatedly pushing back against the creativity that made its sandbox so much fun in the first place, I’m done waiting for it to become the game I kept hoping it would be. This used to be an insanely fun game, even if it has always struggled with the difficulty plateau - early on, it is very hard to survive and you actually have to decide whether a random encounter will result in your player's death and ultimately, how you recover (or don't) depending on game death penalties. Later on, the game becomes far too easy unless you employ mods or know where to edit all the game settings to keep things spicy.  Server/Co-Op play used to be the best way to play with friends; but server chunk data and lags become a larger issue as the game progresses. Rented servers can help some of this to isolate traffic if hosted games cause problems for anyone running the server.  Some of the best features have always been the sandbox-like environment. Nearly everything is destructible and can be used for crafting materials or trading. This has led to a huge debate over releases and game changes which have altered some of the best (and worst) parts of managing the game. Water? Jars with water? No jars? Make up your mind on how this exists in your ecosystem. In a real apocalypse, you'd imagine finding jars or containers almost everywhere, as would be water, provided your biome has it in abundance. Learning to make fire and boil water means, voila, you can drink water without contaminants, which these are (literally) Day 1 skills you acquire.  The 'jars' issue has had it's own heated history.  Also, Devs have historically said they really dislike people using mods to change the game and if your way of playing does not follow how they believe the game 'should be played' has rubbed most people all the wrong ways. It makes zero sense because there's a rather decent modding community dedicated to improving much of what is missing or otherwise gets removed or patched out of the game. (I hesitate to mention jars again...)  Recent releases have made this game less enjoyable as time goes on. The push to sell skins for players as a money grab kind of tells me this is where I get off the train - this isn't fortnite, but I guess that's what we want to monetize: chicken costumes. Because, you know, both of those add to the realism to a game that used to be heavily defined by making health and survival a huge part of the game, but apparently not camouflage or the need to prevent excessive UV exposure in the desert.   Sure, it's a game, I get it, but a strange hill you're willing to die on when it's a life-or-death risk to eat a moldy sandwich because your character is starving but walking in the desert in a sexy bikini doesn't cause excessive dehydration, heatstroke or other negative effects.  Game logic is airtight until you need to add the 3rd grade playground rules, 'because'.  TL;DR - play the older versions of the game (are we still able to force older Alpha versions...????) and then compare with more recent ones. Sure, there are some good things which got added later, but what made this game sooooo good early on was a collection of many things which were later plucked out, one by one and replaced with something less.

Bannerlord is the kind of game where I can lose an entire evening without realizing how much time has passed.  I've played a lot of campaigns in Bannerlord, and every one of them somehow ends up becoming its own little story. Sometimes I'm focused on building an economy and trading between cities, sometimes I'm leading an army across half the map, and sometimes I'm just looking for the next battle because I want to see how my army performs.  One of the biggest differences for me was moving from console to PC. I played Bannerlord on console completely vanilla, with no mods, and I already had a great time with it. But playing it on PC and finally being able to use mods made me realize just how much potential this game has.  Sieges become more interesting, trading becomes deeper, kingdom management gets more options, and suddenly there are dozens of little improvements that make the whole experience feel smoother.  And the armies you can create are probably my favorite part. You can go all-in on cavalry and turn the battlefield into absolute chaos, or build an army around Battanian Fians and watch enemy troops disappear before they even get close. Then you can completely change your approach in the next campaign and play around with a totally different composition.  I've also learned that Bannerlord is more fun when you don't abuse its strongest mechanics. Smithing is probably the biggest example. Once you start exploiting it for ridiculous amounts of money, progression can become way too easy. When I deliberately avoid OP smithing and actually make my money through battles, trading and running my kingdom, the campaign feels much more satisfying.  What frustrates me is that the game often feels like it is one major update away from being much more complete. There are so many systems where you can clearly see what the developers were trying to build, but then you find yourself installing a mod because an important feature is missing or unnecessarily limited.  And that's where the modding community comes in. A lot of Bannerlord mods don't feel like they are changing the game; they feel like they are finishing it. After playing vanilla on console, this became especially obvious to me when I moved to PC.  Despite that, I keep coming back. There is something incredibly satisfying about starting with basically nothing, building your clan, gathering companions, recruiting your army, becoming stronger, taking castles and eventually watching your faction become a serious power on the map.  One campaign can be about trade and diplomacy. Another can be about building the most ridiculous cavalry force possible. Another can end with me sitting outside a castle with an army of Fians and wondering how the enemy thought attacking was a good idea.  That freedom is what keeps Bannerlord installed on my PC.  It's not a perfect game, and I really wish the developers would integrate more of the features that the community has been asking for instead of leaving modders to fill those gaps. But when you combine the base game with the incredible modding scene, Bannerlord becomes an experience with an absurd amount of replayability.  I've already had more campaigns than I can count, and I'm sure there will be another one eventually. Probably with another completely unnecessary amount of mods.

I've played this game with so much love and passion. But recently, the fun and excitement I used to get from it have completely vanished.  First, the good things:  The gunplay is AMAZING. I would always defend this game when talking to other people and tell them that it has some of the best shooter mechanics out there.  The sound design is also absolutely fantastic. You really learn to appreciate how well-crafted it is when using high-end headphones. Being able to hear enemies before they can hear you adds so much to the experience.  If we're talking solely about the game itself, I would always recommend it.  Now comes the bad part.  And I'm saying this from the perspective of a 6-Star MMR player. The lobbies are divided into different MMR ratings from 1 to 6 Stars, with 6 Stars being the highest.  The game has a severe problem with the European servers, where I feel like I'm being matched with Russian and Chinese players most of the time. And when I say most of the time, I mean around 90% of my matches.  The difference between encountering a European team and encountering a high-ping team (usually Russian/Chinese)  is incredibly frustrating.  When I get killed by a European team, I usually don't think twice about it. I know I got outplayed, made a mistake, or simply lost the fight.  But when I get killed in certain situations by players from outside Europe, I often find myself thinking:  "How the hell did I just die there?"  Then I check the player's profile and see where they're from, and it happens far too often. Far too often meaning i feel like i'm only getting killed from High-Ping Teams anymore.  What I'm talking about is the insane difference that high ping can make in gunfights. Whether it's hit registration, peeker's advantage, or simply the way players appear and disappear around corners, the experience can feel completely different.  And honestly, it's becoming so frustrating that it has taken away almost all of the fun and excitement I used to have for this game.  I don't mind losing. I don't mind getting outplayed. That's part of the game.  What I do mind is feeling like the outcome of a gunfight was determined by connection quality rather than by who played the situation better.  It's especially frustrating because I genuinely love this game. The gunplay, the sound design, the atmosphere — all of it is fantastic. I want to enjoy it, but playing at 6 Stars on the European servers has become increasingly exhausting.  And then there's another thing I simply don't understand:  I've encountered players who apparently already have VAC bans on their profiles, yet they're still able to play the game.  How is that even possible?  The lack of communication from Crytek makes this even more frustrating.  The developers have actually acknowledged these problems in the past. Around 1.5 years ago, Crytek talked about potential solutions such as region blocking or preventing players from joining certain servers if their ping exceeds a specific threshold.  At the time, I was genuinely hopeful that something would eventually be done about it.  But since then, there has been very little to no communication about this issue.  1.5 years is a long time when you're dealing with a problem that directly affects the experience of your most dedicated players.  I don't expect the developers to magically fix everything overnight. But I do expect some kind of communication. Tell us what you're working on. Tell us if the proposed solutions aren't technically feasible. Tell us if the problem is more complicated than expected.  Just communicate with the community.  The current lack of communication regarding this particular issue has been really disappointing, at least from my personal perspective.  I really hope the developers take a serious look at the current state of matchmaking and high-ping gameplay.  Because underneath all of this, there is an incredible shooter.

[h1]RimWorld: The Ultimate Story Generator and Why It Might Just Be the Greatest Game Ever Made[/h1]  At a glance, RimWorld looks like a modest, top-down indie colony sim with humble graphics and faceless little pawns sliding across a grid. But peel back those simple visuals, and you find a staggering masterpiece of systemic design—not just a survival game, but an unmatched, endlessly unfolding engine for human drama.   To call it a masterpiece isn't hyperbole; it's an acknowledgment of what happens when mechanics, emergent storytelling, and total player freedom collide.   [h1]The Storyteller, Not the Game[/h1]  What elevates RimWorld into the pantheon of all-time greats is how it frames your experience. Governed by invisible AI "storytellers" (like Cassandra Classic or Randy Random), the game isn't trying to beat you, nor is it just letting you sandbox in peace. It’s actively co-writing a tragedy, a comedy, or an action thriller with you.  One moment you’re peacefully expanding your corn harvest; the next, a heatwave hits, a rabid squirrel bites your best builder, a mechanical dread-cluster drops from the sky, and your resident pyromaniac decides it’s a great time to light the chemfuel storage on fire.  [h1]Emotional Investment Out of Nowhere[/h1]  The true magic of RimWorld is how deeply you care about its inhabitants. Because pawns have distinct traits, flaws, addictions, relationships, and breaking points, they aren't just units—they are characters.  [u]You will remember the pacifist chef who single-handedly held off a raid with a lucky pistol shot.  You will mourn the colonist who caught the plague just days before the rescue transport arrived.  You will laugh, panic, and curse at the sheer absurdity of the situations your people get themselves into. [/u]  [h1]Infinite Replayability and Modding Nirvana[/h1]  No two playthroughs of RimWorld are ever the same. Between the randomized planets, changing scenarios, deep expansion DLCs (like Royalty, Ideology, Biotech, and Anomaly), and one of the most prolific modding communities in PC gaming history, RimWorld can literally transform into whatever game you want it to be. Want a gritty sci-fi survival? Done. A total-conversion fantasy epic with magic and monsters? Easy.   [h1]The Verdict[/h1]  RimWorld is a rare achievement. It challenges your intellect, tests your planning, breaks your heart, and then forces you to immediately hit "New Colony" to try and fix what went wrong. It is a canvas for your darkest choices, your most heroic triumphs, and thousands of hours of unforgettable memories.  If a game is measured by the stories you tell long after you've closed it, RimWorld easily stakes its claim as one of the greatest games ever made.  What kind of colony usually spells your downfall—are you a victim of random Randy chaos, or do your own poorly managed food supplies and pyromaniacs do you in first?

A Convoluted UX Nightmare Burying Deep Potential  •  As someone who has only spent about two hours in RimWorld, please take this perspective for what it is—a raw first impression of the user experience, and I enjoy the discovery of a game, and don't use tutorials. Simply put: the user interface is an absolute mess. It genuinely feels as though the developer went out of their way to overly complicate every single interaction. I spent my entire initial playtime just trying to reverse-engineer the designer's thought process and figure out why things were structured in such a counter-intuitive, fragmented way. It leaves me seriously questioning how this game maintains an "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating. Are these reviews authentic, or is this a case of collective Stockholm Syndrome? My theory is that players who stick around simply develop a high tolerance for these flawed systems. Once you invest dozens of hours learning how the developer’s mind works, you build the muscle memory required to look past the terrible UI. At that point, the sheer mechanical depth and emergent gameplay probably take over, making the experience enjoyable despite the interface, not because of it. While it is incredibly tempting to completely tear this game apart based on how frustratingly unfunctional it feels upfront, I am trying to remain open-minded. There is clearly a massive amount of depth hidden under the hood. However, forcing players to fight a convoluted spreadsheet-management simulator just to execute basic tasks is a massive barrier to entry. The depth of a game should be found in its strategy, not in its menus.

The game certainly has solid foundations and intriguing depth, but I will focus strictly on its fundamental flaws—plenty of people are already singing its praises.     • Misleading Core Premise: The game is advertised as a colony simulator and story generator, but by default, it functions strictly as a brutal Tower Defense game disguised under sim mechanics.     • Punished for Progress: You cannot freely build a grand, beautiful base. Wealth-scaling raid mechanics actively punish prosperity, turning city-building into guaranteed annihilation unless you rely on killboxes.     • Forced Poverty Optimization: The optimal way to play forces you to keep colonists in artificial squalor and micromanage misery, rather than building a thriving, high-standard society.     • Flawed Quest Scaling: Quest difficulty relies on the same broken wealth formulas, offering absurd suicide missions to small settlements and penalizing you for taking good rewards.     • Exploiting Dumb AI Over Real Tactics: Instead of encouraging realistic defense and strategic thinking, the game forces players to build cheesy killboxes to abuse the enemies' flawed pathfinding AI.     • Anti-Economic Logic: The mechanics contradict fundamental economic, strategic, and logistical laws. Real-world power and security rely on capital, surplus, and stockpiles; here, productivity is an existential threat that forces deliberate self-sabotage and asset dumping. Managing labor around penalizing wealth rather than rewarding growth directly mirrors the bureaucratic stagnation and decline of the European Union.     • Reality Check for Potential Buyers: This review is for rational players deciding if the game is worth buying, not for blind fanatics pissing their pants in euphoria over mastering the developer's arbitrary rulebook—rules that have long lost any connection to logic or the real world.     • The Illusion of Depth (The ONI Trap): Much like Oxygen Not Included, the game hooks you early with engaging survival mechanics, but the moment you try applying real-world engineering, logic, or economic principles, you realize the underlying systems are fundamentally degenerate.     • Vanilla Means Vanilla: I refuse to fix broken design with endless mods or cheat through custom sliders just to make a game bearable. This critique applies strictly to the unmodded, default game as intended by the developer—this is the way.

We're still talking a game that's infinitely less complex than dwarf fortress, and has less content in its DLCs than in some of the DF updates. I started playing DF in 2007, I still see new stuff. After a few games of Rimworld in a given biome, I already see the same challenges, the same animals, the situations are roughly exactly the same. I can't recommend to buy it in good conscience.  That aside, the prison architect 1:1 style copy is weird but works well, the game isn't pretty tho but we can excuse that. The OST slaps. It's still a good and somewhat challenging colony sim. I have a bit of an issue with the scope being rather limited (smaller groups of people than I'm used too) but it's a matter of personal preference and I can get it. I'd love to recommend this game to my friends, but every other year it becomes a more expensive product, and I just... can't.  People will use arguments like, "The base game is perfectly fine, just play it and if you want more, get the DLCs later." This ignores the fact that game developers commonly leave out features that feel like they belong in the base game so they can sell them later. I'm not claiming that's what happened here, but it easily could be, and nobody would be the wiser for it.  Fact is, you could probably ignore Royalty and Anomaly, but Biotech and Ideology fit so naturally into Rimworld's futuristic colony setting they feel like they should have been present from the start. They could have been released as free updates. But no. They effectively raise the price of the game from $35 to $80.  It certainly doesn't help that Rimworld and its DLCs have never gone on sale for more than 20% off. What is this? Nintendo? "Our games are timeless and don't depreciate in value"? I understand a developer not wanting to play the sale game, but when you're refusing to meaningfully discount anything AND offering DLC that rival the base game's price, you have to realize what you're doing.  If you want to buy Rimworld, and all its DLCs, at base price, you will pay $150. In another year or two that'll probably be $175.  The question I have is: where will people choose to draw the line, and why?

After 12 hours, it's a solid survival crafting RPG, very nostalgic to my days in Old School Runescape. Many references, skills, and progression mechanics were retained from days past. However, I've encountered several occasional bugs that put a small damper on my experience, but none are game-breaking so far, just a nuisance. Inventory navigation will be unresponsive sometimes with controller, but a simple close/reopen of the inventory screen fixes it. I found myself unable to place new buildings an hour into playing after successfully doing so beforehand with no issue, and I confirmed I didn't activate Ghost Mode or anything else; relogging the world resolved the issue and I haven't encountered it since.  One major point I'd like to make to the developers, though: the crafting system needs more polish, not necessarily an overhaul, but having to press the same button 4 times on controller to smelt/cook/process something at a station becomes very tiresome, especially considering the "GO" button changes to the Y button in certain instances. I would much prefer a small menu in the processing UI where I can select the Item I'd like to process/cook/smelt, and it not only requires just one extra button press to choose a quantity, but also pulls from nearby chests like the other crafting stations rather than having to manually insert the individual ingredients like it's Alpha Minecraft.  Complaints and bugs aside, I would still recommend this game, and I hope to see it flourish into my next favorite game!

The game overall is just okay. The one positive I can truly give it is probably the base building. The fact that you have no real limitations is truly amazing, but it can also be frustrating as hell. The game doesn't properly explain how to build a stable structure, so you could start building a base only to realize that the material you're using isn't strong enough for what you want to make. So, while there are no limitations on how much you can build, there are limitations that the game doesn't inherently explain when it comes to actually building successfully.  Now, the bad:  The combat is really boring and kind of awful. You only get three spells for staffs and wands, and the only two you'll ever really use are air and fire since water is just awful. The weapons all feel the same. You just spam the attack button, which on PC is left click. It doesn't feel satisfying at all, and the animations aren't impressive either.  This is the big kicker: most enemies can be cheesed by simply getting high ground on a rock. Most of the time, I found myself doing this because trying to take on four or five monsters that are even one item level higher than you is just going to result in you dying again and again.  I only fought the first boss, and it literally felt like a boss from a children's game. It had two mechanics that were extremely easy to understand right from the start.  The exploration is pretty boring as well. There isn't much to discover, and the dungeons are just bad. The storage system for exploring the world is also poor. You can barely carry anything around until you reach level 40 Construction, which isn't easy to achieve right away. Once you do, you can get the personal chest, which makes carrying and storing items much easier.  I truly wouldn't recommend this game to anyone unless you're looking to build a big city with some friends, maybe on casual mode so you don't have to deal with the combat. But even then, I'm sure there are better games out there for building a base.
