I originally thought that the full release of RuneScape: Dragonwilds would provide a more complete and better gameplay experience than before, but after actually playing it, I was extremely disappointed. First of all, there was a bug in the Library main quest that left me and my friend stuck for a full two hours. For those two hours, there was nothing we could do except repeatedly try again, restart, and look for ways to solve the problem. This was no longer just a minor bug; it seriously affected the progression of the game. What made the experience even more painful were the problems with the monster AI and attack hit detection throughout the game. I would often take damage and even die repeatedly despite clearly having dodged the attacks. If it happened once or twice, I could accept it, but when it kept happening over and over again, it became increasingly frustrating to play. Even so, I endured all of these problems and continued playing until the final chapter of the main story, thinking that at the very least, I wanted to experience the ending. Then I reached the Boss fight, and whatever patience I had left was completely exhausted. The attack hit detection during the Boss's second phase was extremely unreasonable. The same attack seemed to have multiple damage hitboxes or multiple damage instances, and simply getting hit could result in an instant death within a very short period of time. What I found most unacceptable was that even with relatively complete and decent equipment, I could still be instantly killed by a single attack. If this were simply the result of player error, I could accept it. If my equipment were insufficient, I could always go back and farm for better equipment. But when deaths are primarily caused by obviously problematic attack hit detection, there is practically nothing the player can do through better gameplay or preparation to improve the experience. Throughout the entire process, I was basically enduring one problem after another: enduring the main quest bug, enduring the monster AI issues, and enduring the inexplicable deaths. After finally making it all the way to the final chapter, I just wanted to see whether the ending of the full release could make all the problems I had experienced earlier feel worthwhile. Instead, the Boss fight ended up being the most painful part of the entire experience. This is no longer something that can simply be explained as the game being "difficult." It made me feel like I wasn't losing to the Boss itself, but rather fighting against the game's own bugs and unreasonable hit detection. I genuinely wanted to enjoy this game, but this entire experience constantly wore down my patience. In the end, the sense of accomplishment from completing the game was nowhere near the exhaustion I accumulated from being repeatedly frustrated by bugs, incorrect hit detection, and unreasonable deaths. I hope future updates can genuinely address these issues. The game itself actually has a lot of potential and many aspects that I was looking forward to, but at the moment, these bugs and combat hit detection issues seriously damage the overall gameplay experience.

As much as I want to love this because I love RuneScape (mostly RS3, but I do enjoy OSRS as well), I can't.   They really should have given this game several more months before release.  As of today, the game just feels half-baked, with a fraction of the polish that their other games have and no real differentiators from the 500 other survival/crafters out there which have combat.  I get that they wanted to release while they could still profit off the survival/crafting game craze, but it just doesn't feel like an RS game.  It feels like a very early-access build of Valheim with a RuneScape skin put over it. Yes, a few of the characters we know are there, but otherwise there is both nothing unique/interesting here and also a lot of stuff that just feels like it's not even early-access-ready.    Don't get me wrong, I knew going into this that it was a different type of game than RS3 and OSRS. I just don't think it's actually a better product than either of those games. A solid survival/crafter that FEELS like it's in the RuneScape world would have been EPIC.  This isn't that, beyond some minor visual flair.  This feels like someone tried to mod the 0.5 version of Enshrouded as a RS fan project.  Most disappointing is that nothing is voiced outside a few spare cutscenes.  This is a huge step backwards from RS3, where more and more content is getting voiced. Granted, not everything is silent, but when it feels like it's a huge step down from a game that's been around for over a decade? That's just truly and distinctly a bad move.   There ARE some positives here.  The game plays smoothly (I use GeForce Now), and I haven't run into any massive bugs.  While everything is painfully generic, those generic systems are there and do work.  Building is well done and fluid, even with a controller/gamepad (no small feat). Combat is at least interesting, since the game has melee, ranged, and magic.   Give it at least six months, if they can drag things out that long without a solid playerbase. But right now? I can't even come close to recommending this one.  I'm not refunding, but I'm also not going to be playing until the finish the game - at least to a point where it doesn't feel like every other survival/crafter in a generic world with generic unlocks and generic gameplay.

It's a decent game, but it could be a lot better. I think I got my value out of this because I have time to burn, but that just underlines how grindy the game is. This game fails in several aspects that honestly should've been obvious to the dev team and play testers:  1. Excessive skill grind with tiny, often insignificant and pointless rewards, like 0.085% stamina reduction per point of agility, the hardest skill in the game to grind. I'm sure you're all looking forward to using 8% less stamina 200+ hours into a game. 2. Animation locks for everything. If you shoot your staff once, you'll have to wait 3-4 seconds before you can switch to a new hotbar item. If you cast a spell, you will cast that spell even if you're about to die  and want to move. Because of this, the combat feels very clunky, stilted, and unreactive. 3. Excessively long cooldowns for spells that are meant to save time. Why do I have to wait 60 seconds between watering my crops? And the alternative takes about the same amount of time, so you're either stuck waiting or watering by hand for the same result. 4. The combat is bad. No taunt for melee to control aggro. The heal of the staff is functionally useless. Animation locks make every action a risk, as you might not be able to dodge a fatal attack. Enemy damage is ridiculously high and kills you in 3-4 hits. Spells are almost impossible to cast in combat because of the console wheel system for casting magic and their related animation locks. And worst of all, you'll learn all your attacks and weapons in the first 2-5 hours of the game, and use those for the rest of the game. Only the power level increases. No variety, no innovation, no imagination. Just the same 4-5 attacks all game. The combat is ATROCIOUS and a large part of the game. 5. Limited resource gather points and excessively long respawn times. This is not an issue early on, but when you need 400+ iron ore, having to wait an hour to wait for respawns feels like the devs just want to waste our time. 6. The excessive and offputting EULA basically signing away all you personal information, and the trollish "we'll respond in 45 days when you send us a letter in writing about not using your personal information".  Save your money, wait for Enshrouded, or play one of the games coming out that actually respects its players and their time.

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2 — 4/10  I really wanted to love Space Marine 2, but unfortunately, the game was a huge disappointment for me.  The visuals and atmosphere are impressive, and the Warhammer 40K setting looks fantastic, but good graphics and a great universe aren't enough to carry the entire experience.  The gameplay becomes repetitive very quickly. Most encounters feel like variations of the same thing: fight huge waves of enemies, move to the next area, repeat. After a while, it starts feeling more like a grind than an exciting power fantasy.  The mission design also feels too linear, and I often felt like I was simply being pushed from one combat arena to another rather than actually exploring an interesting world.  There are some great moments, but they are buried under repetitive gameplay and frustrating design choices. I expected to feel like an unstoppable Space Marine, but instead I frequently found myself getting tired of doing the same battles over and over.  Great presentation, disappointing gameplay.

The most flawed masterpiece is the best way to describe Monster Hunter World. It is a game that you'll either adore (like I do) or despise from the bottom of your heart. I personally hate quite a few things about it and I often had to scream at the screen out of frustration of some really horrible design and mechanical issues. Let's get into details, shall we?  First and foremost, the controls are awful, and so is the clunky and confusing UI. You'll eventually get used to it but that's basically like getting used to writing with your feet. It's still awful.   Secondly, you can't use your potions without sheathing your weapon first. And you need 5 business days to sheathe your weapons and 5 more business days to drink the potions. You'll eventually find ways to speed it up but it'll will still get you killed quite a lot because it takes way too long. It adds realism for sure but it also adds more screaming at the screen.   Speaking of realism, apparently it only applies to you because these giant dinosaurs do everything faster than you. They'll hit you, go home and have lunch with wifey, send their kids to school and celebrate an anniversary before you are done sheathing your weapon, drinking a potion or doing pretty much anything. They'll even limp faster than your running or jumping speed when you are chasing them in their final moments. It's like they have an invisible nitrous boost in their rear.  Did someone say chasing? Yeah, get used to these monsters playing Tom and Jerry with you every few minutes leading to you going up and down and down and up until you get to their next place. Oh, and by the time you make it, they may decide, "nope, I am going somewhere else", and down and up and down and up you go again to chase them down. Of course, during this, you move at turtle speed and these guys are like the rabbit, but actually win the race, every time.   Race...yeah that reminds me of something else I disliked initially but eventually got used to. However, I suspect many will never like it. Every mission is timed. You can't take your sweet time. Although most missions are 50 min long so it's a lot of time. But! You can't pause the game, even on solo. So forget long washroom breaks or any emergency because, well, you need to stop trying to have a life! You can go on a free roaming mode that isn't timed, but even then, you can't pause, and if you don't kill any monster quickly, they'll leave the zone.   Finally, I want to address the difficulty, and this is my experience with solo for story and almost all optional content. So far I only joined others for 1 boss that is meant for multiplayer anyway. Story is mostly on the average difficulty side until end game where it gets harder. It depends on your weapon class though and how fast you can adapt to this game's awful mechanics and controls.  What I don't like though is where the difficulty comes from. Basically enemies hit like trucks and have a massive invisible HP pool. Sometimes you'll get one shot or die with 2 hits without the right equipment. You could also be on a stun spree and stand there praying that your partner cat does not do something stupid like bring the monster to you (they'll do it a lot). You also have limited revives per mission and then back home you go to start it all over. It's basically artificial difficulty unlike in games like Dark Souls where you felt you needed to, "Git Gud". Over here, it's basically, "don't get touched".   It's amazing that I almost wrote an essay about the bad stuff, and I didn't even cover half of it. So why do I still recommend it you say? Well...to make it quick...The monsters and stage design and the music are just so amazing that I endured and still endure all those awful things I mentioned. It's simply a masterpiece as I said earlier, despite all the problems. The pleasure and adrenaline you get when you fight the monsters and eventually overcome them is so enormous that it just doesn't matter in the end. It's like climbing a filthy mountain to reach the top where you find Pandora's box. The journey might be full of crap but the destination is so rewarding that you forget about all the bad stuff, and you just can't wait to do it all over again, and again...and again...   TLDR all that : Amazing game that also really sucks. It's SO hard to rate this game properly! I never felt like this before. So many design issues but also so many outstanding moments with the fantastically designed monsters and the music that is unique to every single one of them. It's really breathtaking at times and other times it's rage inducing. Both extremes are present, hurray!   Final Score will be 2 scores for the first time for me : 6/10 if you focus on the issues and 9/10 if you blur it out and focus on what it does best, and that is: Monster Hunting.

Fun fact; The playtime on this game is completley broken as soon as you turn offline mode on, or even just boot up the game offline. The actual playtime I have is over 5K hours on ONE save.... and it keeps dropping below 1K. It seems to be going down. Not too important in the whole scheme of things, I just found that funny and wanted to quickly mention it.  Now onto the real meat; The review.  First things first; Would I recommend this game? Yes. Yes I would. Does it have it's problems? It does, but it's still worth it.  Monster Hunter World, or MHW, is a game where you can choose a weapon out of a fair selection of weapons, and hunt monsters for parts which you can then use to make and upgrade gear. It's not too hard to understand. That's essentially a simplified version of MHW as a whole.  What makes World so damn good is the fact that the performance, quests and overall gameplay is good in all 3 areas. You can easily run this game at 60FPS at a bare minimum with the right settings on a potato. While there are some quests that are freaking butt, most of them are well made and fun to play again. The gameplay is a LOT better than the previous games in the series.  The second main selling point for this game is the DLC. You want amazing graphics? You can easily download them. They don't come shoved into the main game by default, so they won't be a waste of space if you can't run them. You want a whole other chunk of the game with even better quests? Iceborne is there too. Honestly, I would only suggest getting world WITH Iceborne, as Iceborne has some of the BEST designed quests in the series. The endgame quests are actually challenging, but super fun when you get the hang of them.  Now, I will say, if you HAVE played Monster Hunter Rise before World, Rise in simple terms "babies the player a LOT". So things WILL be more of a challenge than Rise. Don't expect them to be easier. Just wanted to mention that.  So, all in all. Should you buy this game and the DLC? Yes, but I'd suggest waiting for a sale as this game goes on sale a LOT. So it's not too bad of a wait. Is it still worth it full price? Yes, but it's also better to just wait for a sale as it's free money saved.

It's a console port of a console game. It claims to be "open world" but it's a series of tightly shaped instances with limited paths in those instances. Bosses are HP sponges which involve multiple phases of sprinting around the map as it disengages. The sheathing and unsheathing animation eats into mobility and time in a way that is painful.  Bladed weapons have to be resharpened mid-fight. You have to find a safe place to back out of combat and several seconds of animation to restore the durability of your weapon. In other words, you're a renowned Monster Hunter with gear whose durability can't even last a single fight.  The first 10-15 minutes of the game are mostly unskippable cutscenes. The quest dialogue is intermittently voiced and then unvoiced. The graphics are beautiful, but that doesn't make the game fun.  Playing Monster Hunter: World feels like visiting an amusement park with weights tied to your legs, then told you can go do anything you want, while having a midget pull you in the opposite direction you're trying to go.

Monster Hunter in my opinion is one of the worst series of all time. I didn't play the earlier ones, but I've heard they're even worse in their setup than this game, and I don't understand how it took off. I'm guessing it was on a handheld, and people desperately wanted anything for their handheld. Monster Hunter probably seemed like it was a good value for the money, and I doubt dark souls was even a thing at that time.  This game honestly has the worst combat I can imagine. You fight the camera, and the controls, as much as you fight the aoe, the knockdowns, and the stuns. Enemies can use collision to damage you. I honestly think most of my frustration comes from the controls being so bad. I can't even face the monster half the time when I want to attack. I actually have to hit forward until my character turns in that direction to attack that way. Camera lock on does not help in this regard. You cannot stay facing the enemy, and have the camera locked on. It does not work like dark souls.  I have wilds, and came back to this one, after spending only like 15 hours with it. Most of my time was fighting pretty easy stuff, and some of the large monsters. I only just now fought the lizard guy, and it was pretty annoying having to dodge his attacks, and then fight the controls to be able to strike him. A lot of it was dodging around, then trying to face the enemy before I counter attack. I can't even imagine how bad this is going to be with later monsters that will chain aoe knockdown attacks together, with high damage.  In Wilds some improvements have been made to the combat. Some weapons are quicker in use. There is a focus mode, so your attacks swing where the camera is targeted, rather than having to move in that direction first. Healing and sharpening your blade are easier, as you can use your mount in combat, to run around evasively, while using your potions and tools. In world using your potions and sharpening is way more dangerous. Going from Wilds to this makes this system even more egregious. I hate the routines I have to go through in wilds, and here they're even worse.  Wilds also have a radial menu selection that uses whichever potion is best for the situation, but it doesn't seem to use max potions. It's radial menu will use less bindings, compared to World. World's radial menu will typically have more bindings used for potions, status recovery, and your whetstone  World has better designed zones. Wilds feel very windy, with too many passages connecting the zones. You basically have to use your mount on auto travel mode to go to a waypoint. Doing it yourself is too confusing. This is a nice benefit to Wilds, however, as getting to a point is faster. The mount also makes it easier to avoid fights with monsters on the way to a waypoint.  World has a better storyline going on. It's faster to unlock capturing. The storyline isn't obtrusive, there are no annoying characters, or any characters really, which I'm okay with. Let the setting, and a basic story set the tone. The world and it's life is the focus. Wilds screws this up. World has better progression. Bounty system is annoying though.  World forces you to have people join your game for multiplayer. Wilds allows you to have AI teammates join you, so it's a 4 hunter game every time without having to wait for people.  I think Monster Hunter games are for people who don't know what a good time is, and are willing to play this because they played it previously. Newcomers will play it because of how many others play it. The game sold a lot. It's like games of the 80s and 90s, that were extremely difficult because not enough stuff was explained, there was no handholding. Nothing was convenient. Many RPG games were made so difficult, and confusing in their design, that you'd have to buy a cluebook to have a chance of solving it. Try playing Wizardry without the cluebooks. They have a part of the series that is linked together, 6,7 and 8. 6 is a nightmare for navigation. You are basically required to use a cluebook.  The masochists who enjoy that stuff, stuff I'm happy to put behind me, are the people that like Monster Hunter.

Title: A Monument to Institutional Malice, Toxic Incompetence, and Betrayed Devotion: The Absolute Extinction Event of Among Us  I used to believe in this game with every fiber of my being. That unwavering, misplaced faith is now my deepest, most agonizing, and most humiliating wound. I didn’t just play Among Us during the 2020 pandemic lockdown golden age; I consumed it, breathed it, and sacrificed thousands of waking and sleeping hours to its colorful, deceptively simple spaceship corridors, treating its social deduction mechanics and frantic emergency meetings as a sacred second home. I spent years defending Innersloth's glacial update cycles, actively rationalizing their glaring server oversights, and aggressively dismissing the dark warning signs whispering through the community as the mere whining of disgruntled casuals. I was a foot soldier of a cult-like devotion, utterly convinced that this was a world crafted by independent creators who understood the fragile, beautiful bond between an indie developer and a passionate player base.  How intensely, unforgivably, and pathetically foolish I was.  What the public sees on the store page is a nostalgic, charming indie social deduction party game—a modest cartoonish masterpiece born from small-team work claiming to channel the ultimate psychological bluffing experience. But beneath that paper-thin, calculatedly deceptive facade lies a predatory, aggressively hostile ecosystem designed to exploit your time, weaponize your passion, harvest your free community moderation labor, and ultimately punish you for the singular crime of actually engaging deeply with public lobbies. The harsh reality of Among Us isn't a love letter to party gaming; it’s an institutionalized insult, a middle finger to anyone foolish enough to invest hundreds of hours into its structurally hollow and fundamentally broken framework.  Let’s pull back the curtain and talk about the unspoken horror that haunts the public lobbies of this game: the arbitrary, indiscriminate, and utterly cowardly ban hammer and chat censorship that targets the most dedicated players the moment they use basic deduction. For weeks, the veteran group chats whispered about it in paralyzing dread. Dedicated players—the exact backbone of the community, the people organizing logical deduction rooms, keeping custom game codes alive, and filling the community spaces with helpful strategy guides—would vanish overnight, or find their chat messages instantly star-filtered into absolute unintelligible gibberish. Their names were silently scrubbed, their accounts restricted, and their appeals locked behind an impenetrable wall of developer silence. I scoffed at the victims. I arrogantly told myself that I played completely legitimately, that hundreds of hours of honest sleuthing, meticulous task management, and raw social persistence would serve as my shield.  Then my inevitable turn came.  Mid-game, deep inside a high-tension emergency meeting where I had successfully tracked down the exact vent usage and alibi inconsistencies of a blatant teamer, the screen seized violently. The dreaded connection error warning flashed across the UI, followed instantly by a forced, unceremonious disconnect to the title screen. My hands shook uncontrollably as I scrambled to hit find game, enter a lobby, and was greeted by the most infuriating, gut-wrenching, soul-crushing notification: temporary suspension or chat restriction for daring to use harsh or direct logical callouts in a game entirely built around accusation and deception.  No warning. No specific rule violation cited other than automated keyword filters catching normal game banter. No human review whatsoever. Just an abrupt, summary execution carried out by a completely inept, automated moderation algorithm that apparently cannot comprehend the basic reality that a human being might actually want to play a social deduction game with passion and intensity. If you dare to actually play their game seriously, to push past the casual meme lobbies, and dedicate real, unbroken hours to mastering map routing, task speed, and psychological tells, their broken, hair-trigger security protocols automatically flag your communication as toxic behavior. They don't want a vibrant competitive social scene because they either haven't built a functional, stable infrastructure to sustain it, or they are utterly terrified of what veteran players discover when the illusion of wholesome casual fun is finally pulled back.  And when you turn to support for even a shred of recourse or human dignity? Prepare to crash headfirst into a brick wall constructed entirely of corporate apathy, cowardice, and automated responses. I poured my bleeding, broken heart into a meticulously written ticket—detailing my exact playtime, my absolute adherence to fair play, and my profound, heartbreaking disappointment. Within minutes, I was hit with the exact same robotic, copy-pasted wall of garbage text that every single restricted victim receives: "Your account action was upheld. This decision is final."  No appeal process. No human being willing to look at your case, check your match logs, or grant you basic respect. Just a cold, algorithmic middle finger from developers who happily take the cultural phenomenon, the active player counts, and the free social media virality of their base while treating us like disposable trash the moment an automated script misfires. The silence from Innersloth is deafening, pathetic, and entirely telling. They hide behind automated systems because facing the human wreckage of their broken chat filters and abysmal matchmaking design requires a spine they simply do not possess.  The technical and design state of the game outside of these tyrannical bans is an absolute disaster anyway, propped up by pure nostalgia and endless crossover merch. The public lobby experience is a chaotic, hyper-toxic mess dictated by trolls, leavers, and Discord cheaters who somehow bypass the very detection tools meant for honest players. Game balancing is practically non-existent, featuring bloated role additions that add artificial confusion rather than tactical depth. The repetitive gameplay loop quickly morphs from a casual throwback into an unrewarding, punishing, soul-crushing chore where nobody takes tasks seriously and everyone leaves the second they aren't assigned the Impostor role. Every single system feels half-baked, held together with digital duct tape and the nostalgic goodwill of players who desperately want it to succeed, only to be brutally kicked in the teeth the second they try to play a real match.  My account—complete with painstakingly unlocked cosmetics, hundreds of hours of irreplaceable memories, and genuine friendships forged in lobby chats—was crippled by automated censorship and broken matchmaking. All of it ruined, vaporized into the ether by developers who couldn’t care less if every single veteran social player walked away.  If you are a new player currently looking at this store page, reading the glowing mobile-port promises, or thinking about downloading this free-to-play trap: Stop. Do not install it. Do not give them your metrics. Do not invest your time, your energy, or your passion into a digital world that fundamentally despises its own community. Play literally anything else. Because if you actually stay, if you actually try to play public lobbies, and if you dare to care about the game too much, the only reward waiting for you is a communication ban screen and developers who refuse to look.  Among Us isn't just another failed multiplayer phenomenon; it is a meticulously constructed psychological trap for the devoted and an eternal monument to bad-faith development. Save your time, save your sanity, protect your peace, and stay far, far away from this toxic wasteland. It stands as a profound, unforgivable insult to anyone who ever believed that passion, time, and genuine emotional investment in a virtual social.

Just downloaded Squad? Welcome! 🎮  Squad can feel a little confusing when you first start, so here are a few tips that will make your first games much easier:  1. Start with the Infantry Tutorial Before jumping into a match, take a few minutes to complete the tutorial. It will help you get familiar with the basics.  2. Find a server and community you enjoy There are hundreds of servers, and every community is a little different. Some are very welcoming to new players, while others are more experienced. Try a few and find one you enjoy. Joining their Discord can also be a great way to meet players and find a community you like.  3. Join a squad and use your mic 🎙️ This is one of the most important things in Squad. Don’t be afraid to talk! If you’re not sure what to do, ask your Squad Leader or other players. Most people will be happy to help you learn.  4. Stick with your squad Try to stay with your squad and follow your Squad Leader. Squad is built around teamwork, so you’ll have a much better experience when you work together instead of going off on your own.  5. Don’t worry about being new Everyone was a new player once. You will make mistakes, get lost, and probably die a lot at first — that's part of learning. 😄  Give it some time, communicate with your team, and enjoy the experience.

review_text: The Witcher 3 is more than just a game for me.  I’ve played a lot of games over the years, but very few have managed to create a world that I actually wanted to get lost in. The characters, the music, the quests, the atmosphere, and especially the little details throughout the world make this game feel genuinely alive.  What I love most about The Witcher 3 is that even after all these years, I can come back to it and still find something that makes me stop and think, “Damn, this game is incredible.”  Geralt’s journey is one of those experiences I’ll never forget. Some quests feel more memorable than entire games, and the expansions somehow managed to make an already amazing game even better.  I absolutely love this game, and honestly, I’m already looking forward to whatever comes next. I’m waiting for the next DLC and, of course, The Witcher 4 with a ridiculous amount of excitement.  CD Projekt Red, take your time. Just give us another world worth getting lost in.  Until then… Wind’s howling.

game_name: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Complete Edition
review_text: I honestly think the unlimited carry weight, removal of equipment durability, and transmog system are some of the worst changes in the remaster.  They may look like harmless quality-of-life features, but they seriously hurt the immersive RPG experience. They turn the game into something much more focused on instant gratification and “just have fun” gameplay.  I know all of these features can be turned off. But I don't think that's a good solution. Developers shouldn't add a bunch of systems that fundamentally change the way the game is played and then simply say, “If you don't like them, just turn them off.”  The problem is that these rules used to exist naturally as part of the game. Now, if I want the original experience, I have to impose those rules on myself.  Those are not the same experience.  Before, the game told me: “You have limited carry weight, so you have to think about what you pick up and what you keep.”  Now the game tells me: “You can carry everything if you want. You never have to repair your equipment if you don't want to. You can use whatever stats you want while looking like something completely different.”  And I have to tell myself: “Okay, I won't use those features because I want to play the game the old way.”  That's not the same thing. The first is a game system. The second is basically a self-imposed challenge.  I think modern game design is increasingly treating friction as something bad: if something slows the player down or forces them to make choices, it must be removed.  But in an RPG, those limitations are often exactly what give your actions meaning. **And it is precisely because the game gets in my way that my actions have meaning.**  If I have unlimited inventory, picking up another item means almost nothing. If my equipment never deteriorates, maintaining it means nothing. If appearance and equipment are completely disconnected, what I'm actually wearing no longer has to make sense in the world.  The problem isn't that these features exist. The problem is that they change the game's rules and then leave the original rules as something the player has to impose on themselves.

game_name: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Complete Edition
review_text: Even after playing through the first two games, I just can not bring myself to finish the Witcher 3. I've tried multiple times over the years to get into the game, but it always leaves me bored to tears. I think the biggest issue is that it sort of over stays its welcome. Mainly with the length of the quests and how they drag on. It's strange to go from the excellence of the first game and its interesting quests to something that attempts more of a "cinematic" approach to dialogue that just drags on.   One of the biggest issues is that the game was made by Europeans or rather Polish dudes, so a lot of the dialogue just sounds poorly translated/low budget or out of place in English. Another game I played recently that had this issue was Crimson Desert, which's story was created by Koreans. Given that the entirety of Witcher 3 relies on its dialogue and story, it really makes it difficult to connect with some of the characters,  One thing that generally confuses me is how people can enjoy the story of Witcher 3 without having played through the first game. When I first played Witcher 3 at release, I didn't know who the hell anybody was, and so there was absolutely no reason for me to care about any character or their intentions. I had briefly played the second game when it had released, and still didn't know anyone besides Geralt or Roche. Well after playing through WItcher 1, I now understand the characters and the general idea of the story. I know who Dandelion, Zoltan, Vesemir, Triss, and all these returning characters are from the first game. The problem is that they don't seem as well written or interesting anymore.  So after getting a general idea of the story and connecting with the characters that the game relies on, I still couldn't even bring myself to find Dandelion and Ciri. That's another issue I have with this game, which is the focus on Ciri. She was mentioned in the first game by name only, and it was interesting to hear when I played it. The problem is that Witcher 3 just sort of expects you to care about Ciri. There really isn't really much backstory given to her, and she just seems somewhat out of place throughout the game. I assume that finishing the story would have it make more sense given that the next game will feature her as the main character, but it still feels somewhat odd/out of place throughout the journey of finding her.   That is where the main quest starts to get boring as hell. Once you end up in Novigrad, you go through a series of investigations putting you through more hours of boring dialogue and a Europeans attempt at making the story seem more cinematic with more pronounced facial animations and such. All of this just to find someone named Whoreson Junior, who still doesn't know where Dandelion is. Well guess what, now you have to go to Skeillage and do the same ♥♥♥♥. The entire time you're just wanting to use fast travel, because exploring the world isn't that fun. Most quests boil down to playing detective and using the "batman Arkham" esque witcher sense mechanic throughout the majority of the game. At this point in my life, that mechanic feels so tiresome and overused in RPG's/open world action RPG's.   Despite the Blood of the Dawnwalker contributing to the ever increasing oversaturation of the gaming market by trying to be a Witcher 3 clone, I actually enjoyed that game and its use of the "Witcher sense" mechanic. It also didn't over stay its welcome with the main quest and is something I actually feel inclined to replay.   Witcher 3 on the other hand never feels like a game I want to replay, and I don't know if I'll ever bring myself to finish it.   On a positive note, the game does feel like a big improvement over the second game. In my opinion, Witcher 1 is the best game in the series and is one of the best CRPG's I have played. After playing 2 right after finishing the first game, I was left really disappointed with how "consolised" it felt in comparison. Despite being on a newer engine, the game felt like it was developed around a controller rather than strictly keyboard and mouse, and thus it didn't control as well as Witcher 1. It also was very QTE heavy and you had to wait for animations to play just to jump off a ledge for example. Its world also felt smaller than 1's, and focused way too much on political jargon between the kingdoms, which made the story boring and fall flat.   Witcher 3 was a big improvement over 2 and brought back some of those PC esque elements, and so it plays significantly better with mouse and keyboard than Witcher 2. It also brought back monster hunting and the open world is beautiful to look at, and is more fun to explore than the second games. I just think that it's too big for its own good and the main story just never clicks with me. Witcher 1's story was just great to me because it didn't need to try and have a focus on cinematic dialogue. It could only do so much with the engine it ran on, so animations could only go so far. For this reason the quests and dialogue never really felt liked they dragged on, and the world wasn't too big to the point where your decisions actually had an impact on most things around you.

review_text: [h2] Game is ok, doesn't do anything amazing [/h2]  I came into this game after cyberpunk and with very high expectations given the reception online. I am sad to say that the game did not meet my expectation. I did not play the previous witcher games nor consumed any of the books since the consensus online was it wasn't mandatory. My review is based on beating the game on hard and doing every side quest in the first region.  [b] Open World [/b] Checklist simulator, the map shows you these question marks on the map and majority of time its just some trash mobs that drops useless gear.  [b] Side quest[/b] Way too many side quest, I didn't keep track but well over 100 on the first region, with majority of them being forgettable, there are some good side quest that in my opinion rival the main story quest or at least more memorable but you have to go through a lot of trash quest to find the far and few good ones. Also the rewards for these quest are unrewarding.  [b] Story[/b] I feel like the story expects you have already consumed past witcher content, I say that because half the game is you trying to rescue this character and the story doesn't do a good job establishing this character I am trying to save. At most you see said character as a kid in the beginning tutorial and then the story starts of with you trying to rescue her for half the game. Also the villains are non existent in the story, they only really start to show up in the second half after you save said character but at that point i already forgot who the villains are and why I should care about them. In general there are many other games that have the same positive reception online as witcher 3 but have infinitely better story.  [b] Combat[/b] Combat is terrible, its as bland as souls like games where you just left click and dodge. But at least in souls like games you have engaging enemies. Enemies are poorly design with very little indication they are going to attack. This created a situation where combat feels more like a rhythm game where you apply your shield spell, auto attack 2 times, dodge and repeat. Sometimes you get greedy and do 3 attacks before dodging. Yes you do have spells but there pretty useless and the dps on them is trash compared to melee combat.  [b] Progression[/b] Progression is shallow and bland. There is a lack of build variety. At the start of the game you start with all your spells unlocked so there is already nothing to look forward to interms of learning new spells. The upgrades for said spells are not really build defining so it doesn't feel good to level up. Gear stats are terrible and it devolves to green arrow up = equip.  [b] Conclusion[/b] For a game that gets glazed to high heavens on the internet I expected it to have at least ONE thing that makes it stand amongst the goats. Many games that came out after witcher 3 have already done everything better then it to the point where this game feels outdated. Because of that if you are someone who hasn't played a lot of games then witcher 3 might be a good game for you but if you are someone who has played a lot of the good modern games in like the past decades then this game might leave you disappointed too.

[h1]The most ambitious open world ever made — just don't expect it to explain itself.[/h1]  [b]245 hours, 100% (34/34 achievements)[/b], and I'd still call it one of the greatest open-world games I've played. It's also one of the most frustrating.  [i]Thanks Gaben — got this for free as compensation after my Steam Controller arrived two weeks late. Worst delivery delay, best compensation package ever.[/i]  [hr][/hr]  [h2]PROS[/h2] [list] [*][b]Breathtaking scale with genuine depth[/b] — five distinct regions, each with its own sub-biomes, and almost nothing feels copy-pasted. Every cave, ruin and settlement feels hand-placed [*][b]The spires and the Abyss[/b] — skyscrapers in a fantasy world that let you climb to a second open world floating above the first, with no loading screens. Best vertical traversal in the genre [*][b]Deep combat sandbox[/b] — three playable characters, a huge weapon roster, dual-wielding, Abyss Gear builds, and dozens of bosses that each get their own arena [*][b]Enormous amount of content[/b] — sanctums, constellations, legendary animals, minigames, fishing, pets, camp management. Completionists will not run out [*][b]Relentless post-launch support[/b] — updates arriving every couple of weeks, many adding real content rather than just fixes [*][b]Excellent PC performance for its scale[/b] — 4K / 60 FPS at max settings with frame generation, even with ray tracing enabled (RX 7900 XTX). Rare for an open world this size [/list]  [h2]CONS[/h2] [list] [*][b]The story is meh[/b] — loosely connected objectives, inconsistent voice acting, and a plot that never quite comes together. It's okay, but don't expect something like The Witcher 3 [*][b]Unexplained mechanics that feel like bugs[/b] — royal trading is live roughly one in-game day a week with no hint anywhere; Residents quests appear one at a time with no indicator; some faction chains silently gate on unrelated progress. You'll often not know whether you're stuck, bugged, or just early [*][b]Trading is pointless[/b] — by late game your camp prints more money than you can spend (I ended with ~4 million), so the whole trade economy exists mostly to feed an achievement. Getting the last royal court meant save-scumming a weekly reset roughly ten times [*][b]Value at full price[/b] — at €70 my 245-hour run works out to ~€0.29/hour. Wait for a sale or a complete edition [/list]  [hr][/hr]  [h2]VERDICT: 9/10[/h2] Crimson Desert tries to specialise in everything — scale, combat, traversal, side content — and mostly succeeds, which makes it unforgettable. But the same "figure it out yourself" philosophy that makes exploration magical turns the completionist grind into reverse-engineering hidden systems.  [b]Highly recommended if you love getting lost in a huge handcrafted world.[/b] If you're chasing 100%, keep a guide open and your patience topped up.

[h1] Crimson Desert Review [/h1]  [h3] *SPOILER FREE* TL;DR: [/h3] Crimson Desert is one of the best games I've played this year. It's clear to me the developers are passionate about their game. There are many great aspects of the game like the hand-crafted world, exploration, combat (most of the time), varying activities, graphics (most of the time), and more. There are also some things in the game that either get annoying as your journey progresses, or are outright infuriating and ruin the experience. Some examples are most all side quests, combat against most bosses or large groups of tough enemies, the many "follow me" quests, same-button syndrome, and, sadly, the main questline. Overall, I still think the game is worth a try at least at a discount if you enjoy RPG games.  [h3] *SPOILERS AHEAD* [/h3]  [i] Disclaimer: I played most of the game BEFORE the "Enhanced Edition" dropped, so if the added cutscenes help fix what problems I have below, I am unaware and I'm not interested in the story enough to see what was added. [/i]  First I will start with the graphics and game performance. The game looks amazing!...until you go indoors, it gets dark, or starts raining. Then for some reason the game gets blurry, a similar effect of turning on frame generation in other titles. It reminded me of the early Star Citizen volumetric cloud technology, where the clouds looked blurry around the edges and had a flickering effect. During the day though, it might be the prettiest game I've seen! Do yourself a favor and turn on the ray-tracing technology if your system can handle it, and go to the Abyss and look at the world when it is dark. It's simply enrapturing! Performance wise, with my specs if I turned everything to cinematic quality and turned on all advanced technology, my game ran at 45fps while standing around. So I ended up turning on DLSS 4.5L, ray reconstruction, and frame generation. With that stuff on, I was able to get 100fps on average, and to me the game still looked incredible.  Now I will go more in-depth with what I enjoyed about the game, what annoyed me, and what I absolutely hated. First let's start with the main storyline. It just starts you off at some cabin with your comrades, you are all mourning for a someone who was lost to battle recently. Then you go inside and shortly after sitting down to eat, you are attacked by this rival clan know as the Black Bears. They end up defeating you and your comrades, and the big baddie slits your throat before tossing you into the river. During this sequence we are not introduced to who Kliff is, who Oongka is, or who anyone is really, like we are supposed to already know. You are just supposed to know that the Greymanes have a rivalry with the Black Bears. Now we are shown that Kliff doesn't actually die, and you are transported to a realm where a short tutorial ensues.  After the tutorial...Kliff is just sitting by a riverside while being hailed by some guy we never met, and I guess he pulled Kliff out of the river and saved him? So yeah, it just kinda skips the part where we learn how Kliff survived. It does this sort of thing throughout the entire main questline. That and Kliff does a thing and then somehow knows "I now need to go talk to this guy to get this thing" suddenly with no explanation as to why we are doing it or how we know it must be done. Basically, the story just jumps around a lot, so I couldn't get into it.  Now on the loot and exploration aspect of the game. It's the best part of the game. There are a lot of things to loot in this game, it's amazing for people who love to hoard loot. There are at least two special chests you can place in your house to-.... oh yeah, did I mention you get a house to decorate? Yes, you can find decorative items in the world, loot it, an bring it to your house to decorate it. One of the special chests I found let me store documents, keys, and other things in it, as sort of a "collectors binder". The other special chest let me store crafting items like iron ore, hide, bones, etc. in it. The best part is anywhere I went that needed these resources would just pull from the chest! Aside from décor, there are many equipment items and upgrades to be found and looted from the world. Exploration is amazing and rewarding! The world is interesting everywhere you go and you are bound to stumble upon a ruin or a puzzle on your travels. Ruins can look empty and boring, but I've found that there is more than meets the eye with them! Puzzles are pretty challenging and offer a change to the usual combat you're doing.  Let's talk about the combat now. It's fluid, it has a number of combos you can perform, it has a parry or block system for defense. It feels good....most of the time. When you start out it will feel excellent fighting the bandits and other fiends even when they are in large groups. However this changes once you get to the tougher enemies, enemies with bows/guns/shields, and most of the bosses (that I fought). They just seems to stun lock you at times, or cause your character to be launched, during which control is taken from you. There are no invincibility frames, so you can die extremely fast. It feels bad when a big dude launches you and then like 10 riflemen just shoot you all while you can't do anything. Later it gets better when you unlock certain abilities, don't sleep on the Spirit skill tree! Bosses though? Man I tried to like them. Some of them are actually fun, most of them are just not. It basically comes down to dodge dodge dodge until they are finally done with their attacks, and then get in there and hit them with a combo, then back out real fast. This was my strategy until I unlocked some Spirit tree skills. Try to fight them normally and you get stun locked and then killed shortly after. That was my experience with 90% of the bosses in this game. I dreaded every encounter I had to face, because I knew the fun I was having might end. It feels like a soul-like boss design in a game that isn't a soul-like. I did not end up fighting every boss in the game and I don't think I will.  Now some things that annoyed me. Most all the side quests I did were fetch quests. Go get me 4x thin hide and bring it back. It gets annoying fast. You can't exactly avoid doing side quests either, because you get 3x inventory  slots for each one you do. In addition to that, side quests and a bunch of the main quests have this annoying "follow me" prompt, where you need to follow a character on horseback. Sorry, but the dialogue in this game isn't even close to Red Dead Redemption II, so I didn't care what was being said. So there's that, but I also noticed that when you are "done" following this person, you aren't always at your destination! Sometimes you just stop like 500m away from where you need to go!  Then there's that one quest with Yann, which I don't even want to get into how much I hated this Yann character, but he messed something up and the camp leader punished him with a chore. Go get some logs for the camp. He brings Kliff into it somehow and then when you arrive at the logging site, he "forgot" his axe. So he just goes back to camp and now you need to get the logs?! How about take my axe and get to work you dillweed!  [h1] Conclusion [/h1]  In conclusion, I think the game does a lot right, but the things that it does wrong do weaken the experience. The game is heavily carried by the exploration aspect, the world that feels alive, and the many things you unlock that expand what you can do. Most of the bosses in the game that I faced were annoying to fight yet visually impressive. The quests are very MMO like and I dislike MMOs these days, so that weakened my experience after seeing it enough times. The main story jumped around right at the start, so it failed to capture my interest right from the start. The looting in the game is awesome and only gets better as your inventory expands. 8/10

Over all, imo, 7.4/10 for a solid comeback from launch.

Crimson Desert is both the best and worst game of the year.  I have debated whether or not to recommend this game for a while now. Crimson Desert is one of the best open world games I have ever played but also one of the most frustrating games I have ever played. (And not in the "good" frustrating way like Dark Souls.)  There is so much to do and the many systems are quite deep. And that is what makes it amazing. However... you are left to figure things out on your own or search google for an explanation of how something works. I'm glad that there is a lot to it, but I'm also constantly frustrated trying to figure out every unexplained obscure game mechanic.  (For reference, here's an example. In the goldenfist unarmed combat arena you can't use your unarmed combat attacks that are grappling or kicking. This is not explained anywhere in the game. You would have to search the internet to know that. But wait, it gets even worse. Nowhere is it explained in game that you are ONLY allowed to use FIST attacks. That means if you are playing the Damiane character you simply can not participate in the arena at all because she uses kicks in every attack chain. And how will you learn this? You just have to figure it out for yourself. For what reason they chose not to explain ANY part of this, I can not fathom. And this is only one example. There are actually, literally dozens upon dozens, if not hundreds of completely unexplained rules that I can only assume seemed obvious to the developers but simply do not make sense to anyone else.)  Unfortunately boss fights are the same. I just google every one by default now. Which feels lame but the gimmicks for each boss are often impossible to decipher in any reasonable amount of time.  The combat is complex but most of the moves end up being pointless. Occassionally you will need some gimmick move you forgot you could even perform (there are hundreds between the three characters) to complete a boss fight or puzzle. Otherwise only dedicated try-hards should bother learning most of the move set.  I have one other criticism. There are three playable characters but you will probably only play Kliff for any length of time. I don't understand why they even bothered adding the other two characters when they force you to play Kliff for the main story. This game should have had a custom character creation system. The fact that it doesn't is the most glaring flaw in the game and another point of great frustration.  This all sounds very negative. But that's not my point. It is a great game. My point is go into it knowing that it will frustrate the living **** out of you. CONSTANTLY. But also know that is worth playing if you enjoy open world RPGs. Most positive reviews have already covered the best parts of the game. They are all true. It's scope is breathtaking.  Bottom line, Crimson Desert is a great game with unbelievably GOOD and unbelievably BAD game design. If you like to explore and don't mind googling hundreds of unexplained quests, puzzles, game mechanics and boss fight gimmicks, have at it.

[h2]50 Hours In...[/h2]  I don't write reviews very often, but Crimson Desert is one of those games that makes you want to talk about it.  I'm over [b]50 hours[/b] in now, and I still keep getting distracted by random things. I tell myself, "Okay, one more thing and then back to the main story," and suddenly I'm on the other side of the map doing something completely different.  That's probably my favorite thing about the game. Exploring doesn't feel like I'm just cleaning icons off a map. If I see something interesting in the distance, I actually want to go there and check it out. Sometimes I find a quest, sometimes an item, and sometimes absolutely nothing useful... but hey, at least the view was nice.   [h2]Combat Is Just Fun[/h2]  The combat is easily one of the best parts for me. It feels smooth, the animations look great, and once you start learning more moves, fights become a lot more fun.  At first, I used the same few attacks again and again. Now I find myself trying combos and doing completely unnecessary moves on normal enemies just because it looks cool.  [b]If the game gives me the option to show off, I'm going to use it. :)[/b]  Another thing I really like is that even after 50 hours, the game still manages to surprise me with new mechanics or things I didn't know I could do. It doesn't feel like the game shows you everything in the first few hours and then just repeats itself.   [h2]Pywel Is Dangerous For My Free Time[/h2]  The world is huge, beautiful, and honestly a little dangerous if you care about your free time.  The landscapes, towns, and overall atmosphere make it really easy to just wander around without even doing anything important. I've had plenty of moments where I stopped just to look around or changed my whole route because something looked interesting.  Of course, it's not perfect. Some systems are more confusing than they need to be, some things are not explained very well, and there are a few technical or animation issues here and there.  But after more than 50 hours, none of that has stopped me from enjoying the game.  [b]I still feel like I have a lot left to see, and that's probably the best compliment I can give it.[/b]  I should probably go back to the main quest.  But I just saw something interesting on the map.  [b]So... maybe later.[/b]

The Greymanes scattered, and during Ch.8, the confirmation that his own choices are what put them in Caliburn's crosshairs. What it never explains is why Umbra. Rebuilding the clan is a motive. Stopping the end of the world is a motive. There's just nothing connecting the two, so when the final fight rolls around, Umbra feels less like the thing Kliff was always headed toward and more like the guy who was still available after the Black Bears and Duke Caliburn died.  The Pailune ambush (which is a prologue) is still the high point of the whole game. And then the game more or less shrugs and converts grief into a to-do list: find survivors, build the camp, take the next contract. Some of those searches should end at a grave. Pailune itself should stay wrecked. I really wanted to like Crimson Desert. The game looks absolutely incredible, the world is massive, and there are plenty of moments where you can see how ambitious this game was supposed to be.  Unfortunately, actually playing it became more frustrating than enjoyable for me.  The controls feel unnecessarily complicated and inconsistent, and the game constantly introduces new systems and mechanics without making them feel like they naturally belong together. There are so many little things that should be simple but instead turn into a slow, awkward process.  The quest design was another major problem for me. I found myself spending way too much time following NPCs around, listening to dialogue I wasn't particularly invested in, or doing tedious tasks just to get back to the parts of the game I actually enjoyed.  And then there are the technical problems.  After playing for a while, the game eventually started crashing on startup for me. I tried updating drivers, verifying the files, changing settings, clearing shader caches, completely uninstalling the game, deleting its leftover files, and reinstalling it from scratch. At one point I basically stripped the game off my PC and started over completely, and I still couldn't get it to reliably behave.  I also opened a support ticket with Pearl Abyss regarding the issue. As I'm writing this review, that ticket has been sitting unanswered for nearly 15 days. Because of the amount of time I've spent troubleshooting and the way the issue has affected my ability to actually play the game, I've also been trying to get a refund if the issue cannot be fixed, but I'm currently unable to get that resolved either.  At this point, I'm spending more time troubleshooting the game and trying to get support than I ever spent actually enjoying it.  There is a genuinely great game buried somewhere in Crimson Desert. The world, visuals, exploration and some of the combat are impressive. I just don't think the game does a good enough job getting me to that good stuff.  Beautiful game, incredibly ambitious, but way too frustrating for me to recommend.

I updated my review after 100% completing the game.  At this point, I have 100% completed RE2R, RE3R and RE4R, and I feel like I'm in a good position to review this game properly.  Bad news first: Resident Evil 4 Remake made me quit the franchise, at least for the near future.  What had already happened to the Dead Space and Dino Crisis franchises has now happened to another great series and, for me personally at least, completely ruined what I loved about it.  A short excursion into what happened with Dead Space and Dino Crisis:  Dead Space 1 and 2 were great games. They were intense, and I was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my pants playing them as a kid. But in trying to reach a bigger audience (something that already started with the second game) they slowly began to move away from what made especially the first game such a great experience.  Dead Space 3 turned into a massive action-based shoot em up with some horror elements sprinkled in, but it wasn't at all what made the first two games so good.  Dino Crisis went down a similar path. It moved away from classic survival horror, with fewer puzzles and survival elements, and instead focused on throwing more enemies at you, giving you more weapons and introducing style/combo systems. None of that really translated into what made the first game a good game in the first place.  From what I remember, some of those changes were received well and helped introduce the games to a wider audience. But even then, they lost a massive part of what had originally made them unique.  And that brings me back to Resident Evil, because I feel like we're looking at the same situation here.  Now, I know this isn't the remake's fault. The original Resident Evil 4 from 2005 already leaned heavily into action, and the remake obviously follows that foundation.  But in the end, that doesn't change what I dislike about this game.  Having spent a considerable amount of time (especially for someone with a full-time job) getting every achievement in RE2R, RE3R and RE4R, I can confidently say that almost everything I loved about RE2R was lost in RE4R.  Going from carefully managing your resources, planning and perfecting routes to conserve ammunition, and constantly thinking about whether an enemy was even worth fighting, to throwing Leon into an arena and having him shoot up an entire village is a massive miss for me.  I hated every arena section. I disliked the combat system, and many of the smaller mechanics felt unintuitive to me - the inventory's automatic sorting being one example.  The bland story of "hey I found Ashley" and "damn it, lost her again" also doesn't correlate with my personal interest. This "plot" repeats like 2 or 3 times over the course of the game and just doesn't do it for me.  For me personally, RE4R lost most of the horror aspects that made me fall in love with RE2R, while also failing to become an action game that I genuinely enjoyed playing.  To be fair, I did somewhat enjoy the Mercenaries DLC, and I had some fun with the Separate Ways DLC and its unique combat mechanics compared to Leon's main story.   At the same time, besides all the gameplay and story critic I definitely want to mention that this game doesn't seem to be fully optimized. I rarely had performance issues playing all sorts of games on my steam deck but definitely had lots of FPS drops in this game. Which made some parts that required fast paced reactions liked boss fights, the shooting range and so on a pain in the ass. If you're planning to play this on Steam Deck be warned!  But other than that, I'm genuinely saddened that this game made me want to step away from the franchise for the foreseeable future.  After putting in the time to 100% complete it, I'm mostly just happy that I can finally uninstall it and never touch it again.  I am aware that a lot of people DO like the game and enjoy it for what it is - I simply want to make clear that you do not get the same type of game that you got with the 2nd and 3rd and that I personally didn't enjoy it and do not recommend it.  Take away from this review what you want.

Resident Evil 4: Souless Edition. It's a one step forward and three steps back kind of game. There will be spoilers. Main game/non-DLC review. The Good: Gameplay is fun. Guns are balanced (apart from OP Riot Gun), a few changes to the story are positive such as making Luis more important. Graphics are good, but can be quite a demanding game due to bloated REngine. Unlockable accessories that gives gameplay advantages across all saves is a very welcome addition. Male character models/outfits are on point and feel close to the OG. Parry mechanic while overused nowadays, is welcome here to give some defense against annoying ranged attacks. The Bad: Pretty much everything else. Starting with the elephant in the room: Ashley is a completely different character here. From her appearance to her personality, the OG Ashley is nowhere to be seen. While the old Ashley was a terrified college girl who got kidnapped and relied heavily on Leon (understandably), this one is a girl boss who wants to be a special agent. I'm not kidding. They tried to make "be a girl boss" her entire personality. It's very jarring and breaks any immersion whenever she's on screen. Her outfit (and Ada's) also got changed because while you can have the goriest, most vomit-inducing death animations ever, a female character showing legs is too much for Capcom nowadays. Ada was also changed albeit nor nearly as bad since she's not the MC. Apart from her new lame censored outfit, her biggest issue is her new monotone-tired-smoker voice. It's just terrible. They also butchered the OG script. Taking away all the iconic, fun and memorable lines out. So no more "Ballistics" or "Overtime" jokes, no more "No thanks, bro!" and "Your right hand comes off?" bangers by Leon anymore, among others. Capcom knows those OG lines are amazing though, so as a big FU to the OG players they simply used them to name in-game Challenges instead. The result? The story is now a homogenized safe slop that feels so stale even AI could write it better. Salazar in particular truly felt like a robot with zero personality. I could almost see ChatGPT churning out his meaningless, non-stop yap during his boss fight. Even the ending got ruined. Instead of Ashley hitting on Leon and him turning her down, implying he already has a woman he likes, now it's just a non-romantic conversation reaffirming that Ashley doesn't need anyone else cuz she's just that good lol.  Lastly (review is getting too long), some enemies were also changed for the worse or cut entirely from the game like U3. Regenerators in particular are just bad now. While the original ones were slow, lumbering, pseudo-immortal scary enemies who spooked you with their weird breathing noises as they slowly approached while you tried to hit their small weak spots, the new ones got hit by mobility creep. They run very fast, spam long-range grab attacks, and while on the ground they seem to move even faster while doing fast leaping attacks. There's nothing scary or unique about them anymore. It's just another fast enemy you need to dodge and shoot.

The very beginning of the game was phenomenal, and after that they outright refuse to throw more than four enemies at you at once. Maybe the chainsaw girls section. I at least appreciate that they didn't make enemies complete bullet sponges like 2 and 3.  The stardew valley of horror, the overall generic entry point for horror action shooters, and an outright meticulous grab of the things they think makes TLOU good. [h1]Preface[/h1] Elden Ring veterans have almost nothing to complain about when it comes to Nightreign. In essence, this title provides more Elden Ring content with added variety, faster pacing, and easy-to-pick-up yet hard-to-master builds and playstyles that provides enough replayability with overall game design that makes it easy to get into another session whenever you have what I call the "Souls itch."  [h1]Positives[/h1] [b]No Time to Waste[/b] Before delving into Nightreign, there were two primary concerns I had from what I knew about the game so far: time-limited runs and boss variety. The time-limited runs is a godsend for players like myself who want more Elden Ring but also seek a fresh experience. The exploration is there (albeit with less freedom from the vanilla title), but the balance between the need to explore and focus on boss fights is all in all well executed. Builds can shift drastically after one or two Nightlord kills and each run can feel unique simply based on how the player approaches each run. As with all games, it all comes down to mindset.  [b]Ten Nightfarers, Ten Playstyles[/b] By this point, most players will settle for the good ol' DR build with most Nightfarer they choose to run. I myself ran mostly solo (a primary reason I held off on Nightreign for so long since solo play was an afterthought a few months into the game's lifespan), and yet with choices like Wylder, Ironeye, and Raider, my runs were not as grueling as I thought they would be. Melee all-rounder, ranged archer, and heavy-hitting bruiser were all on the menu. Now upon completion, I look forward to trying the other Nightfarers to try more technique-based playstyles like the caster-based Recluse and parry-focused Executor. At the end of the day, Nightreign has something for everyone as long as you focus on building each Nightfarer the right - or maybe even wrong - way.  [b]Performance[/b] I rarely mention this as a forte for game reviews, but with all the performance issues AAA games have been launching with lately, a honorable mention is at very least in order. Nightreign ran flawlessly for me, and that may be due to patches that have been released since launch but the point still stands: FromSoftware rarely, if ever, misses in the optimization department. Combat is quick and responsive even more so than it was in vanilla. And in a title with co op multiplayer being one of its appeals, that's saying something.  [h1]Negatives[/h1] [b]Day Phases[/b] This is highly subjective, but granting roughly 13-15 real-time minutes for the exploration cycle before the circle starts closing in might be a turnoff for many players. Time is your greatest enemy in Nightreign, and if anything this can simultaneously be considered a positive as it pushes you to think quickly on your feet and work on your decision-making skills/speed. Granted, you have unlimited time for night/boss phases, but a little more leeway might not have hurt for the less initiated. Just a minor gripe on my end, but not a gamebreaker.  [b]Feels...incomplete?[/b] Perhaps with more dedicated resources, a bigger pull towards ER newcomers, and I daresay more content & horizontal progression(?), I feel the game could have been bigger than it is. As successful as it may have been, many agree that Nightreign just kind of came and went; perhaps not off the grid, but now it's just there for people to enjoy when they feel like coming back to it. Arguably, Nightreign could have started a movement to take the Soulslike genre to the next level entirely, departing from the singleplayer experience we've had for the last decade and causing a chain reaction of games that could give birth to an entirely new genre. But alas, here we are. Nightreign, quite simply put: [i]More Elden Ring[/i].  [h1]Conclusion[/h1] [b]Final Verdict: 9/10 A-[/b] Though not as deep and immersive as the original Elden Ring, Nightreign delivered on its promises and provided the on-the-go Elden Ring experience for veterans and newcomers alike. It may not have been perfect at launch, but FromSoftware has a healthy habit of always striving to satisfy their fans. Patch after patch, they improved solo play and fine-tuned everything they had in place for a memorable experience. Compared to many other companies that recently lose the faith of their supporters with every title they release in this post-2020 era of ongoing hit-and-miss titles, FromSoft remains faithful to its identity and to this day remains in excellent standing with the loyal fanbase. Now, once again, we look forward to what they have in store for us next.

This game is spectacular, when it doesn't crash. Which is totally fixable!  Some people fix the problem by playing in borderless windowed. Some people fix it by *not*. Some people fix it by switching to Linux. Some people only experience the problem on Linux. Some people fix it by updating their GPU drivers. Some people fix it by downpatching their drivers.  I could keep going. I have plenty of time while I wait for the files to verify - if I delete the easy anti-cheat folder then verify the install, *sometimes* I can actually play for a full session without it crashing and rebooting my *entire OS.*  This is a shameful state for a AAA title to be released in. If it weren't a generous gift from a friend who I want to play with, I'd move on and never buy another Fromsoft title.  Edit: After all that, uninstalling and reinstalling did the trick. Apparently EAC gets installed in two different places, and conflicts can arise that get sorted out by doing so. Or perhaps some combination of the above methods was the trick? Who can say!  I did mean it when I said the game was spectacular. There's a cast of characters with storylines that are not impenetrable and varied play styles that are all viable and fun. The random world generation (within reasonable limits) demands on-the-fly decision making, which less experienced players can generally rely on team members to handle while they learn the ropes. The boss fights are at the forefront, and have really always been the most interesting part of FromSoft's library, making this a welcome challenge. And, best of all, you almost never find a cool weapon you want to try only to discover that your build is all wrong, or it's unupgraded and therefore worthless - you can just try it. At worst, you've wasted a few minutes and learned which character would love it. The full breadth of this game is available to people who aren't interested in replaying a 40-hour experience from the ground up.  I've spent a great deal of time here, and I intend to spend a great deal more - and I still don't feel comfortable recommending this, because the crashing issues wouldn't have gotten solved without a serious, focused effort spanning ten days. That's more than most players can justify.

Not fun to play. Camera and movement are horrible to control. The enemies are unforgiving and punishing to fight. There is too much RNG involved. I do not understand the point of the battle royale zones closing in other than to stress the player out after they die to a troll's bomb AOE while climbing the castle walls. Would it not make more sense to have a timer that summons a random boss on the player's location each night, similar to how Margit can spawn as a random encounter? That way the player has more freedom to do what they want to do instead of locking more than half of the content outside the playable area.  The effort to steer away from fake RPG mechanics, unlike other Souls game, is admirable by FromSoftware. I like the addition of relics and passive abilities. I also like that there are different playable characters with unique playstyles so that being knowledgeable about boss attack patterns and dodging at the perfect time is not the only way to guarantee a victory.  Multiplayer is cool. Sometimes frustrating, sometimes invigorating after an epic clutch. Not much to say here.  The graphics, stories, and worldbuilding is phenomenal.
