At the time of the review I had 278 hrs on record, around 60 of which are spent afk reading the wiki and watching guides, I believe. The rating was 95% (Overwhelmingly Positive). Initially, I was going to write a neutral review but after finishing the "Social Season" event I can't recommend buying this game in it's current form.  tl;dr Play only if received for free otherwise avoid. This game is a solid content-creation material but playing it is not as fun/pleasant as watching others do it.  Pros - reject humanity, return to monke - Nice visuals and music. - Core game design is good. If you intend to only play this game casually, fully ignoring any competitive activities and harder maps, just placing your favorite towers, it's an overall pleasant experience. - The "heroes" concept itself is a nice twist on the genre. - There are dozens of official maps and they are quite beautiful. Some of them have fun quirks and easter eggs. There's also a map editor and a challenge editor and the community is pretty productive, so you can always find something new to play with. - Full keyboard shortcut system where you can activate literally anything by a keypress.  Sadly, that's pretty much about all what good I can say about this game. Everything else is very frustrating due to a bad design or implementation.  Cons - *Loving* memory leaks in a Unity game! Each time you restart, exit or enter a level, the game takes more and more time to load. And trust me you will need to replay waves a lot. They even managed to introduce a memory leak related to just using a newly-introduced tower! Do you guys even know how to code? If you are so incompetent, just go find someone who can. - Balancing issues and other bugs that aren't fixed for years. - The game is not deterministic, yet it has a "competitive" modes. Towers have a lot of randomness. Saves doesn't fully store the game state, so reloading a save can either skip some challenges or make it impossible to progress instead. - A lot of content is grind- or paywalled. As I stated, I played 200+ hours already (minus loading time) and still don't have all towers and perks fully unlocked. Granted, I could focus unlocking the towers and leveling my perks, but that assumes playing the way I just don't find fun. There are games where grind can be fun, this one is not one of them. Also some competitive/challenge modes doesn't grant the points needed to upgrading your perks and towers. - The cashgrab is just shameless. Basically it's a typical mobile game with a distinctive monetization model, except that these games are normally distributed for free. Here we pay for the game itself, then they want us to pay even more to play comfortably. At least they don't show us ads, right? Then there are DLCs that are more expensive than the base game yet nobody plays them. And the reviews at the time of writing are "Mixed". - QoL is very very subpar. To begin with while the game has tutorials, neither them or the in-game descriptions do a good job explaining how thing work and what they mean. The tutorials are mostly "this tower can do this and also that, now go have fun with these training waves" and usually leave you more confused than educated. There are also no in-game stats cards for towers, only intentionally vague descriptions. Ok, let's assume this game is just designed to be played through experimentation but it's made painful by the bad QoL (read the next bullet point) and the pain is amplified by the aforementioned memory leaks. So what do you do? Go read the wiki of course! Hence 60 hours of afk. Good fun! (not) - A follow-up of the QoL topic. While you need to restart a lot, there's no way to retry a specific wave other than the current or a special "checkpoint" wave (and this one needs you to pay, lol). Also there's no way to quickly skip easier waves. Granted, there's a "2X speed" button but it doesn't help much when you want to replay waves that begin only after a 10 minutes of gameplay for example. So, be prepared to spend at least half of the time watching the loading screens and/or replaying the same waves if you want to play hardcore. - Competitive modes are specifically designed for only the most dedicated players. If you just want to casually try yourself in a boss challenge or a race you most probably will just leave frustrated and sad and the problem is that it's normally not even your fault. Usually you just don't yet have a perk or tower required to get any significant result in this particular event, or you don't know the particular gimmick that's needed for even a basic full clear of this particular boss or the race. Yeah, the game that is positioned as a casual one tells you to git gud and grind (or pay lol) before you can get ANY place in a leaderboard. - *Loving* micro! I just want to lazily place my turrets and see them go brrrrr, but tower abilities is a core game design feature here so you will need to watch them all the time. In a casual play below "Hard" difficulty and easier maps you can ignore them half of the time but in "Hard+" and bosses you will need to manage them very carefully even if you don't aim for the top score. Efficient mid-wave tower management is a chore too. It would be ok if all this were only required in a race mode. Well at least we have keyboard shortcuts. Anyway this bullet point is more of a "me problem". Still I want you to be warned. - Speaking of gimmicks. The secrets and gimmicks of the maps are almost always of the kind "if you know you know". Yeah, you can find at least some of them through the pure brute forcing or luck or 9000+ IQ puzzle-solving but people who play this game to relax just look up the guide and thank developers with curses. Then there are a lot of maps that doesn't work as you expect, so you can't even guess any valid strategy before you played the map at least once or seen someone else playing it. Wave trajectories and directions can change at any time, map geometry can change too. It could be a fun game design if the maps had some descriptions with them, listing all these nuances. Instead you just grind, restarting the map over and over until you learn all the quirks and not because of skill issue. - Co-op/"social" is just broken. Network connection is a mess, even just launching the game sometimes gives you a connection error. For the 1.5 years I own the game I could connect to the co-op games only couple of times. 99% of the time though I get one of the following: the lobby doesn't even load properly (empty description), me or the other people getting disconnected on attempt to start the game, the game hangs (even mouse cursor doesn't move), UI breaks and I can't return to the main screen. Moreover if you check the internet, you'll see I'm far from the only one having these issues. Now so-called "social" part. For a long time we have "Contested Territory" mode where your team capture tiles on map by playing short games with some random rules. All fun and good except there's no in-game way to have any meaningful communication with people. The game simply doesn't have a chat. In co-op you have a bunch of meaningless reactions (laugh, sad, angry, etc.). And some of them are unlockable cometics, yeah. In the team you don't even have this. You can't even mark a tile to attack or being attacked by you or a team member. Zero. Communication. In a. "Social", team-based activity. *Loving* applause! And "Social Season" event is just a mockery. Not only you have zero socialization here, all but two or three tasks are just lame excuses to make you grind/spend some resources in single-player. The lamest ones are to play with a specific cosmetics. The only "social" tasks are to "finish a daily co-op challenge" and "submit a team boss attack score". And I couldn't finish the latter one plus another one because the tasks are blocked by order and the co-op one comes first. And I just couldn't connect to a co-op game. *Loving* great game design and testing!

This is a pretty fun incremental game. There is certainly no real challenge to it, it's just place more and more machines and split before reaching inputs.   So why do I give it a negative? A few points: - A lot of equipment is straight up useless. You get given a few choices of tools, and only one of them matters within literal minutes.  - Constant upgrading makes you question why you would ever upgrade or use a particular machine, e.g, baling > paper mulching. Apart from the random objectives, you are better off bumrushing cash. - Lack of challenge. It's an incremental game, nothing more. - AI generated descriptions are obvious and distracting. I don't mind AI usage, I do mind when it's distracting. There's also some wonderful, nonsense hints such as "Did you know a wall with an opening you can pass through?" Because the text is all AI generated, it's hard to tell if this is a joke or the developer AI generated hints as well. - Because of the lack of challenge and only one singular input product, once you get to a certain point, you don't feel like there is anything else coming up. The product lines are all one-to-one, meaning there's only a straight path, with exception to only the final machine, which you can fix by.. you guessed it, splitting the hay.  Overall, I would say it's an interesting concept and it is fun for a limited time, but ultimately the base design of it is just kind of blah when there are so many better factory games out there that operate practically the same.

Another year, another full-price update that feels like a bug-riddled beta.  As a long-time fan of the franchise, Football Manager 2026 is a massive disappointment. Instead of delivering meaningful innovation, Sports Interactive has released a product hampered by persistent UI glitches, match engine oddities, and long-standing bugs that have gone unaddressed for multiple patch cycles.  The main issues:  UI Clutter & Overlapping Text: The interface feels messy and poorly tested. Text scaling is broken across several menus, causing data, stats, and squad depth roles to overlap awkwardly—making simple squad navigation frustrating.  Match Engine Anomalies: Defending AI remains deeply flawed. Center-backs still freeze or make bizarre positioning decisions during basic opposition through-balls, while wingers continue shooting into the side netting from impossible angles instead of squaring for an easy tap-in.  Tactics & Squad Depth Glitches: Changing formations on tactical tiles frequently fails to update across related screens, requiring manual menu-refreshing to display accurate player positioning.  Broken Transfer Logic: AI clubs make illogical transfer bids, and mandatory buy-out clauses or loan agreements still trigger bugged upfront payment demands or disappear outright mid-negotiation.  Lack of Real Innovation: Beyond minor visual tweaks, the core gameplay loop feels identical to previous titles—except now you're paying full price to quality-test a release that relies on future patches to become playable.  Unless SI rolls out a major overhaul patch, save your money and stick to an older, fully patched edition.  Verdict: 4/10 — Feels unfinished and unacceptable even after almost a year

Can you enjoy FM26? Absolutely. But unfortunately, I find myself enjoying it in spite of many of its changes and flaws, rather than because of them. The match engine is better than the FM24 generation — although I'd argue only incrementally — and it still produces plenty of moments where you look at an action and think “why the hell did that happen?” because what you're seeing doesn't seem to logically follow from your tactical setup, player roles or instructions. But that's not really my biggest frustration with Football Manager. The issues that have plagued the series for the last decade or more are still there: player interactions that lack nuance, playing-time expectations that don't reflect how real squads are managed, board reactions that fail to understand context, repetitive and increasingly immersion-breaking responses, and a general tendency for the game to evaluate events against arbitrary thresholds rather than understanding what is actually happening in the wider context of your season.  In fact, I think FM26 has actually regressed in one of Football Manager's most important qualities: immersion and its feeling of being a believable football world. Some of that is undoubtedly down to the new UI, which often hides context rather than presenting it clearly, but the deeper problem is much more fundamental. Win a competition you're expected to win and the board essentially treats it like another Tuesday. Rotate your squad because you're playing three games in seven days, get knocked out of a cup you were supposedly expected to reach the quarter-finals of, and suddenly the board is unhappy. Give a player the playing time you agreed to and he'll still complain because the game appears to care more about starts than actual minutes or the circumstances behind them. These aren't necessarily bugs — they're symptoms of a simulation that doesn't understand CONTEXT. Until SI tackles that fundamental problem, I have very little confidence that FM27 will meaningfully address the things that have been frustrating players for years. Football Manager doesn't need more isolated features or more data; it needs to understand what that data means. Give me a game that understands the story of my season, my squad, my decisions and my circumstances — rather than one that simply checks whether individual conditions have been met. That's what would make FM feel like football management again.

Not Recommended — MLS is effectively broken by a known salary-cap bug  I bought FM26 specifically in part because I wanted to manage in MLS, and unfortunately the current implementation has a game-breaking issue with salary-cap calculations during contract negotiations.  In my FC Cincinnati save, the game correctly shows the club’s actual salary-cap position and available GAM in the roster/registration screens. However, when negotiating a new contract, the Budget Adjustments screen displays obviously incorrect salary-cap figures and fails to recognize the club’s available GAM/TAM. Because those incorrect figures feed into the contract validator, the game can disable “Suggest Terms” and prevent you from signing a player even when the deal should be legal under MLS rules.  I was able to reproduce this very clearly with Luca Orellano. The game recognized more than $2 million in available GAM elsewhere, but the contract negotiation screen showed effectively none and would not allow the allocation money to be applied. The result was that a legitimate transfer could not be completed.  More concerning, this appears to be a known issue that has already been reported on Sports Interactive’s own bug tracker and has still not been properly resolved. MLS roster rules are complicated, but that makes it even more important that the game’s cap and allocation-money systems work reliably.  There is a lot I like about FM26, and I would be happy to change this review if the MLS contract/salary-cap system is fixed. But at the moment I cannot recommend the game to anyone who specifically wants to manage in MLS.

I really wish Once Human wasn't an MMO.  The premise of Once Human is genuinely interesting. The world, the atmosphere, the creatures, the weird post-apocalyptic setting — there's a lot here that could make for an amazing survival game.  But unfortunately, I feel like the game quickly falls into the same mechanics and design decisions I've come to expect from NetEase. Instead of focusing on survival, exploration, immersion, and cooperation, it often feels like the game is built around MMO progression, repetitive activities, grinding, seasons, and systems designed to keep you coming back rather than making the world itself interesting.  Personally, I would have much preferred Once Human to be a survival game designed primarily around playing with your friends, rather than an MMO where survival mechanics are built around a persistent online world.  Something closer to No More Room in Hell 2 is what I had in mind. Give me a dangerous world, limited resources, meaningful exploration, tense encounters, and the ability to jump into that world with a few friends and survive together. I don't need hundreds of players, endless progression systems, or a constant stream of MMO-style activities.  That's what makes the game a little frustrating for me. The foundation is there. The setting and concept are good enough to support a fantastic survival experience, but the MMO structure keeps pulling it in a different direction.  I don't think Once Human is a bad game. I just keep thinking about what it could have been if it had focused less on being an MMO and more on being a co-op survival game where the world itself is the challenge.  I'd honestly love to see a new "Once Human" built around that philosophy.

In a Confucian or high-centralization realm, a lawful crown prince succeeding the throne is a supreme moral anchor. Treason is an absolute, unforgivable crime ("乱臣贼子，人人得而诛之"). You need five minutes just to launch the game, and once you finally get in, it runs like an unstable, resource-hogging mess.  And the worst part? There barely feels like there's any actual gameplay. The entire core loop is clicking through endless nested menus, spending arbitrary points to make some hidden modifier go from +3% to +5%, while you watch colored borders slowly move across the map at 5x speed and background dice rolls decide whether anything you did actually mattered.  This isn't deep strategy. It's glorified database administration with historical clip art. If I wanted to spend my free time managing an interactive spreadsheet, I'd get a job in corporate accounting. At least then someone would pay me for wasting my life doing it.  Multiplayer is somehow even worse. The glitches and desyncs get so bad that it becomes completely unplayable.  And don't even get me started on the DLC. Content that absolutely should have been part of the base game being chopped up and sold separately is something I'll never get used to.  The military system is also completely ridiculous. They removed proper docks and ships, and now you can apparently just place a little flag somewhere in Italy and magically spawn your entire army from Norway right into hostile territory. No supply lines, no food, no wages, no transport, no logistical planning whatsoever. Then you steamroll Italy, decide France looks nice, place another little flag in Brittany, magically teleport everyone there, and steamroll France too.  Of course, that's assuming France doesn't decide to do exactly the same thing to you by spawning its entire army in Denmark and flattening your country.  After that, all you're left with are random stress events generated by the game, usually caused by traits, where none of the options are particularly good. You can literally kill a Viking character through stress by executing a few people. Three executions are enough if you have the forgiving trait: critical stress, abdication or death.  Which is especially hilarious considering Vikings can gain piety from executing people.  And after putting hundreds of hours into this game and buying all the DLC, I honestly cannot recommend buying it.  That's probably the most frustrating part. I clearly wanted to like this game. I spent hundreds of hours playing it and paid for all the DLC, yet the more I played, the more obvious it became that the main gameplay loop is fundamentally empty.  The AI is completely brain-dead, whether we're talking about combat AI or character AI. Characters technically have personalities, traits and relationships, but these things rarely feel meaningfully connected to their actual actions. The game constantly tells you that you're interacting with complex human beings, but most of the time you're really just watching RNG select events from a database.  The entire game relies far too heavily on random numbers and scripted events. There is this shallow illusion of emergent storytelling that makes you think the game is naturally creating a unique story around your dynasty, but the characters themselves aren't properly rooted in persistent relationships or a believable world.  For example, you can go on a pilgrimage to a holy site and meet different characters along the way. You would expect to encounter fellow rulers, powerful nobles, religious figures or zealous characters who could become part of your story and create meaningful long-term relationships.  Instead, you often meet completely disposable, one-time-only random characters who exist purely for that particular event and then might as well disappear from the universe forever.  That perfectly represents CK3's biggest problem: it has plenty of interesting mechanics, systems and ideas, but it rarely integrates them in a deep or meaningful way. Everything exists separately, waiting for RNG to randomly throw it at you.  The surface of the game looks incredibly interesting. The characters, dynasties, politics, religions, personalities, warfare and storytelling systems all sound amazing when you describe them individually.  But once you actually spend enough time playing, you start realizing that underneath that impressive surface, the whole thing feels completely hollow.  The game desperately wants to look like a deep and complex grand strategy RPG, but underneath all the menus, modifiers, random events and magical troop teleportation, you're mostly just watching numbers fight each other while occasionally clicking buttons to pretend you're in control.  It gets boring ridiculously fast, and after hundreds of hours and every DLC purchased, I genuinely cannot recommend buying it.

The game itself is really good, but the lack of a proper anti-cheat is becoming a huge problem, especially right now.  If you play Premier, there’s a good chance you’ll encounter at least one cheater in a match, and it seems to get worse the higher your rank is. Unless you’re among the top 5% of players, winning often feels like it comes down to whether the cheater is on your team or the enemy team.  The same problem is becoming more noticeable in Competitive as well. I rarely play a game without encountering a cheater in the lobby. This means that if you want to experience CS as the competitive 5v5 game it’s supposed to be, there’s currently no reliable way to get consistently fair matches without playing on third-party platforms like FACEIT.  I wouldn’t recommend CS to new players in its current state. The game itself has the potential to be one of the best shooters ever made, but until there’s a reasonably effective anti-cheat, the experience is going to be frustrating for a lot of players.
